The Origins of the Śākya Clan:
A Layman’s Humble Discourse on the Buddha’s Entry into China.

*The Comprehensive Examination of the Section on Buddhist Teachings in the Great Compendium of Illustrations and Books of Antiquity and the Present*, Volume One.
In the ninth year of King Zhuang of Zhou, Śākyamuni was born in the kingdom of Kapilavastu in India. According to the *Weishu* (Book of Wei), "Shi Lao" [Buddhism]:...
As for the intent: that which is called "Buddha" was originally titled Śākyamuni, which translates as "Able Benevolent One" (Nengren).

This signifies that his virtue is full and his Way is complete, such that he is capable of saving all things. Prior to Śākyamuni, there were six Buddhas; Śākyamuni succeeded these six Buddhas and has now attained the place of enlightenment.
According to the *Bhadra-kalpa-sūtra*, in the future there will be Maitreya Buddha, who shall succeed Śākyamuni and descend into the world. Śākyamuni...
*Kā* refers to the son of the King of Kapilavastu in India; "India" is the general designation, while "Kapila" is its specific name.
Initially, Śākyamuni was born from his mother’s right side on the fourth night of the fourth month.

Upon his birth, his physical marks were exceptionally sublime, numbering thirty-two in kind; Heaven sent down auspicious omens to correspond with them, also numbering thirty-two. This is the original account.

The *Qǐjīng* (Sūtra on the Arising of Signs) explains this in full detail. When Śākyamuni was born, it was the ninth year of King Zhuang of Zhou, corresponding to the fourth month of the summer in the seventh year of Duke Zhuang of Lu during the Spring and Autumn period, when the fixed stars were not visible and the night was bright. This continued until the eighth year of the Wuding era of the Wei dynasty.
It is said that a total of one thousand two hundred and thirty-seven years have passed. Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood at the age of thirty and guided sentient beings for forty-nine years.
He then entered *parinirvāṇa* between the twin *śāla* trees in the city of Kuśinagara on the fifteenth day of the second month.
*Nirvāṇa* is translated as "extinction" (*mie-du*) or "eternal bliss, self, and purity. This clarifies—
There is no transition, decay, or any burden of suffering. The *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas has two aspects:
first, the ultimate reality (*tattva*); second, the provisional response (*upāya*). The ultimate body refers to the most supreme essence, wondrously transcending all constraints and limitations;

it cannot be anticipated by spatial location, nor can it be restricted by physical dimensions. It responds whenever there is a stimulus, yet its essence remains eternally serene. As for the provisional response body:

This means that he harmonized his light with the six realms and mingled his dust with the myriad classes of beings. His birth and extinction followed the seasons; his longevity or brevity responded to circumstances.

His form arose from conditions; his essence was not substantially existent. Although his provisional form has passed away, his true essence does not shift. It is simply because the times lack a subtle resonance that one cannot perceive him constantly.
This clarifies that the Buddha’s birth was not a real birth and his extinction was not a real extinction. Since the Buddha has departed from the world, the incense...
When wood is used to cremate a corpse, the sacred bones (śarīra) break into fragments as small as grains of rice; yet they cannot be crushed by striking them, nor can they be scorched by burning.

Sometimes they manifest miraculous signs and spiritual efficacy. The barbarians call them *śarīra*. The disciples collect and enshrine them in precious vases, exhausting themselves in offerings of incense and flowers to pay their respects.
They raise halls and buildings for them, calling them *stūpas*. *Stūpa* is also a barbarian term, equivalent to our "ancestral temple" (*zongmiao*). Therefore—

The world calls them stupas and temples. A hundred years later, there was a king named Aśoka who, by means of his supernatural power, divided the Buddha’s relics among the various spirits and constructed eighty-four thousand stupas, distributing them throughout the world; all were completed on the same day.
Today, in Luoyang, Pengcheng, Guzang, and Linwei, there are all Aśoka Monasteries, which likely preserve his legacy. Thus it is said.
Although Śākyamuni entered parinirvāṇa, he left behind his shadow, footprints, nails, and teeth in India, which remain there even to this day.

Those traveling between the Middle Kingdom and that land all testify to having seen them. Regarding the teachings first expounded by Śākyamuni, after his parinirvāṇa, five hundred śrāvaka disciples, including Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda, compiled and recorded them; Ānanda had personally received these instructions.
He was granted the gift of great learning and the power of dhāraṇī, enabling him to synthesize and examine profound principles without any omission.

He then compiled and recorded the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the sūtras; though these differ in their systems like the nine schools of thought, their ultimate aim is fundamentally based upon the Three Vehicles.
Several hundred years later, arhats and bodhisattvas appeared in succession to compose treatises that praised and clarified the meaning of the scriptures.

These include the *Dūṣaṇa-śāstra* (refuting non-Buddhists), the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna *Abhidharma*, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Dvādaśanikāya-śāstra*, the *Śata-dharma-prakāśamukha-śāstra*, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, and others.
All of these rely on the great principles of the various *piṭakas* and schools, posing hypothetical external questions and resolving them through internal Buddhist doctrine.
According to the "Bibliography" (*Jingjie zhi*) section of the *Sui shu*, as for the Buddhist scriptures, they originated from Kāpiśī in Central India (Tianzhu) in the Western Regions.
The Kingdom of Wei. Spoken by Śākyamuni, the Crown Prince of King Śuddhodana.
Śākya was born from the right side of his mother on the eighth day of the fourth month in the ninth year of King Zhuang of Zhou.

His appearance was extraordinary, possessing the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs of excellence. He renounced the rank of crown prince, left the household life to study the Way, and through diligent and arduous practice, attained awakening.
The one who possesses all-encompassing wisdom is called a Buddha; he is also called Fo-tuo and also Fu-tu, all of which are foreign terms.

Translated into the language of China (Huayan), it means "Pure Enlightenment" (Jingjue). His teaching states that although the human body undergoes the differences of birth and death, as for the spirit, it is eternally indestructible.
Prior to this life, it has already passed through immeasurable bodies. Through accumulation and cultivation, [one attains enlightenment].
When the spirit is pure, that is the Buddha-way. Beyond heaven and earth, throughout the four quarters, above, and below, there are further heavens and earths, which likewise have no end or limit.
Yet all of these undergo formation and destruction; one period of formation and one period of destruction is called one kalpa.
Prior to this current heaven and earth, there have already been immeasurable kalpas. In every kalpa, there must be Buddhas who attain the Way and appear in the world to teach.
Their numbers vary. Within this present kalpa, there shall be one thousand Buddhas. From the first until Śākyamuni, seven Buddhas have already appeared. Next, Maitreya shall appear in the world;
he will certainly convene three assemblies to expound the Dharma-treasury and deliver sentient beings.
Those who follow his path shall attain four grades of fruition: the first is called Srotāpanna (Stream-enterer), the second is called Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner)... [and so forth].

The second is the Sakṛdāgāmin; the third is the Anāgāmin; and the fourth is the Arhat. One who has attained the stage of Arhat may enter and exit the cycle of birth and death, coming and going, appearing and disappearing, yet remains untainted by these conditions.
From the Arhat upward to the Bodhisattva, one deeply perceives the Buddha-nature and proceeds toward the realization of the Way.

Whenever a Buddha passes into parinirvāṇa, his bequeathed Dharma is transmitted through three stages: the True Dharma (Saddharma), the Semblance Dharma (Pratirūpakadharma), and the Final Dharma (Antadharma).
The difference between the pure and the turbid, as well as the distance of time in years, each varies accordingly. After the age of the Final Dharma, sentient beings will become dull-witted;
the Buddha’s teachings will no longer exist, and their karmic conduct will turn increasingly evil. Their lifespans will gradually shorten until they live for only a morning and die by evening.
Thereafter, calamities of great floods, great fires, and great winds will arise, sweeping everything away.
As they did so, life was renewed and people returned to a state of simplicity and purity; this is called a minor kalpa (*antarakalpa*). During each minor kalpa, one Buddha appears in the world.
Initially, in Central India, there were many non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) who all worshipped water, fire, and venomous dragons, and were skilled in various magical illusions.
When Śākyamuni practiced asceticism, these followers of heterodox paths all came to harass and torment him in order to distract his mind.
Yet they could not attain it. When the Buddha attained the Way, they all submitted and became his disciples. Male disciples are called *śramaṇa*, which translates as "one who has stilled the mind";
collectively they are called *saṃgha*, which translates as "those who beg for alms. Female disciples are called *bhikṣuṇī*.

They all shave their hair and beards, cast off worldly burdens, and leave the household life. Living together in harmony, they cultivate the mind and practice pure conduct, begging for food to sustain themselves.
With these provisions, one guards the mind and restrains conduct. The monastic community consists of two hundred and fifty precepts for monks and five hundred precepts for nuns.
For laypeople who place their faith in the Buddha’s Dharma, men are called *upāsaka* and women are called *upāsikā*;

they all abstain from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants—these are known as the five precepts. Śākyamuni remained in the world teaching and transforming beings for forty-nine years, even unto [the heavens].
Nāgas, humans, and spirits all came together to hear the Dharma. His disciples who attained the Way numbered in the hundreds of thousands, myriads, and billions.
Subsequently, at the city of Kuśinagara, between the twin śāla trees, on the fifteenth day of the second month, he entered parinirvāṇa.

Nirvāṇa is also called *nirvāṇa*; translated, it means "extinction and transcendence" (*mie-du*), and is also described as "permanence, bliss, self, and purity. This was when Śākyamuni first preached the Dharma.
Because the dispositions, faculties, and karmic actions of people differ, there are teachings of both the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.

When [the Buddha] passed away, his disciples Mahākāśyapa, Ānanda, and others—five hundred in all—pursued the compilation of his words, recording them in writing and arranging them into twelve divisions (*dvādaśāṅga*).
Several hundred years later, arhats and bodhisattvas successively composed treatises.

To clarify its meaning: that which the Buddha taught—namely, that after my parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall endure for five hundred years, the Semblance Dharma for one thousand years, and the Final Dharma for three thousand years—is explained in this way.
In the thirtieth year of the First Emperor of Qin, the Śramaṇas Śrīlaṅka and others from the Western Regions first brought Sanskrit manuscripts of the sutras to Xianyang.
According to the "Basic Annals of the First Emperor" in the *Shiji*, this is not recorded; however, according to the *Fofa Jintang Bian*, it was the First Emperor [who received them].
In the thirtieth year, the *jiashen* year, eighteen Western Region śramaṇas, including Śrīmitra and others, arrived at Xianyang carrying Sanskrit manuscripts of the sūtras.
The officials reported this to the Emperor, who, considering them to be followers of a foreign custom, imprisoned them.
As Śrīmitra and the others recited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, its radiance shone forth and auspicious vapors swirled, filling the prison cells. In an instant—

There was a golden deity, sixteen feet tall, who brandished a vajra and displayed his majesty; he shattered the prison and released him. The Emperor was struck with alarm and remorse, and immediately honored him with lavish gifts before he departed.
In the second year of the Yuanshou era of Emperor Wu of the Han dynasty, Buddhist images were first obtained. According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Wu" in the *Hanshu*, this is not recorded;
however, according to the "Treatise on the Xiongnu," the Han envoy, General of the Light Chariots Qu Ying, led ten thousand cavalry out from Longxi. Having passed through...
The mountains of Yanqi extend for over a thousand *li*. There, he obtained the golden figures used by King Xiutu for the sacrifice to Heaven. (Note: Sima Qian’s son, Sima Guang, says:
"They fashioned golden figures, regarding them as the lords of the celestial deities and sacrificing to them; these are the surviving traces of the present-day Buddhist images.
According to the "Biographies of Śākyamuni and Laozi" in the *Wei Shu*, during the Yuanshou era of Emperor Wu of Han, Huo Qubing was dispatched to campaign against the Xiongnu. Kunye...
The King killed the King of Xiutu and brought his fifty thousand followers to submit. He captured their golden figures, which the Emperor regarded as great deities.
These were displayed in the Ganshan Palace; the golden figures were approximately one zhang in height, and no sacrifices were offered to them—only incense was burned and prostrations performed.
This was the gradual beginning of the circulation of the Buddha-way. Upon opening the Western Regions, he dispatched Zhang Qian as an envoy to the Great [Yuezhi].
He returned in the summer. He reported that beside [the territory] lay the kingdom of Shendu, also known as Tianzhu.
For the first time, he heard of the existence of the teachings of the Buddha (according to the *Weishi benji*, the arrival of King Qunye occurred in the second year of the Yuanshou era).

In the *yǒngpíng* □ year of Emperor Míng of the Later Han, envoys were first dispatched to India, where they obtained the forty-two chapters of the Buddhist scriptures; thus the Baima Monastery was first established.

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Míng" in the *Book of the Later Han*, this is not recorded; however, according to the "Account of the Western Regions," it is found in the [Treatise on the] Western Regions.
In the land of Zhuguo (India), it is traditionally transmitted that Emperor Ming dreamed of a tall golden man with radiance emanating from his crown.
He questioned his ministers about this, and some said, "There is a deity in the West named Buddha; his form is sixteen feet tall and of golden hue.

Thereupon, the Emperor dispatched envoys to India to inquire about the teachings of the Buddha, and subsequently, images of his form were depicted in the Middle Kingdom. — From the *Chu sanzang jiji*.
King Ying began to believe in his arts. Consequently, there were quite a few in China who venerated that Way.
According to the commentary on the biography of King Ying of Chu in Yuan Hong’s *Book of Han*: "Futu" is Buddha. In the kingdom of India in the Western Regions, there exists the Way of the Buddha.
"Buddha" is translated in the Han language as "Awakened" (Jue). It is intended to awaken all living beings. Its teaching takes the cultivation of goodness and a compassionate heart as its core;
it prohibits killing and is dedicated exclusively to purity. Those who are most refined among its followers are called śramaṇas. Śramaṇa is translated in the Han language as "Rest" (Xi).
This refers to resting the mind and abandoning desire to return to non-action (wuwei). Furthermore, they hold that when a person dies, the spirit does not perish.
One receives a physical form again according to these actions; at birth, both good and evil deeds have their corresponding retributions.

Therefore, one should value the practice of goodness and the cultivation of the Way to refine the spirit until reaching the state of non-birth, thereby attaining Buddhahood. A Buddha is sixteen feet tall, with a golden complexion, and bears the light of the sun and moon upon his neck.
His transformations are boundless and penetrate everywhere, greatly saving all living beings. This is the initial clarification.
The Emperor dreamed of a golden man of great stature, with the light of the sun and moon upon his neck.
He questioned his ministers about it, and some said, "There is a deity in the West whose name is Buddha; could what Your Majesty has dreamed not be of him? Thereupon, he dispatched envoys to India.

He inquired after their arts and techniques and drew their images. According to the "Biographies of Śākyamuni and Laozi" (Shilaozhi) in the *Weishu*, in the first year of the Yuanshou era of Emperor Ai of the Han dynasty, Qin Jingxian, a student of the Imperial Academy, received the oral transmission of the *Futu jing* (Buddha Sūtra) from I-tsun, an envoy of the Great Yuezhi King.
When this was heard of in the Central Lands, it was not yet believed or fully understood. Later, Emperor Xiaoming dreamed of a golden [man] at night...
A man appeared with a light like a bowl atop his head, flying through the palace courtyard. He then sought out the ministers, and Fu Yi was the first to identify him as the Buddha.
The Emperor dispatched the Langzhong Cai Yin and the disciple of a *boshi*, Qin Jing, and others on an embassy to India to transcribe the surviving teachings of the *Futu* (Buddha).
Cai Yin subsequently returned to Luoyang from the east with the śramaṇas Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna; thus, the śramaṇas first appeared in China.

The practice of entering through gates and the ritual of kneeling and prostrating began from this point. An Shigao (Yin) further obtained the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* and a standing image of Śākyamuni.
Emperor Ming ordered painters to depict the Buddha’s image and installed them atop the Qingliang Terrace and the Xianjie Mausoleum.
The scriptures were sealed within the stone chamber of the Lantai Library. When An Shigao returned, he brought the scriptures to Han on the back of a white horse.
Consequently, the Baima Monastery was established at Yongguan West in the city of Luoyang. Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna both passed away in this monastery.
"Futu" (浮屠) is the abbreviated designation for *buddha*. "Buddha" and "futu" are phonetically similar; both are Western terms that, upon being transmitted here, became two distinct sounds.
Translated into the language of China (*huayan*), it means "Pure Enlightenment. It signifies the extinction of defilement and the accomplishment of the Way of Radiance.
The Sage’s Awakening: Regarding the essential purport of these scriptures, it is generally said that all categories of living beings arise due to their karma and conduct.

There are the past, the present, and the future; throughout these three periods, the conscious spirit (*vijñāna*) is never extinguished. Whatever good or evil one performs, there will inevitably be a corresponding retribution.
By gradually accumulating superior deeds and refining away the coarse and base, one passes through countless forms, purifying and training the spiritual intelligence until—
One attains the Buddha-way through non-arising. Within this process, the stages and the levels of mental cultivation are not uniform;

all proceed from the shallow to the profound and rely on the subtle to reach the manifest. This generally depends upon accumulating benevolence and compliance, eliminating sensual desires, and practicing emptiness and stillness, thereby achieving pervasive illumination.
Thus, when first cultivating the mind, one relies upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, which are called the Three Refuges, just as [one relies upon] a ruler.
Regarding your three fears, there are furthermore five precepts: abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants.

Their general meaning is the same as benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, wisdom, and sincerity; only their names differ. It is said that by serving [the Buddha] and observing these, one will be reborn in the superior realms of gods and humans.

If one violates these precepts, one will fall into the various sufferings of the realms of ghosts and animals. Furthermore, there are six paths of rebirth where beings are born according to their good or evil deeds.

Those who submit to this Way shave off their hair and beards, cast off worldly burdens, and leave the household life. They establish the relationship of teacher and disciple, observe the rules and regulations, and dwell together in harmony.
Governing their minds and cultivating pure conduct, they beg for food to sustain themselves; these are called śramaṇas, or sometimes sāmaṇas. It is also...
Because their pronunciations are similar, they are collectively referred to as "Seng" (Saṃgha), all of which are foreign terms. "Seng" is translated as "harmonious assembly" (andha-jana).
"Sāman" means "one who has stilled the mind. "Bhikṣu" means "one who begs for alms. Among laypeople who place their faith in the Way and its teachings, men are called "Upāsaka."
A woman is called an *upāsikā*. Those who become *śramaṇas* first practice the ten precepts and are called *śrāmaṇeras*;
when they finally complete the two hundred and fifty, they are fully ordained and become *bhikṣus*. Women who enter the Way are called *bhikṣuṇīs*;

their precepts number five hundred, all of which take the [ten] as their foundation, with the count increasing according to the circumstances. They consist in guarding the mind, restraining the body, and rectifying [the speech].
In speech, one abandons greed, anger, and delusion; in body, one eliminates killing, sexual misconduct, and theft; in speech, one cuts off falsehoods and all other improper words.

These are collectively termed the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*). To be fully endowed with these is called the purity of the three karmas. For ordinary people, practicing to this extent is considered the ultimate;

it is said that through this, one can reach the retribution of evil and good and gradually ascend to the traces of the sages. Regarding those who first ascend to the stage of a sage, there are three types of persons.
Their faculties and karmic capacities differ greatly; these are called the Three Vehicles: the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and the Mahāyāna.

They are so named because they take that which can be mounted as a vehicle to transport one to the Way. These three types of persons have already exhausted their evil traces; they merely cultivate the mind to dispel burdens, rescue sentient beings, and advance in virtue.

Those of the initial faculty are of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and practice the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. Those of the middle faculty are of the Middle Vehicle and receive... [text continues]
Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination: those of superior capacity follow the Mahāyāna and thus cultivate the six perfections.

Although they may proceed through the stages of the three vehicles, they must fundamentally advance through the myriad practices to rescue and deliver billions of beings; only after traversing this vast expanse can they ascend to the realm of Buddhahood.

In the eighth year of Yongping, Prince Ying of Chu offered fine silk to atone for his transgressions; by imperial decree, this was used to assist in providing the magnificent feasts for the *upāsakas* and *śramaṇas*.
According to the *Book of the Later Han*, the Basic Annals (*Benji*) of Emperor Ming do not record this; however, it is recorded in the Biography of Prince Ying of Chu.

In his youth, Ying was fond of the life of a wandering knight-errant and maintained close relations with guests and visitors. In his later years, he took even greater pleasure in the studies of Huang-Lao (Daoism) and observed the fasts and ritual offerings of the Buddhist clergy.

In the eighth year [of the reign], an imperial edict was issued throughout the empire that all those facing the death penalty could redeem their lives by paying a fine of raw silk. Ying dispatched a *langzhong* (Court Gentleman).

He was ordered to present thirty rolls of yellow silk and white gauze. He went to the Regional Inspector (Guoxiang) and said, "Relying on Your Excellency as a vassal and protector, my transgressions and evils have accumulated.
Out of joy for Your Great Benevolence, I present this silk and cloth to redeem my sinful offenses. The Regional Inspector reported this to the throne, and the Imperial Edict replied:
The King of Chu recited the subtle words of Huang-Lao and revered the benevolent temples of the Buddha. Having purified himself for three months, he made a vow with the divine:

"What cause for suspicion or doubt could there be that would lead to regret or failure? I shall redeem [the captured birds] to assist in providing a magnificent feast for the *upāsakas* and *śramaṇas*.
He then issued this proclamation for circulation throughout the various states.
In the [blank] year of the reign of Emperor Ming of the Wei dynasty, the Buddhist monastery (*bìtú*) was moved west of the palace, and a hundred bays of multi-storied galleries were constructed.

The Indian *śramaṇa* Dharmakāla first translated the *Vinaya* precepts and transmitted them to China. According to the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (*Sanguo zhi*), this occurred during the reign of Emperor Ming of Wei.
The *Benji* (Basic Annals) of the Emperor does not record this; however, according to the "Shilaozhi" (Record of Śramaṇas and Barbarians) in the *Weishu* (Book of Wei):

Emperor Ming of Wei intended to demolish the Buddhist stūpa to the west of the palace. Thereupon, a foreign śramaṇa placed a golden basin filled with water before the hall and cast a Buddha-relic (*śarīra*) into the water.
Whereupon, light of five colors arose. The Emperor then sighed and said: "Were it not for its spiritual wonder, how could such a thing be?"
Thus it was. He subsequently moved [the image] to Daocheng, where he constructed a hundred bays of multi-storied pavilions (*zhouge*).

At the former site of the Buddhist temple (*fotu*), he excavated a pond called Mongsī and planted lotuses within it. Later, the Indian śramaṇa Dharmakāla entered Luoyang to propagate and translate the precepts and Vinaya;
this marked the beginning of the transmission of the precepts and Vinaya in China.
In the fourth year of the Chihu era of Sun Quan, the Ruler of Wu, a pagoda was constructed at Fotuo Li. Furthermore, a monastery was established to provide a residence for the monk Kang Senghui.

According to the "Biography of Sun Quan, Ruler of Wu" in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (*Sanguo zhi*), this is not recorded; however, it is recorded in the *Fofa jintang bian* (The Golden Wall and Moat of the Buddha-Dharma). Wu.
In the fourth year of the Chiku era, the Tripitaka Master Kang Senghui of the country of Kangju arrived at Jinling and erected a thatched hut, where he established images and practiced the Way.
When the people of the state first saw this, they were all struck with wonder and amazement. The officials reported it to the throne, and Sun Quan summoned him to question him.

Senghui replied: "The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, entered parinirvāṇa over a thousand years ago; yet his sacred relics, the śarīra, manifest divine responses without limit. Formerly, when King A..."
King Aśoka enshrined them and constructed eighty-four thousand stūpas; this is the legacy of his transformative influence.
Sun Quan considered this to be mere exaggeration and said, "If the śarīra can be obtained, you shall build the stūpas for it. If there is no proof, the state has established laws.
Huì then placed a copper bottle upon a table and requested a period of seven days. When there was no result, he extended the time to fourteen days. Still there was no result, and Sun Quan said:
He proceeded to cook it. At that moment, he silently recited the name of the Buddha, thinking, "How could True Compassion fail me? He requested an extension of the deadline.
When the fifth watch of the seventh day arrived, he heard a tinkling sound from within the jar; looking inside, he found it was a śarīra relic. At dawn, he presented it [to the Emperor].
Sun Quan gathered with his high officials to observe it, exclaiming, "This is a rare omen for the age. He remarked that the śarīra’s majestic power was such that nothing could destroy it.
Sun Quan ordered a strongman to strike it with a hammer, but it suffered no damage and its radiance remained as before.
Sun Quan erected a stūpa for it in Fotuo-li and constructed a monastery to house Huihui, granting it the name Jianchu.

During the □□□ year of Emperor Hu of Wu, an edict was issued to destroy Buddhist monasteries. According to the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (Sanguo zhi), the biography of Sun Hao, the ruler of Wu, this is not recorded.

However, according to the *Continued Comprehensive Examination of Literature* (Xu Wenzhuan tongkao), Emperor Hao of Wu once issued an edict to destroy shrines to deities as well as Buddhist monasteries.
During the Jin dynasty, there were forty-two Buddhist monasteries in Luoyang, and the monks began to wear robes of various colors.

According to the "Account of Śramaṇas and Laozi" (*Shilao zhi*) in the *Weishu*, since the construction of the Baima Monastery in Luoyang, Buddhist shrines were magnificently adorned, and their painted murals were exceedingly exquisite.
There are four styles. Generally, the architectural systems for temples and pagodas were reconstructed based on the ancient forms of India.

Because of this, he left the household life and took the name Huida. He traveled about to worship the stūpas, and eventually arrived at Danyang, though he did not yet know where [the stūpa was].

He proceeded there to pay his respects and found it was indeed the location of the former Stupa of King Aśoka, which had frequently emitted light. From this, he knew for certain that śarīra must be present.
He then gathered a crowd and began digging; at a depth of one zhang, they discovered three stone tablets, each six chi long, one of which contained iron.

There was a casket; within the casket was a silver casket, and within that silver casket was another golden casket, which contained three *śarīra* relics, along with a single hair and a single nail-clipping, each several feet in length.
These were then moved to a stūpa built by Emperor Jianwen nearby to the north. To the west was yet another stūpa.
In the sixteenth year, he again dispatched the śramaṇa Renshang to expand it to three stories; this was the one originally built by Emperor Wu.

This was the opening. Initially, they dug four chi into the earth and discovered a dragon’s lair, as well as various miscellaneous precious objects such as gold and silver rings, bracelets, hairpins, and tweezers left there by people of old.
The excavation reached a depth of about nine chi, where they encountered stone pillars. Beneath the pillars was a stone casket;
inside the casket was an iron jar containing a silver crucible. Within the crucible was a golden filigree flask, which held three śarīras. As it was...
They were the size of millet seeds, perfectly round, smooth, and lustrous. Inside the casket was a lapis lazuli bowl, within which were four śarīras, as well as hair and nail-clippings;

there were four nail-clippings, all of which were the color of agarwood. On the twenty-seventh day of that month, the Emperor again visited the temple to pay his respects, established a Great Unobstructed Assembly, and issued a general amnesty. On this day, he used a golden bowl to hold water and floated the śarīras upon it.

The relics were beneficial; the smallest ones remained hidden and did not emerge. The Emperor performed dozens of prostrations, and the śarīra then emitted light from within the bowl, circling for a long time before coming to rest in the center.
The Emperor asked the Great Sengzheng Hui-nian, "Did you witness this inconceivable event?
Hui-nian replied, "The Dharma-body is eternally abiding, profound and unmoving. The Emperor said, "My younger brother..."
The Prince wished to request one *śarīra* relic to return to the palace for veneration.

On the fifth day of the ninth month, he again convened a Great Unobstructed Assembly (*anāvaraṇa-mahāpariṣad*) and dispatched the Crown Prince, princes, nobles, and high officials to welcome it. On that day, the weather was bright and clear;

the entire populace gathered to gaze upon the spectacle. All the gold, silver, and ritual implements provided for the offering were left at the temple for veneration, along with a donation of one thousand coins.

the empire was granted a general amnesty. In the first year of the Zhongdatong era, [the Emperor] visited Tongtai Temple to lecture on the sutras and establish a Dharma assembly. According to the *Beishu*, "Basic Annals of the Gaozu":
On the gengxu day of the third month in the first year of Zhongdatong, the imperial carriage proceeded to the Great Assembly at Tongtai Temple;

he stayed at the temple offices and lectured on the *Golden Character Sutra of the Three Wisdoms*. On the bingxu day of the fourth month in summer, at Tongtai Temple, he concluded the lectures and established [the assembly].

There were assemblies of the Dharma, general amnesties, and changes of the imperial era. That night, the Tongtai Temple was struck by fire. Furthermore, the Emperor was deeply devoted to the True Dharma and continued to promote the Buddhist scriptures.

He composed several hundred scrolls of commentaries on the meanings of various sutras, including the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* (Great Perfection of Wisdom), the *Vimalakīrti*, and the *Tri-vidyā*.
During his leisure from listening to lectures, he immediately gave expositions at the Chongyun Hall and Tongtai Temple for renowned monks, great scholars, and the fourfold assembly.
The audience was always more than ten thousand people. According to the biography of He Jingrong:

in the third month of the first year of the Zhongdatong era, the Emperor visited Tongtai Temple to lecture on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* (the Golden Threefold Wisdom Sutra). Jingrong requested permission to attend the lectures, and the Emperor granted his request by imperial decree.
Furthermore, there was a decree permitting him to pay his respects during the new and full moons.

In the first year of the Taiching era, the Emperor again visited Tongtai Temple and performed the ritual of "shedding his body. The high officials and ministers redeemed him by offering one hundred million coins.

According to the *Beishi*, in the Basic Annals of the Gaozu: on the gengzi day of the third month in the first year of Taiching, the Gaozu visited Tongtai Temple and established a Great Unrestricted Assembly (*wu zhe da hui*), shedding his body.
The high officials and others offered one hundred million coins to redeem him. On the ding... day of the fourth month in summer...
The tenth month. The imperial carriage returned to the palace. A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the realm. The era name was changed to □□□.

Upon completing this task, he submitted a petition to request ordination. He first burned off his hair and beard as a self-vow, and the Emperor granted his permission.

In the year □□□, Emperor [Gaozu] bestowed upon Jiang Ge the poem “Awakening the Mind. Jiang Ge subsequently submitted a memorial requesting to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
According to the *Beishi*, "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor," this is not recorded. However, according to the biography of Jiang Ge, the High Ancestor was devoted to Buddhism;

many court dignitaries submitted memorials seeking to receive the precepts. Jiang Ge was profoundly faithful in the law of cause and effect, yet the High Ancestor did not yet know of this and remarked that Jiang Ge did not follow [the Buddhist teachings].

The Buddha said: "I have bestowed upon you the poem 'Reviving the Awakening Mind' in five hundred characters, saying: 'One must surely be diligent and energetic; exert oneself in superior cultivation.
How can one act with such negligence, like a prisoner condemned to die? This was told to Jiang Ge and all those of noble station. Furthermore, the imperial hand-edict states:
'The karmic retributions of the world cannot be disbelieved. How could one afford to be negligent, as if facing [an executioner]? "
In the first year of the Yuanyan period, Yuan Yanming was reformed [of his heterodoxy]. He subsequently submitted a petition requesting to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.

In the first year of the Yongding era of Emperor Gaozu of the Chen dynasty, an imperial edict issued the Buddha’s tooth relic, and an Unrestricted Great Assembly (*amogha-mahāpariṣad*) was convened. (According to the *Book of Chen*, Gao...)
The Basic Annals of the Ancestor: On the *yihai* day of the tenth month in winter of the first year of Yongding, he ascended the throne as Emperor.

On the *jingshen* day, an edict was issued to bring forth the Buddha’s tooth relic. It was assembled at the residence of She-mu, where the fourfold assembly gathered for an unrestricted great assembly (*amogha-mahā-pariṣad*).

The High Ancestor personally went before the palace gate to pay homage. Initially, the former State Preceptor of Qi, Faxon, had obtained it in the kingdom of Wuchan; it had long been kept at the Upper Dinglin Monastery.
Temple. At the end of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, it was kept in safekeeping by the śramaṇa Huixing of Qingyun Temple on Mount She.
When Huixing was about to pass away, he entrusted it to his younger brother, Huizhi. At the end of the Chengsheng era, Huizhi secretly sent it to the High Ancestor (Emperor Wu).

It was finally brought out in the fifth month of the summer in the second year of the Yongding era. The imperial carriage visited Dazhuangyan Temple, where the Emperor offered himself as a sacrifice. In the tenth month of winter, [the text] begins.
The title of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. The twelfth month. Furthermore, he visited Dazhuangyan Monastery. Regarding the imperial carriage and ritual objects:

according to the "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor" in the *Chen Shu*, on the *xinyou* day of the fifth month in the summer of the second year of Yongding, the imperial carriage visited Dazhuangyan Monastery and [the Emperor] relinquished his person.
On the *renxu* day, the ministers submitted a memorial requesting his return to the palace. In the winter, the tenth month, on the *yihai* day, the imperial carriage...

The Emperor visited Dazhuangyan Temple and began the recitation of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. On the day of Jiazi in the twelfth month, the imperial carriage visited Dazhuangyan Temple to convene a Great Unobstructed Assembly (*anāvaraṇa-mahāpariṣad*).
The Emperor relinquished his state carriage and ritual regalia; the ministers prepared the ceremonial procession to welcome him.
That very day, the imperial carriage returned to the palace.

On the *xinchou* day of the fourth month of the summer in the fourth year of the Tianjia era of Emperor Shizu, a Great Unobstructed Assembly (*anāvaraṇa-mahāpariṣad*) was convened at the Anterior Hall of the Taiji Palace.
(As recorded in the *Benji* [Basic Annals] of Emperor Shizu in the *Book of Chen*, etc.)

In the second year of the Taian era of Emperor Gaodi [of the Chen dynasty], the Lingcha (Spiritual Pagoda) was constructed. According to the *Chen Shu* (Book of Chen), in the Basic Annals of Emperor Gaozong, this is not recorded;

however, according to the *Xuefo Kaoxun* (Investigations and Training for Studying Buddhism), in the second year of the Taian era of the Chen dynasty, the Lingli (Spiritual Reliquary) was built, fifteen *zhang* in height.

At its base were enshrined Buddha’s fingernails, two inches long and one inch wide, preserved within various precious caskets. Five-colored light radiated forth, and flames rose to a height of one *xun*.
The tradition considers this extraordinary.
In the fourteenth year of the Taijian era, the Later Ruler ascended the throne and established a Great Unobstructed Assembly (*anāvaraṇa-mahāpariṣad*).

According to the *Benji* (Basic Annals) of the Later Ruler in the *Book of Chen*, on the day Dingyi of the first month in the fourteenth year of Taijian, he ascended the imperial throne; on the day Jiashu, he established the Unobstructed [Assembly].

A great assembly was held in the Anterior Hall of the Taiji Palace. On the *bingwu* day of the ninth month of autumn, a Great Unobstructed Assembly (*anāvaraṇa-mahāpariṣad*) was convened in the Taiji Hall.
He relinquished his person, as well as his carriage and imperial robes, and issued a general amnesty for all under heaven.

In the first year of the Tianxing era of Emperor Taizu of the Northern Wei, an edict was issued to construct a five-storied *stūpa* (buddhatu), a meditation hall (*xiuchantang*), and seats for śramaṇas within the capital.

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Taizu" in the *Weishu*, this is not recorded; however, according to the "Treatise on Śākyamuni and Laozi," the state of Wei had already been established previously.

During the Yuanshuo era, customs were pure and uniform; the people maintained themselves through non-action (*wuwei*). Being utterly isolated from the Western Regions, there was no possibility of communication between them.
Consequently, the teachings of the Buddha had not yet been heard of, or if they were heard of, they were not believed.

It was only when Shenyuan established diplomatic relations with the Wei and Jin dynasties—when Emperor Wen was in Luoyang and Emperor Shaoceng arrived at Xiangguo—that the southern [culture] was thoroughly investigated.

Regarding the Buddhist affairs during the Xia dynasty: when Emperor Taizu pacified Zhongshan and campaigned through Yan and Zhao, he encountered monasteries and temples in the various prefectures and states along his route.
Upon seeing the śramaṇas and practitioners there, he treated them with the utmost reverence and respect, strictly forbidding his military forces from committing any transgressions against them.

Although the Emperor was fond of the teachings of Huang-Lao and had perused Buddhist scriptures to some extent, as the empire was newly settled, his war chariots were frequently in action, and all administrative affairs were still in their infancy; thus, he had not yet established [a formal system for Buddhism].
The "Tu Yu" (Hall of the Universe) was built to invite and accommodate the monastic community. However, he occasionally sought them out from other quarters.

Previously, there was a śramaṇa named Senglang who, along with his disciples, had lived in seclusion at Kun’er Valley on Mount Tai. The Emperor dispatched an envoy with a letter and presented him with gifts of silk, felt, woolen cloth, an alms bowl, and a mendicant’s staff.
Even today, this place is still called Lang Gong Gu (Valley of Master Lang). In the first year of the Tianxing era, an edict was issued stating: "Now..."

The rise of the Buddha-dharma has been far-reaching. Its merit in providing salvation and benefit extends invisibly to both the living and the deceased. The divine traces and remaining paths are indeed worthy of reliance.

It was therefore decreed that the relevant authorities should construct and adorn the physical forms [of the Buddhas] and repair the monastic quarters within the capital city, so that those who follow with faith and devotion would have a place to reside.
In this year, the five-storied *stūpa* on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa was first built.

Furthermore, the Hall of Mount Sumeru was embellished with painted decorations; lecture halls, meditation halls, and seats for śramaṇas were specially constructed, all of which were provided with solemn furnishings.
In the [blank] year of Emperor Tai of the Taizong era, the śramaṇa Faguo was posthumously bestowed the title of General of Old Age, and the śramaṇa Tan[...].
[The title] "Certification of the General of Old Age. According to the *Weishu*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Taizong do not record this.

However, according to the "Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism," upon ascending the throne, Emperor Taizong followed the legacy of his grandfather (Emperor Taizu), who was fond of the teachings of Huang-Lao, while he himself also revered the Buddha-dharma.

He established images [of deities] throughout the capital and the four quarters, and further commanded the śramaṇas to instruct and guide the common people. Initially, during the Huangshi era, Zhao...

In the commandery, there was a śramaṇa named Faguo, whose disciplined conduct was refined and profound. He expounded the scriptural teachings of the Dharma. When the Taizu heard of his reputation, he issued an imperial edict to summon him with due ceremony.
After arriving at the capital, he was appointed as the Overseer of Daoists (Dàotǒng) to supervise the monastic community. He frequently engaged in discourse with the Emperor.

He was highly gratified by [the Emperor's] many concessions, and his offerings and provisions were exceedingly generous. Upon reaching the reign of Emperor Taizong, he was further honored with even greater veneration.

During the Yongxing era, the Emperor successively conferred upon him the titles of Fuguo (Aid to the State), Yicheng Zi (Viscount of Yicheng), Zhongxin Hou (Marquis of Zhongxin), and Ancheng Gong (Duke of Ancheng), yet he declined them all.

The Emperor frequently visited his residence in person; because the gate was small and narrow and could not accommodate carriages or litters, he had it expanded and enlarged. He lived to the age of over eighty.
Tai died while in office before his body had been encoffined. The Emperor visited his funeral three times and posthumously conferred upon him the title of General Laoshou and Duke Ling of Zhao.
Previously, Faguo had often remarked that Emperor Taizong was intelligent and wise and fond of the Way, being the Tathāgata of the present age;

he maintained that śramaṇas should offer him full ritual homage. Consequently, Faguo constantly prostrated himself before the Emperor, saying to others: "He who can propagate the Way is the sovereign; I am not."
To pay homage to the Son of Heaven is precisely to pay reverence to the Buddha. Faguo was forty years old when he first became a śramaṇa;
he had a son named Meng, whom the Emperor decreed should inherit the rank bestowed upon Faguo. Later, when the Emperor visited Guangzong, he encountered the śramaṇa Tanzheng on the road;

Tanzheng was nearly one hundred years old, yet he invited the Emperor to meet him and presented him with offerings. The Emperor respected him for his advanced age and his undiminished vigor of will, and likewise conferred honors upon him.
In the year of the Shenyu era of Emperor Shizu,
the General named Lao-shou was ordered by imperial decree to escort the śramaṇa Dharmakṣema from Juqu Mengxun to the capital.
Regarding "Not Recorded": According to the *Shizu benji* (Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu) in the *Weishu*, this is not recorded. Regarding "According to the 'Shilaozhi'":
When Emperor Shizu first ascended the throne, he likewise followed the legacy of Taizu and Taizong, frequently summoning śramaṇas of high virtue to engage in discussion with them.

On the eighth day of the fourth month, the various Buddha images were carried through the broad streets. The Emperor personally ascended the gate tower to observe the procession, scattering flowers as an act of reverence.
Previously, Juqu Mengxun, while in Liangzhou, had also been fond of the Buddha-dharma.
There was the Kasmirian śramaṇa Dharmakṣema, who had studied various sūtras and treatises; in Guzang, he was together with the śramaṇas Zhi Song and others.

He translated more than ten sūtras on the *Nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, he was proficient in the arts of divination and incantations, and his predictions regarding the security and peril of other nations were frequently proven accurate.
Juqu Mengxun constantly consulted him on matters of state. During the Shengu (Shen-ju) era, the Emperor ordered Mengxun to send the *Chen* (prophecy) to the capital;
however, [the Master] regretted it and refused to dispatch it. Subsequently, fearing the retribution of the Wei authority, he sent someone to kill the *Chen*. The *Chen*...
On the day of his death, he said to his disciples, "A guest is about to arrive; you may eat early and wait for him.
When they had finished eating, a messenger arrived. People of the time remarked that he was one who knew his own destiny.
In the fifth year of the Taiyan era, because the number of śramaṇas was so great, an edict was issued to dismiss those under the age of fifty.
According to the *Shi-lao-zhi* (History of Buddhism and Taoism), from the time of Zhang Gui onwards, the people of Liangzhou had for generations believed in the Buddhist faith.

Dunhuang, bordering the Western Regions, saw both monastics and laypeople adhere to their traditional customs; the villages and hamlets were situated close together, and [the population] was numerous.
There was a stupa-temple. During the Taiyan era, when Liangzhou was pacified, its inhabitants were relocated to the capital;
the śramaṇas and all Buddhist rites followed eastward, causing the teaching of the Buddha to flourish even more.

Subsequently, because the number of śramaṇas became excessive, an edict was issued to dismiss those under the age of fifty (according to the Basic Annals, the relocation of the people of Liangzhou to the capital occurred in the fifth year of Taiyan).
In the fifth year of the Taiping Zhenjun era, an edict was issued prohibiting the private maintenance of śramaṇas. According to the *Weishu*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu":

In the first month of spring in the fifth year of Taiping Zhenjun, on the day Wushen, an edict stated: "Ignorant commoners, lacking understanding, place their faith in and are deluded by demons and heresies.

They privately maintain sorcerers and shamans, and harbor prophetic records (*chanji*), books on the Yin-Yang system and celestial portents (*tuwei*), as well as texts on the arts of healing. Furthermore, [they maintain] śramaṇas..."
These individuals, relying on the empty and extravagant claims of the Western Barbarians, give rise to demonic and unnatural growths.
This is not the way to unify the administration and transformation of the state, nor to spread pure virtue throughout the world.

From the princes and dukes down to the common people, anyone who privately maintains śramaṇas, sorcerers, or artisans of gold and silver within their homes must all be sent to the official authorities; they shall not be tolerated.

Concealment is prohibited. The deadline is the fifteenth day of the second month of this year. Should anyone fail to come forward by this date, the sorcerers and shamans shall suffer death, and the masters of their households shall face extermination. This is proclaimed for all to hear and know.
In the sixth year of the Taiping Zhenjun era, an edict was issued prohibiting the burial of śramaṇas within the city walls. Consequently, Huishi was reinterred outside the southern suburb;

more than six thousand people accompanied the procession. According to the "Shilaozhi" (Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism) in the *Weishu* (Book of Wei), the Shizhu (Emperor Shizu) did not record this in his own annals.
Initially, upon the subjugation of Helian Chang, the Emperor obtained the śramaṇa Huishi, whose secular surname was Zhang and whose family was originally from... [text fragment ends].

Qinghe heard that Kumārajīva had produced new scriptures and consequently traveled to Chang’an to meet him. There he studied the classics and practiced dhyāna meditation at the side of the White Canal (Baiqu).
During the day he would enter the city to listen to lectures, and in the evening he would return to his quarters to sit in quietude.
Many discerning people in the Three Commanderies (Sanfǔ) took him as their master. When Liu Yu destroyed the state of Yao Hong, he left his son Yizhen to garrison Chang’an; Yizhen and his attendants—
Everyone held him in deep reverence. When Fayin departed from Chang’an, Helian Chubi pursued and defeated his forces;

both monastics and laypeople, young and old alike, were all massacred in mass graves. Huishi, however, was struck by a blade, yet his body remained unhurt. This was regarded as a most extraordinary marvel by the multitude.
When he spoke of Yuezui, Yuezui became greatly incensed. He summoned Huishi before him and struck him with the precious sword he carried, yet he was still unable to harm him.
Terrified, Yuezui apologized for his transgression. When Tongwan was pacified, Huishi arrived at the capital, where he provided much instruction and guidance;
contemporaries could not fathom his traces. Emperor Shizu held him in high esteem and always treated him with ritual respect. Huishi then began to practice *dhyāna*.
Until his death, he was said to have lived for over fifty years without ever lying down to sleep;

at times he would walk barefoot, yet even when treading through mud and dust, his feet were never soiled, their color remaining increasingly bright white. The world called him the "White-Footed Master" (Baijiao Shi).

During the Taiyan era, he passed away at the Bajiao Temple. He sat upright in pure and dignified composure, surrounded by a full assembly of monks. Remaining still and serene, he breathed his last. His body lay in state for ten days...

On subsequent days, his sitting posture remained unchanged and his countenance appeared as it was at first; the whole world marveled at this divine anomaly. He was subsequently interred within the monastery.
When the sixth year of the Zhenjun era arrived, a decree was issued that no corpses were permitted to remain buried within the city walls, so he was reburied outside the southern suburbs.

Ten years had passed since his death, yet when the coffin was opened, his body was solemn and majestic, showing no signs of decay or collapse. Among the more than six thousand mourners who escorted the funeral procession, there was not one who did not...

Filled with profound grief, Gao Yun, the Director of the Central Secretariat, composed a biography to extol his virtue. He erected a stone monument upon Huishi’s grave and depicted his likeness in a spirit-house (stūpa).
Even during the period when the Dharma was suppressed and destroyed, these remains remained intact and standing.
In the seventh year of the Taiping Zhenjun era, an edict was issued to all provinces to pit the śramaṇas and destroy all Buddha images and Buddhist monasteries.

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu" in the *Weishu*: in the third month of spring in the seventh year of Taiping Zhenjun, an edict was issued to all provinces to pit the śramaṇas and destroy all Buddha images;
two thousand households of artisans from Chang'an were transferred to the capital. In the fourth month of summer...
On the *wùzǐ* day of the month, the five-storied Buddhist stūpa at Ye City was destroyed. From within the clay images, two jade seals were obtained;

the inscriptions on both read: "Received the mandate from Heaven; may his life be long and ever-prosperous. On one of them, the side was engraved with: "The Han Imperial Seal of State received by the Wei.
According to the "Biographies of Śākyamuni and Laozi" (Shìlǎo zhì), when Shizu ascended the throne while still young, he subsequently applied himself with keen resolve.
Regarding military affairs, he always prioritized the pacification of rebellions and calamities.

Although he had returned to the Buddhist teachings and held the śramaṇas in high esteem, he did not yet possess the intent to study the scriptures and doctrines or to seek deeply into the workings of karmic retribution.

Upon encountering the Way of Kou Qianzhi, the Emperor—finding its principles of purity and non-action to be supported by evidence of immortal transformation—thereupon came to believe in and practice those arts. At that time, Cui Hao, the Minister of Works, was a man of extensive learning.
Tao Daowen was widely learned. Whenever the Emperor consulted him on matters of great importance, Hao adhered to the Way of Humility;

he particularly did not believe in Buddhism and frequently spoke in disparagement of it when conversing with the Emperor, often claiming that it was empty and extravagant, a source of waste and harm to the world. Because of his erudition and eloquence, the Emperor placed considerable trust in him.
Hui Gai rebelled at Xingcheng, causing turmoil throughout Guanzhong. The Emperor then marched westward and reached Chang’an. Previously, a śramaṇa had been growing wheat inside the monastery;
the Emperor’s grooms were grazing horses among the wheat. When the Emperor entered to inspect the horses, the śramaṇa offered wine to his attendants.
An attendant entered the monk’s private chamber and saw that there were many bows, arrows, spears, and shields. He brought them out...
The report was submitted to the Emperor. The Emperor said in anger, "This is not what a śramaṇa should employ; he must have conspired with Gai Wu to plot the harm of others.
He ordered the authorities to investigate and execute [the monk] and destroy his entire monastery.

Upon auditing his property, they found a vast quantity of wine-making equipment, as well as goods deposited by regional governors, prefectural magistrates, and wealthy men, numbering in the tens of thousands. Furthermore, he had constructed underground chambers for the daughters of noble families.

I personally engaged in licentious conduct. As the Emperor was already incensed by the monks' violation of the Dharma, and as Seng Hao happened to be in his entourage at the time, he took the opportunity to advance this proposal.

An imperial edict was issued to execute the monks in Chang’an and to burn and destroy Buddhist images. A decree was then sent to the various provinces under the Central Secretariat, ordering them to follow the proceedings in Chang’an exactly.

Furthermore, an edict stated: "Those monks falsely rely on the empty and extravagant doctrines of the Western Barbarians to recklessly give rise to demonic calamities; they are not [to be tolerated]."
To unify the administration and spread pure virtue throughout the world, all those from the princes and dukes downward who privately support śramaṇas must send them to the palace office;
no one shall conceal them. This deadline is set for the fifteenth day of the second month of this year.

Should they not be surrendered by that time, the śramaṇa shall be executed, and the entire household of those who harbor them shall be put to death. At that time, Prince Gongzong was serving as the Regent (Jian) for the Crown Prince.

The state had long revered the Buddhist Way. [The Emperor] repeatedly submitted memorials stating that the execution of śramaṇas was excessive and unjustified, and that their images were not at fault.
Now, having abolished the Way, the gates of all monasteries have been closed and no longer maintained; the plastering, painting, and woodwork will naturally decay.

Although this was requested two or three times, permission was not granted. Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "In the past, the decadent rulers of the Later Han believed in and were deluded by heterodox and false teachings."

This is false. To feign the events of sleep and dreams, using barbarian demons and spirits to disrupt the constant order of Heaven—such a thing has never occurred within the Nine Provinces since antiquity.
These boastful and grandiose claims do not accord with human nature; yet in these degenerate ages, there is no dark-ruling sovereign or chaotic lord who is not deluded by them.
Consequently, governance and instruction fail to prevail, rites and righteousness are utterly ruined, and the way of ghosts flourishes, causing people to view the laws of the King as...

It was treated with utter contempt. Since that time, the world has passed through successive calamities and misfortunes; the punishments of Heaven have been incessantly enacted, and the living people have died out until the lands within the Five Zones have become nothing but desolate ruins.
For a thousand li, all is withered and silent, and no human traces are seen—all of which stems from this.

I, the Emperor, inherit the celestial mandate at a time when the era has reached its nadir; I wish to eliminate the false and establish the true, restoring the governance of the righteous and the farmers. Therefore...
I shall sweep away all Hu deities and extinguish their traces, so that we may not fall short of the legacy of the Feng clan.
From this day forward, whoever dares to serve Hu deities or fashion images—whether of clay or bronze—shall face extermination of their entire lineage.
Although these are called "Hu deities," when I question the Hu people of today, they all say there are none; they are all merely the scoundrels among the Han people of former generations. Liu...

Yuan Zhen, Lü Boqiang, and their ilk have taken the fabricated words of the barbarian [Huiyuan] and, employing the empty rhetoric of Laozi and Zhuangzi, have attached themselves to and augmented them with falsehoods;
none of these are true. This has led to the point where the royal law is neglected and not enforced. They are truly the foremost among great villains.
Only after there have been extraordinary men can extraordinary deeds be performed. Were it not for me, who else could abolish these deceptive objects of successive dynasties?
Let the officials proclaim this to all military governors, regional inspectors, and commandants: as for all Buddhist shrines and images—
He then completely smashed and burned all the Hu scriptures. Monks, regardless of age, were all buried alive in pits. This was in the third month of the seventh year of the Zhenjun era.
Although Emperor Gongzong’s words had not been heeded, he nevertheless delayed the proclamation of the edict so that those far and near could all be informed in advance and prepare their own plans.
Consequently, many monks from the four quarters managed to escape into hiding and avoid capture, while those in the capital cities were spared.
He, too, was fully saved; he obtained golden and silver images as well as various sutras and treatises, thereby gaining great access to the secret treasury.
Yet, as for the earthen and wooden temples and stupas, wherever his teachings reached, none remained undestroyed. At first, Huiqian and Senghao had traveled together with the imperial carriage.
Du Ku contested with Hao. Hao was unwilling to comply, whereupon Du Ku said to him, "You shall now meet an early end and suffer execution; your entire clan will be exterminated.
Four years later, Hao was executed and subjected to the five punishments at the age of seventy. After Hao had been put to death, the Emperor felt considerable regret.
The Emperor had already undertaken the difficult task of restoration; he revered the Dharma and secretly desired to revive it, yet did not dare speak of it openly.

Although the Buddha-dharma had fallen into decline for seven or eight years during the imperial reign, the prohibitions gradually relaxed. Families of devout faith were able to serve the śramaṇas in secret;
those who were particularly devoted even privately donned the dharma-robes to recite and study the scriptures. However, they were not permitted to practice openly within the capital.
Previously, the śramaṇa Tanyao possessed noble character and was personally honored by Emperor Gongzong.

When the Buddhist Dharma was suppressed, many śramaṇas sought audiences by returning to secular life, using their various skills to prove their worth. Tanyao, however, vowed to die rather than comply.
Although Emperor Gongzong personally exhorted him with repeated entreaties, he could not be dissuaded until finally he desisted. He secretly retained his dharma robes and ritual implements.
He was temporarily separated from his body; those who heard of it marveled at and revered him.
In the first year of the Xing’an era of Emperor Gaozong, an edict was issued to restore the Buddha-dharma, permitting the construction of one Buddhist monastery in each prefecture and commandery.
According to the "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor" in the *Weishu*, on the day of Yimao, the twelfth month of winter in the first year of Xing’an, the Buddha-dharma was first restored.
**Dharma:** According to the "Biographies of Śākyamuni and Laozi" (Shilaozhi), Emperor Gaozong ascended the throne and issued an edict stating:

"Now, those who act as emperors and kings must reverently serve the enlightened spirits and manifest the Way of Benevolence. As for those who can bestow kindness upon the people and provide benefit to all living beings, even if they belong to antiquity, their heroic deeds shall still be recorded.
Therefore, the Spring and Autumn Annals praise the rites of honoring the divine, and the Ritual Canon records meritorious achievements."

If even its [the Lesser Vehicle’s] lineage is thus worthy of being bestowed, how much more so is the Śākya Tathāgata, whose merit rescues the great trichiliocosm and whose grace flows throughout the realms of dust?

Those who equate it with the cycle of birth and death praise its profound insight; those who examine its words and meanings value its wondrous clarity. It assists the prohibitions and laws of royal governance and augments the virtuous nature of benevolence and wisdom.
It repels all manner of heterodoxies and expounds the realization of Perfect Enlightenment. Therefore, from previous dynasties down to the present, there has been none who has not revered it.
Furthermore, this is also that which our imperial house has long revered. Emperor Taizu, the Great Wu, opened up the frontier wilderness, and his virtuous bounty reached far and wide.
Śramaṇas and Daoist masters of pure conduct and sincerity, such as Huisi and others, were found everywhere, no matter how distant the place.
Those who respond to one another through wind-like integrity and righteousness are as numerous as a forest. Now, where mountains and seas are deep, strange creatures abound;
likewise, among those of wicked and licentious character, there are opportunities for false pretenses. Consequently, within lecture halls and monasteries, there have even been groups of the violent.

For this reason, the former dynasty took advantage of these flaws and executed those who were guilty. However, the officials misunderstood the imperial intent and prohibited all such activities entirely. Emperor Jingmu frequently lamented this matter.

However, as the state was beset by many affairs of war and governance, I had not yet been able to restore [the Buddhist institutions]. Now that I have inherited this great legacy and preside over the myriad realms, I contemplate carrying forward the will of my predecessors in order to flourish this Way.
I now decree that in all prefectures, commanderies, and counties, one Buddhist monastery (bifu) shall be established at each location where the populace resides.
They shall be permitted to employ their own resources for these purposes without fixed limits on expenditures. Furthermore, those who delight in the Dharma and wish to become śramaṇas...

As for the gates [of admission]: regardless of seniority or juniority, those born into noble families whose natures and conduct have long been sincere, who are free from all blemishes or impurities, and who are recognized by their local communities, are permitted to leave the household life.
From the large continents, fifty people each shall be admitted; from the small continents, forty people each. For those from distant prefectures, ten people each shall be admitted.
Each shall take charge of their respective region, which is sufficient to transform the wicked into the good and propagate the teachings of the Way.
The whole world followed this wind; morning did not suffice for evening’s needs. The monasteries that had been demolished in the past were restored once more.
The Buddha-images, sutras, and śāstras all regained their prominence. At that time, the śramaṇa Sengxian of the capital was of royal lineage from Kapiśī.

Having entered the Way in his youth, he traveled east to Liangcheng; when Liang fell, he proceeded to the capital. During the period when the Buddha-dharma was being suppressed, Sengxian feigned the practice of medical arts.
He returned to lay life; yet, he maintained his commitment to the Way without alteration. On the day the temple was restored, he immediately resumed the status of a śramaṇa.

His five companions were then personally tonsured by the Emperor, and Sengxian remained as the Superintendent of Monks (Dàodàntǒng). In that year, the Emperor issued a decree to the relevant authorities to fashion stone images modeled after his own person.
Once completed, black spots appeared on the faces and soles of the feet of each image, coinciding exactly with the corresponding marks on the Emperor’s own body.
[The Emperor] placed black dots [on his forehead]. Commentators considered this to have been moved by pure sincerity.
In the autumn of the first year of the Xingguang era, an imperial edict was issued to cast images of Śākyamuni for the five emperors, beginning with the Taizong.

According to the "Basic Annals of Gaozong" in the *Weishu*, this is not recorded; however, according to the "Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism," in the autumn of the first year of the Xingguang era, an edict was issued to the relevant authorities.
Within the Five-Storey Great Temple, five standing statues of Śākyamuni were cast for the five emperors beginning with the Founder;
each was sixteen feet in height, and a total of twenty-five thousand jin of red gold was used.
In the Tai’an era, a śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Siṃhala brought a Buddha image three times to the capital.
Furthermore, a Hu śramaṇa from Śākala presented a Buddha bowl and the footprints of the Buddha. According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Gaozong" in the *Weishu*, these are not recorded;

however, according to the "Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism," at the beginning of the Tai’an era, there were the Hu śramaṇas from the Kingdom of Siṃhala, Xiesheyiduo (Kṣemaṅkara) and Fudonantuo (Buddhanandi).

The five men, including Zhi Tandi, brought Buddha images three times to the capital. They all stated that they had traveled extensively through various kingdoms of the Western Regions, where they beheld the Buddha’s shadow-prints and the uṣṇīṣa.
The kings of those foreign lands, following one after another, had all dispatched artisans to copy his likeness.
Nothing could surpass what Nandika had created; viewed from more than ten paces away, it appeared brilliant, yet as one drew closer, it grew increasingly faint.
Furthermore, a śramaṇa from Khotan traveled to the capital, bringing with him the Buddha’s alms bowl and the traces of a miraculously manifested painted image.

In the [blank] year of the Peaceful Era, the Emperor received the śramaṇa Tanyao with the rites due to a teacher. Grain surrendered for entry into the Sengcao (Buddhist Office) was designated as *saṃghika* grain;
those who committed crimes were made *buddhavihāra* households. This is recorded in the "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor" (*Gaozu benji*) of the *Wei shu*.

Not recorded. According to the *Shilaozhi* (Record of Buddhism and Taoism): At the beginning of the Heping era, Shi Xian passed away, and Tanyao succeeded him, with his title changed to "General Overseer of Śramaṇas" (*shamen tong*).
Initially, in the year following the restoration of the Buddhist Dharma, Tanyao was summoned from Zhongshan to the capital. On the road, he encountered the Emperor, who came out to meet him;
the imperial horse stepped forward and bit Tanyao’s robe. At that time, it was considered that the horse had recognized a virtuous man. Later, the Emperor...

He was honored with the rites due to a teacher. Tanyao memorialized the Emperor, requesting that at Wuzhou Sai to the west of the capital city, five caves be excavated from the mountain cliff and one Buddha statue be carved for each, the tallest being seventy feet high and the next sixty feet high;

their carvings and decorations were so marvelous and magnificent as to surpass anything in the world at that time. Tanyao further petitioned that households from the conquered Qi state and other capable commoners be permitted to pay an annual tax of grain.

Sixty *hu*. That which was entered into the Sangha Office became *saṃghika* (monastic) household grain; it served as *saṃghika* grain. In years of famine, it was distributed to relieve the hungry populace.

Furthermore, the state requested that those among the people who had committed grave crimes, as well as government slaves, be made into *buddhavihāra* (Buddhist monastery) households to provide for the sweeping and sprinkling of various temples.
They were also required to cultivate lands and pay grain annually. Emperor Gaozong granted both these requests. Thereupon, the *saṃghika*...
Household-tax fields and temple-tax fields were established throughout the prefectures and commanderies.
Tanyao, moreover, together with the Indian śramaṇas Suchandhara and others, translated fourteen new sūtras.
There were also śramaṇas such as Daojin, Sengchao, and Facun, all of whom were renowned in their time and propagated various divergent teachings.
In the first year of the Huangxing era of Emperor Xianzu, he visited Shiku Temple.

He also founded Yongning Temple and constructed a seven-storied *stūpa* over three hundred feet high, and fashioned a standing statue of Śākyamuni forty-three feet tall. According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Xianzu" in the *Weishu*:
on the day of Dingyou, the eighth month of autumn in the first year of Huangxing, he traveled to Shiku Temple on Mount Wuzhou.

According to the "Biographies of Śākyamuni and Laozi" (Shilaozhi): Upon ascending the throne, Emperor Xianzu was exceptionally profound in his faith. Having perused various sūtras and śāstras, he took a particular liking to the works of Laozi and Zhuangzi.

He frequently summoned śramaṇas as well as scholars capable of discussing the ultimate principle (*yuan*) to deliberate upon the essentials of doctrine. This began at the end of the Tai’an era of Emperor Gaozong.
Liu Jun held a vegetarian feast at Zhongxing Temple in Danyang. There was a śramaṇa whose deportment was exceptionally distinguished;
when the entire assembly turned their gaze toward him, none could identify him. The śramaṇa Huiqu rose and questioned him; he replied that his name was Huiming.

When asked where he resided, he answered, "I have come from Tian'an Temple. Having finished speaking, he suddenly vanished. Emperor Jun and his ministers regarded this as a manifestation of the divine.
[Emperor] Gan changed the name of Zhongxing Temple to Tian’an Temple. Seven years after this, the Emperor ascended the throne, and the era was titled Tian’ian Year One.
In that year, Xue Andu, the Regional Inspector of Xuzhou under Liu Yu, first surrendered the city and its territory. The following year...
He possessed all the lands north of the Huai River. In the year of the High Ancestor’s birth, he established Yongning Monastery and constructed a seven-storied pagoda over three hundred feet high;
its foundation and structure were so vast and magnificent that it was the foremost in the world.
Furthermore, at Tiangong Monastery, he fashioned a standing image of Śākyamuni forty-three feet tall, using one hundred thousand *jin* of red gold and yellow gold.
Six hundred jin (according to the *Benji*, the year of the Emperor’s birth was the first year of Huangxing).
In the second year of Gaozu’s Yanxing era, an edict was issued stating that śramaṇas were not permitted to wander among the common people; those who traveled must do so with official documents.
Furthermore, an edict was issued stating that when constructing Buddhist temples, one must not exhaust one's wealth and property. [He also] [regarded] the Buddha image from Dongping Commandery.
It turned into the color of gold and copper. He issued a proclamation throughout the empire. According to the "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor" (*Gaozu benji*) in the *Weishu*:
in the fourth month of the summer of the second year of the Yanxing era, an edict was issued stating that śramaṇas were not permitted to leave their monasteries to wander among the common people;

those who did so were required to present official documents. According to the "History of Śākyamuni and Laozi" (*Shilao zhi*): when the High Ancestor ascended the throne, the Xianzu moved his residence to the Chongguang Palace in the Northern Garden. He [the Emperor] inspected...
He established the Xiyuan Temple and the Luye Monastery on the western mountains within the park, ten *li* to the right of Chongguang.

There were rock dwellings and meditation halls where Zen monks resided. At Yongning Temple, he established a great Dharma offering and ordained more than one hundred men and women from noble families as monks and nuns; the Emperor shaved their heads and bestowed upon them monastic robes. He ordered—
He cultivated the precepts of the Way to provide merit for his illustrious ancestors. In this month, he issued another edict to rebuild Ming Temple.

In the first year of the Tahe era, he visited Yongning Temple, where he established a vegetarian feast and listened to lectures. According to the "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor" in the *Wei Shu*, this is not recorded;

however, according to the "Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism," in the second month of the first year of the Tahe era, he visited Yongning Temple and established a vegetarian feast, followed by a general amnesty.

Regarding prisoners condemned to death, [the Emperor] granted them a three-month reprieve. He again visited Yongning Temple, where he established a religious assembly, performed ritual circumambulations (*caryā*), and listened to lectures.

He commanded the two secretaries of the Imperial Secretariat to engage in discussions on Buddhist doctrine with the monastics. He bestowed upon the monks robes and precious vessels in varying quantities.

Furthermore, at the site of the former military encampment of Emperor Taizu on Mount Fang, he constructed Siyuan Temple. From the Zhengguang era until this point, the temples within the capital city were newly...

There were approximately one hundred old [monasteries]. There were more than two thousand monks and nuns. Across all temples in the four directions, there were six thousand four hundred and seventy-eight, with seventy-seven thousand two hundred and fifty-eight monks and nuns.
