On the *ding-si* day of the first month of spring in the fourth year of the Taika era, the places where hawks and falcons were kept were abolished, and that land was established as the Hōtoku-ji Temple.
According to the *Wei Shu*, "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor" (*Gaozu benji*), it says...

According to the "Record of Buddhism and Daoism" (*Shilao zhi*), in the spring of the fourth year of Taihe, an edict was issued to establish the Hawk Masters (*ying-shi*) as the Hōtoku-ji Temple. According to the *Xu Wénxiàn Tōngkǎo*, Taihe...
In the fourth year [of the Taihe era], an imperial edict established the grounds of the Eagle-Master (Yǒngshī) as Bào德 Temple (Bàodé Sī) for the merit of Empress Dowager Wénmíng.

In the winter of the tenth year of Taihe, monks and nuns were selected and dispatched; those who were deemed coarse were ordered to return to lay life. According to the "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor" in the *Weishu*, this is not recorded.
However, according to the "Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism," in the winter of the tenth year of Taihe, there was a reference to the second year of Yánxīng.

In the fourth month of summer, an edict was issued stating: "Bhikṣus who do not remain in monasteries but wander through villages and associate with the wicked and crafty for years on end must be dealt with.
Let the people of the countryside form groups of five to provide mutual security, ensuring that they do not harbor unregistered monks.

Conduct a thorough investigation; those found shall be sent to the prefectures and commanderies. Those residing within the capital districts shall be sent to the relevant administrative office. However, if it is for the sake of the Three Jewels..."

Regarding those who travel to instruct and transform the people: those traveling outside [the capital] must carry official documents from the *weina* (administrative head) of the prefecture or commandery;

those remaining at the capital must carry sealed warrants from the *duweina* (head of the central administration). Only then may they proceed. Those who violate this shall be punished. Furthermore, an edict was issued stating:

"Whether among those within or without [the court], when individuals undertake meritorious works or establish monasteries that are lofty, spacious, prominent, and vast, these are sufficient to glorify and exalt the supreme teaching. However..."

Those who lack wisdom each vie with one another for loftiness; the poor and the rich compete with one another, exhausting their wealth and property, striving only to ensure that [their monuments] are high and vast.

They inflict injury and kill insects and all classes of living beings. Yet they believe that if they can simply apply themselves with meticulous care to piling up earth or gathering sand, blessings will accrue to them in imperishable measure.
I desire to establish the causes for merit, yet I was unaware of the karma that harms living beings. As the parent of the people, it is my duty to nourish them with compassion.

From this day forward, I shall prohibit all such acts. Furthermore, the Emperor issued an edict stating: "When sincerity is manifest, its response reaches far; when conduct is earnest, its influence is profound.
Throughout history, we have observed auspicious omens from previous ages, such as birds and beasts changing their colors and plants and trees altering their natures. [In] the east of Jizhou..."
The sacred image from Pingjun emitted a radiant glow, transforming into the color of gilded bronze. Such an extraordinary event was unprecedented in antiquity;

it served to cause the wondrous Dharma to flourish and prosper, a principle most appropriate for the present age. The relevant authorities, together with the *Sramana-tong* (Director of Monks) Tanyao, ordered the provincial government to transport the image to the capital, so that both monastics and laypeople might behold its true form (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This was proclaimed throughout the empire so that all might hear and know of it.
In the first year of the Chengming era, [the Emperor] visited Yongning Temple and ordained over one hundred monks and nuns. He further issued an edict to establish Jianming Temple.

According to the "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor" in the *Weishu*: on the *xinwei* day of the tenth month in the winter of the first year of Chengming, the imperial carriage visited Jianming Buddhist Temple and granted a general amnesty to criminals.
According to the "Treatise on Śākyamuni and Laozi": in the eighth month of the first year of Chengming, the High...

The Grand Councilor submitted a memorial stating that he had previously received an imperial decree to compile the registers. Initially, ignorant commoners had falsely claimed to have entered the Way [to become monks or nuns] in order to evade tax obligations.
Those monks and nuns who lacked official registration were dismissed and compelled to return to lay life. Furthermore, by imperial command, the monks and nuns were to be scrutinized;

the abbots (*vihārasvāmin*) and chant-leaders (*karmadāna*) of each temple were to conduct a thorough investigation. Those among them whose spiritual practice was diligent and exemplary were permitted to remain in the religious life to continue their cultivation.

As for all those who were coarse [in conduct], whether they possessed official registration or not, they were all dismissed and returned to the status of commoners. An edict was issued ordering that those from various provinces who had returned to lay life be selected and dispatched accordingly.
In total, one thousand three hundred and twenty-seven monks and nuns were involved; this was submitted to the throne and approved.
In the sixteenth year of the Taihe era, an imperial edict was issued permitting the ordination of monks and nuns on the eighth day of the fourth month and the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
According to the "Basic Annals" (Benji) of Emperor Gaozu in the *Weishu*, this is not recorded;

however, according to the "Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism" (Shilozhi), the edict of the sixteenth year of Taihe permitted one hundred persons to be ordained as monks and nuns in the Tai Commandery on the eighth day of the fourth month and the fifteenth day of the seventh month.
Fifty persons from the Central Provinces and twenty from the Lower Provinces were established as the standard quota, and this was recorded in the Imperial Decrees.

In the seventeenth year of the Taihe era, an edict was issued to establish monastic regulations consisting of forty-seven articles. According to the "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor" in the *Weishu*, these are not recorded;
however, according to the "Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism," it says as follows.
In the twentieth year of the Taihe era, an imperial edict was issued permitting the master Zhun to wail for the deceased monk outside the gate.
Furthermore, an edict was issued to establish Shaolin Temple for the śramaṇa Buddhabhadra. According to the *Weishu*, "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor," this is not recorded;

however, according to the "Treatise on Buddhism and Taoism," in the fourth month of the nineteenth year of Taihe, the Emperor visited Baitasi Temple in Xuzhou and, turning to address the various princes and [officials], said:
The Emperor addressed the officials, saying: "In this monastery resides the renowned monk Dharma Master Sengsong, who received the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* from Kumārajīva and has propagated it here.
Later, he transmitted it to Dharma Master Fayuan, and Dharma Master Fayuan transmitted it to the two Dharma Masters Deng and Ji.

Whenever I study the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, I find it capable of resolving the deep-seated attachments of men; therefore, I have come to this monastery. At that time, the śramaṇa Daodeng was of refined character...

There was a certain Master Ye, who was highly esteemed by the High Ancestor (Gaozu) and constantly attended his lectures and discussions. Once, while conversing with the Emperor at night within the inner palace, they both saw a ghost together.
He passed away twenty years later; the High Ancestor mourned him deeply and issued an edict granting one thousand bolts of silk as a funeral offering.
Furthermore, he provided a vegetarian feast for the entire monastic community and ordered that rites be performed in the capital for seven days.

He also issued an edict stating: "My teacher, Dharma Master Deng, has suddenly passed away. My grief and anguish are so crushing that I cannot restrain myself. As I am currently attending to the funeral arrangements with medicinal care, I am unable to attend immediately;
therefore, following my teacher’s own instructions, I shall weep outside the gates and wear plain white mourning garments. There was also a śramaṇa from the Western Regions named... [text ends]

Bhadra possessed the path and its practice, and was held in deep reverence and faith by the High Ancestor (Emperor Xiaowen). By imperial decree, Shaolin Monastery was established on the northern slopes of Mount Shaoshi for him to reside in, and he was provided with clothing and provisions from the public treasury.
In the twenty-first year of the Tahe era, an imperial edict was issued to construct a three-storied *stūpa* at the site of the former hall where the monk Kumārajīva had resided.
Furthermore, the Emperor ordered that his son be sought out and reported to him. In this same year, the Jianfu Bureau (Jianfucuo) was renamed the Zhaoyuan Bureau;

this is recorded in the "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor" (*Gaozu benji*) of the *Weishu*. According to the "Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism" (*Shilaozhi*), the Tahe twenty-first year corresponds to [497 CE].

In the fifth month, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "Dharma Master Kumārajīva may be said to have transcended the divine; his talent surpassed the five virtues and his will entered the four practices.
Although the monastery where he once resided still has its remaining grounds, I admire and delight in his cultivated legacy, my profound affection extending both near and far.

You should construct a three-storied stupa at the site of his former hall. Furthermore, seeing how he was oppressed by the cruel and tyrannical, he sacrificed his body for the sake of the Way; having temporarily conformed to worldly ways..."
According to ritual propriety, he ought to have a successor; an investigation should be conducted to report this, so that he may be accorded due recognition and reception.
According to the *Xu Wénxiàn Tōngkǎo*, in this year, the Jianfu Office was renamed the Zhaoyuan, with its official staff fully established to adjudicate monastic affairs.

In the year □□□, Prince Taixing of Jingzhao requested to become a śramaṇa. An imperial edict was issued to the Crown Prince to perform the tonsure ceremony for him on the eighth day of the fourth month.
According to the *Weishu*, "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor," this is not recorded.
According to the biography of Prince Taixing of Jingzhao: initially, when Taixing fell ill, he invited various śramaṇas to perform religious rites; all his assets and wealth—[one].
At that time, he gave alms to those who begged for it so they might recover from their illnesses; this was called the "Scattered-Birth" (Sànshēng) fast.

After the fast, when the monks had all dispersed, there was a śramaṇa who happened to arrive and asked for the leftovers from the meal. Tàixī ridiculed him, saying, "The fast-food is already exhausted;
there is nothing left but wine and meat. The śramaṇa replied, "I can eat those as well. Thereupon, [Tàixī] brought out one *dǒu* of wine and a pair of sheep's feet, which the śramaṇa ate entirely.

He still felt as though he were not yet satiated. After the master had taken his leave, both the wine and the meat remained where they were; yet when he went out the door to pursue him, he could see no one.
Taixing then made a vow before the Buddha: "The teacher from earlier must surely not be an ordinary person.

If this illness is cured, I shall renounce my royal rank and enter the Way. Before long, he recovered. He then requested to become a śramaṇa, and after submitting more than ten petitions, he was finally granted permission.

This was granted. At that time, the High Ancestor was on campaign in the south. He issued an edict to the Crown Prince to have [the monk] tonsured on the eighth day of the fourth month and bestowed two thousand bolts of silk as an offering.

In the □□□ year, the Hall of the Seven Factors of Enlightenment was constructed as a chamber for the four *dhyānas*. According to the "Basic Annals of the High Ancestor" in the *Wei Shu*, this is not recorded.
According to the *Fofa Jintang Bian*, Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty constantly exercised compassion and frequently practiced faith and renunciation.
Reciting the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* with his mouth and maintaining pure precepts with his body, he established a hall for the seven factors of enlightenment and a chamber for the four dhyānas.

In the [blank] year of the Jingming era of Emperor Shizong, an imperial edict was issued to construct two grottoes at Mount Yi’que, south of the cave, modeled after the stone caves of Lingyan Monastery in the capital of Dai (Datong), in honor of the High Ancestor, Empress Dowager Wenzhao. (According to the *Weishu*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizong").

Record: Not recorded. According to the *Shilaozhi* (History of Buddhism and Daoism): At the beginning of the Jingming era, Emperor Xiaowen issued an edict to Bai Zheng, the Grand Chamberlain for the Inner Palace, to construct two stone grottoes at Mount Yique south of Luoyang, modeled after the stone caves of Lingyan Temple in the capital, for the sake of Empress Dowager Wenzhao, the late High Ancestor’s consort.
When first constructed, the summit of the grottoes was three hundred and ten feet above the ground.
In the second year of the Zhengshi era, construction first began by excavating the mountain for twenty-three *zhang*.

When Grand Chamberlain Wang Zhi deemed the excavation too high and difficult to complete due to the great expenditure of labor, he submitted a memorial requesting that it be moved downward to a level spot one hundred *chi* from the ground,
measuring one hundred forty *chi* from south to north.
On the day of Gengyin, the fourth month of summer in the fourth year of the Jingming era, the kingdom of South India presented a tooth of a Pratyekabuddha.
According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizong" in the *Weishu*, it says... [and so forth].
In the [blank] year of the Zhengshi era, an imperial edict was issued for Sun Huiwei to lecture on Buddhist scriptures within the palace precincts at night.

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizong" in the *Wei Shu*, this is not recorded; however, according to the biography of Sun Huiwei, Huiwei originally had the single-character name Wei. During the Zhengshi period...

He served as a Lecturer within the inner palace, where he discussed Buddhist scriptures at night. His views were so well-suited to the Emperor’s intentions that an edict was issued to show him special favor, and he was titled Dharma Master Huiwei.

In the first year of the Yongping era, an edict was issued stating: "Monks who commit crimes such as murder shall be judged according to secular law; all other offenses shall be handed over [to the monastic authorities]."

Regarding "Zhao Yuanshao": According to the *Weishu*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizong," this name is not recorded. However, according to the "Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism" (*Shilaozhi*), prior to this, the Jianfu Office (*Jianfucuo*) was established;

it was subsequently renamed the Zhaoyuan Office (*Zhaoyuancuo*), which possessed a full complement of subordinate officials to adjudicate monastic affairs during the time of the High Ancestor (Emperor Xiaowen).

The śramaṇas Dao-shun, Hui-jue, Seng-yi, Hui-ji, Seng-fan, Dao-bing, Hui-du, Zhi-dan, Seng-xian, Seng-yi, and Seng-li were all esteemed for their profound understanding of the Dharma and their conduct.
In the autumn of the first year of Yongping, during the reign of Emperor Shizong, an imperial edict was issued stating:

"Since the laity and the clergy differ, their laws and regulations are likewise distinct; thus, the teachings of the Way manifest through mutual illumination, and prohibitions and exhortations each have their respective roles."
This is appropriate. From this day forward, if members of the Sangha commit offenses such as murder or worse, they shall continue to be judged according to secular law.
For all other offenses, they shall be entirely entrusted to Zhao Yuan to be adjudicated according to the internal monastic codes and regulations.
In the winter of the second year of Yongping, the Emperor lectured on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra for the monks and court officials.
The Head of the Śramaṇas, Huishen, requested that laws and prohibitions be established for the monks and nuns; the Emperor granted this.

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizong" in the *Weishu*, on the day of Jichou, the eleventh month of winter in the second year of Yongping, the Emperor lectured on the [Vimalakīrti Sūtra] at the Shiqian Hall for the various monks and court officials.

Regarding the *Mojie jing* (Vimalakīrti Sūtra): according to the *Shilao zhi* (Record of Buddhism and Taoism), in the winter of the second year, the Superintendent of Śramaṇas, Huishen, submitted a memorial stating that the monastics—both monks and nuns—are vast in number;

pure and turbid elements flow together, they do not follow the prohibitive scriptures, and there is no distinction between the refined and the coarse. He therefore proposed the establishment of Dharma Masters of Instruction and Discipline.

The assembly deliberated and established regulations: that the *vinaya-dhara*, the *sthavira*, and the *vihāra-svāmin* of all provinces, prefectures, and districts must each cause themselves to cultivate the precepts and strictly abide by internal prohibitions.

Those who do not understand the Vinaya shall be removed from their positions. Furthermore, those who have left the household life must not violate the law or accumulate the eight kinds of impure goods;
however, regarding the provisions of the Sūtras and Vinaya, there are specific rules for what is permitted and what is prohibited. According to the Vinaya, [the use of] carts and oxen...

Lascivious persons and impure objects must not be privately possessed by oneself. Only those who are aged or infirm, sixty years of age or older, are permitted to possess a single vehicle [of transport].
Furthermore, it has recently come to pass that monks and nuns, on account of the Three Jewels, have lent out private property or sought donations beyond the borders of their own prefectures.

Moreover, those who have left the household life have abandoned worldly attachments; originally, there were no funeral rites for them. One should not abandon the Way to conform to secular customs. As for their fathers...
There are three types of masters for a mother. Upon hearing of her death from afar, one may weep for three days; if she was present before one's eyes, the limit is seven days.
There are those who feel uneasy staying in monasteries and instead wander among the common people, creating disorder and committing transgressions—all of which stems from such individuals.

Should anyone commit such offenses, they shall be stripped of their robes and returned to the status of a layperson. As for those wishing to construct monasteries, the number of monks must be limited to fifty or more; only upon reporting this to the authorities and receiving permission may construction proceed.
If anyone should arbitrarily take charge [of such matters], they shall be punished for violating an imperial decree. The monastic community of that temple shall be banished to another province.
According to the laws for monks and nuns, they must not be employed by laypeople; if there are any who violate this, they shall be returned to their original jurisdictions.

As for foreign monks and nuns who came to seek refuge and conversion, those who were sought out for their diligent examination and possessed virtuous conduct in accordance with the Tripitaka were permitted to remain.

If they lacked virtuous conduct, they were to be sent back to their own countries; if they did not depart, they were to be punished according to these monastic regulations. The imperial edict followed this proposal.

In the third year of Yongping, the jade statue was welcomed and enshrined at Baode Temple on the banks of the Luo River. According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizong" in the *Weishu*, this is not recorded;
however, according to the "Monograph on Buddhism and Taoism," previously, a sixteen-foot statue made of white jade (*mín*) had been fashioned at Mount Jing in Hengnong.
In the winter of the third year of Yongping, it was welcomed and enshrined at Baode Temple on the banks of the Luo River, where Emperor Shizong personally went to observe it.
Respectfully submitted.

In the summer of the fourth year of Yongping, an imperial edict was issued stating that the *saṃgha-ṛṣi* (monastic community) grain shall not be left solely to the supervision of the *vina* (steward), but that the Prefectural Governors (*cishi*) must jointly oversee and audit it.
Furthermore, an edict was issued dispatching the *saṃgha-ṛṣi* households, including Zhao Gouzi and others, back to their native villages. [Based on] the *Weishu*, Shizong [era].
The Basic Annals do not record this. According to the "Treatise on Buddhism and Taoism," in the summer of the fourth year of the Yongping era, an imperial edict stated:

"The grain of the Saṃgha is originally intended for relief and charity. It shall be lent out in years of scarcity and collected back in years of abundance; monastics and nuns in the mountains and forests shall be provided for from these distributions."
When the people were in distress and destitution, he would immediately provide relief for them. However, the officials in charge sought profit for themselves, scheming to take excessive interest.
When it came to collecting the debts, they took no account of floods or droughts; sometimes the repayment of interest exceeded the principal, and sometimes they altered the original contracts.

They exploited the poor and lowly without limit, causing the common people to sigh in bitter resentment as the years passed. This is not the way to show compassion for those in dire straits, nor is it the path of noble tradition.
This is the fundamental intent of compassionate rescue. From now on, matters shall not be left solely to the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) and the *duwei* (Commandant).

The Provincial Governors (*cishi*) must jointly oversee and investigate these affairs. The Secretaries-General (*shangshu*) shall inspect all locations where the *saṃghika* (monastic community) holds grain;

they shall list the original quantities for each prefecture, along with details regarding income and expenditure, surplus and interest, the amount of relief distributed, the dates and terms of loans and repayments, and the current status of outstanding debts. [Report this] to the Emperor.

The *Dai lu ji* (Records of the Platform) states: If the interest collected exceeds the principal, or if the original bond has been altered or rewritten, one shall exempt them according to the Vinaya and must not further demand payment.
If there are private debts that have been transferred to repay the Sangha, these shall be treated as gifts to the people and may not be reclaimed.

In the future, when making loans, the poor must be prioritized first; the regulations for debt collection shall strictly conform to the established precedents. Wealthy households shall not be permitted to arbitrarily [seize property].

[The Emperor] granted [the request]. However, as exemptions were still being claimed excessively and indiscriminately, they were to be punished according to the law. Furthermore, Gao Zhao, the Director of the Imperial Secretariat, submitted a memorial stating:

"I have respectfully examined the case of the former Head of the Śramaṇas, Tan-di. In the first year of the Chengming era, he petitioned that two hundred households of military families from Liangzhou, including Zhao Gouzi and others, be designated as *saṃghika* (monastic) households.
He established a quota for the accumulation of grain to provide relief during years of famine, regardless of whether the recipients were monastics or laypeople. All [of these matters]...
This was done to provide relief through almsgiving. Furthermore, according to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the "monastic households" (*saṃgha-ku*) may not be assigned exclusively to a single temple.
Yet, the General Steward (Duweina) Saṃghasīma and Saṃghapriya, in their advancement, violated the imperial decree, and in their retreat, contravened the internal Dharma.

Acting arbitrarily and following their own whims, they submitted petitions to forcibly summon [the monks], causing sighs of resentment to fill the walkways. Consequently, people abandoned their children, harmed their lives, hanged themselves, drowned, and so forth—five [such cases].

With more than ten people, how could this be considered an act of reverently praising Your Majesty’s sagely wisdom and compassionate nurturing? It would deeply betray Your Majesty’s heart of taking refuge [in the Dharma].
Consequently, these individuals would be forced to wail and weep in the streets and alleys, with no one to whom they could appeal.

To the point where white feathers are pierced through their ears and they line up to lodge grievances at the palace gates—even ordinary people would feel deep sorrow for such a sight; how much more so for those of a compassionate nature, who could possibly remain indifferent to it?
Please listen, Mr. Gou and the others. We shall return the official grain quotas to the provinces. In these years of scarcity, let it be used to provide for the poor and widowed;

should there be unforeseen emergencies, let it serve as provisions for defending the borders. As for Xian and the others, who have contravened the imperial intent and violated the laws by submitting erroneous reports, we request that their offenses be handed over to the Ministry of Justice.
The matter was adjudicated according to the monastic code. An imperial edict stated: "As for Xian and the others, they shall be granted special clemency; as for the rest, let it be as reported.
In the [blank] year of the Yanchang era, the number of monasteries for monks and nuns throughout the realm reached thirteen thousand seven hundred and twenty-seven.

According to the *Shi-lao-zhi* (Account of Buddhism and Taoism) in the *Wei Shu*, this is not recorded in the Basic Annals of Emperor Shizong; however, the *Shi-lao-zhi* notes that Emperor Shizong was deeply devoted to [Buddhism].

Regarding Buddhist principles, the Emperor personally lectured on sutras and treatises within the inner palace every year, gathering eminent monks from all quarters to clarify their essential meanings.
The śramaṇas compiled these records as the "Inner Daily Annals. As the sovereign held them in such high esteem, those below him increasingly looked up to and revered them.
By the time of the Yanchang era, there were a total of 13,727 monasteries for monks and nuns throughout the provinces and military districts of the realm.
His followers were exceedingly numerous.
In the [blank] year of the Yanchang era, Empress Dowager Ling, because Li Zang had stated that Buddhism was a teaching of ghosts, punished him with a fine of one *jin* of gold.
(Note: This is not recorded in the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizong" in the *Wei Shu*. According to the biography of Li Xiaobo, Li Zang’s courtesy name was Juruo.)
He was well-versed in historical traditions and possessed considerable literary talent. His temperament was bold and unrestrained, and he was a prominent figure of his time.

Toward the end of the Yanchang era, the Grand Master (Situ) Xian served as a Military Aide (Xing canjun), and the Grand Master’s Chief Assistant Secretary (Chang jian zhubu) and Grand Preceptor (Taishi) Gao Yangwang Yong submitted a memorial recommending Zhang.
He served as the Rectifier of the Main Registrar for his friend. At that time, many among the people were abandoning their households to become śramaṇas.

Zǎng submitted a memorial stating: "Ritual is used to instruct the world, and the Dharma guides those to come. Since their applications differ, their respective domains are also distinct. Thus, regarding the three thousand offenses..."

There is no greater unfiliality than this; among the gravities of unfiliality, none exceeds the severance of ancestral sacrifices. Thus, as for the sin of severing the sacrifices, there is nothing more severe.
How could one lightly indulge sentiments that violate the rites and instead give free rein to an inclination toward the Dharma?
Even if the Buddhist path were to permit it, it should not be so; even if it were permitted, it must still be regulated by the rites. One’s own person and kin—
To abandon one’s family and sever the duty of filial support is contrary to human nature and even more so to the sentiments of ritual propriety (*li*).

It extinguishes the great social relations and, moreover, omits the registration of subjects under the sovereign. While failing to fulfill the rites of the present age, one seeks benefits for the future.

Confucius said, "If you do not know life, how can you know death? These words are ultimate and sufficiently comprehensive. How could one discard such a magnificent governance to follow the ways of ghosts?

Is this not a teaching? Furthermore, the southern regions are currently unsettled, and various levies remain burdensome. The sentiments of the common people are now largely inclined toward evading service;

if we were to permit it again, I fear they would abandon filial piety and compassion, with households everywhere becoming *śramaṇas*. [This was stated by] the Metropolitan Superintendent Sengxian and others.
Fen [accused] Sengzhang of the words spoken by the ghost, claiming that Zhang was slandering the Buddha-dharma. He wept as he petitioned Empress Dowager Ling, who rebuked him.
Zhang defended himself, saying: "I secretly desire to clarify the Buddha-dharma so that both monastics and laity may attain thorough understanding;

it was not my intention to reject true learning or recklessly engage in slander. Furthermore, the names of ghosts and spirits have all been titles used to reach the numinous since the hundred generations."

The orthodox classics state that the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors were all designated as "ghosts" (*gui*). Heaven and Earth are called "spirits" (*shen*) and "deities" (*qi*); when a person dies, they are called a "ghost. The *I Ching* says:
"Know the nature and manifestations of ghosts and spirits. Even the Duke of Zhou, in his own praise, said: "I am able to serve ghosts and spirits. The *Book of Rites* says: [omitted].

"In the realm of light there are rites and music; in the realm of mystery there are ghosts and spirits. Thus, that which pertains to the light is called the 'Majestic Way' (Tangdang), while that which pertains to the mystery is called the 'Teaching of Ghosts' (Guishiao).
It is neither of heaven nor of earth, but originates fundamentally from humanity. To respond to the age and guide the customs, its way is profound and hidden;

it is therefore named 'Ghost. I consider this not to be slander. Furthermore, as for those whose minds are without evil and who take the Buddha-way as their teaching, they may truly be described as follows:"
This merely opens the gateway to all manner of wonders. Although Empress Dowager Ling knew that Zang’s words were correct, she could not avoid the sentiments of Xian and the others;
she alone punished Zang with a fine of one *jin* of gold.
In the first year of the Xiping era of Emperor Suzong, an imperial edict was issued dispatching the śramaṇa Huisheng as an envoy to the Western Regions to collect sūtras and vinaya texts.

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Suzong" in the *Weishu*, this is not recorded; however, according to the "Treatise on Buddhism and Taoism," in the first year of the Xiping era, an edict was issued dispatching the śramaṇa Huisheng as an envoy to the Western Regions to collect various sūtras and vinaya texts.
In the winter of the third year of the Zhengguang era, he returned to the capital with what he had obtained.
One hundred and seventy scriptures and treatises were in circulation at that time.

In the second year of the Xiping era, Empress Dowager Ling issued an edict stating that the ordination of monks must not indiscriminately include those who do not qualify as such, and that monks and nuns may not ordain privately;
those who violate this shall be charged with disobeying the imperial decree. According to the *Weishu*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Suzong," the second year of the Xiping era...
On the day of Yimao in the fourth month of summer, the Empress Dowager visited the Stone Cave Temple at Ique. She returned to the palace on that same day.
According to the *Shilaozhi* (Record of Buddhism and Taoism), in the spring of the second year of the Xiping era, Empress Dowager Ling issued an edict stating:

"Regarding the annual quota for ordaining monks, those from prefectures with a limit of three hundred persons shall have three hundred individuals released and sent forth ten days prior [to the deadline]; as for those from intermediate prefectures..."

Two hundred persons from the large prefectures and one hundred from the small prefectures shall be selected. The Prefectural Governor and the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) shall personally select and refine those to fill the quota.

If there are no individuals of refined conduct, no indiscriminate recruitment shall be permitted. If those who are unworthy are selected, the Prefectural Governor shall be held primarily responsible and shall be charged with violating the Imperial decree.

The Prefectural Governor, the County Magistrate, their subordinate officials, and the various ranks of clerical staff shall be held jointly liable. The *tong* (superintendent) and the *weina* (rector) shall be transferred to a different province more than five hundred li away to serve as monks.
From this day forward, no slaves shall be permitted to leave the household life. Neither the various princes nor those of noble rank shall arbitrarily submit petitions on this matter;
any who violate this decree shall be charged with disobeying imperial edicts. As for monks and nuns who arbitrarily ordain the slaves of others:

Furthermore, those who have moved more than five hundred *li* away to become monks—whether as monks or nuns—and who frequently take in the children of their own relatives or the slaves of others, privately ordaining them as disciples once they reach adulthood:
from now on, this shall be prohibited. Those who violate this shall be laicized; the children they have taken in shall be returned to their original monasteries.

A monastery head may permit only one such person to remain, provided they move five hundred *li* away from the monastery, or two persons if they move one thousand *li* away. As for monks who have privately ordained [disciples], [they shall be dealt with accordingly].

In all cases, because the three village elders were not at fault, many instances of concealment and leniency occurred. From now on, if there is a single person who has been privately ordained, it shall be treated as a violation of imperial decree.

The village elder shall be held primarily responsible; the heads of the hamlets and neighborhoods shall each be demoted by one degree. If fifteen such persons are found within a county, [the magistrate shall be punished].

If there were thirty persons in a commandery, or thirty persons in a prefecture or military garrison, the official in charge was to be dismissed from office. His subordinates and clerks were to be held jointly liable according to their respective ranks.

Those who had been privately ordained were to be conscripted for low-level labor within their respective prefectures. At that time, however, the legal prohibitions were lax, and the authorities were unable to maintain strict discipline.
In the first year of the Xiping era, the Yongning Temple was constructed within the city, and a Buddhist stupa was erected, reaching a height of over forty *zhang*.

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Suzong" in the *Weishu*, this is not recorded; however, according to the "Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism," during the Xiping era of Emperor Suzong, the Yongning Temple was built within the city to the west of the Grand Altar (Dashi).
Empress Ling personally led the hundred officials to mark out the foundation and erect the central pillar (*śāla*).
The Buddhist temple (buddhastūpa) has nine stories and is over forty zhang in height; the expenses for its construction were beyond calculation.
The Buddhist temple of Jingming Temple is also among its peers. As for official and private monasteries and pagodas, their number is very great.
In the summer of the first year of the Shengui era, an imperial edict was issued to establish a *zhai* (fasting retreat) for Hu Guozhen and to permit people to leave the household life.

In the winter, Empress Dowager was buried at Beimang according to the rites for a *ni* (nun). Prince Cheng, Rencheng Wang Chen, submitted a memorial requesting a prohibition against building monasteries within the city walls, stipulating that no monastery with fewer than fifty monks may be newly constructed.
According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Suzong" in the *Weishu*, this occurred in the autumn of the first year of the Shengui era.

On the *wùshēn* day of the ninth month, Empress Dowager Gao passed away at Yaoguang Palace. On the *dīngmǎo* day of the tenth month of winter, she was buried at Beimang according to the rites for a *bhikṣuṇī*.

According to the "Records of Śākyamuni and Laozi" (*Shìlǎozhì*), in the winter of the first year, Rencheng Prince Cheng, Minister of Works and Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs, submitted a memorial stating:
"Looking back upon the High Ancestor, who established the capital at Song and Chan, his prognostication of the dynasty’s longevity was far-reaching, encompassing all considerations..."
From beginning to end, the regulations were comprehensive enough to encompass both gods and men. The Creator opened the auspicious signs and transmitted them for ten thousand generations.

Thus, the regulations for the capital city stated: "Within the city walls, space shall be reserved only for the site of Yongning Temple; within the outer walls, only one nunnery shall be permitted; all other [buildings] must be located outside the city and its suburbs.

This was intended to ensure that these regulations be followed forever, so that no one would dare overstep their boundaries. However, at the beginning of the Jingming era, there were slight violations.

Therefore, the World-Honored Emperor (Emperor Gaozu) revered and cultivated the will of his predecessors, and thus issued a clarifying decree: no stupas or monastic dwellings for monks and nuns were to be constructed within the city walls.
This was intended to eliminate their expectations and aspirations. Did the two Emperors of the Wen-Wu era not love and esteem the Buddha-dharma?

It was simply because the paths of the clergy and the laity have distinct destinations, and it was deemed logically improper for them to be confused with one another. However, the laity were dazzled by hollow reputations, while the monks greedily coveted substantial emoluments.
Despite the explicit prohibitions, people continued to build temples in defiance. In the third year of the Zhengshi era, the Superintendent of Śramaṇas, Huishen, violated the Jingming prohibitions;

he argued that since the temples were already completed, they could not bear to be demolished. He requested that from this time forward, no further construction be permitted, while the previous edicts be relaxed and the current statutes suppressed.
Although the Emperor granted his request with a prior decree, it was subsequently set aside and never implemented. Later—

People came to seek private audiences with increasing frequency, leading to a race for favor. In the second year of the Yongping era, Daoshen and others established further regulations, petitioning that:
"From now on, those wishing to construct a monastery shall be restricted to those with fifty or more monks; only upon such notification shall construction be permitted.

Should anyone establish one without authorization, they shall be punished according to secular law for violating an imperial edict, and the monastic community of that temple shall be banished to a foreign province. This has been the case for some ten years past.
In recent years, private monasteries have flourished, and reports of those being exiled for their offenses have been silent and unheard of.

Is this not because, although the imperial statutes are clear, people rely on their own fortune to collectively violate them; and although the monastic regulations are established in vain, they disregard them out of regard for personal gain?

To act neither as a layperson nor as a practitioner, yet strive only to undermine the Dharma—how can such insatiability ever reach its limit? Indeed, the traces of study are profound and subtle, beyond what a superficial consciousness can discern. The Origin... [text ends]
The gates of the Way are vast and silent; how could brief words suffice to exhaustively explore them? Yet, to enter purity beyond the mundane world is what the Daoists prioritize first.

When merit and conditions are profound and hidden, one does not prize ostentatious withdrawal. If one can simply be sincere and faithful, then even a child gathering sand can surpass the construction of a *bodhimaṇḍa*, and Cunda’s modest offering was sufficient to be presented at the Twin Trees.
Why must one indulge in theft and plunder to provide for the construction of temples and monasteries? This is merely [the way of] the common people...
This is a great misfortune rather than a blessing for the state. Yet, in recent days, private constructions have frequently numbered in the hundreds.

Some individuals have seized public land to plant their own private merit, while others, having obtained permission to build temples, have exceeded their limits and expanded their structures beyond regulation. Such acts of deception and fraud cannot be merely counted by the dozens.

As Your Servant is of inferior talent, I truly feel unworthy of overseeing these public works; nevertheless, I shall respectfully adhere to established regulations and exercise my authority in this matter. All that pertains to...

Having consulted ancient precedents and scrutinized maps and records, I have dispatched Lu Chang, the Commandant of the Prefecture, to assist Cui Xiaofen in conducting a comprehensive inventory of monasteries throughout the capital city and its surrounding districts. There are five hundred such establishments;

however, this count does not include those located on open ground where pagodas and halls have yet to be erected. That the people show such disregard for the law has reached this extreme since the relocation of the capital.
It has been more than twenty-four years since then. Monasteries have encroached upon private residences, taking up one-third of the land.

When the High Ancestor (Emperor Wu of Liang) established his regulations, he did not merely wish to ensure that the monastic and secular paths remained distinct; he also sought to prevent potential evils through profound foresight.

Emperor Xiaowen followed this precedent, yet he did not prohibit the construction of merit-seeking temples; rather, his aim was to block them before they could sprout. Today, Buddhist monasteries exist everywhere, sometimes filling entire cities.
Within these towns, there were sometimes butcher shops overflowing with the slaughter of living creatures, or three or five young monks sharing a single temple.

The chanting of the *brahmanas* and the cries of the butchers resounded together from adjoining eaves; images and stupas were enveloped in stench, and the spiritual nature was submerged in carnal desires.

The true and the false lived in confusion, and those who came and went were a chaotic jumble. The local officials took no action because it was their habitual practice, and the monastic authorities did not enforce regulations against it.
Question: Regarding the defilement of true practice and the corruption of the monastic community—where the fragrant and the putrid are placed in the same vessel—is this not indeed extreme?
In the past, during the Northern Dynasties, there was the plot of Fashou; recently, in Jizhou, the catastrophe of the Mahāyāna occurred.

In both cases, they initially feigned the divine teachings to delude the minds of the masses, and ultimately employed deceit and fraud to indulge their private perversity. As for the regulations of the Taihe era, they were based on the Dharma...

Xiu and Du Yuan [petitioned] during the Jingming era, fearing that the Mahāyāna would fall into disorder; only then did they realize how profoundly the sagely founders had anticipated and restrained such developments.

When the first hoarfrost appears, one must be wary of the solid ice to come; one cannot fail to exercise caution. In the past, when the Tathāgata expounded the teachings, he mostly relied upon mountains and forests.
Now these monks are attached to cities and towns; how could cramped and narrow places be suitable for their practice? Such frivolous clamor must...
In the abode where one dwells in meditation, the mind ought to be guided by the beneficial; otherwise, it cannot be restrained of its own accord.
Those who reside there have already lost their truth, while those who construct them may diminish their merit. Such individuals are the dregs of the Śākya teachings and vermin within the Dharma;

they are not tolerated by internal precepts and should be discarded by royal statutes. This is true not only in the capital, but for the monasteries throughout the provinces and prefectures of the empire.
It is likewise so. They encroach upon and plunder the common people, extensively occupying fields and residences; this harms compassionate sympathy and serves only to prolong sighs of suffering.
Furthermore, human minds differ, and their virtues and vices vary accordingly. There are those who settle their hearts in the ultimate truth, whose spiritual practice is pure and far-reaching;

yet there are also those who outwardly borrow the dharma robes while inwardly harboring perverse morality. Regarding such individuals, one ought to distinguish between the Jing and the Wei rivers; they must not be treated as if they were identical.
Guan: Why encourage virtue? It is because observing the Dharma and praising the good is what ordinary people know. To correct worldly customs and avoid suspicion is a common human inclination.

As for me, why should I alone offer this solitary argument and initiate this unique proposal? Truly, it is because once the national statutes are abolished, it will be extremely difficult to rectify them later.

The net of the Dharma has been momentarily lost, and its regulations and principles are on the verge of falling into disorder. For this reason, I venture to present my humble views, hoping that both [parties] may benefit.

Your servant has heard that the purpose of issuing edicts lies in their certain execution; the establishment of punishments is valued for its ability to bring order to all things. An edict that is not executed is no better than having no edict at all.

Punishment cannot bring about discipline; how does it compare to the absence of punishment? Recently, although clear edicts have been issued repeatedly, those who engage in such acts have increased even further.

Though strict limits have been suddenly imposed, violations do not cease. Is this not because they rely on their merit and entrust themselves to goodness, taking advantage of the fact that no one’s crime will be punished?

To sacrifice one’s private interests for the sake of public officials is difficult; yet if we merely adhere strictly to former regulations without pursuing past transgressions, while subsequent edicts grant leniency from this day forward, the worldly sentiments of the masses will eventually cause established laws to be neglected.
Now, it is appropriate to impose strict penalties and establish special prohibitions to rectify future violations and punish past failures.
If we do not exercise rigorous scrutiny but instead continue to show indulgence, I fear that although the current edict is clear, [the law will remain ineffective].
Furthermore, as was the case in former days, the imperial decree also permits those places designated for offerings and prostrations to remain entirely unrestricted.
Your humble servant considers that the wooden tablets [prohibiting construction] are impermanent and the sites of worship difficult to verify.

If one wishes to claim that there are constructed tablets serving as public evidence for the necessity of building, and point to them as proof of past worship, then such a measure would merely have the name of a prohibition while in reality permitting the construction of roads. Moreover, it would result in mere ostentation.

Since then, four lines of an edict have been issued, yet those who act privately and contravene it do not fear the imperial decree. Is this because the various officials and functionaries are negligent in upholding the law?
Or rather, is it because the governing framework has leaked and prohibitions have become lax, allowing for excuses based on other pretexts?

According to my humble opinion, although there are official markers within the capital, as for the construction of coarse works that ought to be altered or established, I request that they be carried out in accordance with [the regulations].

The previous regulations were established outside the city walls; one may choose any convenient location for them. If the land has been purchased with clear documentary evidence, its transfer is permitted.

If public land has been occupied by theft, it must be returned to the government. However, once sacred images have been completed and cannot be moved or removed, we request that the present edict be followed:
as before, they shall not be restricted and shall be allowed to reside within the wards, provided that the wards themselves are not destroyed.

Do not open gates in such a way as to obstruct the thoroughfares within the village. Those who have received imperial edicts shall not be subject to these restrictions; the same principle applies to those within the city walls.

As for temples where sacred images are solemnly enshrined, yet which are situated in close proximity to slaughterhouses or taverns, please prohibit butchering in the vicinity to ensure the sanctity of the divine abode.
Furthermore, regarding monasteries that house a certain number of monks but whose locations can be relocated, order them to move to spacious sites to avoid cramped and sordid surroundings. As if...
Those who construct [temples] after the amnesty of this year’s first month shall seek to comply with the monastic regulations; they shall be investigated and punished according to the law.

If the number of monks does not reach fifty, they shall be permitted to join together and rely on a larger temple, ensuring that the requirements are met. As for the land sold [to fund the construction], it shall be returned exactly according to the aforementioned procedure.
From now on, if those in other provinces wish to build a temple, provided the number of monks is fifty or more, they must first obtain permission from their home...

The provinces shall submit a formal list. The Emperor will examine the manifest with clarity and deliberation; only after the memorial is heard will the decree be established. Should there be any violations, all shall be punished according to the previous statutes.

If governors and officials below the provincial level tolerate such acts and fail to prohibit them, their offense shall be equal to disobeying the imperial edict. It is hoped that all shall look up to and follow the imperishable legacy of the late Sovereign.
Now that we humbly receive these current edicts of compassionate command, the standards of conduct can be fully restored and the Holy Way shall not fall into ruin. The memorial was approved.

Before long, the empire fell into chaos and turmoil; furthermore, following the atrocities at Heyin, many families of deceased court officials abandoned their residences to bestow them upon monks and nuns.
Consequently, the mansions and dwellings of the capital were for the most part converted into monasteries. The prohibitions issued previously were no longer observed.
Regarding this practice: according to the biography of Prince Chen of Rencheng, Empress Ling was zealous in the construction of religious edifices.
While in the capital, she erected the Yongning Temple, the Taishanggong Temple, and others, at a cost that was not small. In the various provinces, five-storied Buddhist stupas were likewise built.

Furthermore, she frequently held all-day vegetarian assemblies (*sarva-pūjā*), with the distribution of goods often reaching ten thousand units. Consequently, the common people were exhausted by these projects of earth and wood.
The price of gold and silver surged because of this. He stripped the officials of their duties and wealth, causing the state treasuries to be depleted.

Sengcheng submitted a memorial offering earnest admonition; although [the Emperor] ultimately did not follow his advice, he always responded to him with exceptional courtesy. According to the biography of Hu Guozhen:

Guo Zhen’s daughter was Empress Ling. Although Guo Zhen was advanced in years, she held the Buddha-dharma in profound reverence; she frequently observed the fasts and maintained ritual purity, persevering in her prostrations.

On the seventh day of the fourth month in the first year of the Shenguī era, she walked behind the Buddhist image she had erected, proceeding from her residence to the Changhe Gate for a distance of four or five *li*.
On the eighth day, she again stood to gaze upon the image, refusing to sit until late evening.
His exhaustion and fever increased severely, and he subsequently fell ill. He passed away on the twelfth day.

Emperor Suzong issued an edict stating that from the time of his death until the completion of the forty-ninth-day memorial, a vegetarian feast for one thousand monks should be established each time, and seven men were to be ordained as monks. On the hundredth day, a feast for ten thousand monks was to be held, and twenty-seven men were to be ordained.

In the second year of the Shenguī era, Cui Guang submitted a memorial offering earnest admonition against the Empress Dowager’s ascent to the Buddhist temple and her subsequent visit to Mount Songgao;

however, her request was not granted. According to the *Weishu*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Suzong," on the gengyin day of the ninth month in the second year of Shenguī, the Empress Dowager visited Mount Songgao;
on the gui-si day, she returned to the palace. According to the "Biography of Cui Guang," [the events occurred] in the eighth month of the second year of Shenguī.
In the [month of] Yue, Empress Dowager Ling visited Yongning Temple and personally ascended the nine-story Buddha-pagoda. Guangbiao remonstrated with her, saying:

"The precious pagodas within the Buddhist scriptures are lofty and magnificent, containing thousands of chambers; they speak only of offering incense, flowers, and prostrations. How could there be any principle for ascending them?
It is only said that one may ascend the steps of the Triple Gem and descend from above; thus humans and devas meet, both gaining the opportunity to see one another, transcending the mundane world."

It is wondrous and extraordinary, beyond all comparison. While prostrating and kneeling in reverent worship, one remains at the lower levels; yet from afar, gazing out, one beholds the mountains and rivers in their entirety.
Because of this expansive view, laughter and mirth increase, such that one cannot maintain increasing piety at every level or cultivate utmost solemnity at every step.

This will merely cause the men and women of the capital to gather there from both public and private sectors; for the superior to act and the subordinates to follow is a natural consequence of the situation.

We humbly pray that you will cease this personal labor and broaden your transformative influence so that all are moved to emulation. By not treading upon [the sacred ground] yourself, you shall manifest and consolidate your ten-thousand-year reign. The Ninth Month.
Empress Dowager Ling visited Mount Songgao. Sengguang submitted a memorial to remonstrate, but the Empress Dowager did not follow his advice.

In the first year of the Yuangxiang era of Emperor Jing, an edict was issued stating that all newly established temples within the capital were to be demolished. Furthermore, an edict was issued stating that local governors, prefects, and magistrates who constructed temples would be charged with the offense of "perverting the law.
According to the *Weishu*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Jing do not record this; according to the *Shi* [monastic history], it is recorded.
Old Record. In the autumn of the first year of the Yuanxiang era, an imperial edict was issued, stating: "The realm of the Buddha is profound and mysterious; its meaning lies in pure vastness.

A *saṃghārāma* is a land of purity, where principle transcends the clamor of the mundane world. Previously, within the city walls, there were prohibitions against [such establishments]. Since our arrival and the relocation to Ye, we have followed established precedents.
However, when the various officials and the common people first reached the capital, all were provided with residences in the new city outside the walls. Now, regarding the old..."
Within the city, these were borrowed for a temporary period, intended for future necessity rather than permanent use.

I have heard that many people, having obtained land in two locations, abandoned the houses they had borrowed in the old city to establish them as monasteries of their own choosing; yet they knew these places did not belong to them.

I fear that by using this single name, the practice will eventually become excessive and severely undermine established regulations. It is appropriate to entrust this matter to the relevant authorities for a thorough investigation and summary.
Furthermore, as for the old temples and residences within the city, they all have fixed registers; those newly established shall all be abolished and destroyed.

In winter, another edict was issued stating that no governors, prefects, magistrates, or district heads throughout the empire shall be permitted to construct temples. Should anyone violate this, [they shall not...]
Regarding inquiries into the source of funds and the calculation of labor expended for construction, all shall be judged according to the law on the abuse of official authority.

In the spring of the second year of the Xinghe era, an imperial edict was issued designating the old palace at Ye City as Tianping Monastery. According to the *Weishu*, Jìngdì’s Basic Annals, this is not recorded;
however, according to the "Treatise on Buddhism and Daoism," in the spring of the second year of the Xinghe era, an edict was issued [designating] the old [palace at Ye City].

The palace was converted into T'ien-p'ing Temple. From the reign of Emperor Sejong until the end of the Wu-ting era, there were renowned śramaṇas such as Hui-meng, Hui-pien, Hui-shen, Seng-hsien, Tao-ch'in, Seng-hsien, Tao-hsi, Seng-shen, Hui-kuang, Hui-hsien, Fa-yung, and Tao-chang;
all were highly esteemed by their contemporaries. From the time Wei possessed the empire until the transition of the mandate through abdication, [the history of] Buddhist scriptures...
Circulated widely throughout China, there were a total of four hundred and fifteen works comprising one thousand nine hundred and nineteen fascicles.
From the Zhengguang era onwards, the empire faced many perils and royal levies became particularly severe. Consequently, the common people everywhere joined the religious order in groups;
they feigned a devotion to the śramaṇas while actually seeking to evade corvée labor. This state of vulgar excess reached its peak within China.

Since the existence of the Buddha-dharma, such a state has never before occurred. To calculate it roughly, the great assembly of monks and nuns numbers two million, and there are more than thirty thousand monasteries.
That the corruption has reached such an extreme that none are returning to the path is why those who possess discernment sigh in lamentation.

In the sixth year of the Wuding era, eminent monks were assembled in the Xianyang Hall to lecture on Buddhist scriptures. According to the *Weishu*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Jing, this is not recorded.

However, according to the biography of Du Bi in the *Beizhi*, on the eighth day of the fourth month in the sixth year of Wuding, the Wei Emperor assembled eminent monks in the Xianyang Hall to expound upon Buddhist principles; Du Bi was present along with the Minister of Personnel.
Yang Yin, the Palace Secretary-General Xing Shao, the Director of the Imperial Library Wei Shou, and others were all present at the Dharma assembly.
By imperial decree, Sengbi was invited to ascend the lion throne to expound the teachings before the multitude.

Shaoyuan Du Sengda and Seng Daoshun—both paragons of the monastic community—advanced with sharp and piercing questions, engaging in debate for dozens of rounds; yet none were able to best him. The Emperor remarked, "If this worthy man had been born..."
As for the school of Confucius, what was it like?
(Compendium of Illustrations and Writings of the Ancient and Modern Ages, Section on Buddhism, Volume One).
(Compendium of Illustrations and Writings of the Ancient and Modern Ages, Section on Buddhism, Volume Two).
During the Northern Qi dynasty, the Zhao Yuan Temple was established. It appointed various officials, including a *datong* (Grand Overseer), to manage Buddhist affairs.

According to the "Treatise on Official Titles" (*Bai guan zhi*) in the *Sui shu*, following the Later Qi, the Zhao Yuan Temple oversaw all Buddhist matters; it was staffed with one *datong* and one *du* (Director).

There were three *karmadāna* (vinaya-masters), and he also established positions for *gongcao* (merit-officials) and *mainbu* (clerks) to manage the various monastic offices (*śramaṇa-caos*) of the prefectures, commanderies, and counties.
In the second year of the Tianbao era, Emperor Xianzu issued an edict inviting Dhyāna Master Tanyou to the capital city of Ye, where he was established in a monastery to reside.

The Emperor invited him to receive the Bodhisattva precepts. According to the *Beiqi shu*, the "Basic Annals" (*benji*) of Emperor Xianzu, this is not recorded; however, according to the *Fozu tongji*, it is so stated.

In the second year of the Tiānbão era of Emperor Wényí of the Northern Qi, an imperial edict summoned Meditation Master Chóu to the capital of Yèdū. He was established at Yúnmén Monastery to reside there.
The Master sat in meditation within a single room and never once went out to welcome or see off visitors. When the Emperor arrived, his disciples urged him to do so, but the Master said:
Pindola welcomed the king for seven paces, which caused the king to lose his kingdom. Although my virtue does not equal his, my outward demeanor resembles his;
therefore, I did not dare deceive myself, hoping only to bring blessings upon the Emperor. The Emperor, however, was misled by his attendants and treated the Master with arrogance.
He wished to inflict personal harm upon him. The Master merely went twenty *li* outside the monastery and stood with hands clasped by the roadside.

The Emperor, finding this strange, questioned him. The Master said, "I fear that blood might defile the *saṃghārāma*. The Emperor immediately repented and apologized, saying to the Chief Minister Yang Zunyán, "How could one slander such a true man?
He then returned to the palace in the same carriage and asked, "Who was my disciple in a previous life? The Master [replied].

He replied, "I once served as a Rākṣasa king and even now I still delight in killing. He consecrated water in a basin and had the Emperor look into it; there, he saw a multitude of rākṣasas following behind him.
The Emperor was moved to profound reverence and faith, requested to receive the Bodhisattva precepts, and vowed never again to eat meat.
He abolished all instruments for harming living beings used by the Five Parks, such as hawks and dogs, as well as all slaughter within his realm.
In the tenth year of Tenpō, the Emperor visited Kanro-ji Temple at Chion-in to engage in profound contemplation. According to the *Beizhi shu*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Xianzu":
On the day of Jia-yin, the first month of spring in the tenth year of Tianbao, the Emperor went to Kanro-ji Temple in Liaoyang.
On the day of Bing-xu, the second month, the Emperor remained at Kanro-ji Temple for meditative seclusion and deep observation; only matters of great state and military affairs were reported to him.

In the second year of the Dàníng era of Emperor Shìzǔ, on the *rénwǔ* day of the fifth month in summer, an edict was issued to convert the garden of the Double Halls (*Shuāngtáng*) located south of the city wall into the construction site for Dàzǒngchí Monastery.
On the *xīnchōu* day of the eighth month in autumn, an edict was issued to establish the Sāntái Palace as Dàxīngshèng Monastery.
This is recorded in the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shìzǔ" in the *Beizhī shū*.

On the *yisi* day of the third month of spring in the second year of the Tiāntǒng era of Emperor Hòuzhǔ, the Supreme Sovereign (Tàshàng Huángdì) issued an edict to bestow the Three Platforms (*sāntái*) upon Xīngshèng Monastery.
This is recorded in the *Beizhī Shū*, in the Annals of Emperor Hòuzhǔ, et cetera.
In the third year of the Tiāntǒng era, the Retired Emperor issued an edict to completely exempt all miscellaneous households (*záhù*) belonging to various monasteries,
making them equal in status to commoners. According to the "Basic Annals of the Later Ruler" in the *Beizhī shū*, on the day of Jìyōu in the ninth month of autumn in the third year of Tiāntǒng,

the Retired Emperor decreed that those among the miscellaneous protected households (*zábǎohù*) under the jurisdiction of the monastic offices whose surnames were Gāo— despite the favorable edicts granted at the beginning of the Tiānbão era— [were now to be fully integrated].

Regarding those who have not yet been exempted from the provisional employment of their labor and power: they may now all be released from the status of *záhù* (miscellaneous households) and allowed to belong to the prefectures and counties, being treated exactly like ordinary subjects.

On the *xīnhài* day of the first month of spring in the fifth year of the Tiāntǒng era, an edict was issued stating that the three palaces, including Jīnfèng, which had not yet been converted into monasteries...

The Great Xing’eng Monastery was established. On the *jiazi* day of the fourth month of summer, an imperial edict decreed that the Shangshu Province of Bingzhou be made the site of the Great Jishi Monastery, and Jin Temple be made the Great Chonghuang Monastery.

According to the *Beizhi Shu*, "Benji" (Basic Annals) of the Later Ruler, in the first year of Chengguang of the minor ruler [Yezhou], a great Buddha image was carved into the western mountains of Jinyang, and the Great Baolin Monastery was also constructed.
According to the "Basic Annals of the Young Sovereign" in the *Beizhi shu*, whenever there were portents of calamity, banditry, floods, or droughts, the Emperor never diminished his splendor;

he merely established vegetarian feasts (*zhāi*) in various locations, regarding these as the cultivation of virtue. He once excavated the western mountains of Jinyang to create a colossal Buddha image.
One night, ten thousand basins of oil were lit, and their light illuminated the palace interior. Furthermore, for the sake of Consort Hu, he constructed the Daci [Monastery].
The temple was not yet completed when it was renamed Dabolin Temple for Empress Mu. The craftsmanship reached its ultimate limit;
stones were transported and springs filled at a cost exceeding hundreds of millions, with the number of men and oxen who died being beyond reckoning.

In the fourth year of the Kaishuang era of Emperor Gaozu of the Sui dynasty, Xiansi Temple was established, and the monk Lingzang resided there. According to the *Sui Shu* (History of Sui), the Basic Annals of Emperor Gaozu, it is not recorded that the Vice President of the Council of State attended his audiences.
However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the fourth year of the Kaishuang era of the Sui...

In that year, Vinaya Master Lingzang first formed a friendship with the Emperor while they were both commoners. Upon the Emperor’s accession to the throne, he established Daxingshan Monastery to provide a residence for the Master.

By imperial decree, the Left and Right Vice Directors of the Chancellery were to visit him every morning to inquire after his well-being. Once, when the Emperor traveled to Luozhou, the Master accompanied him, and those who sought his guidance became numerous.
The Emperor issued a handwritten edict stating: "I, your disciple, am a secular Son of Heaven; you, Vinaya Master, are a celestial being among men."
"My son, those who wish to leave secular life may be ordained by their teachers as they see fit. Consequently, the number of people he ordained reached tens of thousands.
When some expressed doubt regarding this, the Emperor said, "The Vinaya Master transforms people toward goodness, while I prohibit people from committing evil; our intentions are one and the same."
In the sixth month of summer in the first year of the Renshou era, śarīra relics were distributed to the various provinces.

According to the *Suíshū Gāozǔ Běnjì* (The Basic Annals of Emperor Gāozǔ of the Sui), during the second year of the Dayè era of Emperor Yáng, an edict was issued requiring śramaṇas to pay homage to the sovereign; however, because the monk Míngdǎn and others did not comply...

[The text] stops here. According to the *Suíyángdì Běnjì* (Basic Annals of Emperor Yáng of the Sui), this is not recorded. According to the *Fózǔ Tǒngjì* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs):

In the second year of the Dàyè era, an imperial edict was issued requiring śramaṇas and Daoists to pay homage to the sovereign. Śramaṇas such as Míngdǎn and others resisted the edict and did not comply. The Emperor interrogated them, and they replied:
"If Your Majesty would cause us to disrobe in accordance with the regulations, then we would not dare not to obey. However, if [you know that]..."
"The Dharma may be honored; thus, beneath the dharma-robes, there shall be no rite of monks revering the laity. The Emperor remained silent and desisted.
In the seventh year of the Wude era of the Tang Gaozu, Fu Yi submitted a memorial vehemently denouncing the Buddha-dharma. The Emperor approved of it. (According to the *Tang*...)
In the *Basic Annals of the High Ancestor*, this is not recorded. According to the biography of Fu Yi, the High Ancestor appointed Yi as Director of the Bureau of Astronomy.

In the seventh year of Wude, he submitted a memorial vehemently denouncing the Buddhist dharma, stating: "The methods of the Western Regions recognize neither sovereign nor subject, nor father nor son."
Within the three miserable realms and the six paths of rebirth, they glare at the ignorant and the vulgar, pursuing past transgressions while spying for future blessings.

There are even those who, having personally fallen into wicked rebellion, perform prostrations to the Buddha within the prison and recite Sanskrit mantras in an attempt to evade their fate through deceit.

Furthermore, birth and death, longevity and premature demise, are fundamentally matters of natural law; rewards and punishments, majesty and fortune, depend upon the sovereign. Yet now, these followers falsely claim and rely upon [such powers]. All of this—
It is said that the Buddha usurped the principles of Heaven and encroached upon the sovereign authority. The Book of Documents states: "Only the ruler may exercise blessings;

only the ruler may exercise majesty; only the ruler may enjoy the jade-like delicacies of food. If a minister exercises blessings, majesty, or enjoys jade-like delicacies, it will bring ruin to his house and misfortune to his state.

From the Five Emperors and Three Kings onward, there were no Buddhist teachings; the rulers were enlightened and the ministers were loyal, and their reigns were long-lasting. It was not until the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty that...

He established a shrine for the barbarians (Hus). However, it was only the śramaṇas from the Western Regions who transmitted their own teachings. Prior to the Western Jin dynasty, it was not permitted for those in China to shave their heads and serve the barbarians;

it was only during the chaos of the Shi and Fu regimes that these prohibitions were relaxed. That the rulers were mediocre and the ministers sycophantic, leading to tyranny in governance and a short dynastic tenure—this was brought about by the worship of Buddha.
The cases of Emperor Wu of Liang and Emperor Xiang of Qi are particularly worthy of being held as warnings. In the past, Bao Si was but a single woman, yet she [ruined the Zhou].

The delusions of King You were able to bring his state to ruin; how much more so now, when there are a hundred thousand monks and nuns who carve and paint clay images to delude the world—will the state not perish?
If Your Majesty allows these hundred thousand people to take spouses for themselves, in ten years their offspring will multiply.

The lessons of the ten years [of war] showed that when both military and agriculture are fully provided for, one’s advantage can indeed be decisive. Formerly, Zhang Qiu Zhituo of the Northern Qi said:

"Regarding the monasteries and pagodas of monks and nuns, the ministers saw them as an external threat to their authority, while the consorts saw them as an internal source of jealousy. Through open slander and secret defamation, he was eventually executed in the marketplace.
When Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou entered Qi, he honored his tomb with a noble title; I personally consider him a man of virtue. Furthermore, I have submitted this in twelve [sections].

The discourse was exceedingly poignant. Emperor Yang summoned his ministers for deliberation. Among them, only Dao Yuan supported the petition. Xiao Yu, the Director of the Secretariat, said, "The Buddha is a sage.
There can be no law without a sage. I request that he be executed. Yang Di replied, "According to the rites, one begins by serving one's parents and concludes by serving one's sovereign.
Yet the Buddha abandoned his father to leave the household; as a commoner, he opposes the Son of Heaven, and as one who has renounced his lineage..."
This was to oppose those close to him. Sengyu was not born from the hollow of a mulberry tree; rather, he honored their words. This is what is meant by the saying, "He who is unfilial has no kin.
Sengyu did not answer, but merely joined his palms and said, "Hell is precisely designed for people such as this. Emperor Wendi was skilled at playing *yi* (a board game).

Before he could put [Sengyu’s words] into practice, the succession of the throne came to an end. When Emperor Taizong ascended the throne, he frequently asked Sengyu, "How can you, sir, reject the Buddha-dharma? Sengyu—
He said, "The Buddha was merely a clever man from the Western Hu tribes who deceived the barbarians to deify himself.

Upon entering China, he was adopted by petty children and conjurers who modeled themselves after Zhuangzi and Laozi to embellish his teachings with their texts. This harms the state and provides no benefit to the common people.
The Emperor found this view strange.
In the sixteenth year of the Zhenguan era of Emperor Taizong, he visited Hongfu Monastery to perform merit-making rites for Empress Dowager Mu.
According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Taizong" in the *Jiu Tang Shu*, this event is not recorded;

however, according to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the sixteenth year of Zhenguan, the Emperor visited Hongfu Monastery to perform merit-making rites for Empress Dowager Mu, personally composing a memorial in which he styled himself "the Emperor, Disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts."
He said to the temple master Daoyi, "Recently, because Laozi was my ancestral progenitor, I have ordered his image to be placed before those of the Śākya clan.
Are you not dissatisfied with this? They replied, "Your Majesty honors our ancestors and has established this formal decree; how could we dare to harbor resentment?

The Emperor said, "The relative dignity of the Buddha and Laozi is something that men of comprehensive learning discern for themselves. How can one claim superiority simply because someone is placed above another for a single moment?"
My ancestral lineage traces back to the one beneath the pillar; thus, I have placed Laozi first. All those who possess merit and virtue turn toward the Buddhist gate.
At every site where there were battlefields in the past, I have established Buddhist temples; even my former residence in Taiyuan has been dedicated to the Buddha.
From the beginning, I have never once initiated the construction of Daoist monasteries. You should all understand that such is my intention.
In the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, the śramaṇa Xuanzang and others returned to the capital from the Western Regions.
By imperial decree, they were to translate various sūtras at Hongfu Monastery. According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Taizong" in the *Jiu Tangshu*, this is not recorded;

however, according to the "Biographies of Arts and Techniques" in the *Jiu Tangshu*, the monk Xuanzang was surnamed Chen. Toward the end of the Daye era, he entered the monastic order and extensively studied the sūtras and śāstras. He once said:
There were many errors and corruptions in the translations; therefore, he traveled to the Western Regions to extensively seek out different versions for comparison and verification.
At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, he accompanied merchants on a journey to the Western Regions.

Since Xuanzang was exceptionally eloquent and erudite beyond his peers, wherever he went, he would lecture on and debate the treatises, earning the profound respect and submission of the local people both near and far. He remained in the Western Regions for seventeen years, traversing over one hundred...
