He understood the languages of all the other countries he visited and further compiled the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) in twelve fascicles, incorporating details regarding their mountains, rivers, customs, and local products.
In the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he returned to the capital. When Emperor Taizong saw him, he was greatly pleased and engaged him in conversation.
Thereupon, by imperial decree, he brought six hundred and fifty-seven Sanskrit texts to Hongfu Monastery.
Regarding the translation, he further commanded Fang Yuanling, Right Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs, and Xu Jingzong, Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince,
to extensively summon more than fifty eminent śramaṇas of great learning to assist in the collation and arrangement of the texts.

In the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era, an imperial decree was issued for the relevant authorities to transcribe the newly translated Buddhist scriptures of Xuanzang and to compose an imperial preface, which were then distributed to the Governors-General of the Nine Circuits.
(Note: This is not recorded in the *Beishi*, "Basic Annals" of Emperor Taizong.
According to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era, the Emperor visited the Yuhua Palace in Fangzhou and summoned Dharma Master Xuanzang. Once [there],...
When he arrived, the Emperor said, "While in the capital, I suffered from the heat; therefore, I have come here to the coolness of this mountain’s springs and rocks.
Recalling the Dharma Master, I have sent for you. What sutra or treatise are you translating today? Xuanzang replied, "Recently, I have been translating the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* of Maitreya.

The Emperor examined the treatise himself and said to his attendants, "The Buddha-dharma is vast and expansive, like gazing at the heavens or looking out over the ocean; one can never fully fathom it."

It is most lofty and profound. The classics of the nine schools of thought are like small marshes compared to the vast ocean. The worldly claim that the three teachings lead to the same goal is but a false discourse.
Consequently, he issued an edict to the relevant authorities to transcribe the newly translated sutras and śāstras and distribute them to the governors of the nine circuits.

He also composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka of the Great Tang" to serve as their preface. By imperial decree, the Crown Prince was commissioned to compose the [Preface to the] Bodhisattva...

Postscript to the Tripiṭaka. From that time on, [the Emperor] discussed the principles of the Dharma without ceasing from his lips. He attended upon the Dharma Master with the same reverence as he would a family member.
In the second year of the Yonghui era of Gaozong, on the *guisi* day of the ninth month, Yuhua Palace was abolished and established as a Buddhist monastery. (According to the records:)
The *Jiuzhang* (Basic Annals) of Gaozong in the *Tangshu* does not record this;

however, according to the *Jiu Tangshu* (Old Book of Tang), the Basic Annals of Gaozong, it states that in the first year of the Xianqing era, an imperial edict was issued for Yu Zhining, the Left Vice President of the Department of State Affairs, and others to refine and embellish the scriptures finalized by Xuanzang.
The Emperor went to the Anfu Gate to observe Master Yuanzang receiving the imperial composition for the stele of Ci'en Temple.

By imperial decree, a prince was sent to the Master’s temple to confer the *śaraṇa-gamana* (refuge) precepts upon him. According to the "Basic Annals of Gaozong" in the *Jiu Tang Shu*, this is not recorded;

however, according to the "Basic Annals of Gaozong" in the *Xin Tang Shu*, on the wushen day of the fourth month in the summer of the first year, the Emperor went to the Anfu Gate to observe the monk Yuanzang as he received [the imperial decree].
The Emperor personally composed the inscription for the Stele of Ci’en Monastery. He was escorted by attendants according to Indian ritual protocols, and his retinue was exceedingly grand.

According to the *Fangji zhuan* (Biographies of Arts and Techniques), when Gaozong was still the Crown Prince, he built Ci’en Monastery to perform meritorious rites on behalf of Empress Dowager Wenming.

Furthermore, from within the Translation Institute, a great banner was brought forth. An imperial decree ordered the Ninefold Music (*navavidha-vādya*) as well as the banners, canopies, and various performers from the monasteries throughout the capital to escort Xuanzang, along with the translated scriptures, images, and eminent monks, into Ci'en Monastery.

In the first year of the Xianqing era, Emperor Gaozong again commanded the Left Vice-Director of the Department of State Affairs Yu Zhining, the Palace Attendant Xu Jingzong, and the Director of the Secretariat [to attend].
Li Jiji, Li Yifu, Du Zhenglun, and the Palace Attendant Xue Yuanchao collectively refined and polished the scriptures finalized by Xuanzang.
Fan Yiyun, the State Academy Doctor; Guo Yu, the Master of the Household for the Crown Prince;
and Gao Ruosi, a scholar of the Hongwen Hall, assisted in the further translation. These works were completed as seventy-five sections and submitted to the throne. Subsequently, from the capital...
The people of the capital vied with one another to come and pay their respects. Xuanzang then petitioned for a period of seclusion to engage in translation;
by imperial decree, he was moved to the former Yuhua Palace on Mount Xuanjun, where he remained for six years. He passed away at the age of fifty-six and was buried at Bailu Yuan.

The men and women who escorted the funeral procession numbered tens of thousands. According to the *Fozu tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs): on the eleventh day of the first month of the first year, Empress Wu gave birth to a prince;

a divine light filled the chamber, and he was granted the name Prince Foguang. Over a month later, an imperial decree was issued for him to leave the household life and shave his head at the temple of Dharma Master Xuanzang, where he was conferred the precepts of taking refuge.
In the first year of the Longshuo era, [the Emperor] visited Tiangong Temple and ordained twenty monks.

According to the *Jiu Tang shu*, "Basic Annals of Gaozong," it is recorded that in the ninth month of the first year of Longshuo, he visited Tiangong Temple—the former residence of Gaozu during his time as a hidden dragon—and toured the halls and buildings, remaining moved with emotion for a long time, and then ordained [the monks]. (Note: This is not recorded in the *Tang shu*, "Basic Annals of Gaozong.")
There were twenty monks.

On the *jisi* day of the fifth month in the sixth year of Zhongzong’s Shiseng era (which was the first year of Empress Dowager Yongchang), Xue Huaiyi, a monk of Baima Monastery, was appointed as the Commander-in-Chief of the Military Expeditionary Force for the Xinping Circuit to suppress the Tujue. (According to the *Beishi*, "Basic Annals of Empress Wu").
The record states as follows:

In the seventh year of Sisheng (which was the first year of Empress Dowager Tianshou), the *Dayun Jing* (Great Cloud Sutra) was promulgated throughout the realm, and it was ordered that each prefecture establish a Dayun Temple.
According to the "Basic Annals of Empress Wu" in the *Jiu Tang Shu*, on the seventh month of the first year of Tianshou, the *Dayun Jing* was promulgated.
"Throughout the realm": According to the "Basic Annals of Empress Wu" in the *Jiu Tang Shu*, there were ten śramaṇas who forged the *Dayun Jing* (Great Cloud Sutra) and presented it as a memorial.

It spoke extensively of the divine mandate received by the Shenhuang (Divine Sovereign). An imperial decree was issued to promulgate it throughout the realm, ordering each prefecture to establish a Dayun Temple and collectively ordaining one thousand monks.
In the seventeenth year of Sisheng (the first year of Empress Dowager Jiu-shi), funds were collected from monks throughout the empire to construct a great image for a Buddhist shrine.

This project was halted upon the remonstrance of Zhang Tinggui. According to the "Basic Annals of Empress Wu" in the *Jiu Tang Shu*, on the gengshen day of the eighth month in the first year of Jiu-shi, funds were collected from monks throughout the empire to create a great image.
According to the "Biography of Zhang Tinggui," Empress Wu [levied a tax] upon the monks of the empire...
He donated money to the Buddhist monasteries and established a Buddhist shrine at Baisima Slope, where he commissioned a great statue. Yan Tinggui remonstrated against this, saying:
"To exhaust the wealth of the four seas and drain the labor of the myriad people;

to use the timber of the mountains to build stupas and the finest gold from the smelters to cast statues—though these are grand, such conditioned dharmas are not worthy of high esteem. Furthermore, they fill up mountain ravines and crush insects and ants."
Furthermore, the hundreds of millions of laborers and officials are impoverished; driven by forced service, they suffer exhaustion, and due to hunger and thirst, diseases are now breaking out.

Moreover, while monks and nuns sustain themselves through begging, the prefectures and counties press them with urgent demands for tax delivery like a falling star; thus, they are forced to sell their possessions to fulfill these obligations.

This was not what the Buddhists call "rejoicing" (anumodana). At a time when the world was exhausted and the common people were emaciated and distressed, he proclaimed that the borders were secure and the granaries were full;
thus he nurtured the strength of the people. The Emperor deemed this virtuous and summoned him to the Changsheng Hall, where he bestowed generous rewards and consolation.
Because of this, the labor service was suspended.
In the [blank] year of the Jinglong era, Buddhist temples were extensively constructed. According to the *Jizhuan* (Basic Annals) of Emperor Zhongzong in the *Jiu Tang Shu*, this is not recorded;

however, according to the biography of Xin Tifu, during the Jinglong era, Buddhist temples were extensively constructed, leaving both the public and private sectors exhausted and impoverished. Xin Tifu submitted a memorial, stating:
Now, the borders are in peril and alarm, the granaries are empty and void; the supplies for the soldiers are insufficient, and rewards for the officers have not been reached.

Yet you extensively construct temples and broadly build private residences, felling timber from the empty mountains that fails to provide for the rafters and beams, and hauling earth by the road that does not suffice for the walls.
That which is called "Buddha" is pure and compassionate, embodying the Way to save all beings; he would not desire to benefit himself at the expense of others.
A person does not glorify their own body at the expense of harming the Teaching. Now, during the months of the three seasons, digging into mountains and piercing the earth harms living beings;
exhausting the treasuries and depleting the granaries harms the people; and constructing vast halls and long corridors glorifies the body. To harm life is not compassionate;
to harm the people is not to cherish things; to glorify the body is not pure. How can this be the heart of one who seeks to become a Buddha? Formerly, in the Xia dynasty...
For more than twenty generations, the Son of Heaven was succeeded by the Shang; for more than twenty generations, the Shang was succeeded by the Zhou;
for more than thirty generations, the Zhou was succeeded by the Han. From the Han onwards, the succession of dynasties can be known.

All these lasted long because they possessed the Way, and were short because they lacked the Way. How could one exhaust gold and jade to repair pagodas and temples and thereby enjoy a long-lasting mandate? Thus says your servant.
To reduce the expenses of carving and engraving so as to relieve those who are insufficiently provided for—this possesses the virtue of a Buddha.
To cease the suffering caused by digging and excavating so as to preserve insects and other creatures—this possesses the benevolence of a Buddha.

To divert the funds for construction projects to supply the frontiers—this possesses the merit of Tang and Wu. To redirect surplus stipends to recruit the upright and incorrupt—this possesses the governance of Yao and Shun.
Your Majesty treats what is urgent as non-urgent and what is non-urgent as urgent; you are close to the future while distancing yourself from the present;
you have lost the true and real, hoping instead for the empty and non-existent. You value the deeds of worldly men while disparaging the enterprise of the Son of Heaven. I privately grieve for this.

Nowadays, those who spend their wealth to rely on influence, those who evade service by fleeing their duties, and those of similar standing all become śramaṇas. As for those who have not yet been ordained, they are either impoverished commoners or virtuous people.

[The Emperor] replied: "I have heard that one who uproots the tree of kinship must surely distance himself from factions. To maintain a wife and raise children is not without private affection; this leads others to disparage the Way.
It is not by seeking people for the sake of expanding the Way that one succeeds. Your Majesty has often wished to fill in moats and ditches and abandon the imperial gardens to relieve the poor.
Yet today there are countless monasteries throughout the realm, each as magnificent as one of Your Majesty’s palaces, with expenditures [beyond measure]."
It may even exceed that. If one-tenth of the world’s wealth were possessed by the Buddha, he would have seven-eighths of it; what, then, does Your Majesty possess?
Even if one were to employ those who do not eat and those who do not wear clothes, there would still be insufficiency;

how much more so when one must wait for Heaven to produce and Earth to nourish, relying on the awe-inspiring movement of wind and the moistening of rain, before anything can be obtained? Your servant has heard it said: "A state that lacks a nine-year reserve is called [in peril]."

"This is not appropriate for our country. Now, if we calculate the granaries and measure the treasuries to provide for the hundred officials and the expenditures of ten thousand affairs, I fear we shall not be able to see out the year.
Should war and drought strike one after another, the śramaṇas will be unable to don armor, and the temples and stupas will be insufficient to ward off famine. The Emperor did not heed these words.
In the first year of the Xiāntián era of Emperor Ruìzōng, the śramaṇa Bhara from Western Heaven requested that lamps be lit as an offering to the Buddha.
The Emperor went in person to observe the lantern wheels at Yánxī Gate. [Note: According to the *Tángshū*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Ruìzōng," this is not recorded.

According to the *Fó-zǔ-tǒng-jì*, in the first year of the Xiāntián era of Emperor Ruìzōng, the śramaṇa Bhara from Western Heaven requested that lamps be lit as an offering to the Buddha. The Emperor presided over the ceremony at Yánxī Gate.
He went to view the lantern wheel, which was twenty *zhang* high and featured five hundred gold and silver lamps; from a distance, it resembled a flowering tree.

In the second year of the Kaiyuan era of Emperor Xuanzong, an edict was issued to investigate and audit the monks and nuns throughout the empire. According to the *Jinshu*, in the "Basic Annals of Emperor Xuanzong," this is not recorded;
however, according to the biography of Yao Chong, during the time of Emperor Xuanzong, Yao Chong was enfeoffed as the Duke of Liang and promoted to the position of Director of the Ziwei Department.

During the reign of Emperor Zhongzong, relatives of the imperial clan petitioned for the ordination of monks and nuns; consequently, those from wealthy households and able-bodied men sought ordination to evade taxes and labor service.

At this time, Li Chongjian submitted a memorial stating: "The Buddha does not exist outside [the mind]. Enlightenment is realized within the heart. To act in a way that benefits others and brings peace and stability to the common people—this is what is called the principle of the Buddha.
Why employ deceitful persons to turbidify the True Teaching? The Emperor approved this and issued an edict to purge the monastic community throughout the empire of those who were false.

Over twenty-two thousand people were registered as farmers while retaining their tonsured hair. According to the *Jiù Tángshū*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Xuānzōng," on the *bǐngyǐn* day of the first month in spring of the second year of the Kāiyuán era, Yáo Chóng, Minister of the Zǐwēi Court, submitted a memorial requesting an investigation and accountability of the monks and nuns throughout the empire;
those who had fraudulently assumed the monastic life were returned to lay status, numbering over twenty-two thousand.
In the first year of the Zhìdé era of Emperor Sùzōng, an edict was issued for *shāmen* (monks) to chant and recite sutras for the invocation of blessings.

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Sùzōng" in the *Táng Shū*, this is not recorded. However, according to the *Fózǔ Tǒngjì*, in the first year of the Zhìdé era of Emperor Sùzōng, while the Emperor was at Līngwǔ, the military requirements were insufficient;
consequently, the Chancellor Pèi Miǎn requested that the ordination certificates (*dùchí*) for monks and priests be sold, which were termed "incense-water money" (*xiāngshuǐ qián*). At that time...

As the threat of rebellion was at its height, some advised the Emperor to rely upon the protection of the Buddha. He issued an edict for one hundred śramaṇas to enter the mobile palace to chant and recite scriptures morning and evening.
One night, the Emperor dreamed of a śramaṇa with a golden body chanting the name of Ratnasaṃbhava Tathāgata.
When he questioned his attendants about this, someone replied, "In the White Grass Valley of Helan, there is a Silla monk named Wulou who constantly chants this name. [The Emperor] summoned him.
He saw [the monk] Jinxing there. Before long, Bukong arrived; he subsequently detained him both of them, entrusting him with the task of praying for blessings.

In the second year of the Shangyuan era, because the Emperor was unwell, the Empress pricked her finger to draw blood and transcribed Buddhist scriptures. Furthermore, the various officials held a vegetarian feast for the monks at a Buddhist temple.
(Note: This is not recorded in the *Jiu Tang shu*, "Basic Annals of Suzong"; it is recorded in the *Jiu Tang shu*, "Annals of Suzong").
Basic Annals. On the day of Jia-wu in the first month of the second year of Shangyuan, the Emperor was unwell. Empress Zhang drew her own blood to transcribe Buddhist scriptures.
In the ninth month, the Emperor was again unwell; the various officials held a vegetarian feast for the monks at a Buddhist temple.
In the year □□□, Nanyang was appointed National Teacher (*guoshi*). According to the *Jiu Tang Shu*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Suzong," this is not recorded;

however, according to the *Xue Fulaoxun* (Instructions on Studying Buddhism and Daoism), Emperor Suzong of the Tang dynasty aspired to the Chan school and honored Nanyang as his National Teacher, seeking instruction from him morning and evening.
In the ninth month of the first year of the Yongtai era of Emperor Daizong, he ordered the hundred officials to view the image of the floating Buddha at Guangshun Gate.

He further decreed that the *Ratnaketuparivarta Sūtra* (Renwang jing) be lectured upon at Zisheng and Ximing Monasteries. In the intercalary tenth month, he collected funds from the populace to construct offerings for the floating stupa.
According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Daizong" in the *Jiu Tang Shu*, on the day of Gengyin in the ninth month of the first year of Yongtai, he issued this command.
The hundred officials viewed the floating image at the Gwangsun Gate. On the *gichi* day of the intercalary tenth month, they collected funds from the people to construct a stupa for offerings.
According to the biography of Wang Jin, Jin had long been a devotee of Buddhism; he abstained from pungent vegetables and meat, and in his later years, he was exceptionally reverent and cautious.

After his wife died, he converted his residence in Daowangli into a Buddhist temple. Whenever the various provincial military governors and inspectors came to court, he invariably invited them to his residence and exhorted them to contribute their wealth to assist with the construction.
At first, Emperor Daizong was fond of sacrificial rites but did not hold the Buddhist dharma in high regard;
he would often inquire at leisure about its origins. Li Jin and Yuan Zai then extensively expounded upon the workings of karma and the retribution for one's deeds.

The Emperor’s inclination toward this arose from his practice of worshipping the Buddha within the palace, chanting sutras, and performing incense offerings; this was known as the "Inner Dharma Hall" (Naidōjō).

He summoned more than a hundred monastics daily, providing them with exquisite and abundant meals. When they entered or left, they rode horses from the imperial stables, and the Ministry of Revenue provided them with full provisions and stipends.

Whenever barbarians invaded, he would invariably assemble the monks to recite the *Renwang Jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) for the protection of the state and to ward off calamities. He favored them...

When they departed, they would arbitrarily bestow *sengqie* (monastic staff) and robes upon others, with no known limit. Among the Hu people, those who reached the rank of Minister (*qing*) or Supervisor (*jian*), or were enfeoffed as Dukes (*guogong*), were registered in the imperial precincts;
their influence eclipsed that of princes and kings. Living in groups while relying on imperial favor, they vied with one another for power and seized property.

Virtually all the fertile fields and excellent estates of the capital region fell into the hands of the *futuo* (Buddhists). Although they harbored wickedness and instigated disorder in succession, the Emperor ultimately remained unaware.
An imperial edict was issued to all government offices stating that monks and nuns must not be subjected to flogging or humiliation.

Previously, the shrines of Mount Wutai had been roofed with copper tiles coated in gold, costing hundreds of millions. Li Jin obtained an official tally from the Secretariat and dispatched dozens of Buddhist monks to travel through the prefectures and counties to collect wealth through begging.
Jin submitted a memorial to the Emperor, stating that the nation’s prosperity and long-lasting mandate were sustained by the blessings of these offerings. Although...

At that time, there were many hardships, yet nothing was worth recording. An Lushan and Shi Siming incited poisonous rebellion through their writings, yet both suffered the calamity of their own sons.
Pu Guo Huai’en collapsed amidst the chaos; when the Western Rong tribes rebelled within the borders, they withdrew as soon as the attack began.

These were not matters of human effort. Thus, the Emperor’s faith became even more profound. On the full moon day of the seventh month, he had alms-bowls (ulambana-piṇḍa) fashioned within the palace, adorned with silver and pearls.

They established seven ancestral seats for the High Ancestor and those below him, fully equipped with ceremonial banners, musical instruments, robes, and caps, each identified by the imperial title inscribed upon its banner.

From within the palace, they proceeded in separate processions to the Daoist and Buddhist shrines, accompanied by the clamor of gongs, flutes, drums, and dancing, with participants following one another in rapid succession.

On this day, the ceremonial guards were stationed, and the officials lined up at the Gate of Radiant Compliance (Guāngshùn mén) to welcome and escort the procession; this became the annual custom. Following this precedent, the various ministers all...

Because they spoke of the retributions of birth and death, people neglected their human duties and failed to cultivate them; thus, the administration and penal laws of the Dali era fell into ruin day by day.
This was instigated by Jing, Yuan Zai, and Du Hongjian. According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Daizong" in the *Jiu Tang Shu* (Old Book of Tang):

In the ninth month of the first year of the Yongtai era, two carriages containing the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) were issued from within the palace and entrusted to the two monasteries of Zisheng and Ximing, where they were to be expounded upon a high seat one hundred feet tall.
The lectures were only suspended when the barbarian invaders pressed against the capital region.
In the tenth month of winter, on the day of Jiwu, the *Renwang jing* was again expounded at Zisheng Monastery.
In the third year of the Dali era, an imperial edict was issued granting the monk Huichong of Hangzhou a purple *kāṣāya* from the palace.
This is not recorded in the "Basic Annals of Emperor Daizong" in the *Jiu Tang Shu*; however, according to the *Daizong Shilu*, it states as follows.

In the fourth year of the Dali era, the Emperor established a *dharmapūjā* site (*daochang*), and was moved by the manifestation of Buddha-light. According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Daizong" in the *Jiu Tang Shu*, this is not recorded;
however, according to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the fourth year of the Dali era of Emperor Daizong, the Emperor established a *dharmapūjā* site at the Daming Palace.
He was moved by the manifestation of Buddha-light, and all the princes, princesses, and high-ranking officials in attendance beheld the radiant form of the Buddha from the hour of Zi.
At nightfall, until the crowing of the cock, the Chancellor Pei Mian submitted a memorial offering congratulations.

In the ninth year of the Dali era, an imperial edict was issued to construct a seven-story pagoda on Mount Niushou. According to the *Beishi* (History of the Tang), in the Basic Annals of Emperor Daizong, this is not recorded.
However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the ninth year of the Dali era, the Emperor dreamed of Jiankang’s Mount Niushou.
A mountain. A Pratyekabuddha came and saw it. He commanded Gu Shen, the Prince’s Chamberlain, to construct a seven-storied stupa on the mountain.

In the □□□ year, an imperial edict summoned the monastic community to enter the inner chapel to pay homage to the Myriad Buddha Mountain. (According to the *Book of Tang*, Section on Successive Reigns...)
The *Zongben ji* (Chronicle of the Founding Ancestors) does not record this; however, according to the *Duyang zabi* (Miscellaneous Records from Du Yang):
Emperor Daizong venerated Śākyamuni, and every day he pounded a hundred varieties of incense and mixed them with silver powder to smear upon the Buddha chamber.

When the Kingdom of Silla presented him with a five-colored *qushu* (carpet), its craftsmanship was so exquisite and elegant that it was preeminent for its time. Within every square inch of it, there were figures performing songs, dances, and music, representing various nations.
The imagery of mountains and rivers suddenly appeared as a faint breeze entered the room; upon them, bees and butterflies fluttered and swallows and sparrows danced.

Looking down at them, one could not distinguish whether they were real or illusory. He further presented a "Ten-Thousand-Buddha Mountain" (Wanfo Shan) over ten feet high, which he placed within the Buddha chamber, covering its floor with a woolen rug.
This Ten-Thousand-Buddha Mountain was carved from agalloch, sandalwood, pearls, and jade.
Thus they were completed. As for the forms of these Buddhas, the larger ones exceeded one cun, while the smaller ones were seven or eight fen.

Some Buddha heads were like millet seeds; others were like half a bean. Their eyebrows, eyes, mouths, ears, *śikhā* (topknots), and *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tufts between the brows) were all clearly defined.

Nothing was lacking; moreover, banners and canopies were inlaid with gold, jade, and crystal. Hanging tassels and trees such as the *āmra* and *campaka* were fashioned from a hundred kinds of precious gems.
There were pavilions, towers, and palaces whose forms, though minute, appeared as if they were about to take flight.
Furthermore, before them were monks walking in procession, numbering no fewer than a thousand. Below was a golden bell made of purple-gold, three inches in diameter. Above—
A tortoise’s mouth was used to hold it. Every time its bell was struck, the monks performing their circumambulations would prostrate themselves, their heads touching the ground.
Within it, a deep, resonant sound emerged, called the "Brahma-sound" (*brahmaghoṣa*); this was because the resonance lay within the bell itself.
Although the mountain is named after the Ten Thousand Buddhas, their number is beyond reckoning. Furthermore, nine radiant fans were placed among the peaks of the cliffs. In the fourth month...
On the eighth day, he summoned the two assemblies of monks to enter the inner sanctuary to pay homage to the Myriad Buddha Mountains.

At that time, the onlookers marveled that it was not the work of human hands; furthermore, as they beheld a nine-colored light within the hall, they all called it the "Buddha-light"—this was none other than the Nine-Light Fan.
Consequently, the Emperor commanded the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra to recite a thousand verses of Indian secret mantras before withdrawing.

The first year of the Jiànzhōng era of Emperor Dēzōng, autumn, the seventh month, day *dīngchū*: the practice of providing *āvalambana* bowls from the imperial treasury was abolished, and monks were no longer commissioned for the inner chapel (*nèidàochǎng*).
This is not recorded in the "Basic Annals" (*běnjì*) of Emperor Dēzōng in the *Tángshū*. According to the "Basic Annals" of Emperor Dēzōng in the *Jiù Tángshū*, it states as follows: [text omitted].

In the first year of the Xingyuan era, Dharma Master Fazhao was invited into the inner palace to instruct the palace women in the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) and the Five Assemblies (*wuhui*).
According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Dezong" in the *Jiu Tang Shu*, this is not recorded;

however, according to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the first year of the Xingyuan era of Emperor Dezong’s reign, Dharma Master Fazhao was practicing the Five Assemblies at Bingzhou, teaching people to recite the Buddha's name, while the Emperor [was present] in the inner palace.

He had often heard that in the northeast there were sounds of those reciting the Buddha’s name. He dispatched an envoy to search for them in Taiyuan, where he indeed witnessed the flourishing success of the Master’s exhortations and conversions.
He subsequently invited the Master into the imperial palace, where he instructed the palace ladies in the recitation of the Buddha’s name, extending this practice through five assemblies.
In the third year of the Zhenyuan era, Yu Wenhuan memorialized that the abandoned temples of his local villages should be used as timber for school buildings.

An imperial edict decreed that he be punished for the crime of violating and destroying the Triple Gem. According to the *Beishi* (History of the Tang), the Annals of Emperor Dezong do not record this event.

However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the third year of the Zhenyuan era, Yu Wenhuan, the Governor of Jingzhao, memorialized requesting that abandoned temples in the countryside be converted into schools.

The materials for the temple were abandoned. An imperial edict stated: "To convert a palace dedicated to the Buddha into a Confucian academy is the beginning of an encroachment upon and destruction of the Triple Gem;
the guilt for this shall not be pardoned. Xuán was filled with shame and fear, and that very day he resigned his office and returned home.

In the sixth year of the Zhenyuan era, an imperial edict was issued to send back the Buddha’s bone to Wuyouwang Monastery. According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Dezong" in the *Jiu Tangshu*, this is not recorded;

however, according to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Dezong" in the *Jiu Tangshu*, in the second month of the sixth year of Zhenyuan, there was a finger bone of the Buddha, over one cun in length, at Wuyouwang Monastery in Qizhou.
It had previously been brought to the imperial palace for veneration. On the day of Yihai, an edict was issued.
He was sent back to his original temple.
In the thirteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, because Huo Xianming was ill, he ordered that monks be provided with meals at various temples.

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Dezong" in the *Jiu Tangshu*, this is not recorded; however, according to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Dezong" in the *Xin Tangshu*, it occurred in the thirteenth year of the Zhenyuan era.

In the seventh month of autumn, on the day Jichou, Huo Xianming, the Right Commander of the Shen-ce Army, fell ill. Ten horses were granted to him, and he was ordered to provide vegetarian feasts for the monks at various monasteries.

In the sixth year of the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xuanzong, an imperial decree was issued to Meng Jian and others to translate the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra*. (According to the *Jiu Tang Shu*, the History of the Tang).
The *Benji* (Basic Annals) of the [Xianzong] reign does not record this.

According to the *Jiushi Tangshu*, in the first month of spring in the sixth year of the Yuanhe era, an imperial edict was issued to Meng Jian, Palace Counselor; Liu Boru, Secretariat Drafter; and Gui Deng, Vice Minister of Works.
Xiao Mian, Right Assistant for Omissions, and others translated the *Mahāyāna-mūla-jātaka-citta-bhūmi-avalokiteśvara-sūtra* at Fengquan Temple.
On the gengxu day of the twelfth month in the thirteenth year of the Yuanhe era, they welcomed the Buddha’s bone from Fengxiang. (According to the *Jiu Tang Shu*).
The *Basic Annals* (*Benji*) of Emperor Xianzong state as follows:

"In the fourteenth year of the Yuanhe era, the Buddha’s bone-relics were welcomed to the capital. However, upon consulting the *Annals* of Emperor Xianzong in the *Book of Tang*, this is not recorded.
Furthermore, according to the biography of Han Yu, when Yu was serving as Vice Minister of the Ministry of Justice, Emperor Xianzong dispatched an envoy to Fengxian...
Xiang went out to welcome the Buddha’s relics. After they had been kept within the imperial palace for three days, they were then sent to the Buddhist temple.

Princes, dukes, and scholars rushed about, chanting and prostrating themselves; they even practiced the barbarian rites of branding their bodies and offering up precious treasures and shells, with the fragrance of incense wafting along the roads.

Han Yu heard of this and loathed it, so he submitted a memorial, saying: "The Buddha is merely one teaching of the barbarians. It was only during the Later Han dynasty that it first entered China. Above...
In antiquity, such a thing had never occurred. Formerly, the Yellow Emperor reigned for one hundred years and lived to the age of one hundred and ten.
Shao Hao reigned for eighty years and lived to the age of one hundred. Zhuanxu reigned for seventy-nine years and lived to the age of ninety.
Di Ku reigned for seventy years and lived to the age of one hundred and five. Yao reigned for ninety-eight years and lived to the age of one hundred and one.
At eighteen, Emperor Shun ascended the throne; both he and Yu lived to the age of one hundred. At that time, the world was at peace, and the common people were secure, happy, and long-lived.
Yet, the Buddha had not yet appeared in the Middle Kingdom. Subsequently, Tang also lived to the age of one hundred.
Tangsun Tai served as ruler for seventy-five years; Wuding reigned for fifty years.

Although the historical records do not state their lifespans, by calculating their respective regnal years, it appears they were no less than one hundred years old. King Wen of Zhou was ninety-seven years of age.
King Wu was ninety-three years old when he passed away. King Mu reigned for one hundred years. At that time, the Buddha-dharma had not yet reached China;
it was not because of his worship of the Buddha that this occurred. It was during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty that the Buddha-dharma first arrived.

Emperor Ming reigned for only eighteen years, after which periods of chaos and collapse followed in succession, and his dynastic mandate was not long-lasting. This was also the case with the Song, Qi, Liang, and Chen dynasties.

From the Northern Wei dynasty onwards, the practice of serving the Buddha gradually became more earnest, yet the duration of dynasties was particularly brief. Only Emperor Wu of the Liang reigned for forty-eight years;
during his tenure, he thrice surrendered himself as an offering to the Buddha. He ceased the use of sacrificial animals in ancestral temple rites and observed a single meal per day.
He subsisted on vegetables and fruit. Later, being pursued by Hou Jing, he starved to death at Taicheng, and his state also perished shortly thereafter.
Thus, seeking blessings by serving the Buddha resulted instead in calamity; from this one can see that it is clear the Buddha is not to be trusted.

When the High Ancestor first accepted the abdication from the Sui, he intended to abolish [the Buddhist establishment]. At that time, the officials lacked far-reaching insight and were unable to investigate the matter deeply.
The Way of the former kings has been proclaimed throughout antiquity and the present; yet, despite the propagation of sagely wisdom to remedy these evils, the matter ultimately persisted.
I have long harbored regret for this. I humbly reflect that Your Majesty, the Emperor, of Resplendent Sagacity, Martial Virtue, and Wisdom, is without peer in the thousands of years since antiquity.
At the very beginning of Your accession to the throne, You immediately forbade the ordination of persons as monks.
As for nuns and Daoist practitioners, it was also not permitted for them to establish separate temples or observatories.

At that time, I believed that the will of the High Ancestor would surely be carried out by Your Majesty. Although it may not yet be possible to implement this immediately, how could you allow such practices to flourish unchecked?

Now, Your Majesty has ordered the various monks to welcome the Buddha’s relics from Fengxiang, to observe them from the imperial terrace, and to carry them into the inner palace; furthermore, you have ordered all...

The temples have been successively provided with offerings. Although I am utterly foolish, I must know that Your Majesty is not deluded by Buddhism in performing these acts of veneration to pray for blessings and auspiciousness.

It is simply out of the joy of a bountiful harvest and to comply with the hearts of the people, providing a spectacle of the extraordinary and a source of amusement for the officials and commoners of the capital.
How could one as sagacious and enlightened as you ever be willing to believe [in such things]?
Such are these matters. However, the common people are ignorant and deluded; they are easily led astray and difficult to enlighten.

If they were to see Your Majesty acting in this manner, they would assume it was a sincere devotion to the Buddha, and all would say, "The Son of Heaven is a great sage who still devotes his whole heart to faith. Yet the common people are lowly and humble.
Regarding the Buddha, how could it be appropriate to further begrudge one's own body or life? Thus, they burn their heads and sear their fingers in groups of hundreds;

they strip off their clothes and scatter their money from morning until evening, emulating one another, fearing only that they might be late. Elder and young alike rush about, abandoning their livelihoods.
If you do not immediately impose prohibitions and restraints, as they travel to various other temples, there will surely be those who cut off their arms or slice their flesh as offerings.

"To offer such worship would wound public morality and ruin social customs, becoming a laughingstock throughout the four quarters; this is no small matter. The Buddha was originally a man of the barbarians;
his language was not mutually intelligible with that of the Middle Kingdom, his clothing was of a different style, and his mouth did not utter the legal teachings of the former kings."
Their persons do not wear the ritual robes of the former kings; they know nothing of the righteousness between ruler and subject or the affection between father and son.

Even if their bodies were still alive and they came to the capital to pay court by imperial command, Your Majesty would receive them with no more than a single audience in the Xuanzheng Hall, a single performance of guest-rites, and the bestowal of a single set of robes, before escorting them out across the border and not allowing them to remain.

"To be in two minds about the multitude is improper; how much more so for one whose body has long been dead, whose bones are withered and decayed, and who remains a remnant of the foul and impure—how could such a thing be fit to enter the palace precincts?

Confucius said, 'Revere the spirits and communicate with them. When the feudal lords of antiquity went to offer condolences in another state, they invariably ordered the shamans and priests to precede them with peach branches and bundles of reeds to sweep away all inauspiciousness before entering to pay their respects. Now, there is no such reason here."
To take up such decayed and filthy objects and personally inspect them— without the ritual masters performing their preliminary rites, without the peach branches or the *liè* brooms being employed,
and with neither the ministers speaking of their impropriety nor the Censors pointing out their errors— is truly a source of shame for me. I beg that these bones be consigned to fire and water,
so that their root may be forever severed, the doubts of the world eliminated, and the delusions of previous generations brought to an end, thereby enabling all people under heaven...
One knows that the deeds of a Great Sage transcend the ordinary by tens of thousands of times.

If the Buddha possesses spiritual power and can inflict calamity or misfortune, then whatever transgressions or evils exist should be visited upon this servant’s own person. With Heaven as my witness and overseer, I harbor no resentment or regret.
The memorial was submitted. The Emperor was greatly incensed and showed it to his ministers, intending to condemn Miu to death. Pei Du and Cui Qun said, "Miu’s words are indeed censorious."
This is indeed a grave offense and most fittingly deserves punishment. Yet, were it not for his harboring of ultimate loyalty within his heart, how could he have reached such a point?
I pray that you grant him some leniency so that he may come forward with remonstrance and debate. The Emperor said: "Mou’s claim that my devotion to Buddhism is excessive might still be tolerated;

however, as for his assertion that the emperors of the Later Han dynasty and those who followed all met an early death—that is a most perverse statement! Mou is a mere subject, yet he dares to be so audacious."
"He certainly cannot be pardoned. Thereupon, both those within and without the court were struck with alarm and fear; even the nobles of the imperial clan spoke on behalf of Han Yu.
Consequently, he was demoted to the post of Prefect of Chaozhou. According to the "Annals of Emperor Xianzong" in the *Jiu Tang Shu*:

on the day Dinghai of the first month in the spring of the fourteenth year of the Yuanhe era, the Buddhist relics from Famen Temple in Fengxiang were welcomed to the capital and remained in the imperial palace for three days.
Consequently, they were sent to various monasteries, where kings, dukes, officials, and commoners rushed to offer donations as if they could not wait long enough.
Han Yu, the Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, submitted a memorial vehemently exposing these abuses. On the *gui-si* day, Han Yu was demoted to serve as the Prefect of Chaozhou.
In the fifteenth year of the Yuanhe era, Emperor Muzong ascended the throne. He visited An Guo Temple to observe the *Ullambana* festival and further magnificently adorned various Buddhist temples.
According to the *New Book of Tang*, the Annals of Emperor Muzong do not record this;

however, according to the *Old Book of Tang*, the Annals of Emperor Muzong, on the *bingwu* day of the first month in the fifteenth year of Yuanhe, the Emperor ascended the throne, and on the *yi-mao* day of the seventh month, the Sovereign visited [the temple].
On the *renxu* day, he grandly adorned the An-guo, Ci-en, Qian-fu, Kai-ye,
and Zhang-jing temples and allowed Tibetan envoys to view them.
In the first year of the Changqing era of Emperor Muzong, Liu Zong submitted a petition requesting to become a monk and to convert his private residence into a Buddhist temple.

An imperial edict was issued granting the temple its name plaque and monastic robes; furthermore, he was bestowed the title Dajue. According to the *Tang Shu*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Muzong, this is not recorded;
however, according to the *Jiu Tang Shu*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Muzong, on the *jīmǎo* day of the second month in the first year of Changqing, the Regional Inspector of Youzhou...

The Regional Inspector Liu Zong submitted a memorial requesting to resign his post and shave his head to become a monk. On the *jiǎzǐ* day of the third month, Liu Zong requested that his private residence be converted into a Buddhist temple;
accordingly, an imperial messenger was dispatched to bestow the temple’s plaque with the name "Ba'en" (Gratitude).

When Youzhou reported that Liu Zong was firmly insisting on becoming a monk, the Emperor further bestowed upon him monastic robes. He was granted the honorary title "Dajue" (Great Enlightenment), but that very night he fled from Youzhou.
No one knew where he had gone. On the day of Gengwu in the fourth month of summer, Yiding reported that Liu Zong had already become a monk;

on the twenty-seventh day of the third month, he passed away within the jurisdiction of that province and was posthumously granted the title of Grand Marshal (Taishou). In the second year of the Changqing era, [the Emperor] visited Xingshanyin Temple.
He bestowed one hundred thousand coins upon the Sangha. He also commanded Prince Jing to accompany the Empress Dowager on a visit to Shiweng Temple.

According to the *Jiu Tang shu*, in the Mu Zong benji (Basic Annals of Emperor Mu Zong), it is recorded that on the *jīmō* day of the tenth month in the second year of the Changqing era, the Emperor traveled by way of the double road to Xianyang and stayed at Shanyin Fosi, where he bestowed gifts upon the monks. (Note: This is not recorded in the *Tang shu*, Mu Zong benji.)

One million coins. On the gengwu day of the eleventh month, he commanded Prince Jing to lead five hundred cavalrymen from the imperial guard to attend upon the Empress Dowager as she visited the Huaqing Palace and subsequently the Shiweng Temple.
On the guiyou day, the Emperor visited the Huaqing Palace to welcome the Empress Dowager;
he escorted her back immediately, returning only on the following day. On the jiwu day of the twelfth month, the two military commands within the palace...
The Princess presided over the households of her paternal relatives. As their illnesses were all cured and restored to health, they visited the temple to provide vegetarian meals for the monks.
In the third year of the Changqing era, two hundred bolts of silk were bestowed upon the monks; furthermore, five hundred bolts were bestowed.

(According to the *Tang Shu*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Muzong, this is not recorded. According to the *Jiu Tang Shu*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Muzong, it occurred in the eighth month of the third year of Changqing.)
In the first month, the Emperor traveled by way of the double road to Xingqing Palace; upon reaching Tonghuamen Gate, he bestowed two hundred bolts of silk upon the monk Chiheng.
In the eleventh month, the Emperor presided over Tonghuamen Gate to observe the construction of the Vaiśravaṇa deity, and consequently granted five hundred bolts of silk.
In the fourth year of the Changqing era, Emperor Jingzong ascended the throne. Wang Zhixing, the Prince of Xu and Si, requested the establishment of ordination platforms for monks and nuns.
According to the *Jingzong benji* (Basic Annals of Emperor Jingzong) in the *Jiu Tang shu* (Old Book of Tang), it is not recorded [in the *Xin Tang shu*].

However, according to the *Jingzong benji* in the *Jiu Tang shu*, on the day of Guiyou in the first month of the fourth year of Changqing, the Crown Prince ascended the throne; and on the day of Yiwu in the twelfth month, Wang Zhixing of Xu and Si...

Xing requested the establishment of ordination platforms (*sīmā-maṇḍala*) for monks and nuns. Li Deyu, the Inspector-General of Zhexi, submitted a memorial arguing that Xing was a sycophant and a seeker of favor.

Since the reign of Emperor Xianzong, an imperial edict had prohibited private ordinations and the unauthorized establishment of ordination platforms. Yet, despite this prohibition, Xing petitioned for them;
this was because such platforms had not been established for a long time, and consequently, the śramaṇas throughout the empire were rushing to him as if they could not wait. Xing sought to...
He accumulated great wealth through these means, which was viewed with disapproval by contemporary opinion.

In the second year of the Baoli era of Emperor Jingzong, because Yin Qiu had violated regulations, [the Emperor] requested that ordination platforms for monks and nuns be established; an imperial edict subsequently penalized him with a reduction in his stipend.

According to the *Jinshu* (New History of the Tang), the basic annals of Emperor Jingzong do not record this; however, according to the *Jiu Tangshu* (Old History of the Tang), it is recorded under the reign of Emperor Jingzong.

Record. On the day of Xinwei in the third month of the second year of the Baoli era, Yin You, the Inspector of Jiangxi, requested that a monastic ordination platform (jietan) for monks and nuns be established at Baoli Temple in Hongzhou.
The Imperial Edict stated: "Yin You has willfully violated established regulations by establishing an ordination platform. He shall be penalized with one year’s worth of his emoluments."
In the third year of the Tahe era of Emperor Wenzong, Shen Chuanshi requested that ordination platforms (*jietan*) be established for monks and nuns.
An imperial edict punished him with one month’s salary. According to the *Jiu Tang shu*, Wenzong’s Basic Annals, this is not recorded;

however, according to the *Jiu Tang shu*, Wenzong’s Basic Annals, on the *jyou* day of the tenth month in the third year of Tahe, Shen Chuanshi of Jiangxi memorialized: "On the anniversary of the Emperor’s birth, I request..."
He established a Fangdeng ordination platform for monks and nuns. An imperial edict stated: "It has been repeatedly decreed that no monks or nuns are to be ordained.

You, Master, being a provincial governor by title, ought to uphold these imperial statutes. To entice and lead on those who are ignorant and reckless is contrary to ritual and the Way; you shall be penalized with one month’s salary."
In the ninth year of the Tàihé era, an edict was issued prohibiting the ordination of persons as monks or nuns, following the words of Lí Xuàn;
subsequently, the inner monasteries were abolished and sacred images removed, though these measures were soon restored. According to the *Tángshū*, Wénzōng Běnjì, this is not recorded.
According to the *Jiù Tángshū*, Wénzōng Běnjì: on the dìsī day of the seventh month in the autumn of the ninth year of Tàihé, an edict was issued prohibiting the ordination of persons as...

Regarding Monks and Nuns: According to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the fourth month of the ninth year of the Taihe era, the Hanlin Academician Li Xun requested that the Daoist altar within the Changsheng Palace be abolished and that monks and nuns who were fraudulent or corrupt be purged.

On that day, sacred images were brought forth from the Great Interior; that night, a great wind arose, causing all four *chīwén* (ornamental dragon-heads) of the Hanyuan Palace to shake and fall, and uprooting three trees in front of the hall.
The quarters of the Golden Guard (Geum-u) and the watchtowers inside and out were destroyed, as were dozens of city gates; both the western wall and Gwanghwa Gate collapsed.
The soldiers and citizens were struck with terror. The Emperor, believing that Hyon’s requests had offended the will of Heaven, immediately issued an edict to halt the previous purge.
He restored the ritual images within the Great Palace, and the calamity began to subside.

In the second year of the Kaicheng era, an imperial edict was issued regarding the Qingcheng Festival (the Emperor’s birthday), stating that no extensive banquet assemblies should be held and that the monastic community should not be gathered in large numbers.
According to the *Jiu Tang shu*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Wenzong," on the day of Jia-shen in the eighth month of the second year of Kaicheng, the edict stated:

"The Qingcheng Festival is my birthday; let there be banquets throughout the empire so that all may share in the joy. *Note: This specific edict is not recorded in the "Basic Annals of Emperor Wenzong" in the *Xin Tang shu*.*

I, Tai, do not desire slaughter, using this to manifest my love for life. This is not because I hold the Buddhist gate (the "Empty Gate") in high esteem, nor is it to seek blessings free from falsehood.
I fear that officials and commoners at home and abroad might fail to understand my intentions;

therefore, the extensive arrangement of vegetarian feasts and the large-scale gathering of the monastic community not only waste material resources, but I also fear they may lead the people into delusion. From now on, at banquets, let there be only vegetarian food, and one may serve whatever meat broths or sauces one pleases.
This was established as a permanent precedent.

In the first year of the Huichang era of Emperor Wuzong, the Buddhist law (*bútú fǎ*) was abolished. According to the "Basic Annals" (*běnjì*) of Emperor Wuzong in the *Tángshū*, this is not recorded;

however, according to the "Treatise on Food and Commodities" (*Shíhuò zhì*), upon the accession of Emperor Wuzong, the Buddhist law was abolished, and throughout the realm, four thousand six hundred monasteries were destroyed.
There were one hundred [monasteries] and forty thousand *ārāmas* and *araṇyakas*. Those registered as monks and nuns numbered twenty-six thousand five hundred people;
slaves numbered one hundred fifty thousand; and fields numbered several million *qǐng*. There were over two thousand *muhū* and *xiān* (Zoroastrians) from Daqin (the Roman Empire).

In both the Eastern Capital and the Upper Capital, two monasteries were established in each ward (*jiē*), with thirty monks in each monastery. In the various provinces (*zhūdào*), three monks were stationed [per ward].
[The number of residents] did not exceed twenty. Yu said: "Sell the money and send it to the Ministry of Revenue; provide middle- and lower-grade fields to the temple households.
As for the slaves, let those who are able-bodied become taxpayers (liangshuihu), each receiving ten mu of land.

Since the monks and nuns have been exhausted [of their labor], provide ten *qǐng* of temple fields to the Compassionate Fields (Beitian) and Infirmary (Yangbingfang) in the two capitals, and seven *qǐng* in the various prefectures. Let the masters [of these lands] live out their natural lives."
