In the fourth year of Huichang, an imperial edict prohibited slaughter on the grounds of Buddhist doctrine; it was decreed that on the first day of the first month and the three "Original Days" (Sanyuan), each of these occasions would be observed as a three-day fast from killing, while on the anniversaries of the various emperors' deaths, a one-day fast would be observed.
On other days, there were no prohibitions. This is verified by the *Jiu Tang Shu*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Wuzong. It does not [contradict this].

I have further examined the *Jiù Tángshū* (Old Book of Tang), the Basic Annals of Emperor Wǔzōng. In the first month of spring in the fourth year of Huìchāng, an edict was issued to prohibit the slaughter of animals during the months of fasting, as this custom originated with the followers of Śākya.
Since the founding of our state, it has remained relatively close to the Liáng and Sui dynasties; consequently, some ministers and high officials have perpetuated this corruption.
Butchers have derived substantial profits from it, while those responsible for oversight have secretly accepted bribes. In the first month, by means of ten thousand...
At the beginning of the growth of things, three days of abstention were proclaimed; for the anniversaries of the various sages, one day of abstention was observed.

Furthermore, in accordance with the edict of the twenty-second year of the Kaiyuan era, three days of abstention were set for each of the Three Prime Days (*sanyuánrì*), while no restrictions were imposed during other months.

At that time, the Emperor was intent on studying the arts of the immortals and took Zhao Guizhen as his teacher. Taking advantage of his favor, Zhao Guizhen would, whenever he had an audience, disparage and destroy the followers of Śākyamuni, claiming they were not of the Middle Kingdom.
[His] teachings were said to "devour and exhaust the living beings," and he vowed to eliminate them entirely. The Emperor placed considerable faith in this.
On the *rénwǔ* day of the eighth month in the fifth year of Huichang, Buddhist temples were extensively destroyed, and monks and nuns were returned to the status of commoners.
(As recorded in the *Tángshū*, Basic Annals of Emperor Wǔzōng... According to the *Jiù Tángshū*, Basic Annals of Emperor Wǔzōng, in the fifth year of Huichang... Daoism...
The scholar Zhao Guizhen was especially favored with imperial courtesy. He subsequently recommended the Daoist of Luofu, Deng Yuanqi, who possessed arts for longevity.

The Emperor dispatched an imperial messenger to welcome him. Consequently, Guizhen became closely allied with Liu Yuanjing, a Daoist of Mount Heng, and together they persistently slandered the followers of Śākyamuni.
Thus, their petition to demolish monasteries was carried out. In the fourth month of summer, an edict was issued by the Ministry of Sacrifices.

An investigation was conducted to determine the number of monasteries, as well as the total number of monks and nuns throughout the empire. There were four thousand six hundred large monasteries and forty thousand *āraṇyakas* (hermitages).

The total number of monks and nuns was two hundred and sixty thousand and five. On the day of Gengzi in the seventh month of autumn, an imperial edict was issued to consolidate and reduce the number of Buddhist temples throughout the empire.

The Secretariat and the Chancellery compiled a detailed report to present to the throne; according to the established statutes, on the days of the national memorial services for former emperors in all prefectures and capitals, the officials...

Regarding the distribution of incense at the monasteries: among those [monasteries] of superior prefectures, one monastery each shall be retained. Any sacred images of the successive emperors present there shall be moved into these monasteries.

As for the monasteries of the subordinate prefectures, all shall be abolished. Regarding the two boulevards of the capital and the eastern capital, ten monasteries are requested to be retained, with ten monks for each.
The Imperial Edict states: "One monastery shall be retained from each superior prefecture; those whose craftsmanship is exquisite shall be preserved. As if...
Those that were ruined or had fallen into decay were also declared abolished. On the days when incense was to be offered, officials were dispatched to the Daoist and Buddhist monasteries.

In both the Upper Capital and the Lower Capital, two temples were retained in each ward; thirty monks were stationed at each temple. In the Left Ward of the Upper Capital, Ci’en and Jianfu Monasteries were retained;
in the Right Ward, Ximing and Zhuangyan Monasteries were retained. The Secretariat further memorialized regarding the bronze statues from the abolished temples throughout the empire.

Regarding bells and stone chimes: entrust the Salt and Iron Commissioner with the casting of coins. As for iron images, entrust them to their respective provinces to be cast into agricultural implements.

Gold, silver, brass, and stone images are to be melted down and delivered to the Ministry of Revenue. All gold, silver, bronze, and iron images possessed by members of the gentry and commoners must be surrendered to the authorities within one month following the issuance of this decree.
Should they fail to do so, the Salt and Iron Commissioner shall be charged with enforcing the regulations on the prohibition of copper.

As for the statues made of earth, wood, and stone, they should remain within the temple as before. Furthermore, it was memorialized that monks and nuns ought not to be subordinate to the Ministry of Sacrifices (Cibu), but should instead be subordinate to the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Si).
As for the temples of the Da Qin, the muhu, and the yao, since Buddhism has already been reformed and rectified, heterodox teachings may not be allowed to exist alone;
those individuals shall all be compelled to return to lay life and return to their original places of residence to fulfill their tax obligations.

[The prisoners] were returned to their original places as foreigners would be, and were placed under supervision. The Imperial Edict of the Eighth Month states: "I have heard that prior to the Three Dynasties, there was never mention of the Buddha.
It was after the Han and Wei dynasties that the teachings of the Image [Buddhism] gradually flourished. This was because this strange custom was transmitted during the final age."
The defilements of causal conditions have spread and multiplied until they have come to corrode the national character.

Gradually, without one’s awareness, they entice and delude the minds of men, causing the masses to become increasingly lost and weeping throughout the mountains and plains of the Nine Provinces and within the palace gates of the two capitals.

The ranks of monks increase daily, and Buddhist temples grow more magnificent each day; human labor is exhausted in works of earth and wood, and the people’s resources are plundered for gold and jewels.

To adorn oneself by abandoning one’s parents at the moment of becoming a teacher and disciple, and to violate the bond of spouses within the bounds of the precepts—no practice has ever caused greater harm to the Dharma or more injury to people than this path.
Furthermore, if one man does not farm, there will be those who suffer hunger; if one woman does not spin silk, there will be those who suffer from cold.
Today, the number of monks and nuns throughout the world is beyond counting, yet they all depend on agriculture for their food and depend on sericulture for their clothing.
As for their robes and monasteries—*zhao-ti* temples—their number is beyond reckoning; all are constructed like soaring clouds and elaborately adorned, rivaling the imperial palace itself.
That the material resources of the Jin, Song, Qi, and Liang dynasties declined and their social customs became corrupt and deceitful was entirely due to this.

How much more so in the case of our High Ancestor and the Great Emperor (Taizong), who settled the chaos through martial might and civilized the Middle Kingdom through culture; it was by wielding these two instruments that they achieved such results.

In governing the state, how could one allow the narrow teachings of the West to rival our own? During the Zhenguan and Kaiyuan eras, we likewise attempted reforms, yet they were not entirely eradicated;

instead, they continued to spread and flourish. Having extensively surveyed past precedents and sought out public opinion from all quarters, I have reached the firm conclusion that these abuses must be reformed without hesitation.
Now, loyal ministers both at home and abroad have harmonized with my supreme intention and submitted this detailed memorial.

This is most appropriate and ought to be implemented with determination. It shall serve to punish the source of a thousand-year-old corruption and establish the statutes and laws of a hundred sovereigns.

To benefit the people and aid the masses—how could I decline this? Consequently, of the more than four thousand six hundred monasteries throughout the realm that were abolished, twenty-six thousand five hundred and five monks and nuns were returned to lay life and enrolled as taxpayers for the two taxes.
Furthermore, four thousand *zhao-chi* and *lan-re* (monastic dwellings) were likewise abolished.

There were over ten thousand [monasteries]. He confiscated several million *qǐng* of the most fertile lands and enrolled one hundred and fifty thousand slaves as households subject to the two taxes (*liǎngshuì*).

Those formerly under the jurisdiction of monks and nuns were clearly distinguished; those of foreign faith, such as the Persian *muhū* and *fù*, numbering over two thousand, were returned to secular life.
Thus, they did not intermingle with the customs of the Central Kingdom. Alas! This was something never practiced in antiquity. It seems...

There was a time when things were expected to remain as they were; yet now, all have departed. How could one say there is no such time? Those who are idle, wandering, and devoid of occupation already number more than a hundred thousand.

Abandoned dwellings, painted in vermilion and azure but serving no purpose, exceed a billion in number. From this point forward, let us purify ourselves to instruct the people and aspire to the principle of non-action (*wuwei*);
let governance be simplified and made equitable to achieve the merit of a unified custom. Thus shall the common people throughout the six realms be made to share in [this transformation].

Returning to the Imperial Transformation, I still consider that at the beginning of reforming abuses, the common people are unaware of their daily conduct. Therefore, I issue this decree to the brilliant court to proclaim my intent:

On the *jiachen* day of the eleventh month, an imperial edict was issued for the *Beitian* (Fields of Compassion) and infirmary establishments. Because monks and nuns have returned to lay life, there is no one to preside over them; I fear those who are disabled will have no means of support.
Accordingly, temple lands shall be allocated in measured portions from the two capitals to provide relief. [The same shall apply] to the seven prefectures and commanderies...
The holdings now reached ten *qǐng* each; from among those under their respective jurisdictions, one senior monk was selected for each to manage them so as to provide the ingredients for the gruel.

In the sixth year of the Huichang era, Emperor Xuanzong ascended the throne and issued an edict that, in addition to the four temples previously retained by the two streets of the capital, eight more were to be established.
(This is not recorded in the *Xuanzong benji* of the *Jiu Tang shu*; it is recorded in the *Xuanzong* section of the *Jiu Tang shu*.)

Basic Annals. In the third month of the sixth year of the Huichang era, the Emperor ascended the throne. In the fifth month, the Merit Commissioner of the Left and Right Quarters submitted a memorial stating:

"In accordance with the provisions of the amnesty edict issued on the fifth day of this month, in addition to the four long-established temples remaining in the two quarters of the Capital, eight more shall be established.
Two shall retain their existing names, Xingfu Temple and Baoshou Temple; the remaining six shall have their former names changed."
Baoying Temple was renamed Zisheng Temple; Qinglong Temple was renamed Huguo Temple; Puti Temple was renamed Baotang Temple;
Qingchan Temple was renamed Anguo Temple; Fayun Nunnery was renamed Tang’an Temple;
Chongjing Nunnery was renamed Tangchang Temple. These eight establishments were added to the Right Street. Ximing Temple was renamed... [text ends]
Fushou Temple was established. Zhuangyan Temple was renamed Shengshou Temple.
Of the two old temples retained, Qianfu Temple was renamed Xingyuan Temple, and Huadu Temple was renamed Chongfu Temple. Yongtai Temple was renamed Wanshou Temple;
Wen guo Temple was renamed Chongsheng Temple; Jingxing Temple was renamed Longxing Temple. [The Emperor] honored...
The temple was renamed Xingfu Temple; this was granted by imperial decree in accordance with the petition.
Twelve Daoist practitioners, including Liu Yuanjing, were executed because their doctrines had deluded Emperor Wuzong and they had slandered and destroyed the teachings of the Śākya clan.
The first year of the Dazhong era of Emperor Xuanzong, the intercalary third month: the Buddhist temples were largely restored.
According to the *New Táng Shū*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Xuanzong, an edict was issued in the intercalary third month of the first year of the Dazhong era: [text follows].

In the final years of the Huichang era, monasteries were consolidated and abolished. Although it was claimed that this was a foreign teaching and would not harm the source of governing principles, the people of the Middle Kingdom had long practiced its Way;
thus, the reforms were excessive and the underlying substance of the matter was not fully considered.

Regarding the sacred mountains and superior sites throughout the prefectures and commanderies of the empire, as for the monasteries abolished in the fourth month of the fifth year of Huichang that possessed ancient and established names:
The *saṃgha* may further undertake repairs and renovations; the abbot shall have full authority over them, and the relevant administrative offices must not prohibit such actions.

During the Xiántóng era of Emperor Yìzōng, śramaṇas were ordered to enter the imperial palace to perform rites of prayer. According to the *Tángshū*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Yìzōng do not record this.
However, according to the biography of Xiāo Fǎng, at the beginning of the Xiántóng era, Fǎng served as the Left Grand Master for Ceremonial Attendants (*zuò sànqí chángshì*).
Attendant: Emperor Yizong neglected the affairs of state and took pleasure in Buddhism. He summoned monks into the inner palace to perform rites of prayer and sacrifice.

He frequently visited Buddhist monasteries and bestowed extensive alms. I follow the admonitions [of past sages] and consider that the Indian dharma—which involves severing attachments to attain extinction—is not something a sovereign should emulate or admire.

Rather than now committing these writings to the Sanskrit script and reciting the sounds of the Buddha, it would be better to rectify false rewards and excessive punishments, and to dispel calamities through prayer.

How much more so for the Buddha, who can be apprehended through awakening but cannot be sought through physical marks. Although the Emperor was昏縱 (obscured and unrestrained), he still praised and sighed over these words.
In the fifth year of the Xiántóng era, Páiyán memorialized with a petition urging the construction of Buddhist temples; the Emperor responded with a gracious edict. (According to the records:)
The *Jishi* (Basic Annals) of Emperor Yizong in the *New Book of Tang* does not record this.

However, according to the *Old Book of Tang*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Yizong, in the first month of spring in the fifth year of the Xiancong era, the Censor-in-Chief Pei Tan submitted a memorial arguing that as the empire was mobilizing troops and financial resources were already depleted, it was improper to further promote the construction of Buddhist temples, thereby exhausting the state’s strength. The Emperor responded with a gracious edict.
In the fifth month of the twelfth year of the Xiántóng era, the Emperor visited Ān-guó Monastery and bestowed upon the monks lecturing on the sūtras high thrones made of *candana* (sandalwood).
According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Yìzōng" in the *Tángshū*, this is not recorded. However, according to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Yìzōng" in the *Jiù Tángshū*, it states [as follows].
Furthermore, according to the *Dùyáng zábiān*, because the Emperor revered the teachings of India, he had two high thrones manufactured in the winter of the twelfth year.
The State Temple of Xin’an was bestowed [upon him]. There were two lecture seats: one for the exposition of the Dharma and one for the chanting of the scriptures.

Each was twenty feet high, with a frame carved from polished agallochum and sandalwood and coated in lacquer. Gold and silver were inlaid to form the shapes of dragons, phoenixes, flowers, and trees, which completely covered their surfaces.
Furthermore, small square seats were provided, before which were placed scripture tables, followed by incense basins, and at the four corners stood golden *kāṇḍikās*.
It was thirty feet high, with stone steps and railings all fully provided. In front were embroidered silk curtains and cushions, so exquisite and marvelous as to be unsurpassed in their time.
There, he immediately established a vegetarian feast for ten thousand people and issued an edict that eminent monks should take the lead in delivering lectures.
The Emperor also founded An Guo Temple, where the halls, palaces, corridors, and buildings were grand and magnificent; among them, three bays were particularly adorned and profoundly secluded.
The world acclaimed this as the finest work. The artisans labored day and night to complete it. The Emperor personally visited to reward their toil, and spectators gathered like a wall around him.
On the anniversary of his birth, he had a temple constructed within the palace using colored silks; he bestowed brocade robes upon all officials from the highest ranks downward.
Li Keji once instructed several men to perform a troupe of the "Four Directions" *Púsàmán* dance.
In the third month of the fourteenth year of the Xiántóng era, the Buddha’s relics were welcomed from Fǎmén Monastery in Fèngxiáng.
According to the *Tángshū*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Yìzōng," and according to the *Jiù Tángshū*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Yìzōng":

on the day of Gēngwǔ in the third month of the fourteenth year of Xiántóng, an imperial edict was issued for the monks of the two monastic districts to welcome the Buddha’s relics from Fǎmén Monastery in Fèngxiáng. On the eighth day of the fourth month, the Buddha’s relics [were brought forth].
Upon arriving at the capital, from Kaiyuan Gate to Anfu Gate, colorful pavilions lined the roads, and the sound of chanting the Buddha’s name shook the earth.
The Emperor ascended Anfu Gate to receive him with ritual prostrations. He was welcomed into the inner sanctuary for three days.

When he departed for the various temples throughout the capital, men and women gathered like clouds; his majestic deportment and magnificent attire were beyond compare in antiquity. The Imperial Edict stated: "I, by virtue of my meager merit, have succeeded to..."

Having inherited this vast enterprise, fourteen years have passed. Recently, as bandits have been rampant and the imperial army has not ceased its operations, I, the Emperor, have remained in office with anxious diligence, cherishing and nurturing all living beings.

Consequently, I have honored the Buddhist teachings and held the Primordial Gate (Daoism) in the highest esteem. I have invited the True Body [of the Buddha] to pray for the blessing of the myriad people.
Now, the crowds who come to behold it block the roads and narrow the paths. As I repeatedly think of those in prison, they occupy my thoughts whether I am resting or rising.
I am concerned for you, my common people, who have fallen into the snares of criminal law. Moreover, as the summer heat intensifies, those bound in fetters and shackles suffer;

some remain confined in dark dungeons for long periods, which harms the harmonious vital energy (*qi*), while others are harassed by legal entanglements and interrogations, thereby obstructing their agricultural labors.

Throughout the capital and all the prefectures, provinces, and counties under heaven, the imprisonment of offenders shall be suspended—with the exception of those guilty of the ten heinous crimes, patricide, matricide, intentional homicide, or officials who have committed embezzlement.

The manufacture of poisons, the setting of fires, the carrying of weapons, the exhumation of graves, and other remaining offenses—whether grave or light, according to their respective grades—shall each be reduced by one degree.
Those within the capital’s military garrisons shall be investigated and settled within two days, after which a report shall be submitted to the throne.
For the prefectures and provinces throughout the empire, a report shall be submitted within three days of the arrival of this edict. (According to the *Duyang zabi*: Spring of the fourteenth year.)
An imperial edict was issued for several dozen monks of great virtue to welcome the Buddha’s relics from Famen Temple in Fengxiang.

When the various officials submitted memorials to remonstrate, some cited the precedents of Emperor Xianzong. The Emperor said, "If I can merely see them while alive, I shall have no regrets when I die.
He then had a precious pagoda fashioned of gold and silver, a precious canopy of pearls and jade, and the incense palanquin further adorned with peacock down.
The precious stupas (*caitya*) were adorned; the smaller ones were one zhang high, and the larger ones two zhang.
They were carved from fragrant sandalwood into the forms of flying eaves, flowered railings, tiles, woodwork, steps, and paving stones. These were entirely covered above with gold and silver.

To carry a single stupa required several hundred laborers. The precious canopies and incense carriages were beyond reckoning; their exquisite craftsmanship was so brilliant that it vied with the sun for splendor.
Furthermore, banners and streamers were fashioned entirely from coral, agate, pearls, and musaragalva, utilizing miscellaneous precious gems totaling no fewer than a hundred *hu*.
Approximately ten thousand sets of banners and parasols were crafted from cut silken ribbons.

On the eighth day of the fourth month, when the Buddha’s relics entered Chang’an, the sound of the Buddha’s name shook the earth from the Kaiyuan Gate to the Anfu Lou. Men and women gazed upon them in worship.
The monastic community followed in procession as the Emperor proceeded to Anfu Temple (Anfusi), where he personally prostrated himself in worship, his tears soaking his breast.

He immediately summoned the monks serving in the two streets (the eastern and western monasteries) and bestowed upon them gold and silk in varying amounts. Furthermore, he granted silver bowls and brocade to all the elders of the capital who had welcomed the true remains during the Yuanhe era.
The wealthy families of Chang’an vied with one another to adorn their carriages and attire; they crowded the roads shoulder to shoulder in great numbers. Four...
As people came from all directions—leading the elderly and supporting the young—there were none who did not prepare simple, plain offerings in anticipation of his grace and blessings.
At that time, there was a soldier who severed his left arm before the Buddha and held it in his hand; with every step he took a prostration, blood spilling onto the ground.

Others went so far as to crawl on their elbows and knees, biting off fingers and cutting off hair, in numbers beyond calculation. Furthermore, there was a monk who shaved the hair from the crown of his head, saying:
As he was performing the "refining of the crown" (*zhìdǐng*), fire broke out and pain arose; he immediately shook his head, shouting through the marketplace.
Young men seized him and prevented him from moving, yet the pain was unbearable, so he lay wailing on the road with his head scorched and ruined, his movements distressed.
All who saw him could not help but laugh loudly. When the Emperor went to welcome the Buddha’s bone relics, he entered the inner sanctuary (*nèidào chǎng*). Immediately—
Canopies of golden flowers were set up, and beds of warm and cool temperature were prepared, with mats of dragon-scale and cushions of phoenix-feather.
Incense of jade-essence was burned, and milk of crystal-fat was offered; all of these were tributes presented by the kingdom of Ho-ling over nine years prior.

When the Buddha’s relics were first welcomed, an imperial decree was issued ordering that earthen stupas be constructed along the roadside throughout the capital and the surrounding provinces, reaching heights of one or two zhang.
Reaching heights of eight or nine chi, they were all adorned with gold and turquoise. Within the capital city, there were approximately ten thousand such structures.
At that time, it was rumored that the fragrant stupas shook, and auspicious clouds and Buddha-radiance appeared upon the streets. Those who spoke of these events regarded them as extraordinary omens.

Furthermore, wealthy families in the market districts held great *anivārita* (unrestricted) vegetarian assemblies, constructing pavilions, terraces, and towers made of colored silks along the main thoroughfares.
In the palace halls, they sometimes used mercury to form ponds and gold and jade to fashion trees. They vied with one another to assemble monks and extensively install Buddha images.

Conch shells were blown and gongs struck, while lamps and candles followed one after another in succession. Furthermore, they ordered young boys to wear jade belts and gold forehead-plates, and to go barefoot, shouting out invocations amidst the scene as they indulged in their play at will.
They also fashioned small carriages from brocade and embroidery to carry those who sang and danced, just as [in the previous description].
This was true; while the area surrounding the imperial capital was already prosperous, Yanshou Ward was particularly the pinnacle of splendor.
In the seventh month of the autumn of that year, the Emperor passed away, and the Princess died as well; thus, the title "Tongchang" (Radiant Harmony) became clearly manifest.
In the [blank] year of Emperor Xizong’s reign, an imperial edict was issued to return the Buddha-relics to Famen Temple.

According to the *Basic Annals* of Emperor Xizong in the *Tang Shu*, this is not recorded. However, according to the *Duyang Zabi*, when Emperor Xizong ascended the throne, he issued an edict to return the Buddha-relics to Famen Temple.
Their procession and ceremonial protocol were such that not even one-tenth remained; they were merely a semblance of the former grandeur. Nevertheless, the elders of the capital city...
Men and women vied with one another to see him off. Holding hands, they said to each other, "In sixty years, we have welcomed the True Body but once;
we do not know when we shall behold it again. They then bowed their heads before him, sobbing and shedding tears.
At every incense hall along the way, imperial edicts ordered them all to be demolished; in the capital region, scarcely one or two remained.

In the first year of Kaiping of Emperor Taizu, an imperial decree was issued that monks and nuns were to be transferred from the jurisdiction of the Department of State Affairs (Liubu) to the Department of Sacrifices (Cibu).
The śramaṇa Zhixuan of Quanzhou traveled to India to seek Buddhist scriptures; upon his return, he presented to the imperial court the bone of a Pratyekabuddha and palm-leaf Sanskrit manuscripts.

According to the *Wudai shi* (History of the Five Dynasties), the *Benji* (Basic Annals) of Emperor Taizu of Liang does not record this event; however, the *Fozu tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs) states as follows.

In the third year of the Kaiping era, on the Day of Great Brightness (Damingjie), an imperial edict was issued for the hundred officials to go to the temple to offer incense and pray for [the Emperor’s] longevity.

This is not recorded in the *Beidai Shi* (History of the Five Dynasties), *Benji* (Basic Annals) of Liang Taizu; however, it is stated in the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), and so forth.
In the first year of the Zhengming era of Emperor Mòdi, the śramaṇa Guīxù of the East Pagoda Monastery presented the *Jīnglùn huìyào* (Essentials of the Sūtras and Śāstras).

By imperial decree, it was included in the Great Canon, and he was bestowed the title of Grand Master of Propagating the Teaching (*Yǎnjiào Dàshī*). According to the *Wǔdài shǐ* (History of the Five Dynasties), the Basic Annals of Emperor Mòdi do not record this;
however, the *Fózǔ tǒngjì* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddha and Patriarchs) states as follows.

The first year of Longde (904), the third month of spring, on the day Dinghai, the first day of the lunar month, the private ordination of monks and nuns was prohibited. According to the *Beidai Shi* (History of the Five Dynasties), in the Annals of Emperor Mudi of Liang, it states:

"According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the first year [of Longde], an imperial edict was issued throughout the realm that no one was permitted to privately ordain monks or nuns;
those wishing to leave the household life must enter the capital city and undergo examinations of their mastery of the scriptures."

In the first year of the Tongguang era of Emperor Zhuangzong of the Later Tang, an imperial edict was issued to provide a vegetarian feast for one thousand monks. According to the "Basic Annals of the Tang" in the *Wudai Shi* (History of the Five Dynasties), this is not recorded;

however, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), on the birthday of the [Buddha] in the first year of Tongguang, an edict was issued to the Superintendent of Monks, Huijiang.
The Daoist Cheng Zixiao entered the inner palace to engage in discussion; a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks was provided.
In the second year of the Tongguang era, an imperial edict commanded the monk Huiruan to enter the inner palace to inquire about the methods of Chan.

(According to the *Wudai shi*, the *Basic Annals of Emperor Zhuangzong of Tang*, this is not recorded. According to the *Fozu tongji*, in the second year of Tongguang, an edict was issued to the Three Sages.)

Chan Master Huìràn entered the inner palace to inquire about the methods of Chan. The Emperor said, "Since I descended upon Daliang, I have obtained a priceless jewel, yet no one has offered a price for it.
Huìràn said, "I beg Your Majesty to let me examine this treasure. The Emperor extended the corners of his *fùtóu* (head-wrap) with his hand.

Huìràn said, "As for the treasure of an emperor, who would dare to offer a price? The Emperor was delighted. When Huìràn passed away, the Emperor issued an edict bestowing upon him a posthumous title.
The stupa of Great Master Guangji Tongji.
In the third year of the Tongguang era, the cavalry officer Shi Yingqiang requested ordination; he was granted the title of Great Master Wuxue.

According to the *Wudai shi* (History of the Five Dynasties), the *Benji* (Basic Annals) of Emperor Zhuangzong of the Tang does not record this. According to the *Fozu tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), it occurred in the third year of the Tongguang era.

The cavalry general Shi Yingqiang had achieved merit in battle. Accompanying the imperial entourage into Luoyang, he suddenly attained awakening to the path of Chan. He requested permission to leave the household life and was given the name Qiche;
the Emperor bestowed upon him the title of Master Wuxue and converted his residence into Lide Monastery.

In the fourth year of the Tiānfú era of Emperor Gāozǔ of the Later Jìn, an imperial edict was issued establishing the incense offering and the feeding of monks on the anniversary of the state’s founding as a fixed ritual.

Furthermore, an edict was issued to include Seng Kěhóng’s *Yìnyì of the Great Canon* (Dàzàngjīng yìnyì) into the Great Canon (*Dàzàng*). According to the *Wǔdài Shǐ* (History of the Five Dynasties), in the Basic Annals of Emperor Gāozǔ of the Jìn:

*Bu zai*. According to the *Xīxī cóngyǔ*, the practice of "incense-walking" (*xíngxiāng*) originated during the Later Wei dynasty and continued through the Qi and Liang periods of the Southern Dynasties.

In the sixth year of the Kaibao era, the Emperor visited Xiangguo Temple. He decreed that for each prefecture, no more than one monk per hundred would be permitted to receive ordination annually.
By imperial edict, Indian monks were summoned to the capital and granted purple square-cut robes.

According to the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Taizu," on the Bingzi day of the third month in the sixth year of Kaibao, he visited Xiangguo Temple to view the newly constructed pagoda; on the twelfth month, he limited the number of monks permitted to be ordained.
Regarding the Dharma: it was decreed that from the monastic registers of various prefectures, one person would be permitted to receive ordination per year for every hundred [monastics].

According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs): in the sixth year, Wang Guicong, the Governor of Fuzhou, submitted a memorial stating that the Tripitaka Master Dharmadeva from Central India had arrived.

He translated the *Sūtra of the Holy Amitāyus* and the *Praise of the Seven Buddhas*. The Śramaṇa Facheng of the Fanxue Monastery in Hexing Prefecture served as the scribe to compose the prose. Gui...

From the *Runse* (Chronicle of Imperial Edicts): Emperor Fǎtiān was summoned to the palace. Upon his arrival, the Emperor received him in audience, offered him words of comfort and inquiry, and bestowed upon him a purple square-cut robe (*zifāngpáo*).

According to the *Guītiānlù* (Records of Returning to the Fields), when Emperor Taizǔ first visited the Xiàngguó Temple, he went before the Buddha statue to burn incense and asked whether one should prostrate or not.
The monk Zhànníng replied, "One does not prostrate. When the Emperor asked for the reason, he answered, "The Buddha is currently present."

When paying homage to the Buddhas of the past, Zan Ning was quite literate and possessed eloquence. Although his speech resembled that of a court jester, it happened to suit the Emperor's disposition;

thus, the Emperor smiled and nodded in approval, whereby this became established as a fixed regulation. To this day, when the Emperor goes on imperial tours, incense is burned but no prostrations are made.
Commentators consider this to be in accord with propriety.

In the eighth year of the Kaibao era, he visited a Buddhist temple and paid homage at the stupa of the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi. He personally transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and recited it.
According to the "Basic Annals of Taizu" in the *Song Shi*: "In the eleventh month of the winter of the eighth year of Kaibao, he went to inspect the newly established Longxing Temple.
According to the *Fozu Tongji*: "In the third month of the eighth year, the Emperor traveled to Luoyang and arrived at Longmen."

At Guanghua Temple on Mount Shan, he visited the stupa of the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra to pay homage to his remains. In the fourth month, as the Emperor was about to perform the suburban sacrifice to Heaven, the rain did not cease. He dispatched an envoy to pray at the stupa of Amoghavajra, and by the appointed time, the sky cleared. Upon returning from Luoyang to the capital, the Emperor personally transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and frequently recited it himself. When Prime Minister Zhao Pu saw this while attending to state affairs, the Emperor said: [The Emperor said: "I have heard that the Buddha’s Dharma is profound and subtle, and its meaning is difficult to fathom. Yet, the *Vajracchedikā* is concise and easy to understand; its principles are clear and its words are plain. I have read it many times, yet each reading reveals new insights. It is truly a scripture that can transform the mind. He then ordered the scribe to record these words. Furthermore, he commanded that every day, after the midday meal, the *Vajracchedikā* be recited once in the palace. He also decreed that all officials of the third rank and above must each copy one volume of the sutra and submit it to the imperial library. Thus, the merit of the sutra spread throughout the realm.

It was also reported that whenever the Emperor faced difficulties or undertook military expeditions, he would first recite this sutra before setting out. Consequently, his campaigns were always victorious and his governance was harmonious. This was because the power of the Buddha’s Dharma is vast and inconceivable. Those who encounter it and practice accordingly will surely attain liberation. Therefore, one should know that the *Vajracchedikā* is the supreme vehicle for attaining the Way. One should respect and uphold it with utmost sincerity. If one recites it even once, one will be reborn in the presence of the Buddhas of the ten directions. How much more so if one copies, reads, and explains it! May all beings hear this and believe it. Do not doubt it. It is the true path to the cessation of suffering. Thus ends the account.
He said, "I do not wish for the armored warriors to know of this; it will suffice to say that I am merely reading military treatises.
In the ninth year of the Kaibao era, he visited various monasteries to view the Tripitaka. According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), in the Basic Annals of Emperor Taizu:
on the *jihai* day of the eighth month in the ninth year of Kaibao, he visited Xinglongxing Temple; on the *yisi* day, he visited Dengjue Yuan, and subsequently proceeded to [other sites].
He visited Dongzhuyuan and bestowed money upon the artisans. He also visited Kai bao si to inspect the Tripitaka.
In the first year of Taiping Xingguo of Emperor Taizong’s reign, an imperial edict restored the government granary to become Longxing Monastery.

The Emperor composed the "Preface to the Newly Translated Holy Teachings" and presented it to the Indian monk. (Note: This is not recorded in the *Song Shi*, Taizong Benji; according to the *Leiyi Dianlüe*...)

Yuan. In the first year of the Taiping Xingguo era, Emperor Taizong of the Song dynasty [reigned] initially followed the precedent of Emperor Shizong of the Later Zhou, who had abolished Longxing Temple to convert it into an official granary.

At the beginning of the new dynasty, the monks of the temple beat drums to petition for its restoration; by this time, they had not ceased their efforts. The Emperor dispatched an envoy carrying a sword to interrogate them, saying, "This place has served as a granary for the former dynasty for a long time.
Why do you trouble the imperial court with such persistence? He further gave secret instructions that they were to be executed on the spot if they showed fear. The monks declined.

He remained composed and said, "The previous dynasty was unrighteous; they destroyed images and abolished monasteries. We rely solely upon today’s sagely brilliance to restore them. Why should this poor monk fear death?
The imperial envoy reported this to the Emperor, who was deeply moved and sighed with appreciation. He issued an edict to restore the site as a monastery (according to the *Xu Wénxiàn Tōngkǎo*).
In the first year, the Emperor composed the "Preface to the Newly Translated Tripitaka Holy Teachings" and bestowed it upon Heaven... [text ends]... Monastery.

In the second year of the Taiping Xingguo era, the Tripiṭaka Master Zhuxian was commissioned to rename Longxing Temple as Taiping Xingguo Temple and establish the Kaixian Hall to enshrine the imperial portrait of Emperor Taizu.
The Śramaṇa Śrīghana from India arrived and presented palm-leaf Sanskrit scriptures.
According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), in the Basic Annals of Emperor Taizong, [this event] is not recorded.

However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs) and other sources, in the third year of the Taiping Xingguo era, an imperial edict was issued granting temple names and purple square-cut robes to monks throughout the realm.

Furthermore, posthumous titles for monks and names for their stupas were bestowed. Emperor Taizong dispatched Zhao Rong to welcome the Śāriputra stupa containing the relics of King Aśoka from Mingzhou, appointing him as the Head of Monks (*Sengtong*).
Zanning served as a member of the Hanlin Academy. According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Taizong do not record this.

However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the third month of the third year of the Taiping Xingguo era, imperial plaques were bestowed upon unnamed temples throughout the realm, naming them "Taiping Xingguo" and "Qianming.
Furthermore, the śramaṇas Jicong and others, who had returned from India in the Kaiyuan Temple, presented Sanskrit scriptures and Buddhist images.
A śarīra stūpa, bodhi tree leaves, and a peacock-feather whisk were bestowed, along with a purple square-cut robe.

In the fourth month, an imperial edict conferred the posthumous title "Yuánwù" (Perfect Enlightenment) upon Dharma Master Yuǎn of Lúshān, and his stūpa was named "Níngjì" (Tranquil Stillness). For Dharma Master Yǒng, the title was "Juéjì" (Awakened Stillness), and his stūpa was named "Shízhi" (True Wisdom).
A śramaṇa from Central India, Pánmó, arrived to present a Buddha-śarīra stūpa; an edict was issued for him to be received by an attendant official.
Zhao Rong traveled to Wuyue to welcome the Buddha-relic stupa of King Aśoka from Mingzhou.
When Wang Qian of Wuyue submitted the imperial maps and registers to the court, he ordered the Buddhist Patriarch Zan Ning to escort the Śākyamuni relic stupa for an audience at Zifu Hall.
The Emperor, who had long heard of his reputation, summoned him seven times in a single day and bestowed upon him the title of Great Master Tonghui, appointing him to the Hanlin Academy.
The Academician Tao Gu was among his colleagues. Someone once derided him, saying, "How can such a person find a place in these azure lattice windows and vermilion pillars?
Yet when he engaged in conversation with the scholar, the latter cited the Classics and Histories with an unending flow of erudition. The detractor was thereby struck with awe and submission.
Whenever the Academicians Wang Yucheng and Xu Xuan had doubts, they would consult him; both bowed to him in reverence, treating him with the etiquette due to a teacher. His influence thus grew.
The "Hall of Blessings" (Fùdiàn) is where Buddha images and scriptural treasuries are enshrined, and where pagodas and bells are established; it is the inner sanctuary.

In the fifth year of the Taiping Xingguo era, Buddha images were cast, various Chan monasteries and monk-stupas were constructed, and the Translation Institute was established, marking the commencement of translation activities.
According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Taizong do not record this. According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs)...

General Record. In the first month of the fifth year of the Taiping Xingguo era, an imperial edict was issued to the inner attendant Zhang Tingxun to go to Mount Wutai in Daizhou to cast a gilded-bronze image of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Wan-shan (Myriad Virtues), to be enshrined at Zhenrong Monastery.

An edict was also issued to reconstruct the ten monasteries of Mount Wutai, appointing the śramaṇa Fangrun as the *Sengzheng* (Monastic Rectifier) for the ten monasteries. The ten monasteries were: Zhenrong... [and so forth].
Huayan, Shouning, Xingguo, Zhulin, Jingue, Fahua, Bimi, Lingjing, and Daxian.
By imperial decree, the inner attendant Zhang Renzan was sent to Chengdu to cast a gilded bronze statue of Samantabhadra twenty feet in height.
It was enshrined at Baishui in Puxian Temple on Mount Emei in Jiazhou, where a great pavilion was constructed to house it. An edict was issued to renovate Mount Emei.
The five temples of Mount Emei are Baishui Puxian, Heishui Huayan, Zhongfeng, Qianming, and Guangxiang.
The śramaṇa Fajin of Hedong Prefecture invited the Tripiṭaka Master Fatian to translate scriptures at Putin; the local governor submitted a memorial to present them [to the throne].
The Emperor read this and was greatly pleased. He summoned him to the capital and began the work of translation.
In the second month, the Tripiṭaka Master Tian Xizai from Kaśmīra in Northern India and the Tripiṭaka Master Shi Hu from Oḍḍiyāna arrived.

They were summoned for an audience, granted purple robes, and by imperial decree, the two masters were ordered to collate the Sanskrit manuscripts together. At that time, the Emperor’s resolve toward translation was at its height; he then issued an edict to the Palace Messenger Zheng...
Shoujun established a Translation Institute consisting of three halls to the west of Taiping Xingguo Temple:

the central hall for translating scriptures, the eastern wing for refining the text, and the western wing for verifying the meaning. In the fifth month, the Indian śramaṇa Hualuo arrived to present palm-leaf Sanskrit scriptures;
by imperial decree, he was granted purple robes. The śramaṇa Zhizhe submitted his own work, the *Śrī-Amitāyus-sūtra*.
The commentary on the sutra was completed. An imperial edict conferred upon him the title of Great Master Yanjiao and ordered the construction of Kaisheng Chan Temple at his birthplace.

It enshrined the auspicious sandalwood image of King Udayana, a tooth relic of Śākyamuni Buddha, and the true body, staff, and razor of Master Zhiyi (Zhizong) of Liang, which had been personally sealed within a silver stupa by the Taizu Emperor.
By imperial decree, the inner attendant Wei Qin was dispatched to Sizhou to repair the temple of Master Saṃgha.
The pagoda consists of thirteen stories. The Puzhao Wangsi Temple was renamed Taiping Xingguo [Temple].
In the seventh year of the Taiping Xingguo era, the Weilu Army reported the discovery of Buddha-relics (śarīra), and Shenzhou reported the discovery of a Buddhist image.

An imperial decree was issued to enshrine [the relics] at the local monastery. By imperial edict, the monk Tian Xizai and others were commissioned to translate the scriptures, and the ritual protocols were thereby established.

Furthermore, an edict was issued for the universal ordination of novice monks (*śrāmaṇera*). From Western India, the monk Guangyuan arrived and presented Buddha-relics (*śarīra*). According to the *Song Shi*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Taizu:
on the first day of the ninth month of the seventh year of the Taiping Xingguo era, the year of Jichou, the registers of the various circuits in the Western Capital were updated.
Śrāmaṇera: Order the Cibu (Sectarian Affairs Bureau) to issue a certificate.

According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the first month of the seventh year [of the Kaiyuan era], the Weilu Army submitted a report stating that while excavating earth for the construction of a city wall, they discovered five nested containers—a stone casket, an iron casket, a copper casket, a silver casket, and a gold casket—within which was a lapis lazuli bottle containing Buddha śarīra. An inscribed stone record stated: "The twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era."
The Imperial Secretariat respectfully dispatched an official to report that Wang Xu, a resident of Luzhai County in Shenzhou, while tending cattle in a field, saw a white rabbit;
he pursued it as it entered a burrow in the earth, and upon probing the hole, he discovered fifty stone Buddha statues.
Their craftsmanship was remarkably ancient, each being over a foot in height. By imperial decree, they were enshrined in a local monastery, where the images frequently emitted white light.
In the sixth month, the Translation Institute was completed. An imperial edict ordered Tian Xizai and others to reside therein. Tian Xizai was conferred the title Great Master Mingjiao;
Fatian, Great Master Chuanjiao; and Shi Hu, Great Master Xianjiao. They were commanded to each translate one scripture from the Sanskrit manuscripts they had brought with them.
An edict further appointed the Sanskrit scholars Fa Jin, Chang Jin, Qing Zhao, and others to serve as scribes and editors for the texts. The Court of Imperial Sacrifices...
The Minister Yang Shuo and Zhang Lurun, an official of the Ministry of War, composed the text; Liu Su, a Palace Attendant, provided supervision;

and Tian Xizai described the ritual for translating the scriptures. In the Eastern Hall, facing west, a sacred altar was prepared with lime plaster and four gates were opened, each presided over by a foreign monk (*brahmacārin*).
They maintained secret mantras for seven days and seven nights. Furthermore, a wooden altar was set up, upon which the names of the holy ones were inscribed.
The Wheel-Eyed One said: "This is the Great Dharma Maṇḍala. Invite the noble sages to bathe with *āgama* water.
Present offerings of incense, flowers, lamps, water, and various delicacies and fruits. Perform prostrations and circumambulations, and pray for divine protection to eliminate demonic obstacles.
The primary translator shall sit facing outward and proclaim the Sanskrit text. The second, the Proof-of-Meaning (Arthasiddhi) master, shall sit to his left and deliberate with the translator."
The Sanskrit manuscript was placed third; the person sitting to its right listened as the Chief Translator read the Sanskrit aloud, verifying it for errors.
Fourth was the Sanskrit scholar who transcribed the characters, carefully listening to the Sanskrit and recording them in Chinese script while still following the Sanskrit phonology.
Fifth was the scribe who translated the Sanskrit sounds into the Chinese language. Sixth was the editor who refined and arranged the written characters to form coherent sentences.

7. Regarding the meaning: the seventh stage involves consulting the texts of both lands to ensure there are no errors. 8. Regarding the finalization: the eighth stage involves excising redundancies and determining the precise phrasing and meaning.
9. Regarding the refinement of the text: the officials shall take their positions facing south among the assembly of monks to deliberate and polish the language.
The monks shall bathe daily; their three robes, sitting mats, and deportment shall be strictly orderly, as shall all necessary articles of use.

All [materials] were provided by the government offices. Tian Xizai stated: "In the translated texts, there are instances where characters coincide with the Emperor’s personal name or temple names (*miaohui*).

In previous dynasties, these were not avoided. If the wording were altered to evade them, I fear it might obstruct the essential meaning of the scriptures. I now wish to follow the practice of the Nine Classics of the National Academy, merely omitting certain strokes.
The imperial edict replied: "Regarding the usage of characters in Buddhist scriptures, they shall follow the original text. Temple names and the Emperor’s personal name need not be avoided."
In the seventh month, Tian Xizai presented the newly translated *Sūtra of the Holy Buddha-Mother*, one fascicle; Fa Tianshang presented the *Sūtra of the Auspicious World-Protector*, one fascicle;

and Shi Hu presented the *Sūtra of the Adornments of the Tathāgata*, one fascicle. An imperial edict was issued to the monks of the two monastic districts, ordering them to select one hundred śramaṇas learned in the exegesis of the scriptures to carefully determine the meaning of these texts.
At that time, Shen Yao, the Superintendent of Monks for the Left District, and others submitted a memorial stating that the translation bureaus had long been neglected and their traditions lost.

The translation was extremely difficult. Tian Xizai and others took the Sanskrit manuscripts and first translated the Sanskrit meanings; they then verified these with Chinese literary standards to ensure they were brilliant and elegant.
By imperial decree, the new scriptures were admitted into the canon and woodblocks were carved for their circulation. The Emperor personally visited the Translation Institute.

He summoned the assembly of monks, granted them seats, and comforted them with words of encouragement. He bestowed upon them bedding, silk fabrics, and various articles of daily use, and ordained ten youths from that monastery.
He then took all the Sanskrit manuscripts preserved within the palace and ordered them to be translated.

In the twelfth month, by imperial decree, he selected śramaṇas specializing in Sanskrit studies to serve as scribes (*bi-shou*), and ten śramaṇas specializing in doctrinal studies (*yi-xue*) to serve as proofreaders of the meaning (*zheng-yi*). From then on, this became the custom for every anniversary of his birth.

He was required to present the newly translated scriptures; all were summoned to take their seats and granted a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*). The scriptures were entrusted to the Tripitaka Repository. An imperial edict stated:

"I am currently promoting the teachings of the Dharma to bring blessings upon the state and the family. Therefore, let all the novices (*tóngxíng*) from the various provinces, both internal and external, be ordained.

The Chengdu śramaṇa Guǎngyuǎn returned from traveling to the Western Heaven (India) and went to the palace gate to present a memorial from the Prince of West India, Mòtúnǎng, as well as the *Fóding yìn* (Buddhōṣṇīṣa-mudrā).
On a palm leaf [inscribed with] Bodhi tree leaves, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Shi Hu by imperial decree, the preface states:

"I humbly hear that in the land of China there is a Great Son of Heaven, most sagely and most divine, possessing sovereign wealth and power. Yet, as my own merit gradually diminishes, I have had no means to pay court in person.
From afar, I have received the Imperial Grace, being bestowed with one set of the Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s saṃghāṭī robes from the Vajrāsana; I have already donned them."

I offer this hanging [relic] as an offering. I humbly pray that the Emperor of China may be perfected in merit and wisdom, that his lifespan may be prolonged, and that all sentient beings may be delivered from their drowning.
I respectfully enclose these Śākyamuni relics and present them through the śramaṇa Guangyuan.

In the eighth year of the Taiping Xingguo era, an imperial edict was issued to compile the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. Furthermore, an edict was issued bestowing the name "Chuanfa" (Dharma Transmission) upon the Translation Institute.
Selected youths were sent to the institute to receive instruction. The monk Fayu was granted an imperial decree to travel to Central India.

An edict also commanded an inner attendant to enshrine a relic beneath the base of the Saṃgha Stūpa. Additionally, an edict was issued for the construction of Shouchang Temple. (According to the *Song Shi*, under Taizong.)

Basic Annals: Not Recorded. According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the sixth month of the eighth year of the Taiping Xingguo era, an imperial edict was issued for Zanning of the Hanlin Academy to compile the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*. Zanning requested permission to return to Qiantang to undertake the composition, and the Emperor granted his request.

Furthermore, by imperial decree, the Translation Institute was renamed the "Chuanfa" (Dharma Transmission) Institute, and the Yijing (Sutra Printing) Institute was established to its west. Tian Xizai and others stated:
Throughout successive dynasties, all translations have relied upon Indian monks; had they not come from afar, the translation of scriptures would have ceased.

Desiring that fifty youths be selected from the two monastic streets to study the Sanskrit script, an imperial edict was issued to the high-ranking official Wang Wenshou to select ten individuals, including Weijing, for an audience in the private palace.
By imperial decree, they were sent to the Translation Institute to receive instruction. As for Weijing, he was from Jiang...

Nanli was the nephew of Li Yu. Having received the Sanskrit texts orally, he immediately understood their meaning. After more than a year, he was ordained as a monk and ascended to the Buddhist academy to serve as a scribe for the lectures.
He was granted purple robes and the title Great Master Guangfan. The śramaṇa Fayu came from the Western Heaven and presented Buddha-crown relics and Sanskrit scriptures on palm leaves.
Fayu exhorted the masses to create a dragon-jewel canopy and a golden-robe *kāṣāya*, which he then...
He traveled again to the Vajrāsana in Central India to make offerings. He requested letters of introduction for the various countries he would pass through;
an imperial edict was granted, bestowing official decrees upon the kingdoms of Sribhoja, Kāñcī, and Koḷam, and he was dispatched with them.

Si-zhou reported that the Saṃgha Stūpa emitted light during the day, and that more than a thousand people daily offered incense by burning their heads and arms as an act of devotion. An imperial decree was issued accordingly.
He attended upon the Śākyamuni relics, enshrining them beneath a stūpa and placing newly translated scriptures above them. He showed these to his ministers, saying:
"The teaching of the Buddha is beneficial to governance and brings universal benefit to all living beings. Those who are enlightened realize its profound source for themselves;

the ignorant, however, give rise to groundless slander. As for this Way, I have a slight understanding of its essence. Whenever one acts as a ruler, if one rectifies the mind and remains free from partiality, then—"
This is the practice of self-benefit. Generally, performing a single act of goodness to bring peace to the world is the practice of benefiting others.
For instance, Emperor Wu of Liang’s sacrifice of himself as a slave was a biased view of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and is not the Dharma proclaimed for later generations. Zhao Pu replied:

Your Majesty governs the world with the Way of Yao and Shun and cultivates the mind through the conduct of the Tathāgata. Your sagely wisdom is lofty and far-reaching, beyond what your ministers can comprehend.

By imperial decree, the *Lotus Heart Reversed-Text Gāthā* composed by Your Majesty and the *Eulogy on the Sealed Treasury of the Meaning of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra* were presented to your close ministers.
An edict was then issued to the inner attendant Zhang Chenggui to travel to Mount Tiantai to rebuild the [Long]shou Temple.
Shouchang Temple. This was requested by the śramaṇa Zixun.

In the first year of the Yongxi era, the Japanese śramaṇa Ryōnen came to court; by imperial decree, he was granted the Tripitaka and an edict was issued to have five hundred and sixteen statues of arhats fashioned, which were enshrined at Shouchang Temple.
(Recorded according to the *Song shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Taizong.")

[The] *Ji* [Annals] does not record this. According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs): In the third month of the first year of the Yongxi era, the Japanese monk Ryōnen came to court.
Ryōnen stated that his country had passed through sixty-four generations and eighty-five sovereigns until reaching Emperor Ōjin, at which time the Chinese script was first transmitted.
It was during the *wenshen* year of the reign of Emperor Kinmei that the Buddha-dharma was first transmitted.

The instruction to release [the envoys] was given during the early years of the Liang dynasty’s Chengsheng era. Upon the accession of King Yongming, there was a crown prince named Shōtoku (Śrīmat), who at the age of seven attained an awakening to the Buddha-dharma.
At Bodai-ji Temple, he lectured on the Śrīmālā-sūtra, moving the heavens to rain down flowers.
He was the first to dispatch an envoy to China to seek the Lotus Sūtra, which occurred during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. Upon the accession of Emperor Kōtoku, [he] petitioned...
In the fourth year of the Chōwa era, he dispatched the monk Dōshō to China to receive the Dharma from Dharma Master Xuanzang; this was during the fourth year of the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty.
Subsequently, when Empress Suiko ascended the throne, she ordered the monk Chitō to enter China to seek the Mahāyāna teachings;

this was during the third year of the Xianqing era. Following that, when Emperor Tenmu ascended the throne, in the second year of the Hōkyū era, he ordered the monk Genbō to enter China to seek [the Dharma].

The Dharma [was established] during the fourth year of the Kaiyuan era. Next, under Emperor Xiaoming, in the fourth year of the Tenpyō-Shōhō era, an envoy was dispatched to China to seek the scriptures of both internal (Buddhist) and external (non-Buddhist) teachings; this coincided with the Tianbao era.
Next, under Emperor Kanmu, the monk Kūkai was dispatched to China to transmit the teachings of Zhiyi; this occurred during the Yuanhe era. Next, under Emperor Juntoku, the monk Jō... was commanded.
In the early years of the Dàzhōng era, he entered China seeking the Esoteric Teachings of Śākyamuni.

Upon hearing that the king of that island was succeeded by members of a single clan while all the ministers held hereditary offices, the Emperor said to his chief ministers, "The ruler and subjects of this island barbarian are able to maintain such enduring and perpetual sovereignty.
Subsequently, Nanyue (Nanjo) requested an audience at Mount Wutai; upon returning to the capital, he petitioned for the imperial bestowal of printed copies of the Tripitaka.

An imperial edict was issued for the relevant authorities to provide these [resources] to him. An edict was also issued to have five hundred and sixteen statues of Arhats fashioned, which were enshrined at Shouchang Temple on Mount Tiantai.

In the second year of the Yongxi era, the Indian monk was granted the title of Chaoqing Dafu (Court Petitioner of the Fourth Rank), and an edict was issued to search for and procure Sanskrit scriptures, for which he was provided with quarters in the West [of the capital].

Those among the celestial monks who were proficient in Sanskrit were summoned to the Chuanfa Yuan (Court for the Transmission of the Dharma). Furthermore, by imperial decree, monks were invited to the inner palace to establish a *dōjō* (sacred precinct).

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Taizong" in the *Song Shi* (History of the Song), on the day of Yiwu, the second intercalary month of the second year of the Yongxi era, it was prohibited for monks to maintain wives and children.
On the day of Bingwu, the tenth month of winter, the Indian monks Tian Xizai, Shihu, and Fatian were all [appointed as...].
Chaoqing Dafu; Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial. According to the *Fozu Tongji*:
In the second year of the Yongxi era, the Emperor examined the newly translated scriptures and said to his ministers, "Tian Xizai and others have mastered the essence of translation.
He then issued an edict appointing Tian Xizai as Chao-san Dafu, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, and both Fata and Shihu as Chao-feng Dafu.

The Grand Master (Dàfū) was appointed as the Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglù Qīng). Fǎtiān changed his name to Fǎxián; both were granted monthly stipends of butter, curd, and cash according to their respective ranks.

Newly translated sūtras and śāstras were all carved onto printing blocks and distributed. Tiexīzāi and others submitted a memorial stating that they had heard that in various prefectures of Shǎnxī, there were many monastics and laypeople who possessed and preserved Sanskrit manuscripts.
They requested that an order be issued to search for them, so as to provide resources for further translation. The Emperor’s decree granted this request. Furthermore, an edict was issued:
The monks who served in the two monastic streets established ritual sites within the inner palace to pray for the welfare of the people; this became an annual custom.
Any Indian monks proficient in Sanskrit who could assist with translation were all accommodated at the Translation Institute (Chuanfa Yuan).

As for monks from south of the Ling Mountains who had taken wives and established households, an imperial edict was issued to the local officials in those regions to admonish and exhort them to conform to the orthodox teachings.

In the third year of the Yongxi era, an imperial edict was issued that all temple boys registered in the registers were to receive full ordination (*pravrajyā*). The Imperially Composed Preface to the Sacred Teachings (*Shèngjiào xù*) was then placed at the beginning of newly translated scriptures.

According to the *Song shǐ* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Taizong do not record this; however, according to the *Fózǔ tǒngjì* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddha and Patriarchs), it is so stated.
In the third year of the Yongxi era, an imperial edict was issued that all registered novices throughout the empire were to be ordained.
From this time forward, only those who had read three hundred sheets of scripture and whose mastery of their studies was proficient were permitted to be registered.

Furthermore, the Emperor’s own preface to the *Sacred Teachings of the Tripiṭaka* was bestowed upon Tian Xizai and others, ordering it to be placed at the beginning of the newly translated scriptures.
In the fourth year of the Yongxi era, an imperial edict was issued to an inner attendant to deliver a jeweled crown, necklaces, and monastic robes to Puxian Temple on Mount Emei.
According to the "Treatise on the Emperors" in the *Song Shi*, this is not recorded;

however, according to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the fourth year of the Yongxi era, an edict was issued to an inner attendant to deliver a jeweled crown, necklaces, and monastic robes to Puxian Temple on Mount Emei. On that day, the assembly...
He beheld the Great Being Samantabhadra riding upon purple clouds as he traveled through the air; after a long while, he vanished.

In the first year of the Duan-gong era, an imperial edict ordered that the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) be included in the Great Canon. Furthermore, an edict was issued to provide annotated commentaries on the Emperor’s own collection of Buddhist writings, the *Focheng wenji*.
According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Taizong" in the *Song Shi*, this is not recorded. According to the *Fozu tongji*, [the entry for] the Duan...
In the first year of the Guangong era, Zanning, Grand Master Tonghui of the Hanlin Academy, submitted a memorial to present the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* in thirty fascicles.

An imperial edict praised his work and ordered it to be included in the Great Canon (*Dazang*). By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Tianshou Temple in the capital, and the two street records of monks, Ke Chao and others, requested that he provide annotated commentaries on the Emperor’s own collection of Buddhist writings; the Emperor granted this permission.
In the second year of the Duangong era, the pagoda of Kai bao Temple was completed. The Emperor personally enshrined the śarīra relics within it.

He then issued an edict to an inner attendant to repair Buddhist statues and temple buildings at Mount Emei. According to the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Taizong," on the day of Guihai in the eighth month of the second year of Duangong, an imperial decree was issued for the construction of the Kai bao Temple Śarīra Pagoda, which was subsequently completed. According to the *Fozu Tongji*: Duangong...
In the second year of the Guangong era, the construction of the jeweled pagoda at Kai Bao Temple was completed. It has eight corners, eleven stories, and measures thirty-six *zhang* in height.
At the top, it enshrines a pagoda for a thousand Buddhas and ten thousand Bodhisattvas; at the base, a celestial palace is fashioned to house the reliquary stupa of King Aśoka’s Buddha relics.
All were constructed by Yu Hao, a master stonemason from Hangzhou. The work was completed in eight years. The Emperor bestowed upon it the name Fusheng Stūpa Courtyard.
On the day the śarīra relics were enshrined, the Emperor traveled incognito in a shoulder-carried palanquin and personally placed them within the stūpa.

A white light rose from one corner of the small stūpa, and the great stūpa emitted a radiance that illuminated heaven and earth. Noble and commoners, burning incense and making offerings, filled the roads. The inner attendants...
About several dozen people came forward to seek ordination to sweep the pagoda. The Emperor said to his close ministers, "In my past lives, I have personally sat upon the Buddha’s throne;
it is only that I have not yet attained the knowledge of past lives. He issued an edict to Zhu Ang, a scholar of the Hanlin Academy, to compose an inscription for the pagoda.

The Emperor said to him, "Many Confucians disparage the Buddha. Previously, the monk Fayu from Central India requested me to erect a stele for the Buddha’s Vajrāsana in our own country. As for learning..."
The scholar Su Yijian had previously produced it, referring to the Buddha as a "barbarian. I detested his insolence and consequently commissioned another to produce it.
You should understand this intent. By imperial decree, the eunuch Xie Baoyi was ordered to lead the artisans of the Directorate of Works;

three hundred taels of gold were granted to reside at Mount Emei to adorn the image of Samantabhadra and to rebuild the temple buildings, and the Emperor’s own collected writings were also granted for this purpose.
The record was composed by Xu Xuan, Director of the Imperial Academy.

In the first year of the Chunhua era, an imperial edict was issued to establish Chunhua Temple to enshrine a stone Buddha image. Furthermore, an edict was issued for the "barefoot practitioner" to enter the imperial presence.
He was granted the Tripitaka of the Great Koryo Kingdom, along with the Emperor’s own collected writings on the Buddha Vehicle (*Buddhayāna*). [According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), Tai...]
The *Zongben ji* (Record of the Essential Origins) does not record this; however, according to the *Fozu tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs):

In the first year of the Chunhua era (990 CE), while excavating the ground to build a city wall in Tongli Commandery, ten stone Buddha statues were discovered at the site of an ancient temple. An imperial decree was issued to establish Chunhua Temple to enshrine these images.

Furthermore, an edict summoned the "Barefoot Wayfarer" (Chijiao Daozhe) for an audience. The Emperor asked, "How do the Chan and Vinaya masters of the South transform sentient beings? He replied: [text follows].

He said, "To investigate it, there is but one principle. He then rose and circumambulated the dragon bed once, saying, "Is this Chan? Is this Vinaya? The Emperor replied, "To investigate it, there is but one principle.
The Emperor further stated that the King of Goryeo had sent an envoy to request the bestowal of the Tripitaka and the Imperially Composed Collection of Buddhist Writings (*Busung Munjip*).
An imperial edict was issued granting them.
In the second year of the Chunhua era, the purple robes were bestowed upon the śramaṇa Chongda and a monk from Central India.
An imperial edict appointed the monk Zanning as a compiler for the Historiography Institute (*Shiguan*). According to the *Song Shi*, in the Basic Annals of Emperor Taizong, this is not recorded.
According to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the second year of the Chunhua era, the śramaṇa Chongda of Taiyuan returned from the Western Heaven after a journey of ten years, and presented [the following]:
The Buddha’s relics, palm-leaf Sanskrit scriptures, and purple robes were bestowed [upon him]. He resided at Guang’ai Monastery in the Western Capital.
By imperial decree, Zan Ning was appointed as a compiler for the History Bureau. The śramaṇa Puttaka from Nālandā Monastery in Central India came to court;
he presented Buddha relics and Sanskrit scriptures and was granted purple robes. The śramaṇa Jingjie from the kingdom of Champa in the South Seas arrived...
[Missing]. He presented a *cintāmaṇi*, a bronze bell and *vajra*, and *kunkuma* incense.

In the fourth year of the Chunhua era, an imperial decree was issued stating that all Sanskrit scriptures brought by Buddhist monks from the western regions who had come to China, as well as those carried by Chinese monks returning from the west, must first be reported in detail;
their titles were to be sealed and submitted to the throne. King Chong of Goryeo dispatched an envoy.

A Memorial of Thanks for the Bestowal of the Tripitaka and the Imperially Composed Collection of Writings. According to the *Basic Annals* of Emperor Taizu in the *History of the Song*, this is not recorded.

However, according to the *Chronicles of the Buddhas and Patriarchs*, in the fifth year of the Chūnhua era, a śramaṇa from the Kingdom of Khotan presented the Mahāyāna *Zhùzàng jīng*. Based on the words of Fǎxián, an imperial edict was issued.

Burn and discard it. According to the *Song Shi* (History of the Song Dynasty), the *Basic Annals of Emperor Taizong*, this is not recorded. According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs):

Dharmabhadra submitted a memorial stating: "This scripture is written in the script of Khotan; it is not in Sanskrit. Within it, there is no..."
He questioned the author and the assembly that had heard the Dharma; it was found that across sixty-five passages, both the text and its meaning were incorrect.

The Emperor summoned Xian and admonished him, saying: "To allow such heterodoxy and falsehood to circulate is not the way to honor the Buddha-dharma. You should burn and discard these works to prevent future delusion."
In the first year of the Zhìdào era, an imperial edict was issued for three hundred monks from each province to ordain one person per year, and for one hundred nuns to ordain one person per year.
Furthermore, an edict was issued to promote the *Yúlánbōn* (Ullambana) ritual. According to the *Song Shǐ* (History of Song), the Basic Annals (*běnjì*) of Emperor Tàizǔ do not record this;

however, according to the *Yānyì Yímóù Lù* (Record of Bequeathing Counsel to Posterity), Emperor Lǐ [Zhòu] was a devotee of Buddhism and the number of people he ordained as monks is beyond counting. Since Emperor Tàizǔ...
He traveled south to Jiangnan and conducted a rigorous purge once again; the number [of monastics] remaining was still large. Emperor Taizong therefore established a prohibition.

On the *jichou* day of the sixth month in the first year of the Zhizhao era, he issued an edict stating that from among the various prefectures in Jiangnan, the Two Zhe, Fujian, and other regions, one monk shall be ordained annually for every three hundred monks, and one nun shall be ordained annually for every one hundred nuns. (According to the *Fozu Tongji*).
In the first year of the Zhìdào era, the śramaṇa Karāśanti from Central India came to court and presented a *buddhoṣṇīṣa* relic and palm-leaf Sanskrit scriptures.
An imperial edict was issued decreeing that monks and nuns must recite one hundred sheets of scripture and read five hundred sheets of scripture to qualify for ordination.
Furthermore, an imperial edict was issued for the two monastic offices to have Senglu Shengcai present the *Yulanpen* ritual.

In the second year of the Zhidao era, an edict was issued for the twenty fascicles of the *Mizangquan* (Exposition of the Secret Treasury), the five fascicles of the *Yuanshi* (Commentary on the Origins), and the ten fascicles of the *Xiaoyao yong* (Verses on Recluse-like Ease), all composed by the Emperor himself, to be annotated by the two monastic offices and included in the Great Canon for circulation. An imperial decree then charged the Historiography Institute with commissioning Zanning to compile [the records].

According to the *History of the Song*, Basic Annals of Emperor Taizong, it is recorded that in the ninth month of the third year of the Zhidao era, the śramaṇa Rāhula from Western India came to court and presented a Sanskrit scripture written on palm leaves (*palm-leaf vaipulya-sūtra*).
He was subsequently granted purple robes. (Note: These details are not recorded in the aforementioned [standard] histories. According to the Buddhist [records]:

He bestowed purple robes upon the Indian śramaṇa [Fǎ]zàn and appointed Zànníng as the Right Street Monk Registrar (*yòujiē sēnglù*). (According to the *Song shǐ*, Zhēnzōng...)

Basic Annals: Not Recorded. According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the first year of the Xianping era, the Emperor composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka" (*Sanzang Shengjiao Xu*) and bestowed it upon the Great Master Mingjiao Faxian and others, instructing them to place it after the "Preface to the Holy Teachings" of the late Emperor.

The śramaṇa Kesheng then annotated the preface and presented it for imperial review. An edict was issued appointing Zhu Ang, Director of the Bureau of Imperial Edicts, as the concurrent official for refining the translated texts. [From] Central India.
The śramaṇas Youminī and others came to court and presented Buddha-relics, Sanskrit scriptures, bodhi-tree leaves, and rosaries made of bodhi seeds;
they were granted purple robes. The śramaṇa Buddhagupta from Western India came to court and presented Sanskrit scriptures; he was granted purple robes.
By imperial decree, Shi Guan Bianxiu Zan Ning was appointed as the Right Street Superintendent of Monks (Youjie Senglü).
In the second year of the Xianping era, the *Preface to the Holy Teachings* (Shèngjiào xù) was bestowed upon the Translation Court (Chuányuànyuàn).
Chen Shu requested that the Translation Institute be abolished, but this was not permitted. By imperial decree, Zan Ning was promoted to the rank of Left Street Monk Registrar (zuòjiē sēnglù).

According to the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Zhenzong," on the day of Renyin in the seventh month of the second year of Xianping, the *Preface to the Holy Teachings* was composed and bestowed upon the Translation Court. According to the *Fozu Tongji*...

In the second year of the Pinghe era, Chen Shu, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, submitted a memorial stating that the Translation Institute had long been a source of excessive expenditure for provisions and supplies, and requested its abolition.
