The Emperor, considering it a grand legacy of the previous reign, did not grant permission. By imperial decree, the Historiographer Zanning was promoted to the position of Chief Registrar of the Left Street Monastery.

In the eighth month of the third year of the Xianping era, Tian Xizai, who held the rank of Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, passed away. He was posthumously granted the title of Dharma Master Huiben, and an imperial decree ordered the relevant authorities to provide the full rites for his funeral.
In the fifth month of the fourth year of the Xiánpíng era, Fǎxián, the Minister of the Court of State Ceremonies (Hónglù Qīng), passed away. He was posthumously titled Dharma Master Yuánjué.
An imperial decree ordered that his funeral rites be conducted according to the protocol used for Huìbiàn. [Note: These details are not recorded in the *Song Shǐ*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Zhēnzōng.
They are recorded as stated in the *Fó-zǔ Tǒngjì*.]
In the sixth year of the Xianping era, an imperial edict was issued to select suitable monks to travel to India to retrieve Buddhist scriptures.
Furthermore, an edict was issued to compile and edit the teachings and works of the Sui dynasty monk Zhiyi, bestowing upon them the title *Tiantai Zonglu* (Comprehensive Record of Tiantai).

According to the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Zhenzong," this is not recorded; however, according to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the sixth year of the Xianping era, Chen Shu, the Governor of Kaifeng...

The Emperor said, "Regarding those who claim to be monastics going to the Western Heaven to fetch scriptures: I have summoned them for questioning on several occasions, and they are rarely proficient in their scriptural studies, while their physical appearance and character are mediocre and coarse.
Should they travel to the various provinces, they will surely provoke contempt and disdain. From now on, it is appropriate to test their mastery of the scriptures and examine their talents."

He selected those that were suitable and ordered them to be sent. The imperial decree was granted. In the second month, an edict was issued for the Master Zhizhe of Sui to categorize his teachings and scriptures and compile them into a written record;

in total, there were one hundred and fifty-four sections, which were titled the *Tiantai Zonglu*. The Translation Bureau requested that this be appended to the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu* (The Kaiyuan Era Catalogue of Buddhist Teachings) as the "Eastern Land Collection. The imperial decree stated: "So be it."
In the first year of the Jingde era, purple robes were bestowed upon the śramaṇas of various countries. Due to a drought, a monk from India was summoned to perform incantation rites.

An edict was issued for Yang Yi to compile and promulgate the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp). According to the *Song shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Zhenzong," this is not recorded.
According to the *Fozu tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the first year of the Jingde era, the Japanese śramaṇa Jizhao came to present [offerings].
An image of Amitāyus Buddha; the *Lotus Sūtra* written in golden characters; a crystal rosary; and a purple robe with square-cut sleeves were bestowed.

The Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla from India arrived to present Buddhist relics and palm-leaf Sanskrit scriptures; he was granted a purple robe and a bundle of silk, and lodged in the Translation Institute.
The Śramaṇa Śīlabhadra from Northern India arrived to present Sanskrit scriptures; he was granted a purple garment. In the seventh month, there was a severe drought.
A monk from India was summoned to the Jinnming Pool (Jinmingchi). An altar was established in the middle of the water, and he performed incantations to summon the dragon.
Clouds and mist emerged from within the pool; in a short while, rain arrived. Thereafter, whenever there was a drought, he invariably performed these incantation rites with great efficacy.

The śramaṇa Daoyuan of Eastern Wu presented the *Chanzong chuanteng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp of the Chan School) in thirty fascicles. By imperial decree, Yang Yi, the Hanlin Academician, was commissioned to finalize the work.
It was promulgated.

In the second year of the Jingde era, [the Emperor] visited the Translation Court (Chuanyuan) to inspect newly translated scriptures. He summoned the monks to the Jianbiadian (Audience Hall) to examine and test their religious practice and conduct.
According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Zhenzong" in the *Song Shi*: on the gengwu day of the ninth month in the second year of Jingde, he visited Xingguo [Monastery].

The Temple’s Translation Court: Observing Newly Translated Scriptures. According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the third month of the second year, the śramaṇa Jñānaśrī from Kaśmīra arrived and presented Sanskrit scriptures written on bodhi-tree leaves.

In the seventh month, the śramaṇa Dharmapāla from the Western Heavens arrived and presented Sanskrit scriptures; the Emperor bestowed upon him purple robes. In the ninth month, the Emperor visited the Translation Court in person.
He ordered the various monks of the Tripiṭaka to be seated and bestowed upon them incense, tea, and silk brocades according to their respective ranks.

Regarding the abbots of the various monasteries, as their appointments had previously been made through the transfer of monastic offices rather than based on their actual talent, the Emperor summoned them to the private hall to examine and test their religious practice and conduct.
In the third year of the Jingde era, Sun Shangzhi memorialized requesting a reduction in temple construction and the ordination of monks. This was not permitted.

According to the *Song Shi*, in the "Basic Annals" (*Benji*) of Emperor Zhenzong, this is not recorded. However, according to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the third year of the Jingde era, Sun Shangzhi, the Attendant Reader to the various royal princes, memorialized requesting a reduction in temple construction and the ordination of monks. The Emperor said: "The two traditions of Buddhism and Daoism are of assistance to the world."

Regarding the Teaching: some people, due to biased views, often disparage it. Even though there may occasionally be instances of laxity among monks and Daoists, how can the Teaching be abolished on that basis?

In the fourth year of the Jingde era, an imperial letter was sent to the Buddhist community in Jiaozhou; when court officials requested that the Teaching be prohibited, the Emperor did not grant their request. (According to the *Song [History]*)

*The Veritable Record of Emperor Shenzong*: On the day of Yihai, the seventh month of autumn in the fourth year of Jingde, Jiaozhou presented tribute; the Emperor bestowed Buddhist scriptures upon them.
According to the *Fozu Tongji*, in that same year, a ministerial official submitted a memorial stating: "Ignorant commoners lack understanding and are excessively devoted to Buddhism.

They claim that by giving wealth one may seek blessings, and by performing offerings one may extinguish sins. This corrodes the state and harms the administration; it is fitting that measures be taken against it."
[The Emperor] prohibited [it]. He said to his chief ministers, "Buddhism causes people to reform their conduct; it truly has its benefits. How can it be prohibited?
Moreover, the reach of the Buddha-dharma is extremely vast; even the various states of the remote borderlands all know of it and believe in it.
Only the Way of the Daoists existed originally within the Central Kingdom, yet it was not very flourishing. Wang Dan replied, "Recently, a Liao envoy ascended the Kai Bao Pagoda."
He paid his respects with great devotion and vowed to abstain from killing. However, upon reaching the Shangqing Palace, he no longer prostrated himself.

This shows that among the four barbarian tribes, they value Buddhism alone and do not revere the Way (Daoism). The Emperor said, "It is so. He then issued an edict dispatching an envoy to present him with a golden-embroidered *kāṣāya*.
He traveled to Zhongge Temple on Mount Luofu in Huizhou to enshrine a miraculous image of Śākyamuni Buddha and established a site for prayers and blessings for the state;
thereupon, auspicious birds of five colors were moved to gather at the place where the offerings were made.
In the *Jingde* era, it was first ordered that the Chancellor lead the palace officials (*neizhi*) to Buddhist temples to offer incense.
According to the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Zhenzong," this is not recorded. According to the *Wen Zheng Bi Lu* (The Pen Record of Wang Wenzheng):

Under the former regulations for national memorial services (*guoji*), one member of either the Chancellor or the Vice-Chancellor was alternately appointed to lead the civil and military officials of regular attendance (*changcan*) to Buddhist temples to offer incense, along with the palace officials.

He was not included among them. During the Jingde era, Wang Gong Qinruo and Chen Gong Yaosou, both serving as Directors of the Chancellery for Military Affairs (Shumiyuan Shi), led the palace officials to attend together.

It was then decreed that from this time forward, at the Great Taboo (the anniversary of the Emperor’s passing), the Directors of the Chancellery for Military Affairs, the Palace Officials, the Academicians (Xueshi), the various Palace Commanders (Neizhisi Shi), and military officers down to the rank of regimental commander (Liejiao) would all form a single class. They were first to proceed to the West Upper Gate (Xishanggemeng) to present their names and offer [homage].

The Chancellor and the Vice-Chancellors, along with the civil and military officials of the hundred ranks, form one group. They next proceed to the Gate of the Hall (Gedmen) to present their names for the expression of condolences, after which they withdraw.
They then go together to a Buddhist temple to offer incense; this is omitted for the minor memorial anniversaries.
In the second year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, the destruction of Buddha images fashioned from gold and precious materials was prohibited.

An imperial edict appointed the monk Weijing as Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Guanglu Qing) to participate in the translation of Buddhist scriptures. Princess Wuguo Dachang was granted the title of Master Baoci Zhengjue.
According to the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Zhenzong," on the day of Guichou in the second month of the second year of Dazhong Xiangfu, the prohibition against destruction was issued.
Gilding and sculpting stupas and images: According to the *Fozu tongji*, in the second year [of the Tianxi era], Chongsheng Temple in Shengzhou was renamed Chengtian;

a "Ganlu" (Nectar) ordination platform was established there, and Imperial Edict appointed Grand Master Guangfan Weijing as Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices to participate in the translation of scriptures.
In the ninth month, the Princess of the Great State of Wu entered the monastic order, receiving the dharma name Qingyu and the honorary title Baoshou.
The Great Master Cizheng was the seventh daughter of Emperor Taizong. From childhood, she abstained from meat and blood.
When the Emperor visited Yansheng Temple, he took her onto his lap before the Buddha and vowed that she should become a nun; thus, she now requested ordination.

An imperial edict established Ziseng Monastery for her residence, and by command, the ritual protocols of the Śramaṇa community and the musical troupes of the Jiaofang were employed to escort her. At that time, there was also the daughter of Prince Mi and Prince Cao...

The Empress and more than thirty ladies of the inner palace all followed her into the monastic life. An imperial decree was issued on that same day to universally ordain ten youths from throughout the empire;

one such youth was ordained. Furthermore, an edict was promulgated to establish Yingtian Temple at Jiamaying in Luoyang, the site where the Great Ancestor was born, in order to enshrine his sacred remains.
In the third year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, an imperial edict was issued to all circuits throughout the realm to establish ordination platforms (*śīlākṣepa-maṇḍala*).

It prohibited officials and commoners from insulting or defaming monks and nuns. An edict was also issued to provide the titles of scriptures and treatises for the examination of *śramaṇas*. The monk Yunhuo was hosted at the Northern Imperial Garden.
A Śramaṇa from Central India in the Western Heaven came to court. According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Zhenzong do not record this;

however, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (General Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the third year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, an imperial edict was issued to establish the Fengxian Ganlu Precept Platform at Taiping Xingguo Temple in the capital, and precept platforms were established in all circuits throughout the realm, totaling seventy-two locations. The capital...
The Master [resided] at Cixiao Temple. He separately established a Mahāyāna ordination platform. By imperial decree, no official was permitted to insult or humiliate monks or nuns without cause;
anyone who spoke the word "bald-head" (tú) would be suspended from their current office, while commoners so offending would be banished a thousand *li*.

An edict was issued to Li Wei, the Director of the Bureau of Imperial Edicts, to provide titles from the sutras and treatises for the examination of śramaṇas, based on which they were promoted or appointed. Regarding the order of the Left and Right Quarters (Jiē): the Left Quarter was headed by the Chancellor (Xiang).
At the Guosi Temple in the Right Street, there was Kaibao Si. Furthermore, by imperial decree, the Chan Master Yunhuo of Xifeng in Jizhou was invited to reside at the Northern Imperial Garden.

He remained in meditative absorption for over a month before requesting to return to his native mountains; the Emperor granted him permission. Whenever the Master entered samādhi, he would sometimes not emerge for an entire year.
The Śramaṇa Zhongde from Western India came to court and presented śarīra relics, Sanskrit scriptures, and the Bodhi Seal. [From] Central India...
The Indian śramaṇa Juecheng (Jiachi) arrived at court, presenting śarīra relics, Sanskrit manuscripts, a portrait of the Vajrāsana, and leaves from the Bodhi tree.
He was summoned to the private hall, where he was received with great courtesy and provided lodging in the Translation Institute.

Juecheng presented a hymn of praise for the Emperor, which was translated by Wei Jing by imperial decree. Juecheng said to the scholar Yang Yi: "Upon entering this country, I saw pigs being slaughtered."

In the sheep market stalls, the carcasses were hung inside; their suffering was so unbearable that one could not bear to look upon them. In Western India, those who eat meat or the five pungent roots are driven out of the city;
therefore, those without goods do not wish to dwell here for long. They pray to reach Mount Wutai to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, and then immediately return to their native lands.
Duke Ding Wei of Jin asked him, "Having traveled from such a great distance of tens of thousands of li, what else do you intend to do?

He replied, "I also wish to pay my respects at the stupa of Vinaya Master Xuan. Upon his return, an imperial edict was issued granting him a gold-embroidered *kāṣāya* robe for enshrining on the Vajrāsana, along with funds for travel expenses and offerings of tea and fruit.
In the fourth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, the Emperor visited Guanghua and other monasteries to pay homage to the stupa of Vajrabodhi and the true body of Kāśyapa Mātanga.
He issued an edict to repair Puxian Monastery and provide vegetarian meals for thirty thousand monks. Four monks were ordained annually.

Furthermore, he summoned the practitioner Shoujian for an audience and ordered all the palace ladies to come forth to burn incense. He bestowed purple robes upon a śramaṇa from the country of Bamiyan. (According to the records...)
The *Veritable Record of Emperor Zhenzong* in the *History of the Song* does not record this.

According to the *Chronicle of the Buddhas and Patriarchs*, in the third month of the fourth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, the Emperor visited Guanghua Temple on Mount Longmen in Luoyang to pay respects at the stupa of Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi;

he composed a eulogy, which was engraved on stone and placed within the stupa. He then proceeded to Baima Temple to pay respects at the true body of Tripiṭaka Master Kāśyapa Mātanga. The Emperor said:
An attendant said, "Since Kāśyapa Mātanga arrived until now, a thousand years have passed, yet his entire body remains undecayed. This is truly worthy of veneration;

it is fitting that the monks of the temple be strictly instructed to guard it with diligent care. Consequently, the Emperor composed a work to praise him and issued an edict granting three thousand taels of gold.
He renovated the Puxian Temple on Mount Emei, provided vegetarian meals for thirty thousand monks, and ordained four monks each year.
Furthermore, he issued an edict summoning the Daoist practitioner Jian Dao of Lianshui Commandery to have an audience. He ordered all the palace ladies to come forth and burn incense;
as each lady approached, the Emperor addressed her, saying, "She is the Empress. The Master replied that she was not. This continued with dozens of women until the Master suddenly rose and said:
"Your Majesty should favor the nurturing of this man; one day he will surely become the master of our house. This refers to Empress Dowager Zhangxian.
The Master requested to return to the mountains, and the imperial decree granted his wish. While in the mountains, he constantly wore paper robes and kept his door closed, never meeting anyone.

When someone placed food before him in the courtyard, he would take it himself once the person had withdrawn. In the fifth month, the Śramaṇa Jixian from the country of Pāṇi arrived to present Sanskrit scriptures on the Bodhi...

[The Emperor] bestowed the seal of office and purple robes. In the eleventh month, Li Shiheng, the local governor of Yizhou, presented forty fascicles of the *Shishi huoyao* (Essentials of Buddhist History), compiled by the śramaṇa Renzan of Daci Temple.

In the fifth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, an edict was issued for the śramaṇa Mózhen to have an audience with the Emperor. Furthermore, an edict was issued to establish a temple in the Kingdom of Japan, and it was granted the name Shenguang.
According to the *Song Shi*, in the "Basic Annals of Emperor Zhenzong," this is not recorded; however, according to the *Fozu Tongji*, it is so stated.
In the second month of the fifth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, an imperial edict summoned the śramaṇa Mózhen of Mount Emei in Jiazhou to have an audience with the Emperor.
The Emperor bestowed a poem upon him and lodged him at Jingde Temple. Prince Yuancheng of Shu dreamed of a youth in blue robes holding a letter and presenting it to an imperial messenger;
the youth’s feet stepped upon yellow clouds and he vanished into the distance. The Prince questioned the Master about this, and the Master replied, "There will soon be an heir apparent."

Soon after the auspicious news of the imperial conception was announced, Emperor Renzong was born. The Japanese government dispatched an envoy with tribute, reporting that a "radiant light" had appeared in the eastern part of their country.
According to ancient tradition, such an omen appears when the Son of Heaven in the Central Plains is sagacious and enlightened.

The Emperor was delighted and issued an edict to establish a temple in Japan, granting it the name Shinkō-ji (Divine Light Temple). He further commanded his literary ministers to compose a record for the temple.

In the sixth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, an imperial decree was issued that only those who had passed examinations on the scriptural studies of novice monks (*śrāmaṇera*) were permitted to undergo tonsure and ordination.
The name of the pagoda at Kaiyuan Temple was bestowed, and a catalog for the compilation of the Tripitaka was also granted, titled the *Dazhong Xiangfu Fabao Lu*.
A śramaṇa from Western India arrived and was granted purple robes. The monk Chongju was summoned to the inner palace to lecture on the sutras. (According to the *Song Shi*).

The *Shinzō Honki* (True Sect Fundamental Chronicle) does not record this; however, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), on the second month of the sixth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, an imperial edict was issued to all officials throughout the realm requiring that candidates for the tonsure and ordination must first pass examinations on the scriptures and their doctrinal studies.

On the fifth month, a golden light was seen atop the spire of the Fushō Pagoda at Kōfuku-ji Temple, and holy monks were seen circumambulating the pagoda. On the following day, five [relics] were obtained.

The physical relics were highly favored by the Emperor, who personally visited and venerated them. He beheld the relics atop the stupa, as large as the moon, translucent like crystal, and moving back and forth upon the bell-strings.
The common people and the officials alike gazed upon them. On the brick floor, he enshrined more than five thousand grains of relics.
By imperial decree, the stupa was bestowed the title "Stupa of Miraculous Response" (Linggan Zhitai). At that time, Xingci Monastery in the capital...
At the stupa, there were also relics visible atop the *cakra* (wheel). An inscription above read: "The auspicious signs of the Image-Dharma (the Buddhist teachings) are the blessing for the people.

In the eighth month, Zhao Anren, Vice Minister of the Ministry of War and Official for Polishing the Texts of the Translation Bureau, received an imperial decree to compile the catalog of the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*).

Upon completion, it consisted of twenty-one fascicles and was granted the title *Dazhong Xiangfu Fabao Lu* (Record of the Dharma-Treasures of the Dazhong Xiangfu Era), with an imperial preface further bestowed.
The preface states: Since the Taiping Xingguo era, a total of four hundred and thirteen fascicles of sutras, vinayas, and śāstras have been translated.
These were compiled by Yang Yi, Director of the Imperial Library, and the Great Master Guangfan Weijing, among others.

Furthermore, they requested that the collections of Buddhist writings composed by the imperial pen during the two reigns be included in the Tripitaka; an edict was subsequently issued granting approval and bestowing the posthumous title of "Great Master Sengqie of Sizhou."
The Master Shibo Zhao Mingjue was one whose name could not be mentioned, whether in public or private.
In the ninth month, śramaṇas from Western India, including Zhi Xian and others, arrived to present śarīra relics and Sanskrit scriptures; they were granted purple robes.
In the eleventh month, the śramaṇa Pūrṇabhadra from Vārāṇasī in Western India presented Sanskrit scriptures written on leaves from the Aśoka tree. The Dharma Master Chongju of Fushí arrived.

In the capital, the Emperor heard of his reputation and summoned him into the inner palace to lecture on the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*. He eloquently expounded upon its profound principles, which greatly delighted the Emperor’s mind.
The Emperor bestowed upon him purple robes, gold, silk, incense, and medicinal herbs.

In the eighth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, an imperial edict was issued to include the *Miaojue ji* (Collection of the Wondrous Enlightenment), composed by the Emperor Taizong, within the Great Canon (*Dazang*).
The Kingdom of Zhu’er (Jūrṇa) in Nanyhai dispatched an envoy to present Sanskrit scriptures from India. According to the *Song shi*, Zhenzong benji, this is not recorded;
however, according to the *Fozu tongji*, in the eighth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, an edict was issued naming the Nan’an Rock in Tingzhou.

Junqingyuan was granted one hundred and twenty scrolls of imperial calligraphy by Taizong. By imperial decree, the five fascicles of *Miaojue* composed by Taizong were entrusted to the Chuanfa Yuan to be included in the Tripitaka.
An envoy from Zhu’nan in South India arrived to present tribute, offering Sanskrit scriptures from India.
The envoy stated, "For forty years, there has been no wind or waves at sea; this signifies that [the Emperor] of the Middle Kingdom possesses..."
When the Sage appeared in the world, in the ninth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, śramaṇas from various kingdoms of India arrived and presented śarīra relics and Sanskrit scriptures.

By imperial decree, the stone niches for Buddhas at Longmen Mountain were repaired, and the śramaṇa Zhiwu was summoned by edict to pray for rain. (According to the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Zhenzong")
Record. Not recorded. According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs):

In the second month of the ninth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, the śramaṇa Tianjue from the country of Udyāna in Northern India, the śramaṇa Miaode from the country of Siṃhala in Southern India, and śramaṇas from the country of Kaśmīra in Western India arrived at court.
Each presented śarīras and Sanskrit scriptures, and each was bestowed with purple robes and gold and silk.
In the fourth month, the śramaṇa Dharmaruci arrived from the country of Śrāvastī in Central India; he presented Sanskrit scriptures and was granted purple robes.
In the fifth month, the śramaṇa Buddhasānta arrived from the country of Varṇu in Eastern India; he presented Sanskrit scriptures and was granted purple robes.
The stone niches containing Buddha images at Longmen Mountain in the Western Capital had fallen into ruin over many years.
The Emperor ordered the śramaṇa Xi Yan to provide craftsmen for their restoration, totaling seventeen thousand three hundred and thirty-nine statues.

When no rain fell in the ninth month, an edict was issued for the śramaṇa Zhiwu of Guishan in Sizhou to enter the capital and reside at Kaibao Temple to pray for rain. Zhifu had previously prayed for rain in Sizhou.
It rained. Moved by this, Huiwu once severed an arm; now he said again, "If it rains within seven days, I shall sever another arm.
On the fifth day, there was heavy rain, and he then cut off an arm. The Emperor dispatched an envoy to bestow medicine upon him, but Huiwu said, "It does no harm.
Those who saw that the severed arm had no blood were greatly amazed. The Governor of Si and the people of the commandery all dreamed of the monk Śāṇakavāsin, who said to them, "Wu..."
He was one among these five hundred arhats who came here to save the world.
In the first year of the Tianxi era, an imperial edict prohibited the inclusion of the newly translated *Piṇāyaka Sūtra* in the canon.

[The Emperor] bestowed more than four thousand printed volumes of the *Zhiyi Jiaowen* (Texts of the Teachings of Zhiyi) from Mount Dongye in Taizhou. According to the *Song Shi*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Zhenzong:
Not Recorded. According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the fourth month of the first year of the Tianxi era, an imperial edict stated:
"The teachings of the Golden Immortal (the Buddha) truly benefit all living beings. The texts upon palm leaves ought to be supported through translation.

Yet, if the lineages of transmission differ, then heterodoxy and orthodoxy will inevitably become intermingled. Once precision and detail are lost, errors gradually accumulate. Moreover, the offering of meat and blood is a profound sacrilege."
Regarding the True Vehicle, such expressions of revulsion and cursing are all the more contrary to the sublime principle.
Consequently, the four-fascicle *Piṇāyaka Sūtra* of the new translation was not permitted to enter the Canon; from this time forward, no scriptures similar to this text shall be translated.
In the seventh month, an imperial edict granted four thousand six hundred and twenty printed copies of the teachings of the Master Zhizhe from Dongye Mountain in Taizhou.
Zhuzhan Benru was a native of Guan County. He constructed a library pavilion to enshrine [the scriptures].

In the third year of the Tianxi era, an imperial edict ordered that the Emperor’s annotated Buddhist scriptures be included in the canon and distributed. Furthermore, an edict was issued granting the Tripitaka of the Daizhou Kingdom.
According to the *Song Shi*, in the Basic Annals of Emperor Zhenzong, this is not recorded. According to the *Fozu Tongji*, Tian...

In the third year of the Xì era, Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others requested that the *Imperial Commentary on the Sūtra of Forty-two Sections* and the *Imperial Commentary on the Sūtra of the Bequeathed Teachings* be included in the canon and promulgated;
the Emperor’s decree granted this. In the eleventh month, the kingdom of Eastern Jurchen presented tribute and petitioned for the bestowal of the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*);
the Emperor issued a decree to provide it.

In the fourth year of the Tianxi era, an imperial edict was issued to include the *Shidian fayin ji* (Collection of Dharma Sounds from the Buddhist Canon), composed by the Emperor, within the Great Canon (*Dazang*).
Furthermore, a purple robe was bestowed upon the śramaṇa from Western India, and the monk Zhili was specially granted the title Fazi (Dharma Wisdom).

According to the *Song shi*, in the Basic Annals of Emperor Zhenzong, this is not recorded. According to the *Fozu tongji*, in the first month of the fourth year of Tianxi, the Right Street Lecturer on the Sūtras... [text fragment ends].
Yan et al. requested that the Emperor’s own composition, the *Shidian fayin ji* (Collection of Dharma Sounds from the Exegesis of the Buddhist Canon), be commissioned for monastic annotation.

It consisted of thirty fascicles, and they petitioned that it be included in the Great Canon (*Dazang*). The imperial decree granted permission. Initially, Yang Yi was appointed to oversee this project.

Within the collection, there was a passage concerning the "six kinds of earth tremors. One monk annotated it with nearly three hundred characters; the prose was obscure and fragmented, rendering it unreadable. Yang Yi struck it out and annotated it himself.

It is said that the essence of the earth is fundamentally still; movement inevitably brings change. The people were impressed by its simplicity. A śramaṇa from Western India named Puxian arrived to present Sanskrit scriptures and was granted purple robes.
Li Zunzui, the Commandery Marshal Attached to the Household, memorialized that the Dharma Master Liaoli of Siming had maintained lofty conduct and sacrificed his life for the Dharma.
The Emperor sighed with admiration and praise without ceasing, specially bestowing upon him the title "Fazhi" (Dharma Wisdom) and decreeing that he remain in residence.

While he was expounding the teachings to the world, he did not permit them to leave their bodies behind. At that time, twenty-three individuals from the Translation Institute, including the Proofreaders and Chief Editors, each composed poems to praise his virtue and character.
In the fifth year of the Tianxi era, an imperial edict was issued dispatching an inner attendant to invite the monk Fazhi to lead the assembly in performing the Lotus Sūtra Repentance Ritual.
Furthermore, an edict was issued to establish Zisheng Chan Monastery for the posthumous merit of soldiers who had died in battle.

According to the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Zhenzong," this is not recorded; however, according to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the fifth year of the Tianxi era, an edict dispatched the inner attendant Yu Yuanqing.
He traveled to Yanqing Monastery in Siming and invited Master Fazhi to lead the assembly in performing the Lotus Sūtra Repentance ritual to pray for the blessing of the nation.

The Master composed an essential summary of the repentance practice and submitted it. By imperial decree, a Zisheng Chan Cloister was established in Bingzhou to perform merit-making rites for the soldiers who had died in battle.
Ding Wei, Chief Counselor and Minister of the Department of State Affairs, concurrently served as the editor for the translated scriptures.
The Hanlin Academicians Chao Hui and Li Wei were concurrently appointed as Officers for Refining Writings.
In this year, the number of monks throughout the empire was 397,615, and the number of nuns was 61,240.
In the first year of the Qiánxìng era, Rénzōng ascended the throne. Empress Dowager Zhāngyì dispatched an envoy to request that the monk Zuǎnshì perform repentance rituals for the state.

He was granted purple robes, as were the monks from the kingdom of Kucha. According to the *Basic Annals of Emperor Rénzōng* in the *History of Song*, he ascended the throne on the wùwǔ day of the second month in the first year of Qiánxìng.
According to the *Chronicle of the Buddhas and Patriarchs*, in the first year of Qiánxìng, Empress Dowager Zhāngyì...
Later, an envoy was dispatched to Tiantian (Tianzhu) in Qiantang to invite Master Zunshi to perform repentance rites for the sake of the state.

The Master presented the *Jinguangming Huguo Daochang Yi* (The Ritual Manual for the Golden Light Sutra’s Protection of the State). Consequently, he submitted a memorial requesting that the works of the Tiantai teachings be included in the Tripitaka.
A monk from Kucha named Huayan arrived to present Buddha-relics and Sanskrit scriptures; the Master was subsequently granted a purple robe.
*The Comprehensive Collection of Illustrations and Writings on Antiquity and the Present* (Gujin Tushu Jicheng), Section on Buddhist Teachings, Compendium of Investigations, Volume Three.
*The Comprehensive Collection of Illustrations and Writings on Antiquity and the Present*, Section on Buddhist Teachings, Compendium of Investigations, Volume Four.
Song Dynasty II.

In the first year of the Tiānshèng era of Emperor Rénzōng, an imperial edict was issued for an inner attendant to descend with incense to Mount Lìngshān in Tíanzhú to pray for the blessing of the state.
The Zhùliǎn Country of the South Sea presented a *Tíanzhú* Sanskrit scripture written on gold leaves. (According to the *Song Shǐ*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Rénzōng.")
Not recorded. According to the *Fozu tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs):

In the first year of the Tiānshèng era, an imperial edict was issued to the eunuch Yang Huáigǔ to descend with incense to Mount Ling of Tiantai to pray for the blessing of the state. The Dharma Master Cíyún Shì further petitioned that the Tiantai teachings be included in the Tripitaka.
Huáigǔ memorialized this to the Emperor, who took notice. The King of Zhùliǎn in Nánhǎi then dispatched an envoy to present gold leaves.
The Indian Sanskrit scriptures were translated by Imperial Decree by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmapāla.

In the second year of the Tiānshèng era, an Imperial Decree was issued granting the Tiantai teachings and texts entry into the Canon, and one hundred taels of white silver was bestowed for a meal offering to a thousand members of the monastic community at Mount Ling.
The Śramaṇas from West India, Axián and Hùxián, arrived to present Sanskrit scriptures on palm leaves; an Imperial Decree was issued granting them the purple robe.
Regarding the "Fú" (entry): According to the *Song shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Rénzōng," this is not recorded. According to the *Fó-zǔ tǒng jì* and other sources:
In the third year of the Tiānshèng era, Xià Sǒng and others presented seventy fascicles of the *Xīnyì jīng yīnyì* (Phonetic Meanings of Newly Translated Scriptures).

An imperial edict was issued prohibiting the admission of those who had previously committed serious crimes or those with tattooed bodies. According to the *Song shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Rénzōng," this is not recorded.

According to the *Fozu tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the third year of the Tiānshèng era, Xià Sǒng, the Academician of the Hanlín Academy, together with the Tripiṭaka Master Wéijìng and others, presented seventy fascicles of the *Xīnyì jīng yīnyì* (Phonology and Meanings of Newly Translated Scriptures).
Mǎ Liàng, the Director of the Department of State Affairs, remarked that the Buddha-way is most honorable and weighty.

"May you, the teacher of gods and men, please not permit those who have previously committed grave offenses or those with tattooed bodies to receive ordination. The Emperor’s decree granted this request.

In the fifth year of the Tiānshèng era, a monk from the Western Regions presented a Sanskrit manuscript, and Wéijìng submitted the catalog for the Tripitaka, which was bestowed the title *Tiānshèng Shìjiào Lù* (The Tiānshèng Record of Buddhist Teachings).
According to the *Song Shǐ*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Rénzōng, on the day of Dīng in the second month of the fifth year of Tiānshèng...
Year Chou. Monks from the Western Regions, including Dharmakṣema (Fa Jiāng), arrived to present Sanskrit manuscripts.

According to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the fifth year, the Tripitaka Master Weijing presented the catalog of the Great Canon (*Dazangjing*) in two bundles. It was bestowed the title *Tiansheng Shijiao Lu* (Tiansheng Record of Buddhist Teachings) and comprised a total of 6,197 fascicles.

In the sixth year of the Tiānshèng era, the annual tribute of woven Buddha images from the two circuits of Szechwan was abolished; an imperial composition of hymns in praise of the Triple Gem was also produced.

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Rénzōng" in the *History of the Song*, on the *jǐyǒu* day of the first month in spring of the sixth year of Tiānshèng, the annual tribute of woven Buddha images for the Qiányuán Festival from the two circuits was abolished.
According to the *Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs*, in the sixth year of Tiānshèng, the Emperor composed hymns in praise of the Triple Gem and bestowed them [upon the clergy].
The Prime Minister and the Translation Institute [reported].

In the seventh year of the Tiānshèng era, an imperial edict was issued to establish Cíhuà Temple for the posthumous merit of the late Emperor. According to the *Song Shǐ* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Rénzōng do not record this.

However, according to the *Fó-zǔ Tǒngjì* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the seventh year of the Tiānshèng era, an edict was issued to construct it extensively in the capital.
At Cihua Temple, he said to his ministers: "This was intended as a memorial service to recommend merit for the late Emperor.
Henceforth, no labor services shall be mobilized arbitrarily or without cause."
In the ninth year of the Tiānshèng era, an imperial edict was issued to welcome the robe and alms bowl of the Sixth Patriarch and install them in the Qīngjìng Hall of the Imperial Palace.

A decree was also issued for the monk Huáiwèn to travel to India to construct a stupa and to welcome the Buddha’s tooth from Kāibǎo Monastery to be enshrined within the Forbidden City. Subsequently, these were returned to the monastery.

According to the *Song Shǐ* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Rénzōng do not record this. However, according to the *Fó-zǔ Tǒngjì* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the ninth year of the Tiānshèng era, an edict was issued... [text continues].
The presiding official of Shaozhou went to Nanhua Temple on Mount Baolin to welcome the robe and alms bowl of the Sixth Patriarch and bring them into the imperial capital for veneration.

Upon their arrival, they were enshrined in the Qingjing Hall within the Great Palace. By imperial decree, Yan Shu, Vice Minister of the Ministry of War, was commissioned to compose the "Record of the Sixth Patriarch’s Robe and Alms Bowl.
The Translation Court reported that the śramaṇa Huaiwen had previously traveled to India for the sake of Emperor Zhenzong.

A stūpa was erected beside the Buddha’s Vajrāsana. Now, wishing to go once more to build two further stūpas for the Empress Dowager and the current Emperor, he requested that the "Preface to the Holy Teachings" from the previous reign, the "Vow Text of the Empress Dowager," and the "Hymn to the Triple Gem" of the Sovereign be inscribed upon stone beneath the stūpas, as well as the manufacture of monastic robes to be offered to the image of Śākyamuni.
The imperial decree granted permission, and the court scribes were further ordered to compose the necessary texts.
The Record of Three Journeys to the Western Heaven by the Śramaṇa Huaiwen. Initially, Emperor Taizu doubted that Vinaya Master Xuán’s Buddha tooth was genuine;

he dispatched an envoy to retrieve it from Luoyang. When it was subjected to the intense heat of a blazing fire, its color did not change. The Emperor’s heart was filled with reverence for this divine marvel, and he subsequently composed a text of aspiration.
During the reign of Emperor Taizong, the tooth was again tested by fire, and the Emperor composed verses of praise to express his veneration, whereupon he enshrined it within the Great Image.
The Hokke-in of Kokusei-ji once invited [the image] to be enshrined and offered before the Inryaku-tō at Kōhō-ji.

On the night of its veneration, a divine light radiated forth brilliantly; he subsequently composed verses of praise. Because the Emperor had served it with reverence for three reigns, he then invited it into the imperial palace.
He irrigated it with rose water. Suddenly, from within the hole, he obtained a single śarīra, its five colors dazzling the eyes.
He then composed a hymn of praise for it and enshrined it within two nested golden caskets. He then offered it back to the monastery.

In the first year of the Jingyou era, the unregistered monasteries throughout the empire were demolished. Buddhist scriptures were bestowed upon Zhao Yuanhao, and an imperial edict was issued to test the recitation of the *Lotus Sūtra* by novice monks;
only those who passed the selection were permitted to receive ordination. According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Renzong" in the *Song Shi*:
on the day of Yihai, the intercalary sixth month of the first year of Jingyou, the unregistered monasteries throughout the empire were demolished; on the day of Guiyou, the twelfth month.
The Bestowal of Buddhist Scriptures upon Zhao Yuanhao, Prince of Xiping. According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs):

In the first year of the Jingyou era, an imperial edict was issued to examine the novice monks (*tongxing*) throughout the realm; those who could recite the *Lotus Sūtra* successfully were granted ordination. The Vice-Chancellors Song Shou and Xia Song were appointed to jointly supervise the examinations.
There was one novice who failed to pass his recitation of the sūtra. When asked how many years he had been practicing his studies, he replied, "Ten years."
The two gentlemen laughed and felt pity for him. They agreed that upon his return, each would take up a scripture to recite:
Sui finished his in ten days, while Song completed his in seven, without omitting a single character. In that year, there were 385,052 monks and 40,874 nuns throughout the empire.

In the second year of the Baoyuan era, the monks Huaiwen and others returned from Central India; they were summoned for an audience, comforted with imperial favor, and granted titles, purple robes, and gold and silk.
According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Renzong" in the *Song Shi*, this is not recorded; however, according to the *Fozu Tongji*:
In the fifth month of the second year of the Baoyuan era, he traveled three times to the Western Heaven (India) with a heart full of inquiry.
Accompanied by the śramaṇas Deji and Wudingdean, he returned from Madhyadeśa in the kingdom of Magadha, bringing with him Buddha-relics, śarīra, palm-leaf Sanskrit scriptures,
*pippala* seeds, leaves from the Bodhi tree, leaves from the Aśoka tree, a rosary of bodhi seeds, and nineteen Indian stone inscriptions.
The Emperor summoned him for an audience and comforted him, bestowing upon him the title of Great Master of Manifest Teaching (Xiàojiào Dàshī), along with purple robes and gold coins.

In the first year of the Qìnglì era, the monk Wéijìng and the Vice Minister of the Court of Judicial Review Kǒng Fǔdào requested that the translation of scriptures be discontinued; this was not permitted.
[Note: This is not recorded in the *Song Shǐ*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Rénzōng. According to the *Fó-zǔ Tǒngjì*, in the first year of the Qìnglì era, the Tripitaka...]

The Dharma Master Weijing said, "In the western lands, tens of thousands of scrolls of new and old scriptures have been submitted. The establishment of the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu) incurs significant expenses for its stipends and provisions.
I request that the translation of scriptures be discontinued. The Emperor replied, "How could I dare to immediately abolish the ancient legacy of the Three Sages?
Furthermore, the records of precious tributes cannot be identified without the Court of State Ceremonial. Not long after, the Censor-in-Chief Kong Fudao submitted a memorial requesting its abolition.

Regarding the translation of the scriptures, the Emperor presented the *Jingshu* (Pure Commentary) for his inspection and exhorted him that the grand ceremonies of the previous dynasty must not be abruptly discontinued.
In the second year of the Qingli era, he conferred the title and a purple square robe upon the monk Benru, and further granted the plaque for the White Lotus Society (*Bailianshe*).
According to the *Song Shi*, in the Basic Annals of Emperor Renzong, this is not recorded. However, according to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the second year of the Qingli era, at the beginning...
On Mount Dongye, Dharma Master Benru convened a hundred monks to perform a year-long *dharmaparyāya* repentance ritual based on the *Lotus Sūtra*.
In the seventh month of that year, Li Zun, the Prince Consort, petitioned the court on his behalf. Consequently, the Master was granted the title Shenzhao and bestowed with a purple square-cut robe.
Once, while at the southwest of the mountain, he saw a tiger lying down; striking it with his staff, he said, "This is not your dwelling place. The tiger lowered its head.
He departed first. Later, at the place where the tiger had lain, he built a hut to serve as a hermitage. In that year, he retired to this location;
admiring the spirit of Mount Lu, he formed the White Lotus Society with the worthy Xu Zhong and Zhang Dexiang. For six or seven years, they remained there.
It gradually developed into a great monastery. His Majesty, having long heard of its reputation for the Way, subsequently bestowed upon it the name "White Lotus.
In the third year of the Qingli era, an imperial decree invited the Buddha’s tooth relic into the inner palace to pray for rain; a golden hall was constructed to enshrine it.
According to the *Song Shi*, in the Basic Annals of Emperor Renzong, this is not recorded. According to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the sixth month of the third year of the Qingli era...

During a prolonged drought, an imperial edict was issued to invite the Buddha’s tooth relic from the Xiangguo Temple. The Emperor entered the inner palace in person to offer prayers; in a mere moment, rain poured down in torrents.

He then had a golden pavilion with four gates constructed to emulate a celestial palace, wherein the relic was enshrined. Furthermore, he composed a text of aspiration to manifest his devotion and reverence.
The Chancellor Zhang Dexiang concurrently served as the Commissioner for Translating Scriptures and Polishing Their Text. (Based on the *Xuefo kaoxun*, Volume 3)

In that year, an imperial edict was issued to welcome the Buddha’s tooth relic into the inner palace to pray for rain. It was bathed with rose water from the sea, and a single *śarīra* (relic) was obtained.
This was stored in a lapis lazuli bottle, adorned with the seven precious gems, resting upon white silk floss, and covered with necklaces and robes embroidered with dragons and phoenixes.
It was venerated there for over a month.
In the fourth year of the Qingli era, the Linggan Pagoda was destroyed by fire. An imperial edict was issued to retrieve the śarīra from the pagoda’s foundation for veneration within the palace.

According to the *Song Shi*, in the "Basic Annals" (*Benji*) of Emperor Renzong, this is not recorded. However, according to the *Fozu Tongji*, it occurred in the sixth month of the fourth year of the Qingli era.

The Pagoda of Miraculous Response at Kai Bao Si was destroyed by fire. An imperial messenger was ordered to retrieve the śarīra relics enshrined within the pagoda’s foundation for veneration within the palace, with the intent to rebuild it.
The remonstrating official Yu Jing earnestly petitioned against this, but the Emperor did not heed his words.
In the seventh year of the Qingle period, an imperial edict conferred the title of Great Master Ciren Ningji upon the Purple-Robed Divine Monk.
An imperial composition, the *Eulogy on the Translation of Scriptures*, was bestowed upon the monk Fahu. According to the *Song Shi*, in the Basic Annals of Emperor Renzong, this is not recorded.

According to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the spring of the seventh year of the Qingle period, there was no rain; the Emperor dispatched an envoy to Da Hong Mountain in Suizhou to pray for rain. The envoy...
A person rose at dawn and knocked at the hall, where he encountered a divine monk clad in purple robes who looked at him with his eyes; the following day, there was a heavy rain.
An imperial edict conferred upon him the title Great Master Ciren Ningji, and the Emperor composed a verse on the translation of scriptures to bestow upon the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmapāla.

In the eighth year of the Qingli era, an imperial decree was issued to invite the monk Fahua to perform a vegetarian feast at the Huacheng Hall. According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Renzong do not record this event.

However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), the Censor-in-Chief Sima Guang repeatedly submitted memorials requesting that an heir apparent be established.
Upon hearing that Fahua of Kaibao Temple possessed extraordinary conduct, the Emperor burned incense and offered silent prayers at night; the following day, he invited Fahua.
On the day of the vegetarian feast in the Huacheng Hall, Emperor Hua donned his ceremonial robes at dawn and waited expectantly.

Suddenly, an inner attendant reported that the Dharma Master Fahua had entered through the Right Aisle Gate; as he approached the inner palace, the Emperor could not stop him from proceeding. The Emperor smiled and said, "I summoned him myself.
Upon arrival, the Master went straight to the imperial couch, sat cross-legged, and received the meal. When the Emperor inquired about the matter of an heir to the throne, the Master asked for paper.

He inscribed thirteen characters, repeated three times. Later, when Emperor Yingzong succeeded to the throne—as the thirteenth son of Prince Puzi—in the first year of the Renshou era (1049), he issued an imperial decree to rebuild the Linggan Pagoda.
An imperial messenger was dispatched to Baguan Temple in Chenliu to welcome the Buddha’s finger-bone relic (*śarīra*).
According to the *Song Shi*, in the "Basic Annals" (*Benji*) of Emperor Renzong, this is not recorded; however, according to the *Fozu Tongji*:
In the first year of the Huangyou era, an imperial decree was issued to rebuild the Linggan Pagoda to enshrine śarīra relics.

An imperial messenger was dispatched to Baguan Temple in Chenliu to invite the Buddha’s finger-bone śarīra. Some suspected it was a forgery, so the Emperor ordered that it be tested with a fierce fire and struck with a golden mallet;
it suffered no damage whatsoever. Suddenly, the śarīra flew forth and radiated light toward the west. The Emperor remarked, “This is true merit.”
Desiring to return it to propagate the teachings, he placed it within a precious crystal casket. An imperial edict composed a text of aspiration to welcome it back to the temple.
Originally, this was a resident of Chenliu who had built a monastery for the śramaṇa Yijin and requested the name "Chanjiao" (Propagating the Teachings) for its plaque.
Suddenly, a monk from India arrived and said, "I have brought a relic of the Buddha’s finger-bone from India, wishing to seek an auspicious place to enshrine it;
none but you, Master, can protect it. Having spoken, he gave it to him and departed. Thereafter, auspicious lights appeared repeatedly, and prayers were frequently answered.

In the second year of the Huangyou era, with Prime Minister Wen Yanbo concurrently serving as the Commissioner for Translating Scriptures and Polishing Texts, an imperial edict was issued for the monk Huailian and others to enter the Chenghuang Hall for an audience.
Shun Laofu was granted permission to remain as a monk as before. According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), the Renzong Basic Annals does not record this;

however, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the second year of the Huangyou era, Prime Minister Wen Yanbo concurrently served as... [text continues].

The Imperial Commissioner for Translating Scriptures and Polishing Texts, Yanbo, while in the capital, joined with Chan Master Jingyan to lead a gathering of one hundred thousand monastics and laypeople in the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation), making a vow to be reborn in the Pure Land.
By imperial decree, Chan Master Huailian of Jingyin Chan Temple in the Left Ward was summoned to have an audience at Huacheng Hall.
He ascended the seat, and Zen Master Zhilin of the Right Ward’s Office of Monastic Records and others engaged him in formal dialogue. His responses to the questions were deemed most excellent.

The Emperor granted him the title "Great Awakened" (Dàjué). Initially, when Shun Laofu resided at Qixian on Mount Lu, the Magistrate of Nankang, out of personal resentment, stripped him of his monastic robes.
Dàjué welcomed him to Jingyin Monastery and provided him with the main quarters. Whenever the Emperor summoned the Master to the inner palace, he never spoke of this matter.
One day, when Prince Jia arrived at the temple, he saw Dàjué standing in attendance beside Shun with great reverence; finding this strange, he questioned him.
The attendants learned that Dajue had once entered the chamber of Emperor Shun; they returned to report this to the Emperor. The Emperor summoned him for an audience in the private hall.

Seeing his dignified appearance and extraordinary bearing, the Emperor respected him, remarking, "A man of lofty spirit from the mountains and forests. He then inscribed upon a fan the characters "Xiao Shun" (曉舜) as a gift and granted him permission to remain a monk as before.
He was further appointed to reside at Qixian Temple, where he was bestowed with purple robes and a silver alms bowl.
In the fifth year of the Huangyou era, the Śramaṇas from Western Heaven, Zhijixiang and others, came to court to present Sanskrit scriptures; each was bestowed with purple robes.
According to the *Song Shi*, in the Basic Annals of Emperor Renzong, this is not recorded. According to the *Fozu Tongji*, it says as follows...

In the first year of the Zhìhé era, imperial edicts were issued bestowing titles upon various monks. According to the *Song Shǐ* (History of Song), the *Běnjì* (Basic Annals) of Emperor Rénzōng does not record this;

however, according to the *Fó-zǔ Tǒngjì* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddha’s Lineage), in the first year of the Zhìhé era, an edict was issued stating that the Tripitaka Master Fǎhù, whose virtuous precepts were lofty and eminent, should be specially granted a six-character master title:
"Great Master Pǔmíng Cíjué Chuánfàn. This was because the Emperor had dreamed of visiting Jìngdé Temple.
At the gate, he saw a dragon coiled upon the ground; startled, he woke up. He dispatched a messenger to investigate and found a monk lying outside the gate named Daolung.

The next day, the Emperor summoned him for an audience; his responses were detailed and敏捷 (agile). The Emperor bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Mingwu and issued an edict to construct the Huayan Monastery outside the Cao Gate for him to reside in.

In the first year of the Jiayou era, on the Qianyuan Festival, an imperial decree was issued for the Fusheng Pagoda Cloister of Kaibao Temple to hold a Great Fast and bestow monastic robes upon the monks.
(This is not recorded in the *Song Shi*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Renzong.

According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the third year of the Jiayou era, the State of Xixia submitted a memorial stating that a new monastery had been established within their realm and requesting the grant of the Tripitaka scriptures.
The imperial edict granted permission. According to the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Renzong," this is not recorded.

According to the *Fozu Tongji*, etc., in the □□□ year, because the number of monks ordained annually was too great, the quota was first reduced by one-third. According to the *Song Shi*, Emperor Ren...
The *Zongben ji* (Chronicle of the Founding Patriarchs) does not record this; however, according to the biography of Zhang Dong:

when Dong was serving as Director of the Ministry of Sacrifices, the population throughout the empire was increasing daily, and many people were leaving secular life to become monks. Consequently, in the first year of the Zhìhé era, Dong submitted a memorial requesting an imperial edict to increase the annual quota for monastic ordinations.

While previous edicts had stipulated that one person could be ordained for every three hundred households across the various circuits, he subsequently proposed that one person be ordained for every one hundred households. Furthermore, among the civil and military officials within...
"Regarding the practice of establishing monasteries upon the graves of ministers, this has proliferated in recent years.

If those with meritorious service are to be granted such privileges, they should instead be provided with households from antiquity to guard their tombs, with only the restriction that no timber may be cut or gathered there. Currently, the registers of the Ministry of Sacrifices list more than three hundred thousand monks;
if we fail to curtail this number, the state will not be able to sustain the offerings required for them in the future. The court adopted his words and began to reduce the number by one-third.
One [entry] is omitted.

In the fourth year of the Zhìpíng era of Emperor Yǐngzōng, Shénzōng ascended the throne. He issued *duésēngjié* (monk-certificates) to the Shǎnxī Transport Commissioner, ordering them to purchase grain to relieve the drought.
He also bestowed official titles (*é*) upon all monasteries throughout the empire. According to the "Basic Annals of Shénzōng" in the *Sòngshǐ*, this occurred during the Zhìpíng era.

In the first month of the fourth year, the Emperor ascended the throne. In the tenth month of winter, on the day gengxu, the Shaanxi Transportation Commission was granted ordination certificates for monks, ordering them to purchase grain to relieve the counties and prefectures suffering from frost and drought.

According to the *Fozu Tongji*, an imperial edict of the fourth year decreed that all private temples constructed throughout the realm containing thirty rooms or more were to be granted the title "Shousheng" (Longevity-Saint).

In the first year of the Xīníng era of Emperor Shénzōng, the sale of monk ordination certificates (*dùdí*) began. According to the *Shìngshǐ* (Veritable Records of the Song Dynasty), this is not recorded in the biography of Emperor Shénzōng.

However, according to the *Fózǔ Tǒngjì* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddha and Patriarchs), on the seventh month of the first year of Xīníng, Qián Gōngfǔ, the Palace Censor, submitted a memorial stating that since the Ministry of Rites had encountered a year of famine and river flooding, he requested that ordination certificates be sold to assist in the immediate emergency. From this point forward, [the practice continued] during the Imperial Birthdays...
He bestowed [ordinations] and also reduced [the number of certificates]; the sale of ordination certificates began from this point.
In that year, there were 220,660 monks throughout the empire and 34,030 nuns.

On the *dingmao* day of the fourth month of summer in the third year of the Xīníng era, the Ministry of Revenue issued ordination certificates (*duésēngdié*) to the Two-Zhejiang Circuit Transport Commission to recruit commoners to contribute grain.
(As recorded in the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shenzong" in the *History of Song*).
In the fifth year of the Xīníng era, an imperial edict was issued for the Tiānzhú Guānyīn Temple in Qiántáng to ordain one monk annually to attend to the incense and lamps.

This is verified by the *Sòng Shǐ* (History of the Song Dynasty), *Běn jì* (Basic Annals) of Emperor Shénzōng; however, it is not recorded therein. According to the *Fó zǔ tǒng jì* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddha’s Lineage), it states as follows...

On the day of Dingchou in the eighth month of the seventh year of Xining (1074), the Huayan Circuit Pacification Commandery was granted ordination certificates for monks to recruit grain for the relief of Han and Tibetan famine-stricken people.
(As recorded in the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Shenzong," etc.)

In the third year of the Yuanfeng era, an imperial edict was issued to provide a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks. Those translation monks who had been granted the title of Acting Assistant Director were renamed as Dharma Masters of the Tripiṭaka (*Sanzang Fashi*).

According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), Shenzong’s Basic Annals, this is not recorded. However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (General Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the first month of the third year of the Yuanfeng era, an edict was issued to provide a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks within the Great Palace, bestowing upon them *kāṣāya* robes and copies of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* for the sake of [the deceased] Cizong.
The Imperial Grandmother performed memorial rites for his merit. Officials were appointed to meticulously determine the regulations for the bureaucracy and court ceremonies.

It was decreed that from the Tang dynasty until the present reign, those who served as monks-officials for the translation of scriptures had all been granted the rank of *Shi* (Provisional) Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Guanglu Qing*) or Minister of the Court of State Ceremonies (*Honglu Qing*).

Hereafter, they shall instead be conferred the title of "Translator of the Tripitaka Dharma Master" (*Yijing Sanzang Fashi*). Those granted the rank of *Shi* Junior Minister (*Shaoling*) shall be conferred the title of "Tripitaka Dharma Master. Furthermore, the Vinaya Monastery of Donglin in Jiangzhou was reformed into a Chan seat.
Mingchang was appointed to reside there as the Abbot.
In the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, an imperial edict summoned the monk Zongben to have an audience at the Yanhe Hall. (Note: This is not recorded in the *Shenzong Benji* of the *Song Shi*.
According to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, an edict was issued for the Xiangguo Temple to open sixty [new halls]).
The four courtyards were established as the two monasteries of Baizhan and Erlü; the eastern and western corridors were designated as the two great monasteries of Hui-lin and Zhi-hai.

By imperial decree, Chan Master Zongben of Jingci was appointed to reside at Hui-lin, and Chan Master Changzong of Donglin was appointed to reside at Zhi-hai. Changzong firmly declined the appointment, which was granted.
When Zongben entered the audience at the Yanhe Hall, he performed the "mountain cry" greeting and immediately sat cross-legged upon his seat, causing the attendants to look on in astonishment.

The Master remained composed. When the Emperor offered him tea, he took up the cup and swirled it about. The Emperor asked about his place of training; he replied, "Chengtian Yong'an. The Emperor was greatly pleased.
They conversed for a long time, and upon retiring, the Emperor remarked to those around him, "A jewel among monks. An attendant asked, "What did Your Majesty say?
He replied, "We were merely having casual conversation while drinking tea. According to the *Ketan*, during the Yuanfeng era, an imperial edict was issued to the monks... [text ends]
Ciben was summoned to the Huelin Chan Monastery for an audience and granted tea, which he regarded as an honor. When the late Master [Ciben] attended upon the Emperor, he was given this proclamation:
the Emperor remarked that the capital is bustling and its common people pursue superficial pursuits; "I have summoned you," he said, "to exhort the people to do good. There is no other purpose."

In the seventh year of the Yuanfeng era, Wang Anshi requested that the garden and residences of Jiangning Prefecture be converted into a Buddhist monastery, and it was granted the name Baoben Chan Monastery.

According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), Shenzong Benji (Basic Annals of Emperor Shenzong), this is not recorded. According to the *Fozu Tongji* (General Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), it states...

According to the *Xifeng Rili* (Calendar of the Xifeng Era), in a memorial submitted by Wang Anshi, he wrote: "Fortunately, we have encountered Your Majesty’s sagely destiny, which has transcended and elevated [the common lot]..."

I, Yi, am aware that you have extended your grace and compassion to me, encompassing both my father and myself. Bearing heaven upon my head and the earth upon my back, my tears of gratitude are beyond measure. Yet, looking upon my own decrepit and failing body, what benefit can I possibly provide?
Driven by a humble wish no greater than that of an ant, I now reside in a garden house in Shangyuan County, Jiangning Prefecture;

I have established a Buddhist monastery there to perpetually pray for the prolongation of Your Majesty’s divine longevity. If you would deign to grant this, I beseech you to bestow it as a special favor.
The name has been granted. It is a rare and expansive honor, a meeting with glory for this one time. Relying upon Your Majesty’s majestic spiritual power, I vow to repay this kindness without end.
I await further instructions. Having received the Imperial decree, it shall be granted as requested: the temple shall be named Baoben Chan Temple.

In the eighth year of the Yuanfeng era, the Crown Prince personally transcribed Buddhist scriptures to pray for the Emperor’s longevity. According to the *Song Shi*, in the Basic Annals of Emperor Zhezong:

in the second month of the eighth year of Yuanfeng, Emperor Shenzhong was bedridden with illness. The Chancellor Wang Gui petitioned that the succession to the throne be established early as a measure for the sake of the ancestral temple and the altars of state.
He further submitted a memorial requesting that the Empress Dowager temporarily assume joint governance of affairs. Emperor Shenzhong first...
Agreed. On the first day of the third month, the Jia-wu day, the Empress Dowager held court behind the curtain in the Funing Hall and addressed Guo Tai and the others, saying:

"The Crown Prince is by nature grave and dignified; he is quick-witted in his studies. Since the Emperor began taking medicine, he has personally transcribed Buddhist scriptures to pray for His Majesty’s recovery.

I have brought these forth to show you. The characters he had written were extremely upright and careful. Guo Tai and the others offered their congratulations, whereupon they received the imperial decree.
[He] was established as the Crown Prince.
In the first year of the Yuanyou era of Emperor Zhezong, the Korean monk Uichon came to court. According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Zhezong do not record this.
However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the first year of Yuanyou, the Korean Prince Yu-se, [ordained as a] monk...
When Wŏnhyo (義天) came to court, the Emperor issued an edict for Su Shi of the Ministry of Rites to serve as his host. The relevant authorities prepared the accommodations with great care.

Wŏnhyo submitted four memorials requesting to receive the teachings of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. Thereupon, an edict was issued for Yang Jie of the Ministry of State Affairs to escort him to Qiantang, where he received the Dharma from Master Jingyuan of Huizhen Temple.
He subsequently traveled to Tiantai to visit Master Cibian Jian and receive the teachings of the Tiantai school.
He studied under Master Lingzhi Zhao, requesting the *Śīla-dharma* and the *Zizhi ji*. He then traveled to Jinshan to visit Chan Master Foyin Yuan, who accepted his prostrations while seated.
Yang Jie asked him in surprise for the reason. Master Yuan replied, "Yitian is merely a monk from a foreign land.
If I were to bend the Way to conform to worldly custom, how could I demonstrate the teacher-disciple dharma to the people of China? When the imperial court heard this, they [honored] the Master...
To ensure the preservation of the Great Dharma, once Yitian had returned to his country, he established monasteries and propagated the teachings, honoring Cibian as the founding patriarch.
Furthermore, he entrusted the three translations of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—both the old and new versions—written in golden script to Huiyin, where he constructed a pavilion to house them.
In the third year of the Yuanyou era, an imperial edict ordered an inner attendant to carry gold to Donglin Temple to adorn the Buddha images in the Five Divine-Dynasty Halls.
This is not recorded in the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Zhezong," but is stated in the *Fozu Tongji*.

In the fifth year of the Yuanyou era, an imperial edict was issued bestowing the title Shenzhi (Divine Wisdom) upon the monk Sheng. According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Zhezong do not record this;

however, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the fifth year of Yuanyou, the Dharma Master Shenzhi Sheng arrived and resided at Xingfu Monastery in Yue.

At that time, Zhao Qingxi, whose courtesy name was Gongbian, served as his patron. It happened that there was a severe drought and a great epidemic, yet despite long prayers, no response was received.
He then requested the Master to welcome the Great Being (Mahāsattva) into the government offices. After he prayed earnestly for one night, rain fell like pouring water and the epidemic subsided.
Han Bi reported this to the court; the Emperor bestowed the name "Yuántōng" upon the Master's residence and conferred the honorary title "Shénzhì" upon the Master.

In the seventh year of the Yuanyou era, an imperial edict was issued granting a plaque for the name of the stūpa temple of Buddhatāpali. According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), in the annals of Emperor Zhezong, this is not recorded.

According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the seventh year of the Yuanyou era, Su Shi, the Governor of Yingchuan, submitted a memorial stating: [text follows].

The stupa courtyard of Buddhapāli was frequently efficacious in granting the fulfillment of prayers. A request was made for an imperial plaque, and by imperial decree, it was bestowed the name "Guangfan" (Radiant and Pure) Courtyard.
While Buddhapāli was in the Tang, he returned to India at the beginning of the Yifeng era to retrieve the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, which he brought back to translate and disseminate.
Later, he died while traveling in Ying. The villagers lacquered his body and constructed a stupa to honor him with solemn rites.
In the first year of the Shaosheng era, monks were summoned to the imperial palace to perform a memorial service (*daochang*) for the first anniversary of Empress Xuanren’s death.

According to the *Song Shi*, in the Basic Annals of Emperor Zhezong, this is not recorded. According to the *Daoshan Qinghua*, in the ninth month of the first year of the Shaosheng era, the prohibition...
For the occasion of the first anniversary of the mourning period (*xiǎoxiáng*), a ritual altar was established within the palace to proclaim benevolence. Elder Xuānlóng Bào ascended the seat;

the Emperor had set up his imperial curtained pavilion nearby to listen. The monk offered this prayer: "We humbly pray that Your Majesty, the Emperor, shall love the state as you love your own person and regard the people as your own children.

May you ever recall the protection and preservation of the Grand Empress Dowager, and always maintain the same anxiety and diligence as the late Emperor. [May] all the high officials and the hundred functionaries..."
"I shall reverently uphold the laws and institutions of the House of Han. From the four quarters across ten thousand *li*, it shall forever remain the domain of the Zhao clan.
Subsequently, a monk asked a question, saying, "Where does Your Majesty currently reside? He replied, "I reside in the Dragon Palace of the Buddha-dharma above the heavens."
Her heart was set upon her descendants and the state. At that time, as these accounts were circulated, there was no one who did not offer praise. Alas! How sagacious was the Empress Dowager!
Both Chinese and barbarians hailed her as a female Yao or Shun. While she presided from behind the curtain, every edict she issued was received by the people of the world with [reverence].
This is called the "Pleasant and Coherent Account.
In the third year of the Yuánfú era, Huīzōng ascended the throne and issued an edict to restore the monasteries of Shàogāng and Shǎolíng.

According to the *Sòngshǐ* (History of the Song Dynasty), in the first month of the third year of Yuánfú, the Emperor ascended the throne. According to the *Fózǔ Tǒngjì* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddha and Patriarchs)...

In the third year of the Fú era, by imperial decree, Lóu Shēng, the Magistrate of Dēngfēng who was overseeing the construction of Tàilíng, requested that the remaining labor force be used to repair the Shaolín Monastery on Mount Sōnggāo.
Officials and commoners worked together, and it was completed in a single day. It was named the Miànbì Ānruò (The Cave of Facing the Wall).
Shortly thereafter, twelve stalks of *zhīcǎo* (mushrooms) grew from within the grove; nectar rained down upon the pond, and at night, a light reached toward the heavens. Afterwards...
Shan Chen Wusi composed a record for it.
In the first year of the Jianguojingguo era of Emperor Huizong, a monk was summoned to the inner palace to lecture on the sutras.

According to the *Song Shi*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Huizong, this is not recorded; however, according to the *Ketan*, in the first year of the Jianguojingguo era, a monk was summoned to the inner palace.

He lectured on the sutras and was granted the title of "Ten Chan Masters," as well as the Imperially Composed Preface to *Seng Weibai’s Continued Record of the Lamp*. These events were considered particularly momentous by the monastic community.

In the second year of the Chongning era, an imperial decree was issued to establish Chongning Temples throughout the empire, and posthumous titles were conferred upon various monks. (According to the *Song Shi*, [Biography of] Emperor Huizong...)

The Annals of the Founding Patriarchs. On the *gēisi* day of the ninth month in the second year of the Chóngníng era, an edict was issued for all prefectures throughout the empire to establish Chóngníng Temples.

According to the *Fó-zǔ Tǒngjì*, in that same second year, the posthumous title Dàoshì Fǎhuì (Great Master of the Way and Wisdom) was bestowed upon the Táng dynasty Vinaya Master Dào Xuān of Zhōngnán Mountain;
the posthumous title Dàshī Fǎbǎo (Great Master of the Dharma Jewel) was bestowed upon the Great Master Cíyún Zūnshì of Tiānzhú Mountain; and [the title] Nánpíng... [was bestowed].
Fanzhen was posthumously titled Dashi Baoxiang; Gushan Zhiyuan was posthumously titled Dashi Fahaha.
In the third year of the Chongning era, an imperial edict was issued to welcome the Buddha’s tooth relic from Xiangguo Temple into the palace for veneration.

Regarding the bestowal of posthumous titles upon various monks, the *Song shi* (History of Song), in the "Basic Annals" (*benji*) of Emperor Huizong, does not record this. According to the *Fozu tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the third year of the Chongning era, an edict was issued...

The Imperial Relics of Śākyamuni Buddha, which had been venerated by the three successive dynasties at Sangwangsi Temple, were welcomed back and enshrined within the palace for offerings. Enclosed within a crystal casket, the *śarīra* relics emerged like falling raindrops.

By imperial decree, the title "Dharma Master Who Opens the Way and Perfects Penetration" (*Qidao Yuantong Fashi*) was posthumously conferred upon Kāśyapa Mātanga of Baimasi Temple, and the title "Dharma Master Who Opens the Teaching and Holds All" (*Kaiao Zongchi Fashi*) was bestowed upon Dharmaratna.
Furthermore, the titles "Great Master Who Transmits Awakening through Emptiness" (*Jingkong Shaojue Dashi*) were granted to Fu Dashi of Shuanglin Temple and others.
Scholar. Regarding Li Zhangzhe of Fangshan, known as Xianjiao Miaoyan Zhangzhe:

In the fifth year of the Chongning era, an imperial edict was issued to abolish the Buddha-dharma. According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Huizong do not record this.

However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (General Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), on the tenth month of the fifth year of Chongning, Emperor Huizong issued an edict stating: "Those who possess the empire must honor and serve [the Buddha]."
"The Supreme Lord (Shangdi). Should there be any who dare to be irreverent toward Him, yet the teachings of the Śākya [Buddhism] place the Heavenly Emperor within the ranks of ghosts and spirits;
no offense against the deities and transgression of one's proper station is more extreme than this. The relevant authorities shall expunge it. Furthermore, by imperial decree:

"Within the Water-Land Ritual Assemblies (shuilu daochang), the positions of the Three Purities (Sanqing) and others were established. The edict issued during the Yuanfeng era prohibits this; the matter must be strictly investigated and enforced. [Old Record]
In the monasteries where monks reside, images of the Three Teachings are often displayed together, such that they have become the central icons of the temple halls.

Śākyamuni occupies the center, Laojun occupies the left, and Confucius occupies the right; this does not accord with the intent of venerating the True Lord (Tianzhen) or the principles of the Confucian teachings.
