These images should be invited back to the Daoist observatories and Confucian academies to rectify their proper placement. Upon reading the imperial edict, the śramaṇa Yongdao of the capital wept and said:

Within this realm, Confucius and Laozi established their teachings by emulating Heaven; thus, they did not contravene Heaven. The Buddha’s Dharma appearing in the world is that which all gods and humans take as their teacher;
thus, it does not contravene the Buddha. That enlightened kings of antiquity served the Buddha while also attending to the Supreme Deity was because they understood this principle.

The Buddha-dharma is impartial; therefore, although its teachings are bestowed such that both sages and ordinary people may gather together, the distinctions between ruler and minister, and honor and humility, are each uniquely preserved.
Since the time of our ancestors, the adherence to the Dharma has been firmly established.
Were these suddenly abolished, I fear the calamity of destroying the Dharma would find its omen herein. Those who heard this were filled with dismay.

In the third year of the Daguang era, it was prohibited for high-ranking officials and members of the imperial clan to claim possession of monasteries with official names to serve as funerary temples or for the merit of ancestral rites.

According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Huizong do not record this. However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), an imperial decree was issued in the third year of Daguang stating that for funerary temples established by meritorious ministers and members of the imperial clan, they were permitted to build their own buildings and acquire land; they were merely granted the official name and exempted from taxes and levies.
Proclamation: Monks shall be invited from their own homes to serve as abbots; it is not permitted to claim or occupy designated monasteries for the merit of ancestral grave temples.
The Censorate and the Inner Service Office (Neishicheng) are authorized to investigate and take action against any violations.

In the fourth year of the Daguang era, on the *xinyou* day of the first month in spring, an imperial edict was issued stating that for commoners and officials to prostrate before monks would be considered the great offense of irreverence (*badaogong*).

On the *gengwu* new moon of the second month, the burning of the crown, the cauterizing of the arms, the shedding of blood, and the severing of fingers were prohibited. On the *renyin* day of the fifth month, the issuance of monastic certificates (*sengdie*) was suspended for three years.
This is recorded in the *Song Shi*, in the "Basic Annals" (*benji*) of Emperor Huizong.

The fourth year of the Zhenghe era: The finger of the Buddha from the Bāguān Temple in Chenliu was brought for examination. According to the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Huizong," this is not recorded. According to the *Fozu Tongji*:
In the fourth year of the Zhenghe era, local officials reported that the so-called "finger of the Buddha" at the Bāguān Temple in Chenliu was actually the finger of a sea dog (*hai-gou*).
An imperial edict was issued to bring it for verification; it was subjected to fire and struck with iron hammers for over ten days, yet its color remained [unchanged].
[The Emperor] did not change [his mind]. He issued an edict to treat him with greater courtesy and send him back.

In the first year of the Xuanhé era, an imperial decree was issued to destroy the Buddha-dharma. According to the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Huizong," on the day Yimao of the first month in the first year of Xuanhé, an edict was issued to change the title of the Buddha to "Great Enlightened Golden Immortal" (Dàjué Jīnxiān), while others were designated as "Immortals" (Xiānrén) or "Great Beings" (Shìdà). Monks were [to be...]
The virtuous practitioner changes their attire and adopts [the Chinese] surname; the temple is termed a "palace" (*gong*), the cloister a "sanctuary" (*guan*), and the *bhikṣuṇī* a "virtuous woman.

According to the *Fozu Tongji*: In the first month of the first year, an imperial edict stated: "Since the influence of the former kings has exhausted, the foreign teaching has begun to prevail within the Middle Kingdom.
Although their words differ, their ultimate aim is one with the Way. Though the teaching may not..."

Yet it still harms the rites and righteousness of the Middle Kingdom; therefore, it must be reformed. We shall designate the Buddha as the Great Awakened Golden Immortal (Jinxian), requiring him to wear the robes of a Celestial Honored One (Tianzun).
Bodhisattvas shall be called Great Beings (Dashis), monks shall be called Virtuous Beings (Deshis), and nuns shall be called Female Virtuous Beings (Nü Deshis).

They wore ceremonial caps and headbands, and carried wooden tablets (muh). Temples were designated as palaces (gong), and monasteries as observatories (guan); the abbots were appointed as "Officials in Charge of Palaces and Observatories.
They were strictly prohibited from possessing bronze gongs, stupas, or statues. When Buddhism was first suppressed, none in the outer court supported the movement;
it was only when the Prefect of Kaifeng, Sheng Zhang, was incited by wicked men regarding matters of personal interest that he began to comply, subsequently issuing an imperial edict to this effect.
Cai Jing said, "The state has enjoyed peace for a long time, and thus heroes have had no use; many of them have hidden among these followers.
If one day their dwellings are destroyed and their food and clothing taken away, where will they turn? They will surely give rise to great resentment and gather to cause a rebellion.
On a future day, whom will you, my lords, allow to bear the blame? When the Emperor heard this, he was enraged and said:
"These people merely wish to intimidate me. When his family members urged him [to flee], Jing said, "I shall face this with my own body to repay the Buddha.
It happened that the monastic community was about to submit a petition to the capital seeking a formal debate.

Li Chengzhang obtained this information through his investigations and arrested the two leading high monks, Dayuhua and Mingjue, both of whom were Vinaya masters. He had them all bastinadoed seventy times and executed.
Yongdao, the Great Master Baojue of the Left Street, submitted a memorial stating: "From antiquity, the Buddha-dharma has never failed to wax and wane in tandem with the fortunes of the state.
When Emperor Taiwu of the Wei dynasty and Cui Hao suppressed the Buddha-dharma, within less than three or four years, Cui Hao’s entire clan was exterminated.
When Emperor Wencheng extensively restored it, and when Emperor Wu of Zhou and Wei Yuansong suppressed the Buddha-dharma, within five or six years, Wei Yuansong..."
He was demoted and died. Emperor Wen of the Sui dynasty greatly revived it. During the Tang dynasty, Empress Wu, Zhao Guizhen, and Li Deyu suppressed the Buddha-dharma;
yet within a year, Guizhen was executed and Li Deyu was exiled to his death. Emperor Xuan greatly revived it.

In our own nation, the Taizu and Taizong emperors, along with their successive sagacious successors, translated scriptures, examined monks, and greatly promoted the Buddha-dharma. These established laws remain intact; even if ten thousand...
The world can be preserved. How can Your Majesty bear to follow the words of a treacherous man on a single occasion and commit such a world-shocking act?

Does Your Majesty not reflect upon how Emperor Taiwu was assassinated by the hands of eunuchs, how Emperor Wu of Zhou became a prisoner in an iron dungeon, and how Emperor Wu of Tang suffered the retribution of having his life-span shortened and his throne usurped? These are all precedents that may be observed as warnings. Your Majesty—

"How can you, my subordinate, tread upon the calamity that befell a wicked ruler and contravene the laws of our ancestors? When this memorial was submitted, the Emperor was greatly incensed and issued an edict to exile him to Daozhou.

Because Liang Ji insisted on refusing to carry out the order, the Emperor consequently abandoned the deliberations on the reorganization of the administration and instead made all decisions solely through his attendants.
Liang Chengzhang coerced the Buddhist Registrar Hongbing into submitting a memorial to receive imperial instructions; thereupon, all monks were changed to "Virtuous Scholars" (deshi).
They all followed this by changing their attire; otherwise, they would have been destroyed. [The Emperor] repeatedly petitioned before the Sovereign, saying:

"The Buddhist images throughout the realm were not created by the monks themselves. They were all made by sons for their fathers and by ministers for their sovereigns, solely to pray for blessings and repay their debts of gratitude.
To now destroy them on a large scale is precisely enough to disturb the hearts of the people; I consider this to be of no benefit to the state. The Sovereign’s intention—
He was moved slightly by this.
In the second year of the Xuanhua era, an imperial edict was issued to restore the Buddhist titles and designations. According to the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Huizong":

on the dinghai day of the sixth month in the second year of Xuanhua, the names of monasteries were restored; on the yisi day of the ninth month, those who had become *deshi* (lay practitioners) were restored to the status of monks.
According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the eighth month of the second year of the Xuanhua era, an imperial edict was issued stating:

"Previously, due to the proposals of wicked men, the titles of those of the Śākya clan were altered; this was deeply improper. Those previously designated as 'De-shi' (Virtuous Men) and 'Nü De-shi' (Virtuous Women) shall henceforth be called monks (*seng*) and nuns (*ni*) as before.
In the ninth month, an edict was issued to fully restore the status of monks and nuns throughout the empire.
In the sixth month of the seventh year of the Xuanhua era, Daozhou Yongdao received an imperial decree to be released and returned home.

By imperial edict, he was to reside at Zhaoxian Chan Monastery and was granted the name Fadao to honor his protection of the Dharma. (This is not recorded in the *Song Shi*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Huizong;
it is according to the *Fozu Tongji*, etc.)

In the eighth year of the Xuanhua era, an imperial edict was issued prohibiting the defilement and humiliation of monks and nuns. According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Huizong do not record this;

however, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the seventh month of the eighth year of Xuanhua, Princess of the Wu Kingdom held the Buddhist gate in high esteem.

An imperial decree was issued to officials and commoners: "Should anyone insult, humiliate, revile, or address monks and nuns with the derogatory term 'shaven-headed,' they shall be punished in accordance with the instructions of the third year of the Xiangfu era.

In the second year of the Jingkang era of the Qinzhong reign, when the Gaozong Emperor ascended the throne, he summoned the monk Kechen to the temporary capital to preach the Dharma and issued an edict.

Sengfadao served as a Military Counselor (Canmou) to the Commander-in-Chief (Zongguan) with the rank of Xuanjiao Lang. According to the *Song Shi*, in the Basic Annals (*Benji*) of Emperor Gaozong, this is not recorded.
However, according to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the fifth month of the second year of the Jingkang era, the Prince of Kang ascended the throne at Songzhou;
on the tenth month, the Emperor traveled to Yangzhou and dispatched eight envoys to summon Chan Master Kechen of Jinshan.

He went to the imperial encampment and expounded the methods of *dhyāna*. He was granted the title Yuanwu. Under the authority of Zong Ze, the Guardian of the Eastern Capital, the Dharma Master Fadao was appointed to reside at Tiansheng Temple in the Left Ward.
He was also granted the rank of Xuanjiao Lang and appointed as a military advisor to the Commander-in-Chief, charged with performing rites for the state and providing protection for the army.
The Master traveled to the Huai and Ying regions, where he exhorted the local elites to provide grain.
He assisted the state, and the army relied upon him for its salvation.

In the fourth year of the Jianyan era of Emperor Gaozong, the former residence of Lin Lingsu was established as Zifu Monastery, and by imperial decree, the monk Fadao was conferred the title of Great Master Yuantong Faji.
According to the "Annals of Emperor Gaozong" in the *Song Shi*, this is not recorded. According to...

*Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs): On the *yihai* day of the second month in the fourth year of the Jianyan era, the Emperor visited Jiangxin Temple and issued an edict designating the former residence of Lin Lingsu as the Zifu Jiaoyuan.
Prime Minister Lü Yihao nominated the Dharma Master Yuanbian Daochin to preside over it.
On the *jweiwei* day of the third month, the Emperor departed from Jiangxin; by imperial decree, the Dharma Master Fadao was to accompany the imperial entourage.

They deliberated on matters of state and military affairs. The Emperor wished to invest him with the ceremonial crown and robes, but the Master declined with great earnestness. By imperial decree, he was conferred the title of Great Master Yuantong Fazhi.
In the fourth month, while the Emperor’s camp was stationed at Kuaiji, there was a severe drought; the Emperor issued a decree for the Dharma Master Dao to offer prayers at Yuantong Temple.
On that very day, rain fell. The Emperor was greatly pleased.
In the second year of the Shaoxing era, while the Emperor was reading a Buddhist scripture within the inner palace, he issued an edict to construct the Avalokiteśvara Hall.
(This is not recorded in the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Gaozong. According to the *Fozu Tongji*, it was in the first month of the second year of the Shaoxing era.

The Emperor halted his progress at Qiantang, which was elevated to the status of Lin’an Prefecture. Within the inner palace, the Emperor frequently inscribed the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-pūrṇamukha-parivarta*, the *Bhadracarī-praṇidhāna*, and the verses of the Seven Buddhas;
in his leisure time, he would regularly read them himself to inspire sacred understanding.
Furthermore, he personally inscribed the Ashoka Mountain Śarīra Stupa as the "Stupa of the Radiance of the Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa. In the second month, he issued an edict once again.
The Hall of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara was constructed in India.
In the third year of the Shaoxing era, an imperial decree ordered the monk Judo to reside there. According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Gaozong do not record this;

however, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), on the second month of the third year of the Shaoxing era, the Dharma Master Judo of Mount Lu submitted a memorial to the Department of State Affairs.
Since the reign of Emperor Shenzong, Daoists have arrogantly assumed official ranks; those such as Lin Lingsu and Wang Chundao were so numerous that they rivaled the two highest civil offices.

Consequently, Daoists were permitted to rank above the monks. Although during the Jingkang and Jianyan periods the titles of office held by Daoists had already been rescinded and revoked, they still dared to remain haughtily at the head of the assembly during incense offerings for the national memorials and during congregations at monasteries. This...

They hold the national laws in contempt. Such being the case, we now wish to restore the ancient regulations of our ancestors. This is fully recorded in the *Sengshi lüe* (A Brief History of the Sangha). Whenever there is an assembly at court, the monks precede the Daoists;

they stand side by side in the palace courtyard, with the monks to the east and the Daoists to the west. On occasions such as the suburban sacrifice to Heaven (*jiaotian*), the Daoists are on the left and the monks on the right.

We have recently sent an official to the Ministry of Rites (*Lilbu*) and obtained a formal document from the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Taichangsi*) concerning the *Yinge li* (Rituals of Adoption and Abolition), which states that during the Qian... [text truncated].
In the first year of the Dede era, according to the established custom for the general amnesty at Xuande Gate, monks were positioned to the left and Daoists to the right.

Furthermore, upon consulting the Jiayou Compilation of Decrees and the Shaoxing New Code, both of which arrange the textual order with monks preceding Daoists, the entries within the Zhenghe statutes that placed Daoists, Buddhist observers, and Buddhist postulants above monks have all been deleted and are no longer in effect. Subsequently, we received an imperial decree to this effect.

The regulations were revised accordingly, placing the monks at the head. In the eleventh month, the Court of Imperial Sacrifices issued circular edicts to all circuits stating that for incense offerings, formal processions, and assemblies in all locations, one must follow the established laws of the imperial ancestors by placing the monks on the left.

In the fourth year of the Shaoxing era, an imperial edict was issued to establish a Great Water-Land Feast (*shuilu daizhai*) to deliver those who had perished in battle. According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Gaozong, this is not recorded.
However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the fourth year of the Shaoxing era, Liu Yu of the illegitimate Qi state...
As the Jurchen invaders had entered the borders, the Emperor issued an edict for a personal campaign.

On the ninth month, the Emperor personally visited the Hall of the Great Being of India (Tianzhu Dashi Dian) to burn incense and offer solemn prayers for the early pacification of the northern barbarians. Subsequently, Han Shizhong, the Pacification Commissioner of Huaidong, defeated the Jurchen and Qi people at Chengzhou.
Han Shizhong presented the captured prisoners to the imperial presence and, taking advantage of the occasion, petitioned for the posthumous honors of those who had fallen in battle.
Regarding the granting of funeral benefits and condolences, the Emperor sighed with distress and said, "To die by the edge of a blade is truly pitiable.
He immediately commanded Hu Songnian, Director of the Hanlin Academy, to draft the formal text for holding a great *shuilu* (water-land) vegetarian feast for the salvation of the deceased.

That evening, many spirits and ghosts were seen gathering at the assembly, and those who had dreamed of their comrades killed in battle all rejoiced together, believing that from this point forward they would attain [liberation].
Regarding those born into the happy realms, the Emperor heard of this and was greatly delighted.

In the fifth year of the Xiaosheng era, he issued an imperial decree for Dharma Master Dao to enter the palace to pray for rain; he was subsequently granted a golden bowl, as well as a monastic certificate (*du-ji*) and silver coins for the monk Yingru.
This is not recorded in the *Song Shi* (History of Song), *Gaozong Benji* (Basic Annals of Emperor Gaozong). According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs):

In the fifth year of the Xianhe era, there was a great drought for an entire month. An imperial edict summoned Master Daofa to enter the palace to pray for rain. He established a ritual altar and performed the rites;
using four golden vases, each filled with fresh carp, he sprinkled water and offered silent prayers, then dispatched four swift messengers to cast them into the river.

Before they had even returned, the rain had fallen in abundance. The Emperor was greatly pleased and specially bestowed upon him a golden bowl. In the ninth month, the Emperor traveled to Tianzhu Monastery.

The officer of the palace burned incense. The Abbot responded with fluency, as if in a formal audience before the Emperor. The Emperor was pleased and bestowed upon him the "Wansui Xiangshan" (Myriad Years Fragrant Mountain) for the service of the Great Being (Bodhisattva), along with ordination certificates, silver, silk, and other gifts.

In the seventh year of the Shaoxing era, an imperial edict was issued stating that those monasteries with official endowments that had been converted into memorial temples for ancestral graves should all be rectified.

According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), in the Annals of Emperor Gaozong, this is not recorded. However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the seventh year of the Shaoxing era, Chen Gongfu, the Left Palace Counselor, submitted a memorial requesting that the established laws of the founding emperors be followed and that no officials in the executive branch be permitted to designate [monasteries] for such purposes.

Regarding titled monasteries: as for those previously petitioned by officials to be designated as titled monasteries to serve as ancestral grave temples for the accumulation of merit, all such instances shall be rectified, and permission granted to provide them with small, untitled monasteries instead. The imperial decree was accepted.

Initially, Chief Administrator Li Gang had occupied the Puli Monastery in Changzhou and the Xingsheng Monastery in Shaowu. When a court official remonstrated, it was determined that both locations were already titled monasteries.
Regarding the obstruction [caused by this], an imperial edict was issued to separately allot a small, unregistered courtyard for him; the scholarly community considered this a relief.

Furthermore, the Chief Secretary Shen Yiqiu submitted a memorial stating that although the Miaoyan Monastery at his ancestral grave had been built by his own family, it already possessed an original imperial plaque and thus should not be reallocated as a gift.
The Emperor, considering it a building constructed by himself, deemed there was no need to rectify the matter. At that time, the remonstrance officials praised Yiqiu for his capability.
He embodied the ancestral methods and intentions, reforming the currency of the present day. His request was granted by imperial decree.

In the ninth year of the Shaoxing era, an edict was issued to all prefectures and commanderies to establish Baoen Guangxiao Chan Monasteries as dedicated sites for the solemn commemoration of Emperor Huizong.
This is not recorded in the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Gaozong," but is verified in the *Fozu Tongji*.
The chronicle records as follows:
In the fifth month of the twelfth year of the Xiangxing era, the issuance of *du-seng-die* (monk certificates) was suspended.

According to the relevant entries in the *Basic Annals of Emperor Gaozong* in the *History of Song*, and according to the *Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs*, in the twelfth year, Jian Shuyi, a Left Assistant Official of the Department of State Affairs, offered his private wealth [to support the Sangha].

A memorial was submitted requesting that the sale of ordination certificates (*duòdié*) be suspended; the court granted this request. At that time, the Lin’an Prefecture requested ordination certificates to repair the Hall of the Great Being at Tiantzhu.
An imperial decree granted fifty thousand strings of cash for the purpose. The Emperor then said to his attendants: "I observe the sovereigns of antiquity..."

If one wishes to eliminate the two teachings of Śākya and Laozi, whether by destroying their images or abolishing their followers, such efforts will not last long; rather, they will often only cause them to blaze all the more fiercely.
Now, if one simply does not issue ordination certificates (duòdié), then [the heterodox teachings] will naturally diminish over time, and we shall achieve victory.

In the thirteenth year of the Shaoxing era, an imperial edict was issued to establish the Shouxing Monastery (Shoushengyuan). Monks requested the allocation of ordination certificates (*dudie*), which was not permitted.

According to the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Gaozong," this is not recorded. However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), in the thirteenth year, an edict was issued to construct Tianshen Wanshou Yuanjue Monastery on the northern mountains of West Lake, and to renovate the West Lake Shouxing Monastery, with [a certain monk] appointed as the presiding official.
The petitioner requested the allocation of ordination certificates (*duòdì*). The Emperor said: "Those who speak of this all desire to sell the certificates to provide for the state's revenue.

However, what is obtained from a single certificate does not exceed two hundred strings of cash, yet one man is deprived of his labor. If the allocation were suspended for ten years, their numbers would naturally diminish."

In the twenty-fourth year of the Shaoxing era, an imperial edict designated Upper Tianzhu as an Imperial Court Dharma Assembly (Oqian Daochang), specifically exempting it from levies and other such matters.
In the eleventh month of the thirtieth year of the Shaoxing era, Chan Master Daochang, abbot of Lingyin, submitted a memorial requesting that these provisions be promulgated.
Regarding the *duòdié* (ordination certificates):

[the Emperor] did not grant them. In the thirty-first year of the Shaoxing era, Wu Zicai, Vice Minister of the Ministry of Rites, submitted a memorial requesting that the issuance of *duòdié* be promulgated.

Those who commented on the matter dismissed him as a sycophant to the Buddha; he was subsequently dismissed and returned to his rural estate. (According to the above, from the *Song Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Gaozong").
[The *Ji* (Chronicle) does not record this in either case. According to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), etc.:
In the thirty-second year of the Shaoxing era, Emperor Xiaozong ascended the throne and presented jade artifacts from the inner treasury to the Hall of the Great Being (Guanyin).
[This is not recorded in the "Basic Annals" of Emperor Xiaozong in the *Song Shi* (History of Song]. According to the *Fozu Tongji*, the thirty-second year of the Shaoxing era...
In the fifth month of that year, he abdicated the throne to the Crown Prince. In the tenth month, torrential rains did not cease. The Emperor dispatched an inner attendant to pray at Shang Tianzhu;

as soon as the smoke from the incense offerings rose, the morning sun broke through the clouds and the weather cleared. Delighted, the Emperor presented three grades of jade vessels from the Inner Treasury.
He donated the Dashida (Great Being) Hall; Empress Dowager Shoucheng donated a crown of the seven precious gems.
In the first year of the Qiandao era of Emperor Xiaozong, the monk Zilin was summoned for an audience, and an edict was issued prohibiting the mistreatment and humiliation of monks and nuns.

According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), the Basic Annals of Emperor Xiaozong do not record this. However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), it occurred in the second month of the first year of the Qiandao era.
He summoned the Dharma Master Lin of Mount Ling to an audience. The Emperor asked, "I wish to read the scriptures; what do you consider to be the essential?

The Master replied, "The *Vajracchedikā* and the *Awakening of Faith* (or *Perfect Enlightenment*) are the most essential paths. The Emperor asked about the method of Zen meditation (*chán*). The Master replied, "One must simply realize it for oneself."

The Emperor was pleased and conferred upon him the title "Cishou" (Compassionate Reception). In the third month, Princess of Zhengguo entered the monastic order. An imperial edict was issued to officials and commoners:
those who insult or humiliate monks and nuns, or address them with the derogatory term "bald-head," shall be punished according to the edicts of the Xiangfu and Xuanhua reigns.

For officials, their appointments shall be suspended; for commoners, they shall be banished one thousand *li*. All provincial governments throughout the empire were ordered to post this notification everywhere for public understanding, and it was further permitted for monks and nuns to record such offenders.

The white command and the ordination certificate shall accompany [the monk] at all times as a permanent official warrant. Regarding any offenses committed by monks or nuns, local officials shall not adjudicate them privately;
they must report the matter to the throne and await imperial decree before taking action.

In the third year of the Qiandao era, the Emperor visited Shang Tianzhu. He conferred upon the monk Ruone the title of Right Street Monk Registrar (Youjie Senglü) and issued an imperial edict to construct the Neiguan Hall within the Forbidden City, strictly following the architectural regulations of Shang Tianzhu. According to the *Song Shi*, in the biography of Emperor Xiaozong, this is not recorded;
however, according to the *Fozu Tongji*, in the second month of the third year of the Qiandao era, the Imperial Carriage visited Shang Tianzhu to pay his respects to the Great [Buddha].

The scholar Wen Zhushan Ruone asked, "Before a Great Being (Mahāsattva), is it appropriate to prostrate or not? The Master replied, "If one does not prostrate, each person claims their own superiority;

if one prostrates, there is mutual respect. The official was delighted and performed a prostration. He asked again about the meaning of performing the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* repentance at the beginning of the year.
The Master said, "The Buddha preached the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-samādhi* for Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings."

He entrusted him with the protection of the state and its people. Later, the Patriarch established this as a ritual for repentance (*chanyi*), which was practiced on New Year’s Day to pray for blessings upon the nation.
This is a rite of a flourishing era. The Emperor was pleased and appointed him as the Right Street Monk-Registrar (*youjie senglu*).

Furthermore, he was granted money to establish the Hall of the Sixteen Contemplations at the former residence of Dharma Master Daoyi; he commissioned the Palace Secretary Lou Yao to compose a commemorative inscription.
In the third month, an imperial decree was issued to construct the Inner Hall of Contemplation within the Forbidden City, strictly following the architectural regulations of Upper Zhusi.
In the fourth year of the Qiandao era, the monk Ruonuo was summoned to lead fifty monks into the Neiguantang (Inner Contemplation Hall) to perform Buddhist rites.
According to the *Song Shi* (History of Song), in the Basic Annals of Emperor Xiaozong, this is not recorded.

However, according to the *Fozu Tongji* (Comprehensive Record of the Buddhas and Patriarchs), on the eighth day of the fourth month in the fourth year of Qiandao, the Dharma Master Ruonuo of Shangzhu was summoned to lead fifty monks into the Neiguantang to perform the "Protecting the State" (*Huguo*) ritual.
After the meal, he preached the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* Samādhi. The Emperor remarked, "The Buddha-dharma is indeed wondrous; how could there be such a vast number of scriptural volumes?
The Master replied, "That which has its source is thus. The Emperor was pleased and promoted him to the position of Hui Guang Dharma Master, Registrar of the Left Street.
From that time on, every year on the Buddha’s birthday, fifty bolts of silk were granted to the monks of the Inner Quarters for the performance of Buddhist rites.

A Memorandum by Ruo Ne, Monastic Registrar of the Left Street: It is truly the case that our Sacred Court follows the institutions of the Tang dynasty by establishing the examination for the transmission of scriptures (*jingdu seng*) as a formal requirement for ordination.

[The Master] said: "This sutra is the sublime proclamation of the Tathāgata’s singular transformation upon appearing in the world; it is the ultimate goal for all living beings.

It consists of seven fascicles, a length that strikes the perfect balance between prolixity and brevity. Therefore, those who study and recite it are free from the afflictions of excess or deficiency."
From the Tang dynasty until the present, five hundred years have passed. Although the imperial statutes have been obscured, they remain applicable and executable even unto ten thousand generations.

This is the underlying intent. It was the practice that those who were novices throughout the realm would first undergo examinations in their respective prefectures and commanderies; only after passing these would they enter the capital.

There, the officials in charge would open the examination hall and personally supervise the re-examination. Once the rankings were determined and submitted to the throne, the Ministry of Sacrifices (Cibu) would issue the official certificates.

However, in cases where special imperial edicts granted favor—such as the eight thousand monks during the Jianlong era or the seventeen thousand in the general ordination of the Taiping era—these individuals were exempt from the scriptural examinations.

Regarding those who claim this will deplete the state’s revenue, one should respond to them as follows: "Let it be that for each year, a thousand certificates (*qian-die*) shall be designated as the quota for the scriptural examination;
the funds for these thousand certificates shall then be distributed equally among the remaining certificates.

Thus, even those who cannot recite the scriptures but possess ample wealth may also seek ordination. At present, the number of monks throughout the realm is excessive; [therefore,] let the scriptural examination be established.

To follow the ancient way, it is fitting to restrict ordinary people by means of official documents; this would truly suffice to restore the established laws of our ancestors and remedy the redundant abuses of the current era.

One *chih* (official), one *ti-dian* (supervisor), one *ta-shih* (chief envoy), and one *fu-shih* (vice-envoy).

In the twenty-eighth year of Zhizheng, the Shangdu Guiyun Ti dian So (Office of the Supervisor of Provisions for the Northern Capital) was established. Its rank was the fourth grade of the upper class.
It consisted of one *Daluhuachi* (ethnic leader), one *ti-dian*, one *ta-shih*, one *fu-shih*, and one *zhi-shi* (administrative officer). Up to...
In the twenty-eighth year of the Yuan era, the Daidu Tiju Zishanku (Capital Directorate for the Zishan Treasury) was established. Its rank was from the fifth grade.
It consisted of one Daluhuachi (official of Mongol descent), one Tiju (Director), one Tongtiju (Assistant Director), and one Futiiju (Deputy Director).

He was in charge of matters concerning currency and silk. In the twenty-sixth year of the Zhiyuan era, the Shangdu Lizhen Ku (Shangdu Treasury for Beneficence) was established, with a rank of the seventh grade from below.
It was staffed by one Director-General and one Deputy Director, who were responsible for managing provisions, delicacies, and various items of gold and silver.

In the first year of the Yuanzhen era, the Dajici Jiang (Supervisor of the Great Relief Granary) was established, consisting of one Official in Charge of Disbursements and Receipts and one Chief Administrator.
Xingjiao Temple Administrative Office: One Superintendent. The Pacification Commission for Tibet and Adjacent Regions (Tufan dengchu Xuanweisi) Du Yuanshuai Fu, rank second class from above:

Five Pacification Commissioners (Xuanweis), two Assistant Administrators (Jingli), two Secretaries (Dushi), one Archivist (Zhaomo), two Robbery-Apprehending Officials (Budao guan), one Confucian School Professor (Ruxue jiaoshou), and one Town Pacifier (Zhenfu).
Two officials. Its subordinate units include the Tusi Malu Military-Civil Myriarchy (Tuo-si-ma-lu jun-min wan-hu fu).

Its rank is the third grade, regular. One Daluhuachi (Darughachi), one Wanhu (Myriarch), one Vice-Daluhuachi, one Vice-Wanhu, one Jingli (Administrator), one Zhishi (Secretary), and one Zhenfu (Pacification Commissioner). [Western Xia Section]
Established the Military-Civil Administration Commission (Junmin Zongguanfu) for Hexi Prefecture and other areas. Its rank was the third grade of the first class.

Personnel included: one Daluhuachi (Yuan official), one Zongguan (Commissioner), one Tongzhi (Assistant Commissioner), one Zhizhong (Vice Commissioner), two Fupian (District Magistrates), one Jingli (Chief Clerk), and one Zhishi (Administrative Officer).

The Military-Civilian Thousand-District (Junmin Qianhusuo) is ranked as a subordinate fifth rank (cong wu-pin).

The Military-Civilian Thousand-District of Lidian Wenzhou for Mongol, Han, and Tibetan Troops is ranked as a fourth rank (zheng si-pin). It consists of one Daluhuachi...

The *Tusi* Route New-Attached Army *Qianhusuo* (Centurion Commandery) is of the Grade Five, Inferior. The *Daluhuachi* (Commandant).

The Myriarchy (*wan-hu fu*) of Wenfu Prefecture, West Route, South Route, Ditya, and other areas: rank is *cong-san-pin* (third class, lower grade). One *darughachi* (president). Two *wanhu*.

Prefecture. Rank: Following Grade Three. One Daluhuachi (Darughachi) and one Thousand-Household Commander (Qianhu).
The Military Thousand-Household Commandery for the Han and Tibetan Troops in places such as Jiawen and Fuzhou. Rank: Regular Grade Five.
One Daluhuachi and two Thousand-Household Commanders. Guizhou Prefecture. One Daluhuachi and one Governor (Zhizhou), respectively. Same as above.

The Military and Civil Pacification Commission (*Junmin Anfu Shisi*) for Songpan, Kedai, Weimozhou, and other areas; rank is the third grade, regular. One *Daluhuachi*.
One Yuanfu (Commissioner); one Tongzhi (Assistant Commissioner); one Qianshi (Deputy Commissioner); one Jingli (Registrar), one Zhishi (Administrator), and one Zhaomomo (Scrutiny Officer);
and one Zhenfu (Pacification Officer). Weizhou, Baoning County, Maozhou, Wenshan County, and Wenchuan County are all subordinate to it.
[The jurisdiction also includes] Jingzhou, Chashang, Bilixi, Anxiang, and twenty-six other districts.
The Zujunmin (Tribal Military-Civilian) Thousand-District Commandery: one Daluhuachi (Darughachi) and one Qianhu (Thousand-District Officer).
The Longmoutou (Dragon Head) Duliu (District Chief) et al. Twenty-Two Tribes Military-Civilian Thousand-District Commandery: one Daluhuachi (Darughachi).

One *Daluhuachi* (Darughachi) and one *qianhu* official: the *Wanhusuo* (ten-thousand-household) of Zhecang.

Duo-gan-si (Tögan-si) Fields...

The Grounds Office for the Commandery of Military and Civil Affairs (Dili Guanjunmin Duyuan-shuai Fu): one Commander-in-Chief (Duyuan-shuai), one Administrative Assistant (Jingli), and one Pacification Officer (Zhenfu).
The Office of the Commissioner for the Recruitment of Troops in Lame’er Kang and Other Areas (Lama’er Gang dengchu Zhaotao Shisi): one Darughachi.

The Pacification Commission for Military and Civil Affairs in Ningyuan and other areas is of the third rank of the regular grade.

It consists of one Daluohuachi (Yuan official), one Pacification Commissioner, one Vice Commissioner, one Assistant Commissioner, one Acting Commissioner, one Director of Records, one Administrative Officer, one Examiner of Documents, and two Garrison Commanders. The Six Tribes Subduer’s Commission is likewise established.
One *Daluhuachi* (Darughachi), one *Zhaotaoshi* (Jatushi), one *Jingli* (Niyabi), and one *Zhishi* (Yayunji).
The counties of Yandao and Mingshan in Ya Prefecture were subordinate to it. The Tianquan *Zhaotaoshi* (Jatushi):
One *Daluhuachi*, two *Zhaotaoshi*, and one *Jingli* and one *Zhishi* respectively. The Yutong Road.
The Wanhufu (Myriarchy): one Daluhuachi (Darughachi), one Wanhushi (Myriarch), one Jingli (Administrator), and one Zhishi (Secretary), each. Lizhou is subordinate to it.
The Diao-men Yu-tong dengchu Guan-jun Shou-zhen Wanhufu (Myriarchy for the Military Garrison and Defense of Diao-men, Yu-tong, and other areas):
one Daluhuachi, two Wanhushi, one Jingli, and one Zhishi, each; and one Zhenfu (Pacification Commissioner).

The Changhe Xi Li Guanjun Zhaotaoshi Si (Changhe West Interior Military Pacification Commission): Two *zhaotaoshi*, one *jingli* (administrative secretary). Dogan... [text ends]

At the Yisimargan Myriarchy (Wanhufu): one Darughachi and two Myriarchs (Wanhuis). At U-Tsang Nalisugu...

In the sixth month of summer in the first year of Emperor Xianzong’s reign, the monk Haiyun was appointed to oversee the affairs of the Buddhist teachings. According to the *Yuan Shi* (History of Yuan), *Basic Annals of Emperor Xianzong*, it states:
"In the twelfth month of the first year of Zhongtong of Emperor Shizu, the Indian monk Ha-shi-ha (Haghasibha) was appointed as Imperial Preceptor (*Dishi*) and invested with [the title]."
He governed the Buddhist teachings with a jade seal. According to the *Yuan Shi* (History of Yuan), *Benji* (Basic Annals) of Emperor Shizu:
In the third year of Zhongtong, Buddhist rites were performed. According to the *Yuan Shi*, *Benji* of Emperor Shizu:

On the day of Yibyou, the eleventh month of the third year of Zhongtong, Venus (Taibai) encroached upon the Hook and Key (Gouqian) asterism. On the day of Dinghai, an imperial edict was issued to Sheng'an Temple to perform the *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-cakravartin* rite.
Meeting. In the twelfth month, Buddhist services were performed at Haotian Temple for seven days and nights; fifteen thousand taels of silver were bestowed.
In the fourth year of Zhongtong, Buddhist services were held for the construction of the Imperial Ancestral Temple (*Taomiao*).

According to the *Yuan Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu," on the *gui-mao* day of the third month in the fourth year of Zhongtong, the Imperial Ancestral Temple was first established. According to the *Xu Wenxian Tongkao*, [the construction of] the Imperial Ancestral Temple...
The temple mandated that monks perform Buddhist rites for seven days and nights; this became an annual custom.

In the first year of the Zhizhi era (1260), monks were dispatched to pray for rain. According to the *Yuanshi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu," on the *renzi* day of the fourth month in the first year of Zhizhi, droughts occurred in Dongping, Taiyuan, and Pingyang;
imperial edicts were issued to dispatch Western monks (*xiseng*) to pray for rain in each region.

In the second year of Zhizhi (1265), an imperial edict was issued to establish the offices of the Monk Registrar (*senglù*) and others in the prefectures and commanderies, and to institute lectures on the Three Studies (*sanxué*) and assemblies for the Three Meditations (*sànzhèn*).

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu" in the *Yuanshi*, on the day of Jiazi in the second month of the second year of Zhizhi, an edict was promulgated to the Bureau of the General Overseer (*zǒngtǒngsuǒ*).
Those among the monks who have mastered the five great canonical collections shall be selected as the central cadre.

Those possessing virtuous conduct and achievements shall be appointed to official positions such as Provincial and Prefectural Monk-Registrar (*senglù*), Director (*pànzhèng*), and Vice-Director (*fùdūgāng*). Furthermore, in each administrative circuit, the three studies shall be established and three Chan assemblies shall be convened.
In the third year of the Zhizhi era, an imperial edict was issued for monks and Daoists to pray for blessings, appointing the monk Ji as General Superintendent (*zongtong*).

According to the *Yuanshi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu," on the gengwu day of the fourth month in the summer of the third year of Zhizhi, an edict was promulgated ordering monks and Daoists to pray for blessings at the temples and monasteries of the capital;
the monk Ji was appointed as General Superintendent and resided at Qingshou Monastery.

In the first month of spring in the fourth year of Zhizheng, the involvement of monastic officials in civil litigation was prohibited. (As recorded in the *Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu* in the *History of Yuan*, etc.

In the sixth year of Zhizheng, Buddhist rites were performed at the Imperial Ancestral Temple; an edict was issued to elevate the National Preceptor (Guoshi) Phagspa, bestowing upon him the title "Great Treasure" (Dabao).

The Dharma King bestowed the jade seal. According to the *Yuanshi* (History of Yuan), in the twelfth month of the sixth year of Zhizhi, Buddhist rites were performed at the Imperial Ancestral Temple for seven days and nights.
According to the *Biography of P’ags-pa*, P’ags-pa was of the Sakya clan of the Tufan (Tibetan) people and belonged to the Kün family.
When the Shizu ascended the throne, he honored him as State Preceptor and conferred upon him a jade [seal].
The Emperor ordered the creation of a new script for the Mongols. In the sixth year of Zhizhi, an edict was issued for its promulgation throughout the empire. The edict stated:

"I, Your Majesty, consider that characters are used to record speech, and speech is used to chronicle events; this has been the universal system from antiquity to the present. My dynasty first established its foundation in the northern regions."

The customs favored simplicity and antiquity; they had not yet had the leisure to create and implement a written script for practical use. Consequently, they employed Han-style characters and Uyghur script to convey the language of their own dynasty.
Examining the cases of the Liao and Jin dynasties, as well as various distant nations, it appears that each has its own respective script.
Now that civil governance is gradually flourishing, there are deficiencies in the script for writing, and the institutional systems of this era remain truly incomplete.

Therefore, the Imperial Preceptor Phagspa was specially commissioned to create a new Mongolian script, intended solely for the purpose of transcribing all written characters so as to facilitate the expression of speech and the communication of affairs.
From this day forward, all imperial edicts issued with seals shall be written in Mongolian.

He created new characters for ancient terms and supplemented them with the respective scripts of each nation; he was subsequently elevated to the title "Pa-spa" (Phags-pa) and designated as the "Great Dharma King of the Precious Jewel," further being granted a jade seal.
In the seventh year of Zhizhi (1270), the practice of monks illicitly occupying private fields was prohibited, and their clerical vestments were redefined.

In that same year, the ritual service of the White Parasol (*Sitatapatra*) was inaugurated and established as an annual tradition. The Vajra Master Dampa was invited to serve as the abbot of Renwang Temple.
According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu" in the *Yuanshi*, on the intercalary eleventh month of the seventh year of Zhizhi, an imperial edict was issued to the former territory of Xixia.

The civilian officials under the jurisdiction of the Office of the Surveillance Commissioner for the Investigation of Law (Ti-xing An-cha Si) were ordered to prohibit monks from falsely claiming possession of civilian farmland.

In the twelfth month, Da Huguo Renwang Temple was established at Gaoliang River. An imperial decree was issued to revise the colors of monastic robes. (According to the "Treatise on Sacrifices" [Ji-si-zhi]).

In the seventh year of the Zhizhi era, following the words of the Imperial Preceptor Phagspa, a single white parasol was placed upon the imperial throne in the Hall of Great Brilliance (*Daming Dian*).
Upon it, Sanskrit characters were inscribed in gold leaf on plain silk. It was said that this was to suppress malevolent spirits and to protect and pacify the state.
Thereafter, every year on the fifteenth day of the second month, the *Shvetachattra* [White Parasol] rite was inaugurated in the Great Hall.

The *chattra* ritual service: Various colored ceremonial insignia and temple attendants (*shouzhi*) were employed to escort the *chattra* on a circuit throughout the interior and exterior of the imperial city, proclaiming that it would cleanse all inauspiciousness for sentient beings and usher in blessings and prosperity.
On the fifteenth day of the first month of the year, the Xuanzheng Yuan, together with the Zhongshu Sheng, submitted a memorial requesting [the performance of this rite].
Prior to this, the Zhongshu had received an imperial decree and issued a formal document to the Shumiyuan.
The Guard (Wei) shall provide one hundred and twenty persons for the umbrella-bearers and drummers; five hundred armored cavalrymen for the rear guard;
and five hundred miscellaneous laborers for the sedan chair carriers of the Han General Guan Yu’s divine palanquin used at the ritual altar.

There are three hundred and sixty monasteries under the jurisdiction of the Xuanzheng Yuan, which are responsible for providing the Buddha images, altar decorations, banners, streamers, jeweled canopies, and the heads of the ceremonial carriages and drums.
There were three hundred and sixty altars with banners. At each altar, twenty-six persons carried and bore [the offerings], while twelve monks played cymbals and drums.
From the Daidu Road (Dadu Lu), one hundred and twenty teams of various colored "Golden Gate" (Jinmen) grand ritual societies provided services.
The Yunhe Bureau of the Jiaofangsi (Music Office) oversaw the Great Music (Dale), including drums, clappers, hand-drums, double-reed pipes, long flutes, lutes, and zithers.
The Seven-Colored [Troupe] consists of four hundred persons. The Xinghe Bureau oversees one hundred and fifty performers of various female roles and theatrical troupes.
The Xianghe Bureau oversees one hundred and fifty men and women of various acrobatic troupes.
The Yifeng Office oversees three types of refined music—Han, Hui, and Hexi—with three troupes for each type, totaling three hundred and twenty-four persons. Altogether...
The attendants were all provided with armor, robes, and weaponry by the government; they took pride in being bright, colorful, and well-ordered.

Adorned with pearls, jade, gold, and embroidery, their accoutrements were remarkably ingenious. Arranged from head to tail, they extended for over thirty li. The men and women of the capital, as well as those in the villages and neighborhoods, gathered to watch.
Officials of the Ministry of Rites inspected the various types of military parades, while officials of the Ministry of Justice patrolled to suppress any clamor or disorder. The Chancellery...
Officials of the Imperial Preceptor’s Court were assigned to guard the city gates, while one official of the Secretariat (Zhongshusheng) acted as the general supervisor.
Two days prior, the Crown Prince was welcomed at the West Zhenguosi Temple for a tour of the four gates; they carried a large statue and entered the city with full ceremonial retinue.
On the fourteenth day, the Imperial Preceptor led five hundred Indian monks to perform Buddhist rites within the Daming Hall.
On the fifteenth day, the ceremonial parasol was respectfully invited to be placed upon the imperial throne; various ritual guards and military banners were arrayed before the hall.
The various *shezhí* (corporate guilds) and the various altar attendants lined up outside the Chongtian Gate to escort the procession out of the palace.
Upon arriving at Qingshou Temple, they partook of vegetarian fare. Having finished their meal, they rose and proceeded.
From outside the wall of the West Palace gate, they entered the Hongmen Gate of Houzai City from the south bank of the Haizi moat.

Passing through Donghua Gate and crossing Yanchun Gate toward the west, the Emperor, the Empresses, and the Princesses watched from the *taji* (pavilion with a golden ridge) atop the Wude Hall and the *wudian* (colored pavilion). And so forth.

The military escort and the local shrine officials escorted the golden parasol back to the palace. It was then respectfully placed upon the imperial couch, where the Imperial Preceptor and the assembly of monks performed Buddhist rites until the sixteenth day, at which point they dispersed;
this was called "Wandering through the Imperial City. In the sixth month, the same procedure was followed in the Upper Capital.
According to the *Continued Wenxian Tongkao*, in the seventh year of the Zhizhi era (1270), an edict was issued inviting the Imperial Preceptor Zhanpa Vajra to reside [there].
He took charge of Renwang Temple and oversaw the general ordination of monks.
On the *jisi* day of the fifth month in the eighth year of the Zhizhi era, he performed Buddhist rites on Qionghua Island.
(As recorded in the *Yuan Shi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu," etc.)
In the ninth year of Zhizhi, an envoy was dispatched to offer sacrifices at Xingguo Temple; furthermore, monks were assembled to recite the Tripitaka.

According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu" in the *History of Yuan*, in the first month of spring in the ninth year of Zhizhi, an imperial edict was issued for Prince Yan to dispatch an envoy carrying incense and banners.
He made offerings at Xingguo Temple on Mount Wutai. In the seventh month of autumn, he assembled the monks of the capital to recite the Tripitaka in nine assemblies.
In the twelfth month, he established Dashingengshou Wan'an Temple.
In the eleventh year of the Zhizong era, Yelünzhen succeeded to the position of Imperial Preceptor (*di-shi*). According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu" in the *History of Yuan*:
in the third month of the eleventh year of Zhizong, the Imperial Preceptor Haosiba returned to the kingdom of Tibet and appointed his younger brother, Yelünzhen, to succeed him.
He then completed the construction of the Great Huguo Renwang Temple.
In the thirteenth year of the Zhizhi era, the Zaijie (Precepts for the Deceased) Assembly was established, and the Imperial Preceptor was again commanded to perform Buddhist rites.

According to the *Yuanshi* (History of Yuan), in the Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu: on the day of Xinyou in the second month of the thirteenth year of Zhizhi, the imperial carriage proceeded to the Upper Capital.

A Great Zaijie Assembly was held at Kaiyuan Temple in Shunde Prefecture. On the day of Jiazi in the intercalary third month, it was prohibited for monks from the Western Regions to [hold]... (the text is incomplete).
Regarding military implements: on the first day of the ninth month, the day of Renshen, the State Preceptor Yilin Zhen was ordered to perform Buddhist rites at the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
On the day of Xinyou, a *zijie* (precept-merit) assembly was convened in the capital.

In the second month of the fourteenth year of Zhizhen, an imperial edict was issued appointing the monks Kangjigiyin and Jinagagava as Joint General Superintendents (Zongshe) of the Buddhist Teachings for Jiangnan,
exempting them from monastic taxes and levies, and prohibiting disturbances at temple precincts. (As recorded in the *Yuan Shi*,
"Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu," etc.)
In the sixteenth year of the Zhizhi era, San-du was ordered to perform Buddhist rites, and the General Administration of Dahuoguo Renwang Temple was established.
Upon the death of the Imperial Preceptor, an edict was issued to hold a memorial vegetarian feast and bestow a posthumous title.

According to the *Yuanshi*, "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu," in the fourth month of summer in the sixteenth year of Zhizhi, it was decreed that monks from Quanzhou should pay taxes according to the Song precedent to provide for military provisions. In the fifth month...
In the Bingyin year, an imperial edict was issued stating that official correspondence from the Buddhist administration of Jiangnan must not be sent through the postal relay system.

In the seventh month, an order was given to disperse the various monastic centers to perform fifteen days of Buddhist rites. In the eighth month, the General Administration of Dahuoguo Renwang Temple was established.
In the twelfth month, Shengshou Wan'an Temple was constructed in the capital. The Imperial Preceptor Yilianji also passed away. An edict was then issued for all National Preceptors.
There were one hundred and eight Chan masters. At the Wan’an Temple in the capital, a vegetarian feast was held, the precepts were completed, and robes were bestowed.

"The One Above All Under Heaven, the Proclaimer of Literature and Assistant in Governance, the Great Sage of Ultimate Virtue, the Universal Awakened True [Buddha]."

The Imperial Preceptor (Dishi) of the Great Yuan, the Son of Buddha from the Western Heaven, the Dharma King of the Great Jewel that Fulfills Wishes and Protects the State, established the Office for Meritorious Works of the Capital in the seventeenth year of Zhizhen. He was granted the seal of the National Teacher’s Office for Governing the Teachings.

Furthermore, he commissioned the printing of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* and distributed it to the monastics throughout all circuits. According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Shizu" in the *Yuanshi*, this was in the seventeenth year of Zhizhen.

In the nineteenth year of the Zhizong era, the Office of Imperial Merit was abolished. An edict was issued appointing the Imperial Preceptor Darma Bhalala Ji to preside over the Buddhist teachings.

On the *bǐngwǔ* day, the Censor Liu Heng requested the establishment of public granaries (*yìcāng*) and the revocation of official positions held by monks and Daoists. In the sixth month, an epidemic broke out in the capital; Buddhist rites were performed for its relief.
Wanshoushan. In the year of Xinyou, an imperial edict was issued exempting monks from miscellaneous corvée labor. In the year of Xinwei, Buddhist rites were performed at Qinchalu in Ningxia;
2,120,000 strings of cash were disbursed. In the seventh month of autumn, on the day of Yiwu, 15,000 strings of cash were granted to the Western monk Sajja.
In the ninth month, on the day of Jiashen, Shouanshan Temple was constructed; 10,000,000 strings of cash were disbursed. Winter.
On the *renzi* day of the tenth month, Buddhist rites were performed at Wende Hall. On the *gengshen* day, the fortieth day, an imperial edict was issued to translate Buddhist scriptures.

On the *yichou* day, the Emperor visited Dahuoguo Renwang Temple; the Imperial Preceptor requested that Qabir Jinchang be appointed as the Chief Administrator (*duyuanshi*) of the Xuanweisi Commission for Tibet, and the request was granted. On the *gengwu* day, Bayuzhu was ordered to supervise the construction of Shouanshan Temple.

On the *dinghai* day of the eleventh month, Buddhist rites were performed in the Gwangjeon Hall. On the *dingyou* day, an edict was issued to all prefectures to construct temples for the Imperial Preceptor (Dishi) Phagspa;
their architectural scale was to exceed that of Confucian temples. On the *gengxu* day of the twelfth month, a copper Buddha image was cast and installed in the Okdeung Hall.
On the *renxu* day, the Western monk Nianzhen Halasi was summoned to the capital by imperial decree.

In every prefecture and county he passed through, officials welcomed him with solemnity. On the day of Jisi (the 25th day of the first month), an imperial decree was issued to discontinue the welcoming of the Buddha on the eighth day of the second month of the following year.
In the first year of Yingzong’s Zhizhi era, grand Buddhist temples were constructed, Buddha images were fashioned, and golden stupas were erected;

furthermore, the Western Regions scriptures were transcribed in gold, and an imperial robe of pearl-embroidered *kāṣāya* was produced. Additionally, the monk Fahong was appointed as Minister of Education (*Situ*), and an envoy was dispatched to bestow honors upon him.
Gold, silver, coins, and silks for the monks from Western Fan were distributed according to their rank. According to the *Yuan Shi*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Yingzong:
on the day of Dingchou, the first month of spring in the first year of Zhizhi, Buddhist services were performed in Wende Hall;

a temple was constructed at Shouanshan to house the treasury for managing wealth and silks, with a rank of the seventh grade from below. On the day of Jiyou, the second month, the Imperial Shrine for Renzong was built.

At Pukkyeong Temple, three thousand five hundred men were mobilized for military service in the *xinhai* year. Construction was carried out at the Hwaryangsa Temple in the Capital (Uldum) and the Daewongboksa Temple was completed;
the Emperor granted five hundred taels of gold, two thousand five hundred taels of silver, five hundred thousand *kwan* of paper currency, and ten thousand bolts of silk.
The Censor-in-Chief Gwaninbo Sogyoer Hadimishil and Seonggui Li [were appointed].
Qianheng remonstrated against the construction of the Shaoyanshan Buddhist Temple. Guan Yinbao, Suo Yao’er, Haidimisi, Zhang Gui, and Qianheng were executed;
Qianheng fled to the Nurkan region. In the Dingmao year, the monk Fahong was appointed as the Patriarch of Shiyuan.
On the Bingzi day of the third month, the Di-shi Basiba Temple was established. The title of Rongluk Dafu Sifu was conferred.

In the capital, on the day of Xinsi, an envoy was dispatched to bestow upon the monk of Sasa-kha-di in Western Tibet two hundred and fifty *liang* of gold, two thousand two hundred *liang* of silver, twenty thousand *kāṣāyas*, and various amounts of silk, banners, and tea.
On the day of Renwu, the mantra-master Duerzhi was dispatched to the twelve kingdoms of Yaji-ban to retrieve Buddhist scriptures. On the day of Guiwei, the Imperial [edict] was drafted.

He donned a *kaṣāya* adorned with pearls. On the day of Yiyou (the 26th), the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* written in gold characters in the Tangut script was completed at Baoji Temple and enshrined in the Incense Hall of the Inner Palace.

On the day of Bingzi in the fifth month, the military laborers engaged in the construction of temples on Mount Yishou were dismissed; the site of the former Huizhou Huihui Temple in the Capital was then used to establish the Imperial Preceptor’s Hall (*Dishi Dian*).
On the day of Dinghai, Buddhist rites were performed in the Dajian Pavilion. In the sixth month, [a statue] was fashioned in gold.
The Buddha’s śarīra relics were enshrined in the capital. In the twelfth month of winter, the imperial carriage proceeded to the Xiseng Guanding Monastery.
An edict was issued for the Imperial Preceptor (Dishi) Gonggar Gulru Sijian Cang Bangzangbu to travel to Western Xia to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
He was granted one thousand three hundred and fifty taels of gold, four thousand and fifty taels of silver, and ten thousand bolts of silk.

A draft was made for five hundred thousand *kuan*. In the year Yichou, the Zhongshui Si (Office of Central Auspiciousness) was established. Fifty thousand *jin* of copper were cast to create Buddha images for the Shou'an Mountain Temple.

In the second year of the Zhiyi era, a Western monk was appointed as Minister of Education (*Situ*). Furthermore, due to the illness of a Western monk, an imperial edict was issued to release prisoners. He was restored [to his position].
He was granted paper currency. An envoy was dispatched to welcome the Imperial Preceptor (Di-shi) at Xuande Prefecture.
In this year, the fields of monasteries in Jiangzhe were taxed, and those monks who had wives were conscripted as commoners. According to the *Yuan Shi*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Yingzong:

on the day of Guisi in the first month of spring in the second year of Zhizhi, the Western monk Luo-zang was appointed Minister of Education (Situ). In the second month, the Western monk Yisilaman Zhanpu...
[The Emperor] fell ill. He issued an edict to commute the death penalty for one prisoner and reduce the punishment for twenty individuals charged with offenses punishable by flogging.

On the *gengchen* day of the third month, he decreed that as for the temple lands in Jiangzhe: those held as perpetual endowments from the Song dynasty and those granted by Emperor Shizu shall be exempted from taxation;

all others shall be subject to tax. On the *jiumao* day of the intercalary fifth month, he prohibited the religious rites of the White Lotus Society. On the *xinhai* day of the ninth month, he visited Shaolin Temple on Mount Shou’an and bestowed [gifts].
The supervising official was granted five thousand *gyo* of paper money. On the day of Bingyin, the Western monk Bangi fell ill; he was granted fifty thousand *gyo*.
In the eleventh month, those among the monks in Jiangnan who had wives were conscripted as commoners. On the day of Yi-mao, the Western monk Gaozhuwa was dispatched.
In the twelfth month of the Xuande era, when the Imperial Preceptor arrived at Xuanzhengfu, a Western monk requested the immediate release of prisoners for the purpose of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

The Emperor said, "Releasing prisoners to pray for blessings—how could this be done out of consideration for the Master? I have considered that if evil people are repeatedly pardoned, they will instead bring harm to the virtuous; what blessing could there be in that?"

In the third year of Zhizhi, a Buddhist temple was constructed. An imperial edict ordered the transcription of the Tripitaka in golden script. Furthermore, an edict was issued to all offices throughout the empire, commanding monks to recite one hundred thousand sections of scripture.
Another edict ordered the release of prisoners and the setting free of living creatures. In this year, Emperor Taiding ascended the throne and performed great Buddhist rites.
According to the *Yuan Shi*, the Basic Annals of Emperor Yingzong, on the day of Renyin in the first month of spring in the third year of Zhizhi, [the following] was decreed:
The Taipushi (Court of the Grand Stables) was granted one hundred mares for the sacrificial rites at the Imperial Portrait Hall of Emperor Shizu Renzong.

On the first day of the second month, the *geng* day, work commenced on the construction of the Huayan Monastery in Shangdu—the monastery of the Imperial Preceptor Eight Banners—and the residence of Bayizhu;

six thousand two hundred laborers were assigned to these tasks. On the *ding* day, the *hai* day, an imperial decree ordered the transcription of two sets of the Tripitaka in gold, and Bayizhu and others were charged with this duty.

In summary, on the first day of the fourth month of summer, the *Renxu* day, an edict was issued to all offices throughout the empire to command monks to recite one hundred thousand sections of scripture.
On the *Jiaxu* day, the Imperial Commissioner for Merit, Kuerlu, was dispatched to the capital;

there, thirty-one prisoners facing the death penalty were released, as were sixty-nine persons sentenced to fifty-seven lashes or more, and one hundred thousand caged birds were set free. The relevant authorities were ordered [to carry out these measures].

He paid the full price for them. By imperial decree, the four temples of Wanan, Qingshou, Sheng’an, and Puqing in the capital, as well as Jinshan Temple on the Yangtze River and Wansheng Youguo Temple on Mount Wutai, were to perform the Water and Land Buddhist rites for seven days and nights.

According to the Basic Annals of Emperor Taiding, he ascended the throne in the eighth month of the third year of Zhizhi. On the day of Guihai in the tenth month of that winter, these Buddhist rites were performed.
In the Daming Hall, in the eleventh month, the imperial carriage proceeded to Zhongdu, where Buddhist rites were performed in the Qungang Hall.
On the *bingzi* day of the twelfth month, he commanded the various princes guarding the borders north of the Ling Mountains to perform Buddhist rites for one month in order to repel enemy troops.
On the *jimao* day, he ordered monks to perform Buddhist rites within the Great Interior (*Danei*) to suppress thunder. He also had the image of Mahākāla sculpted.
In the first year of the Taiding era of Emperor Taiding, a Buddha image was carved beneath the Huicheng Pavilion of the Yanchun Gate.
Great Buddhist rites were performed, and [the Emperor] received the precepts from the Imperial Preceptor (Dishi).

Furthermore, he had a portrait of the Imperial Preceptor painted and distributed it to each provincial government, ordering that it be sculpted and enshrined for worship. In this same year, Song Ben and others petitioned to abolish the excessive bestowal of noble titles upon monks.

Guī and others petitioned to abolish the Office of Merit (Gōngdéshīsī), to exempt the tax on monastic lands, and to allow monks with wives to return to civilian life; however, these requests were not granted.

According to the *Basic Annals of Emperor Tàidìng* in the *Yuán Shǐ*: in the first month of spring in the first year of the Tàidìng era, he ordered monks to chant the Tibetan scriptures in the Guāngtiān Hall;
on the jǐwèi day of the second month, he performed Tibetan Buddhist rites at Shòu'ān Mountain Temple.
It was said that there were the Xingjisikela, the Kuerlufubu, and the Shuidu’erma.
There were forty monks from the Sajian Shili Nanjia [sect]. After three years, it was discontinued. In the Jiazi year, Buddhist rites were performed;

one hundred and eight monks, along with performers of the hundred arts, were ordered to escort the Imperial Preceptor on a tour of the capital. In the Guiwei year, the Yeli [Muslims] were issued an imperial edict.
It may be warmed. Each [matter] shall be handled according to the prescribed rules of the precepts.

In the third month, Censor-in-Chief Song Ben, Li Jiabin, and Zhuan Yanqi submitted a memorial stating that the offices of the Three Dukes—Grand Marshal, Minister of Education, and Minister of Works—had been improperly conferred upon monks, and that the two monasteries, Huifu and Shuxiang, had both been dishonorably granted noble titles and ranks;
they requested that these be abolished. No reply was given. In the fourth month of summer, Buddhist rites were performed at Shou...

At Changdian, on the day of Jiashu, the Emperor commanded the mantra-reciters (zhoushi) to perform Buddhist rites for the subjugation of thunder. On Dingmao in the sixth month, the Great Awodien (Dawodidian) was completed;
there, rites for the pacification of thunder were performed. On Xinwei, rites for the deity Heiya Mandahe were performed at the Shuishjingdian.

On Guiyou, the Emperor received the Buddhist precepts from the Imperial Preceptor (Dishi). In the autumn, on Bingwu of the seventh month, [an edict] was issued in the Uyghur script via the postal relay system.
The Tibetan scriptures were deposited at Changqing Temple, and the eunuch Ayibei was appointed as the Abbot (Sijing) of the temple.

On the *xinwei* day of the eighth month, eleven portraits of the Imperial Preceptor (Dishi) Pakpa were painted and distributed to each provincial government, ordering them to have statues made for worship.
On the *yisi* day of the ninth month, Buddhist rites were performed on the anniversary of the death of Empress Xiaoxian Yuansheng, providing meals for ten million monks. The tenth month of winter.

Bingzi (the third day of the fifth month): An edict was issued for the Imperial Preceptor to perform Buddhist rites at the Yanchun Pavilion. Xinchou (the eighth day of the fifth month): A golden jeweled canopy (*suvarṇa-cchattra*) was constructed and adorned with the seven precious substances;

it was to enshrine the relics of the Buddha. According to the biography of Zhang Gui, in the sixth month of the first year of the Taiding era, while the imperial carriage was at the Upper Capital, the Emperor had previously issued an edict due to portents and anomalies, summoning the various officials to convene a discussion. Zhang Gui, together with the Chumu Yuan (Secretariat for Military Affairs) and the [Imperial]...
The officials of the two academies—the Historiography Bureau (Shitai) and the Hanlin and Jixian Academies—discussed at length the merits and defects of the current age.

Together with Song Wenzan, an Extraordinary Councillor of the Left and Right Secretariats, they traveled to the Upper Capital to present their memorial. Their proposal stated: "The *wakh-a'ur* (imperial hunting camps) established by successive dynasties..."

The Changqiu Palace shall inherit the prestige [of the former] at Changning Temple. As for the military garrisons stationed along the borders, they shall be dealt with according to separate deliberations.
Since antiquity, sagely rulers have relied solely on sincerity in their governance; this alone can move heaven and earth and stir the ghosts and spirits.

From the outset, they never sought blessings from monks or Daoists to oppress the people or bring disease upon the state. To cite the year 30 of the Zhizhi era (1293): regarding the performance of *zhao* rituals and Buddhist services—

The categories [of expenditures] originally numbered one hundred and two. In the seventh year of the Dade era, the Office for the Supervision of Meritorious Works was re-established, and the items accumulated to over five hundred.
This year, a certain monk expanded the categories; next year, he immediately took this as a precedent, more than doubling the previous total.

Furthermore, the monastic community has engaged in managing affairs for close attendants and purchasing items for Buddhist rites, using divination to justify their requests and deceiving the authorities to increase [their allowances].

They cultivate the practice of *maṅzhai* (vegetarian feasts) and claim to offer special devotion; they transmit these offerings to the relevant authorities, who dare not question them for fear that the provisions might be delayed.
Moreover, since the Buddha takes purity as his foundation—neither rushing nor desiring—yet the monastic community greedily covets wealth and profit, thereby contravening his teachings themselves.
For every single necessity, gold, silver, paper currency, and silk are counted in no small measure; annually, several thousand strings of cash are consumed.
[Ten] thousand ingots—more than several times the amount during the Zhizhen era. All the offerings provided were entirely for his own possession;

furthermore, the paper currency from alms and donations was taken beyond that. He exhausted the fat of the common people according to his whims, seizing it for his own profit to support his wife and children.
Since his conduct was neither refined nor pure, he was merely insulting and profaning the heavenly deities; how could he hope to obtain blessings? In recent years, the Buddha...

Matters have become increasingly complex. The reigns of successive dynasties have not been long, and calamities have arrived with ever-greater speed. It can be known with certainty that these matters yield no corresponding efficacy.
We, your servants, propose that the Office of Merit and Virtue (Gongde Shisi) be abolished.

As for the ritual offerings and Buddhist services held on the anniversaries of imperial deaths from the thirtieth year of the Zhiyuan era onward, as well as those of successive reigns, let the Xuanzheng Yuan alone be responsible for overseeing their performance. All other [matters]...
All [such practices] shall be abolished. Those in the immediate retinue shall not, under any pretext, devise schemes to memorialize the throne for the arbitrary addition of official titles.
Should there be any special imperial decrees or transmissions from the Central Secretariat, they must be submitted again for review before being implemented.
In the second year of the Taiding era, an imperial edict was issued to allow monasteries to continue acquiring land and subject them to the same corvée labor as the common people;

furthermore, the performance of Buddhist rites by Western monks (Sogdians) and the gold-lettered transcription of the Tripitaka were abolished. In that same year, both the Emperor and the Empress received the Buddhist precepts from the Imperial Preceptor (Di-shi).

The inhabitants of Tu Yao’s Tomb at Fosi in Juancheng County, Puzhou, requested [the relocation of the tomb]. The Censorate petitioned for the rectification of the laws concerning the provision of postal stations for monks.

Neither [party] replied. According to the *Basic Annals of Emperor Taiding* in the *History of Yuan*: In the first month of the second year of the Taiding era, ministers of the Zhongshu Sheng (Secretariat) submitted a memorial stating:

"The people of Jiangnan are impoverished while the monks are wealthy. As for the fields and lands belonging to various temples and monasteries—none of which were originally established by the Song dynasty nor granted by successive dynasties—it is requested that the old regulations be restored, so that these lands may be subject to the same labor services as those of the common people. This was granted. On the *jihai* day of the second month, [the Emperor] ordered the West...

The Sangha performed Buddhist rites for the cremation altar at the Yanhua Pavilion. On the day of Dingyou in the fourth month, the district of Juancheng in Puzhou reported that there was a Buddhist temple atop the tomb of Yao to the west of the city, requesting that it be relocated;
no reply was received. On the day of Guihai in the seventh month, the Da Qianyuan Temple was renovated.
On the day of Gengwu, due to insufficient state funds, the transcription of the Tripitaka in golden characters was suspended. On the day of Renshen, the Censorate...
The Minister submitted this memorial: "The Western monks perform Buddhist rites at an immense cost that provides no benefit to the state; they should be abolished.
This was granted. On the day of Yiwu in the tenth month of winter, the Empress, who was also a devotee of Linzhenbala, received Buddhist precepts from the Imperial Preceptor.
On the day of Dingyi, the Emperor visited Dachenhua Puking Temple to offer sacrifices to Empress Zhaoxian Yuansheng in the portrait hall and bestowed paper currency upon the monks.
One thousand ingots. On the day of Yiyou in the twelfth month, the Emperor again received the Buddhist precepts from the Imperial Preceptor (Dishi).

According to the biography of the Imperial Preceptor Phagpa, in the second year of the Taiding era, Li Changyan, an Inspector of the Western Circuit, once traveled through Pingliang Prefecture and the prefectures of Jing, Hui, and Dingxi.
He observed Tibetan monks traveling in succession along the roads, wearing circular golden insignia and riding swift horses.
The number of such missions reached several hundred. When the official guest houses could no longer accommodate them, they were forced to take up lodgings in private residences;

consequently, they would harass and drive out the men, and defile the women. Along the route from Fengyuan, between the first and seventh months, there were one hundred and eighty-five round trips, utilizing over eight hundred and forty horses.
Compared to the envoys of the various princes and provincial governments, these figures are ten times greater.
