Seventh: The postal station attendants have no one to whom they can appeal, and the Censorate has no means to investigate them.
Furthermore, the state’s manufacture of circular tokens was originally intended for the purpose of alerting border defenses against alarms. For what reason do monks suddenly wear them?

We beg that the law regarding the provision of postal stations to monks be rectified, so that the Censorate and the Constitutional Courts may exercise their authority to investigate and correct abuses. No report was received.
In the third year of Taiding, Buddhist affairs were extensively promoted. Temples were constructed, scriptures were transcribed, and bronze Buddha statues were cast.

The Imperial Preceptor was granted a princess as his consort and bestowed with the rank of Prince; the Imperial Preceptor was further awarded gold, silver, paper currency, and silk in the tens of thousands. Additionally, paper currency and land were granted to various monasteries.
According to the "Annals of Emperor Taiding" in the *History of Yuan*, this occurred in the second month of the spring of the third year of Taiding.

The year Yiwei (1455): Buddhist rites were performed at Chongtammun Gate to exorcise thunder. The year Bingshen (1456): The Shrine for the Imperial Spirit of King Hyeonjong was constructed at Yasu-ri Temple;
it was granted the name Daecheonyeonju-sa, and an imperial edict provided the *Kanjur* (Tibetan canon) written in gold with the West蕃 (Xifan/Tibetan) script.
The year Jiyou (1459): Shuxiang-si Temple was constructed on Mount Wutai, and three hundred *qing* of land were granted. The third month, Ji zi day.
The Office for the Supervision of Meritorious Deeds (Ming-gongde-sishi) was ordered to conduct annual Buddhist rites, totaling one hundred and twenty-seven.

Monks were dispatched to perform Buddhist rites at Lin-tao, Feng-xiang, Xing-ji-er-zong-shan, and other locations. On the day of Yi-si in the fifth month, thirty-one sites were designated for the performance of the "Subduing Thunder" (Zhen-lei) rites.
On the day of Yi-mao, the Imperial Preceptor’s elder brother, Suonan Zangbu, was appointed to lead the three routes of Western Tibet (Xi-fan).

On the affairs of the Xuanweisi (Commission for Pacification): [The Emperor] bestowed a princess in marriage and conferred the rank of Prince. In the seventh month of autumn, on the day of Renzi, the Empress received the *yama* initiation from the Mian Da’ge at the Shuijing Hall.
On the day of Jia-yin, he visited Dagan Yuan Temple and issued an edict to cast copper statues of the Buddhas of the Five Directions.

On the day of Xin-hai in the ninth month, he commanded the Imperial Preceptor to return to the capital to perform the *sajing* (sprinkling of consecrated water) Buddhist rites at the Daming and Xingsheng [Temples].
At the Three Palaces of Longfu, on the *renwu* day of the tenth month in winter, the Imperial Preceptor returned to the land of Tsetisga due to illness.

The Emperor bestowed upon him tens of thousands of pieces of gold, silver, paper currency, and silk. An edict was issued to the Zhongshu Sheng (Secretariat), ordering officials to accompany him and provide all necessary provisions.
Furthermore, Dayuan Yansheng Si was granted twenty thousand *ding* of paper currency and one thousand *qing* of land in the two prefectures of Jixian and Linjiang. The Zhongshu Sheng...
Your servant submits that the provision and support of the military and the common people must necessarily rely upon the advantages of the land.
When Emperor Shizu established temples such as Daxuanwen and Hongjiao and granted them perpetual lands, they were already considered at the time to be a wasteful expenditure;

yet Chengzong further constructed Tianshou Wan’ning Temple, which, compared to those of Shizu, increased the expenditure by one and a half times. As for Wuzong’s Chong’en Fuyuan and Renzong’s Chenghua [temples], the same applies.

At Puming Temple, the revenue from rents and taxes increased even more significantly. Emperor Yingzong excavated mountains to open the temple, causing loss to both soldiers and farmers, yet it ultimately yielded no benefit.
Land is the possession of our ancestors; descendants ought to cherish it together.
I fear that henceforth this will be used as a pretext to recklessly initiate construction projects, seeking blessings and profit to satisfy private desires. May Your Majesty examine this.
The Emperor received this with appreciation and accepted it. On the *guǐmǎo* day of the eleventh month, a minister of the Zhongshu Sheng (Secretariat) reported:

"The Western monks frequently take advantage of auspicious days to petition for the release of heavy prisoners, which contravenes the statutes of governance. We request that this practice be abolished. An edict was issued stating: "From now on, those who are to be released must have their cases reviewed by the Zongzheng Fu (Bureau of the Imperial Clan).
Because the young Prince Xiao Xue cried incessantly, the Emperor ordered the Imperial Preceptor (*Dishi*) to perform Buddhist rites; [he subsequently] released the heavy prisoners.
Three prisoners were detained at the General Administration Office of Dachenhua Puqing Temple. The Bureau for the Supervision of Transport was abolished.
According to the Biography of the Imperial Preceptor Pakṣapati (Bisiba): When the Yuan first rose in the north, they already held Buddhism in high esteem.

Upon their acquisition of the Western Regions, the Great Ancestor (Emperor Kublai) considered that because those lands were vast and rugged, and their distant inhabitants were fierce and fond of strife, he sought means to govern them accordingly.

To civilize and soften the people, the territories of the local tribes within the commanderies and counties were governed by appointing officials and assigning them duties under the supervision of the Imperial Preceptor (Dishi).
Consequently, the Xuanzheng Yuan (Court of Administration for Buddhist and Tibetan Affairs) was established; the second-highest official in this office was invariably appointed from among the clergy.

Those appointed by the Imperial Preceptor to oversee both internal and external affairs—including from the rank of "Teacher-Minister" (shishi) downward—were necessarily drawn from both the monastic and lay communities, and they governed both military and civil populations.
Consequently, for a period of a hundred years, the edicts of the Imperial Preceptor were implemented alongside imperial decrees throughout the Western Regions.
Regarding the reasons why the court treated him with such reverence and placed such trust in him, there was nothing [that could be surpassed].
There is no greater honor than this. Even emperors, empresses, consorts, and princesses all prostrate themselves before him upon receiving his precepts.
During formal audiences in the main palace hall where the hundred officials stand in ranks, the Imperial Preceptor (Gongma) may even occupy a seat of his own at the side of the throne.

Furthermore, at the beginning of every emperor’s reign, an edict is issued to praise and protect him; it is customary to command that a string of pearls be fashioned into characters as a ceremonial gift. This is because...
He was esteemed to such an extent that, before he had even arrived, the Grand Secretaries and high ministers dispatched several hundred couriers on horseback to welcome him.

At every station along the way, provisions and escorts were provided in abundance; upon his arrival at the capital, the Emperor issued an edict for the Metropolitan Commandery to provide half of the ceremonial imperial procession as a vanguard, and commanded the officials of the Ministries, the Court of Judicial Review, and the Censorate, as well as all other government offices, to don silver-fur robes.
Regarding the *qizun* (monastic robes), on the eighth day of the second month each year, the imperial procession for welcoming the Buddha was used to escort them.

Furthermore, the Minister of the Court of Ceremonials and the Director of the Bureau were ordered to specifically supervise the reception. Upon their completion and the subsequent enshrinement of the *śarīra* relics, the officials were again ordered to depart from the city walls to offer a farewell sacrifice.
In the ninth year of the Dade era, the Chancellor Temür was specially dispatched to provide protection and escort them by imperial carriage.
The funeral expenses consisted of five hundred taels of gold, one thousand taels of silver, ten thousand bolts of silk, and three thousand ingots of paper currency.

In the second year of the Huangqing era, these were increased to five thousand taels of gold, fifteen thousand taels of silver, and seventeen thousand bolts of brocade, fine silks, and various colored fabrics.
Even for the travel and accommodations of his brothers, sons, and descendants, the relevant authorities provided for them all without deficiency. Thus it was with Tai.

During this interval, as the Imperial Preceptor’s younger brother, Gongga Yisijian, was about to arrive, the Zhongshu (Secretariat) was ordered to present offerings of sheep and wine to welcome him at the outskirts of the capital.
His elder brother, Suonan Zangbu, subsequently married a princess, was enfeoffed as the King of Bailan, granted a golden seal, and issued with a circular tally (*yuanfu*).
As for his disciples, those titled *Sikong*, *Situ*, or *Guogong* were permitted to wear seals of gold and jade. [The preceding...]

Looking back at what followed, those who were his followers relied on his power to act with unrestrained arrogance; their influence grew day by day, their fiery aura scorched all around, and the harm they inflicted spread to the four quarters beyond description.
In the fourth year of the Taiding era, the Crown Prince received the Buddhist precepts at Zhiguo Temple. A Western monk was appointed as Imperial Preceptor (Dishi), and he was granted a jade seal.
According to the "Basic Annals of Emperor Taiding" in the *History of Yuan*: on the gengshen day of the first month in the spring of the fourth year of Taiding.
The Crown Prince Yundan Zangbu received the Buddhist precepts at Zhiguo Temple. In the second month, the Imperial Preceptor Champa Yesi Jisibuchangcu Yesidachub passed away;
the Emperor ordered Tashi Temür Niuzai to supervise the Buddhist funeral rites.
In the third month, he ordered the Western monks (Xiseng) to perform rituals to stop the winds. On the Jiawu day of the fourth month in summer, [he] with the West...
The monk Gongke Leshiba Chongnas Si Jianzang Banzangbu was appointed as Imperial Preceptor (Dishi) and granted a jade seal.

He was further commanded by imperial decree to address the monastics throughout the realm. On the *guimao* day of the tenth month in winter, the Emperor ordered the Imperial Preceptor to perform Buddhist rites at Dayuan Yansheng.

In the first year of the Zhìhé era, Buddhist rites were performed. The Emperor received the Buddha-precepts from the Imperial Preceptor (*di shī*). According to the *Yuán Shǐ* (History of Yuan), the Basic Annals of Emperor Tàidìng:
In the first month of spring in the first year of Zhìhé, an edict was issued for the Imperial Preceptor to perform Buddhist rites within the palace.

On the *yǐmǎo* day of the third month, the Emperor presided over the Xīngshèng Hall and received the precepts of Amitāyus Buddha from the Imperial Preceptor. On the *gēngchén* day, [an edict was issued...]

One thousand monks performed Buddhist rites at Zhenguosi Temple. In the year Bingxu, an imperial edict was issued to the Imperial Preceptor (Dishi), ordering monks to perform Buddhist rites in Yanguanzhou and to construct two hundred and sixteen stupas to suppress the flooding of the sea.
In the first year of the Tianli era of Emperor Wenzong, the Buddhist temples were extensively constructed.

According to the *Basic Annals of Emperor Wen* in the *History of Yuan*, in the ninth month of autumn in the first year of Tianli, he ordered monks from Gaochang to perform Buddhist rites at the Yanchun Pavilion.
He also ordered the Yelüke’u-wen (Yelüke’u) to perform Buddhist rites at the Shrine of the Empress Xianyi Zhuangsheng. On the day of Jichou in the tenth month of winter—
The first day of the month, he commanded the Western monks (Xiseng) to perform Buddhist rites.

On the *xinwei* day of the eleventh month, he dispatched the Western monks to perform Buddhist rites within the new inner palace of Xinghe. On the *wuyin* day, they performed Buddhist rites at Wutai Temple.

On the *bingwu* day of the twelfth month, he visited Dachong'en Fuyuan Temple to pay respects at the Shrine of Emperor Wuzong. He then separately commanded various monks to [perform rites] at the Daming Hall and Yanchun Hall.

He established Buddhist temples at the Gexing Palace, the Longfu Palace, and Mount Wansui. Furthermore, he commanded one hundred Western monks to perform Buddhist rites at the Huigyou Pavilion for seven days.

In the second year of the Tianli era, a Buddhist temple was constructed and a General Administration Commission (Zǒngguǎn Fǔ) was established, along with an Office for the Supervision of Construction.
These bodies were charged with overseeing all labor services, and permanent landholdings (*yǒngyè*) were granted to them. Furthermore, grand Buddhist rites were performed;

[the Emperor] received the Buddhist precepts from the Imperial Preceptor (*Dìshī*), provided gold, silver, paper currency, and silk, and sent the remains of the late Imperial Preceptor’s *śarīra* back to his native country. All corvée labor and taxes were exempted for monks and nuns. (According to the *Yuán shǐ*).
The *Basic Annals* of Emperor Shizu state: In the second year of the Tianli era, on the day of Bingyin in the first month of spring, the Emperor visited Dachong’en Fuyuan Temple.
On the day of Jisi, he bestowed one ingot of paper currency upon each of forty-two thousand two hundred and seventy soldiers of the inner and outer guards to perform Buddhist rites.
A minister of the Zhongshu Province remarked that the annual expenditure for these Buddhist rites was greater now than it had been in the past.

One thousand one hundred and fifty *liang* of gold, six thousand two hundred *liang* of silver, fifty-six thousand two hundred *ding* of paper currency, and thirty-four thousand or more rolls of silk were presented;

[the Emperor] ordered that all these be reduced or eliminated, and they complied. In the second month, the Buddhist services for the "Wandering through the Imperial City" (*you huangcheng*) were established.
On the *jisi* day of the third month, he decreed that the former residence of his youth at Qijing be converted into the Great Longxiang Qijing Monastery (*Dalongxiang Jiqing Si*).
On the day Dingyou of the fourth month in summer, ten thousand ingots of paper currency were granted to establish permanent endowments for the Great Longxiang Temple of Jiqing.

The Henan Surveillance Commission reported that because the Henan administrative region was suffering from military conflict, drought, and famine, they requested to requisition the surplus grain of monks and Daoists from Jianghuai to provide relief;
this was granted. In the fifth month, three thousand ingots of gold and one hundred [ingots] of silver held by the Chupi (Storehouse for Accumulated Prosperity) were [allocated].
[He] established the Great Chengtian Husheng Temple. In the year Yihai, he visited Dashingou Wanan Temple and performed Buddhist rites at the Shizu Shenjudian (Ancestral Shrine of Emperor Shizu).
He also performed Buddhist rites at the Yudedian and the Datiany Yansheng Temple.
On the gengzi day of the eighth month in autumn, he commanded A-rong and Zhao Shian to supervise the construction of Longxiang Jiqing [Temple] in Jiankang.

Temple. On the day of Jiayin, the Longxiang General Administration (Lóngxiáng Zǒngguǎnfǔ) was established, ranked as the third grade of the regular order, to oversee the construction labor for the Great Chengtian Husheng Temple.
On the first day of the ninth month, the day of Yimao, Buddhist services were performed in the Daming Hall and the various palaces of Xingsheng and Longfu.
On the day of Jiwu, the former fields of Empress Dowager Quan of the former Song dynasty were purchased to serve as the permanent endowment for the Great Chengtian Husheng Temple. Jiwu.

The Office for the Supervision of Construction at Longxiang Wanshou Monastery and the Office for the Supervision of Construction at Hainan Monastery were established, both ranked as the fourth grade of the regular order and subordinated to the Longxiang Prefectural Administration.
On the *jichou* day of the tenth month in winter, the Office for the Supervision of Construction at Dachengtian Husheng Monastery was established, ranked as the fifth grade of the regular order.
On the *jiachen* day, one hundred and eight monks from the Uyghur region performed Buddhist rites.

At Xingsheng Hall, on the wu-shen day, Buddhist rites were performed at Guanghan Hall. On the geng-xu day, having completed the personal sacrifice at the Imperial Ancestral Temple, an edict was issued to the empire to suspend construction work at Dachengtian Husheng Monastery.
On the yi-mao day of the eleventh month, an edict was issued to the empire regarding the installation of the Empress.
[The Emperor] received the Buddha-precepts from the Imperial Preceptor and performed Buddhist rites for sixty days. The Empress... eight.

He did not request [the Emperor] to clarify the fundamental tenets for the sake of posthumous merit, but instead commanded the Imperial Preceptor (Imperial Master) to lead a multitude of monks in performing Buddhist rites for seven days at Dayuan Yansheng Temple.
The Empress contributed fifty thousand taels of silver to assist in the construction of Dachengtian Husheng Temple.
The State Preceptor of the Western Xia, the Duke of Guo, Chongbu, passed away; his younger brother, Jiansang Banzangbu, succeeded him.
He succeeded to the office; the imperial seal and insignia were likewise conferred upon him.

On the day of Bingyin, the Bureau for the Supervision of Artisans at Pukingxiu Temple was renamed the Office of the Director of Construction and Repair (*Yingshan Tiandiansuo*), with a rank of Grade Five (Lower). It was subordinated to the Longxiang Prefectural Administration.
One hundred and fifty *qing* of official fields in Pingjiang were granted to the Great Longxiang Jiqing Temple, as well as to the Great Chongxi Wanshou Temple.

At the temple, in the twelfth month, the Western monk Lien-chen-k’i-la-si was appointed as Imperial Preceptor (Ti-shih). An edict was issued to monks and nuns stating that they were exempt from all corvée labor and levies.
On the day of Xinmao, the Emperor commanded the Imperial Preceptor to lead his disciples in performing Buddhist rites at the Ninghui Pavilion.
An edict was further issued to all monasteries regarding their lands: those held since the Jin and Song dynasties, as well as those granted by successive reigns, were all to be exempted [from taxes].
Regarding taxes: those who were liable for tax payments were exempted from corvée labor. Those monks who had returned to lay life were permitted to re-enter the monastic order.

In the year Jihai (1359), an envoy was dispatched by relay station to return the relics of the late Imperial Preceptor to his own country, providing him with five hundred taels of gold, two thousand five hundred taels of silver, fifteen hundred *dian* of paper currency, and five thousand bolts of silk. In the year Rentyin (1362), an edict was issued to the Jiangzhe Provincial Administration...

Memorandum: Twenty-seven *piṭaka* of Buddhist scriptures were printed. In the year Jiachen (1504), for the anniversary of Emperor Wuzong’s death in the first month of the following year, three hundred and forty monks from Goryeo and China were ordered to recite two *piṭaka* of Buddhist scriptures in advance at Dachong’en Fuyuan Temple.
On the day Renzi (January 29, 1504), the imperial portrait of Emperor Wuzong was completed; Buddhist services were then performed in the Shenyudian (Hall of the Imperial Spirit). [End of] Record.

Miao’s Transmission. Miao was promoted to Censor-in-Chief. At the beginning of the Tianli era, Emperor Wen issued an edict to convert the former imperial residence in Jiankang into a Buddhist monastery, intending it to be as magnificent as possible.
Over seventy households were demolished for the project, and he appointed the Grand Censor to supervise the labor.
Miao submitted a memorial stating: "I have heard that since antiquity, the people have been employed according to the seasons, and ministers have been treated with propriety."
There have been those who attained great prosperity and peace not by this path. When Your Majesty was still a hidden dragon in Jianye, the residents were already burdened by the demands for supplies;
fortunately, they have now witnessed the current era of fortune. The common people stand on tiptoe and lift their heads, awaiting extraordinary grace.
Yet now, you deprive them of the season for farming to construct Buddhist temples, and further demolish their dwellings, causing their households to fall into ruin.
To squander resources on such matters—how could this be the Way of a Sage for governing the world? In the past, when Emperor Gao of Han rose from Fengpei, he restored two counties;
when Guangwu achieved the Restoration, he exempted Nanyang from taxes for three years.

Since you do not pursue these [traditional] practices, yet instead honor and exalt the Buddha, how can you satisfy the expectations of the people? Furthermore, the Buddha takes compassion as his heart and skillful means as his practice.
The teaching now honors the Buddha, yet you harm the common people; does this not contravene his teachings of skillful means?
It is the duty of the Palace Officials (Taisō) to specialize in investigation and to rectify the hundred offices. To now entrust them with the labor of construction—how could this be proper?
The memorial was submitted. Consequently, the Grand Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Yushi Dafu) was indeed relieved of his supervision of labor services.
In the first year of the Zhishun era, the Emperor, the Empress, Prince Yan, and the Crown Prince Mingzong all received the Buddhist precepts.

They bestowed great largesse upon various monasteries in the form of paper currency, silk, and land as permanent endowments. An envoy was dispatched carrying gold and silver to Hangzhou to transcribe Buddhist scriptures.
He ordered the various provinces south of the Yellow River to recite the Tripitaka.

In this year, at the request of officials of the Zhongshu Sheng (Secretariat), the number of Buddhist services performed annually at Shangdu was reduced from one hundred and sixty-five to one hundred and forty, which became the permanent standard.
According to the *Yuanshi* (History of Yuan), in the first month of spring in the first year of Zhisun, he dispatched envoys carrying fifteen hundred taels of gold and silver.

Five hundred taels [of silver]. He visited Hangzhou to have Buddhist scriptures copied. Ten thousand ingots of paper money were granted for the purchase of permanent land for Daxinglong Puming Temple in Hainan.
On the wuyin day, one thousand *qing* of fields were granted to Longxi Zongguanfu. On the dingyou day of the second month.
The Emperor and the Empress Dowager, as well as Prince Yan Aratnadara, all received the Buddhist precepts. On the day of Jihai, he commanded Crown Prince Mingzong to receive the Buddhist precepts.

He issued an edict to the Shumi Yuan (Secretariat for Military Affairs) to provide ten thousand ingots of paper currency from the proceeds of military屯田 (tuntian) grain to assist in the construction of Buddhist temples, and exempted the soldiers from labor service for building works.
He further ordered the purchase of the lands formerly belonging to Zhao Xian, the former Prince of Ying.
[The Emperor] established [the land] as perpetual endowment for Dàlóngxiáng Jíqìng Temple. An official of the Censorate stated that it was unnecessary to pay its value in cash.
The Emperor said, "I have built this temple for the sake of my descendants and the common people. If I were to take land from others without providing compensation, it would not be my intention.
On the first day of the fourth month, the *renwu* day, he ordered Western monks to perform Buddhist rites in the Rénzhì Hall. From then on...

The service began on the first day of the month and concluded at the end of the twelfth month. Due to the famine in Shaanxi, an imperial edict was issued for the relevant authorities to perform Buddhist rites for seven days.
On the *renchen* day, the four hundred *qǐng* of land confiscated from the sons of Zhāng Guī were granted to Dàchéngtiānhùshèng Temple as permanent property.
On the *rentiǎn* day, sixteen thousand two hundred and ninety *mù* of fallow land in Yìdū, Bānyáng, and Nínghǎi were surveyed.

One thousand *qǐng* were granted to Dàchéngtiānhùshèng Temple as permanent property. The Yìdū Guǎngnóng Administration Commission (*Tíjǔsī*) was established, along with the Yìdū, Bānyáng, and Nínghǎi various Administration Offices (*Tílǐngsuǒ*), all of which were subordinated to the Lóngxíng Prefectural Government (*Zǒngduàn Fǔ*).
On the *jǐmǎo* day of the fifth month, an envoy was dispatched to Mount Wútaí to perform Buddhist rites. In the sixth month, [the Emperor] commanded [officials] from Henan, Húbǎng, and Jīngxī.
In the Gansu Provincial Administration, six hundred and fifty volumes of the Tripitaka were recited and thirty thousand ingots of paper money were distributed.
In the seventh month of autumn, an order was issued for Western monks to perform Buddhist rites for the Crown Prince, the Yan Wang.

In the intercalary seventh month, the treasuries, fields, houses, slaves, and livestock of Söjü Yarlya and others were inventoried and granted to the Great Chengtian Husheng Monastery as its permanent endowment. [End of middle section]

The Secretariat officials submitted a memorial, stating: "There are three hundred and sixty-seven Buddhist temples within and without the capital, consuming immeasurable amounts of gold, silver, paper currency, and silk.

As state expenditures are currently insufficient, these should be reduced. The Emperor ordered the Secretariat personnel and the officials of the Xuanzheng Yuan to reduce the number of temples performing annual Buddhist rites in Shangdu from one hundred and sixty-five to one hundred and four, and commanded the relevant authorities to maintain this permanently.
This became an annual custom. In the eighth month, it was reported that silver was produced in Guangling County of Weizhou.
An imperial edict was issued to the Zhongshu and Daxi Yuan offices to dispatch officials to oversee the matter; the silver obtained each year was to be returned to Dachengtian Husheng Temple.
On the day of Xinyou, as this month was the birth month of the Great Emperor (Shizu), he ordered one hundred and seventy monks from the capital to perform Buddhist rites. In the ninth month...
Bingwu (the 14th day of the eleventh month). An edict was issued for Western monks to perform Buddhist rites in the Daming Hall.

At the beginning of the Zhizhi era, lands belonging to the Baiyun school had been granted to Shouanshan Monastery as permanent property; now, the monk Shen Mingqi petitioned on this matter, and an imperial decree was issued ordering the Zhongshu Sheng to rectify the situation.
On the first day of the eleventh month, an edict was issued commanding the Imperial Preceptor to lead Western monks in performing Buddhist rites within the palace.

There were eight locations for lay practitioners (*bāiwán*). These began on this day and concluded at the end of the year. On the twelfth month, an imperial decree was issued for the construction and Buddhist services at Longxiang Jiqing Temple;

the Jiangnan Provincial Administration Commission provided all necessary supplies. On the *dingmao* day, an edict was issued for Western monks to perform Buddhist services at sixteen locations within the Xingsheng Guangtian Palace.

In the second year of the Zhishun era, Seng Baofeng was promoted to the rank of *Situ*, and the Guangjiao General Directorate (*Guǎngjiào Zǒngduàn Fǔ*) was established to oversee the administration of monks and nuns.
Furthermore, he was appointed as National Preceptor (*Guoshi*) and granted a seal of gold and jade. Extensive temples were constructed and Buddhist services performed;

Buddhist scriptures were transcribed in gold. In this same year, at the request of officials of the Xuanzheng Yuan, the Imperial Shrines of the successive sovereigns and the Buddhas of various monasteries [were restored].

Matters. Two hundred and sixteen [items] per year; by imperial decree, sixteen were eliminated to establish the fixed standard. According to the *Wenzong benji* (Basic Annals of Emperor Wenzong) in the *Yuanshi* (History of Yuan):

on the gengchen day of the first month of spring in the second year of Zhishun, the monk Baofeng, who presided over Dachengtianhusheng Temple, was promoted to the rank of Minister of Education (*Situ*).
On the dinghai day, because the temple built by Emperor Yingzong at Shouanshan had not yet been completed, an imperial edict was issued to the central government...
The Secretariat issued one hundred thousand *ding* of paper currency to provide for his expenses. Furthermore, Yan Tie-mu-er and Sa-di were ordered to supervise the labor services.

On the wu-day of the first month, over twenty-four thousand households of subjects from the Jin Prince’s domain, including Liu Yuan-liang, were assigned to Shou-an Mountain at the Da-zhao-xiao Temple as perpetual land-holding households. On the wu-shen day of the second month, the Guangjiao [Monastery] was established.

The Prefectural Offices (*Zǒngguǎnfǔ*) were established to administer the affairs of monks and nuns; there were sixteen such offices in total: namely, the Capital Region and Mountains-to-the-West Circuit;
the River-East and Mountains-to-the-Right Circuit; the Liaodong and Mountains-to-the-North Circuit; the Henan and Jingbei Circuit;
the Two Huai and Jiangbei Circuit; the Hubei and Hunan Circuit; the Zhejiang and Jiangdong Circuit; and the Zhedong and Fujian Circuit.
The circuits were as follows: the Jiangxi and Guangdong Circuit; the Guangxi and Liaohe Circuit; the various routes of Yunnan;
the various routes of Shandong; the various routes of Shaanxi; the various routes of Gansu; the various routes of Sichuan; and the various routes of Yunnan.
Their rank was the third grade of the regular class. In each prefecture, a Daluohachih (Darughachi) was appointed as the Governor-General, along with an Assistant Governor and a Vice-Governor.
Each office shall have one official; the Xuanzheng Yuan shall select candidates from among the officials within the current registers, draft appointments, and report them for approval.

As for the *zongguan* (General Manager), a monk shall serve in this capacity. In the year Jih-wei, the Emperor commanded that a Western monk perform Buddhist rites for one full year on behalf of the Crown Prince Guṇadara.

In the year Jiazi, the ministers of the Zhongshu Sheng submitted a memorial stating: "Your Majesty has established the Dachen [Great Vehicle] Monastery without expending state funds and without taxing the people."

Regarding the Imperial Temple of Great Protection (Dacheng Tianhusheng Si): We, your subjects, wish to offer one hundred thousand ingots of paper money and six hundred ingots of silver as an offering toward the construction needs of this temple.
This was granted. In the Jiaxu year, an edict was issued ordering the General Administration of Land Taxation to remit the tax on mineral silver to the Imperial Temple of Great Protection.
In the third month, a special decree was issued appointing Shazhen Aihu to hold the position of Biladute Naishili.
He was appointed as State Preceptor of the Tripitaka and granted a jade seal.
On the wuzi day, the Western monk Xuni Dieba Dalaban was appointed as State Preceptor of the Tripitaka and granted a golden seal.

The assets of Jie Ruru Bandan Cheli Temür were confiscated and bestowed upon Dachengtianhusheng Temple as its permanent endowment. On the gengzi day, he prepared for an imperial journey to the Upper Capital.
He ordered Western monks (Xī-sēng) to perform Buddhist rites at the halting stations along his imperial carriage route.

In the fourth month of summer, he commanded Western monks to perform Buddhist rites at Mount Wutai and Mount Wulíng for one month each, on behalf of the Crown Prince Gūndata-la, to pray for blessings.
He dispatched three thousand soldiers from the Guard to assist with the construction work at Dàchéngtiānhùshèng Temple, issuing an edict to gild the temple with gold leaf.
One thousand copies of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* were transcribed in Uyghur script. On the *bingxu* day of the fifth month, a minister of the Taisi Zongyin Yuan reported:

"The twelve monasteries, including Dawan'an, established during successive reigns, originally had an authorized quota of three thousand one hundred and fifty monks who were granted annual grain stipends.
Now that their numbers have become excessive, we request that nine hundred and forty-three be reduced."

[The Emperor] granted permission. On the day of Yiwei, an edict was issued to transcribe one entire collection of Buddhist scriptures using gold ink. On the day of Jiachen, a minister of the Xuanzheng Yuan reported:
"According to the old regulations, there were two hundred and sixteen Buddhist services performed annually at the Imperial Shrines of the successive emperors and at various monasteries;

we now reduce this by sixteen to establish a fixed standard. [The Emperor] granted permission. In the seventh month of autumn, he commanded the Western monks (Sangha) to [perform rites] at the Great...

Buddhist rites were performed at Mingzhong Pavilion on Mount Wansui in the capital, beginning on the eighth day of the eighth month and continuing until the imperial carriage returned to the Great Capital.

On the ninth month, an official of the Censorate reported that Yan Jixiang, the State Counselor and presiding master of the Da Shengshou Wan’an Temple, had misappropriated public property and maintained a wife and children;
it was decreed that he should be relieved of his positions as State Counselor and presiding master. This was granted.
On the *xinyou* day of the tenth month in winter, imperial edict was issued to have Western monks perform Buddhist rites at Xingsheng Palace.
On the fifteenth day, in the third year of Zhishun, the Xingshui Office was established to oversee Buddhist affairs for the Inner Palace. In order to perform these rites, prisoners were released.

An envoy was dispatched to the residence of the Imperial Preceptor (*Tishri*) to deliver an edict woven with pearls to his subordinates, while further gifts of paper currency and silk were distributed. Furthermore—
The seal of the Monk Minister (Seng Situ) was granted. This was the year Emperor Ningzong ascended the throne.

According to the *Wenzong Benji* of the *Yuanshi*, in the third month of the third year of Zhishun, the Xingshui Si (Bureau of Prosperous Auspices) was established to oversee the annual Buddhist rites performed for the Inner Palace;
its rank was the third grade of the first order. On the day of Yiwei, the Imperial Preceptor (Dishi) traveled by boat on the Gaoliang River at the Western Hills.
Ha. Three hundred guards were mobilized to tow the boat. In the fourth month, Buddhist rites were performed to pray for blessings.
He released Liu the County Magistrate of Dingxing and twenty-six prisoners from the Ministry of Justice who had been held at the Censorate.

In the fifth month, he dispatched an envoy to the residence of the Imperial Preceptor (Di-shi) at the site of Teshikya, where he issued a decree woven with pearls to proclaim his instructions to the Preceptor’s subordinates. Furthermore—

He bestowed four thousand *ding* of paper currency and five thousand bolts each of silk and cloth, distributing them accordingly. On the day of Xinmao, he further conferred the seal of the Minister of Education (Situ) upon the monk Yan Jixiang of Wanshan Temple;
by imperial decree, fifty thousand *ding* of paper currency were granted for the restoration of the Hall of the Shadow of the Imperial Preceptor Phags-pa.
In the seventh month of autumn, on the day of Yihai, he ordered monks to perform Buddhist rites at the Iron Banner Pole (*tie fan gan*), bestowing one hundred *jin* of gold.
Two thousand taels of silver; five hundred rolls each of silk and brocade; two thousand rolls of cloth; and ten thousand ingots of paper currency.
According to the Basic Annals of Emperor Ningzong, in the tenth month of the third year of Zhishun, the Emperor ascended the throne.
He had his younger brother, Yantiesigusi, receive the precepts from the Western monk Jialama-wala.

In the second year of the Yuantong era of Emperor Shun, an edict was issued to curtail the excessive expenditures on Buddhist rituals. According to the *Basic Annals* of Emperor Shun in the *History of Yuan*:

on the *gui-mao* day of the first month of spring in the second year of Yuantong, an imperial decree was issued that monks and Daoists were to be conscripted for labor service on the same basis as the common people.

On the *jia-chen* day of the third month, a minister of the Zhongshu Sheng (Secretariat) reported that the construction of a Buddhist ritual site in the Xinghe Prefecture had incurred expenses amounting to [blank] *chao*.

There were over 13,530 ingots [of gold]. It was decreed that they should follow the precedent of the Capital (Daidu) and the Upper Capital (Shangdu) regarding the provision of food and monetary allowances for the clergy, thereby curtailing wasteful expenditures.
This was granted. On the *yǐyou* day of the fourth month in summer, a minister of the Zhongshu Sheng stated that the expenses for Buddhist services and offerings were far too extensive.
Compared to the era of Emperor Shizu, the annual expenditure had increased by thirty-eight ingots of gold and two hundred [ingots] of silver.
Three hundred and forty *ding* [of gold], over sixty-one thousand six hundred rolls of silk, and over twenty-nine thousand two hundred and fifty *zhao* [of paper currency].
With the exception of the anniversary memorial services for successive reigns, all others were abolished.
This was granted.
In the twelfth month of winter in the first year of the Zhizong era, an edict was issued ordering that all monks who had wives were to return to lay life as commoners.
Subsequently, however, they were again permitted to remain as monks. (As recorded in the *History of Yuan*, in the Annals of Emperor Shun, etc.)
In the second year of Zhizhi, on the *ding-si* day of the eleventh month of winter, the Chancellor of the Henan Provincial Administration, Yue Luo Pu Hua, was dispatched to Xifan to become a monk.
In the twelfth month, the residence of Yan Tie-mu-er was bestowed upon the Guanding Guoshi Nang-xie Xing-ji;
it was named Dajue Hai Temple, and within it, statues of the Thousand Buddhas were fashioned.
In the twelfth month of winter in the third year of the Zhizong era, the Saṃgharāma monks from the Western Regions were summoned to the capital.
They were titled Guǎngdìng Guóshī (State Preceptor of Consecration) and granted jade seals.
On the day of Guihai, the first month of spring in the fifth year of Zhizhen, the bestowal of monastic names and titles upon those who did not merit them was prohibited.
On the first month of spring in the first year of Zhizheng, an order was issued for Yongming Temple to transcribe one complete set of the Buddhist canon in golden characters.
According to the aforementioned entries in the *Veritable Record of Emperor Shun* of the *History of Yuan*.

In the second year of the Zhizheng era, following the petition of Na lin, the Xuanzheng Yuan established the Chongjiao So (Office for the Propagation of the Teaching) to adjudicate the legal disputes and litigation of the clergy.
[Note: This is not recorded in the *Shun Di Ben Ji* (Basic Annals of Emperor Shun) of the *Yuanshi* (History of Yuan). According to the biography of Na lin:

In the second year of Zhizheng, Na lin was appointed as the Administrator of the Xuanzheng Yuan. At that time, Mi jie, a senior monk of Upper Tianzhu Monastery, and Hui [yuan], a senior monk of Jingshan Monastery...]
In the various provinces, those who committed offenses with impunity were all sentenced to severe punishments by Nalin.

He petitioned for the establishment of a Chongjiao Office (Office for the Propagation of the Teaching) under the Xuanzheng Yuan, proposing that its officials be modeled after the Liwen Officers of the provincial administrations and ranked at the fourth grade to adjudicate the legal disputes and litigation involving monks. This was granted.
On the *bingshen* day of the twelfth month of winter in the third year of Zhizheng, an edict was issued to transcribe the Tripitaka in golden characters.
On the *jia Shen* day of the twelfth month of winter in the sixth year of Zhizheng, an edict was issued to re-establish the Great Huguo Renwang Temple.
Furthermore, an edict was issued [appointing] the Yinggong Caiyong Guiyun Tongzong Guanfu; in total, twenty-six myriad and several thousand ingots of money were loaned from the private sector.

In the second month of spring in the seventh year of Zhizheng, on the first day of the cycle (Jiaxu), Buddhist services were performed at Xingsheng Palace, for which two thousand ingots of paper currency were bestowed.
On the renshen day of the third month, an envoy was dispatched to repair the Great Qianyuan Temple in the Northern Capital.
In the eleventh month of winter, sixteen hundred and twenty thousand *qǐng* of land in Shandong were allocated to the Great Chengtian Husheng Temple.
On the first day of the first month of spring in the thirteenth year of Zhizheng (the gengwu day), at the request of the Imperial Preceptor, the prisoners in the capital were released.
On the jia-shen day of the third month, an edict was issued to repair the Dachen Tianhusheng Temple, and twenty thousand ingots of paper currency were granted.
(The above details are recorded in the *Veritable Records* of Emperor Shun of the Yuan Dynasty.)
In the fourteenth year of the Zhizheng era, Toghon Temür performed meritorious deeds for the sake of the Dosi-ge-er and constructed a Buddhist temple.

Consequently, the Crown Prince released prisoners as part of these Buddhist rites. According to the *History of Yuan*, in the first month of spring in the fourteenth year of Zhizheng, on the day Dingchou, the Emperor said to Toqtu Temür:
"I have previously performed meritorious deeds for the sake of the Dosi-ge-er and invited the White Parasol (Śvetachattra) [deity]."
The tour of the Imperial City was truly for the sake of the living beings of the world.

It has now been decreed that one hundred and eight *lama* monks shall be selected to continue performing the meritorious deeds of the Dusi Ger. All items required shall be provided by the government; do not cause disturbance to the people.
In the second month, the Great Shouyuan Zhongguo Temple was established at Qinghe, and the lands of abandoned temples in Jiangzhe were transferred to it.
In the eleventh month of winter, the Crown Prince performed Buddhist rites. He released all prisoners in the capital with death sentences or lighter terms.

According to the biography of the Imperial Preceptor Phagspa, his regular practice of offering prayers and performing sacrifices for the state at various times of the year was commonly referred to as "performing good deeds" (*hǎoshì*).
These activities were manifold; among them were those called *zhènléi ālánàsì*, which in the Chinese language means "celebratory praise," and those called *yīsī*.
*Man lan*: In the language of China, this means "Medicine Master Altar. *Suo si chuan bu*: In the language of China, this means "Protecting the City. *Du'er chan*:
In the language of China, this means "Great Bestowal of Food. *Du'er zhi lue duo si*:
In the language of China, this means "Exquisite Vajra Ritual for Averting and Bestowing Food. *Cha'er ga duo si*: In the language of China, this means "Averting."

There is that which is called *Lónggē’ér*, which in the language of China means "wind-wheel" (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). There is that which is called *Zǎnduōsì*, which in the language of China means "performing the offering of food.
There is that which is called *Chūduō’ér*, which in the language of China means "emerging from water to rescue the six realms of existence.

There is that which is called *Dǎnglàduōsì*, which in the language of China means "warding off the offering of food. There is that which is called *Diǎnduō’ér*, which in the language of China means "constantly and perpetually offering food."
One is called *Tso-ting* (Sitting in Stillness); one is called *Lu-chao* (Lüzhāo), which in the Chinese language means the "Dharma-assembly of the Lion’s Roar" (*siṃhanāda-maṇḍala*).

One is called *Heiya Man-dage* (Hēiyá Mánduōjié), which in the Chinese language means "Lord of the Black Prison. One is called *Shuosi Jiang-duer-ma* (Suǒsī Jiāngduōrmá), which in the Chinese language means "Offering Food to the River-Guardian Deity.
One is called *Chisigu lin-shuo* (Chìsīgǔ Línshuō), which in the Chinese language means "Self-Receiving of the Master’s Precepts."
Some say *zhèn léi zuò jìng* (鎮雷坐靜), others say *chīlàchá zuò jìng* (吃剌察坐靜); in the Chinese language, this means "Secret Seated Meditation" (*guīmì zuòjìng*).
Some say *zhēnrě* (斟惹); in the Chinese language, this means "Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. Some say *gǔlín duōsī* (古林朵思);

in the Chinese language, this means "The Supreme Great Black Deity’s Rite for Averting and Bestowing Food. Some say *xièbái zālà* (歇白咱剌); in the Chinese language, this means "Mahāsukha" (Great Bliss).

There is also that which is called Bisitsen (必思禪), the Chinese equivalent of which is Amitāyus (Immeasurable Life). There is that which is called Dutsigor (覩思哥兒), the Chinese equivalent of which is the Śvetaparājaya Dhāraṇī (White Parasol Mantra).
There is that which is called Shozhashala (收札沙剌), the Chinese equivalent of which is the Pañcarakṣā Dhāraṇī Sūtra (The Scripture of the Five Protective Dhāraṇīs).
There is one called *A-xi-da-sa-da-xi-li*, which in the language of China is the *Prajñāpāramitā in Eighty Verses*.
There is one called *Sa-si-na-tun*, which in the language of China is the "Great Li Heavenly Deity Mantra. There is one called *Kuo-er-lu-fu-bu-tun*.
"Mahācakra-vajra-mantra" in the language of China; there is one called "Cha-pa-mi-tun," which is the *Amitāyus-sūtra* in the language of China;
there is one called "Yi-si-lo-pa," which is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttamarāja-sūtra* in the language of China; and there is one called "Sa-si-na-tun."
In the language of China, this is called "protective deity mantra. There is one called *nam-chen-tun*, which in the language of China means "Vajra of Embracing Form.
There is one called *p'u-lu-pa*, which in the language of China means "mantra method. Furthermore, there are those who fashion *tsa-tsas*, which are small stupas made of clay.
There are also those who fashion *dza-er-kang*. As for those who fashion *dza-er-kang*, they may be made as one or two units. By...
He traveled to the seventh site, where he fashioned *tsa-tsas* numbering one hundred thousand, two hundred thousand, and up to three hundred thousand.
Furthermore, he once constructed two hundred and sixteen stupas, filled with the seven precious gems and jade;
half were placed on the seashore and half were placed within the water to suppress maritime calamities.
In the twenty-second year of the Zhizheng era, the Crown Prince summoned monks from Xifan (Tibet) and Goryeo to sit in rows within the Qingning Hall.

According to the *History of Yuan*, in the Basic Annals of Emperor Shun, it records that in the twelfth month of winter in the twenty-second year of Zhizheng, the Crown Prince sat regularly in the Qingning Hall, where long mats were spread out and the monks from Xifan and Goryeo were seated in rows. The Crown Prince...
The Crown Prince said, "Master Li Haowen has taught me the Confucian classics for many years, yet I still do not comprehend their meaning.
Now, having listened to the Buddha-dharma, I have been able to understand it in a single night. Thereupon, he came to hold Buddhist studies in high esteem.
In the eighth month of autumn in the twenty-fourth year of Zhizheng, the practice of "seeking favors" by Western Tibetan monks was prohibited.
This is recorded in the *Veritable Record* (Benji) of Emperor Shundi in the *History of Yuan* (Yuanshi), as follows.

*The Comprehensive Collection of Illustrations and Writings on Antiquity and the Present* (*Gujin Tushu Chengji*), Section on Buddhist Teachings (*Shijiao Bu*), Compendium of Investigations (*Huikao*), Volume Five.
*The Comprehensive Collection of Illustrations and Writings on Antiquity and the Present*, Section on Buddhist Teachings, Compendium of Investigations, Volume Six. Ming Dynasty.
In the fourth year of Taizu’s Hongwu era, an imperial edict was issued to summon eminent monks for a grand Buddhist memorial service (*guǎngjiàn fohuì*).

According to Song Lian’s *Record of the Grand Buddhist Memorial Service at Jiangshan Temple*: "In the twelfth month of winter in the fourth year of Hongwu, ten eminent monks from Jiangnan were summoned by imperial decree.
The Imperial Observatory selected the auspicious date, and the *jiàn* (memorial) dharma assembly was established at Taiping Xingguo Chan Temple on Mount Jiangshan."
The Emperor stayed overnight in the fasting chamber and abstained from all pungent meats for one month. He further commanded the Right Chancellor of the Central Secretariat,

Wang Guangyang, and the Left Chancellor, Hu Weiyong, to send a letter to the deities of the city and the soil, fully proclaiming the Emperor’s intent and requesting that they inform the netherworld to ensure everyone assembled by the appointed time.

In the fifth year of Hongwu, a grand Dharma assembly was held at Zhongshan Temple. According to the *Lichao shiji* (Collection of Poetry from Successive Dynasties), on the fifteenth day of the first month in the fifth year of Hongwu, the imperial court convened a great Dharma assembly at Zhongshan Temple to universally deliver the spirits of the netherworld.

On the fifteenth day of the twelfth month in the fourth year, the Emperor presided over the Fengtian Hall, assembled the dukes, marquises, and various officials, and issued a proclamation regarding its establishment.

Regarding the causes for this assembly: the Emperor prohibited slaughter throughout the realm. Having first observed the fast for one month to solemnize the rite, on the thirteenth day of the first month at the third watch, the Emperor ascended the Fengtian Hall and assembled the dukes, nobles, and officials to present the memorial to the Buddha.
He commanded the Minister of Rites to carry [the relics] to Mount Zhongshan to inaugurate a Dharma assembly and cremate them.

On the fifteenth day, the Emperor donned the *gǔnmian* robes and ascended the imperial carriage to attend the assembly. At sunset, he welcomed the Buddha; leading the dukes, marquises, and hundred officials, he attended the Dharma feast to make offerings to the Buddha.
For the performance of the great rites and music, the melodies of the "Shanshi" (Benefiting the World) suite were employed. Prior to this, on the fourteenth day, there was a light snowfall.

Auspicious signs were manifested. Soon thereafter, the sky cleared. That evening, stars and the moon shone in the heavens; the wind and dew were profound and still. Strings and flutes played in alternation, while lamps and candles gleamed together in brilliance.
The grandeur of the rites and ceremonies was such that it could not have been matched by any previous age.

In the sixth year of the Hongwu era, Tibetan monks were enfeoffed as Guanding Guoshi (State Preceptor Consecrated with Water) and Zanshan (Assistant Good) Wang (Kings), all of whom were granted golden seals and official edicts.

According to the *Mingtongji* (General Record of the Ming): in the eighth month of the sixth year of Hongwu, an imperial decree was issued to the chieftains of the various tribes of Western and Native Tibet, ordering them to nominate those who had previously held official positions so that they might come to the capital to receive their offices and seals, and thereby govern according to local customs.
For this reason, the Yuan-appointed Imperial Preceptor Namkha Zangpo was appointed as the State Preceptor for the Flourishing Buddha-Jewel (Chisheng Fobao).
He established two Commanderies of Regional Military Commissioners (Duweishi) for Ü-Tsang and Kham-Ga.

From these, down to the various Pacification Commissions (Xuanwei), Pacification Commands (Zhaotao), and so forth, including the Myriarchies (Wanhu fu) and chiliarchies (Qianhu suo), there were thirty-three such offices in total to appoint the local chieftains. From that time on...

Among the monk-officials, there were those enfeoffed as Imperial Preceptors with Consecration (Guanding Guoshi), Zanshan Wang (Prince of Good Counsel), Chanhua Wang (Prince of Propagating the Teaching),

Zhengjue Dasheng Fawang (Dharma King of the Mahāyāna of Perfect Enlightenment), and Rulai Dabaofawang (Dharma King of the Great Jewel of the Tathāgata). All were granted golden seals and edicts, governing their respective subjects and presenting tribute every other year.

In the fifteenth year of the Hongwu era, the Shanshi Yuan (Office for the Propagation of Goodness) was reformed into the Senglusi (Bureau of Buddhist Affairs), establishing the positions of Left and Right Shan-shi, Chan-jiao, Jiang-jing, and Jue-yi to oversee matters pertaining to the Buddhist teachings. In that same year, an imperial edict was issued to select eminent monks to serve as attendants to the various princes.
According to the Ming Huidian, the Shanshi Yuan was established at the beginning of the dynasty and was reformed into the Senglusi in the fifteenth year of Hongwu.

The sixth category consists of the Zheng (Correct) Offices. These offices established the positions of Left and Right Shan-shi (Good World), Left and Right Chan-jiao (Expounding the Teachings), Left and Right Jiang-jing (Lecturing on the Scriptures), and Left and Right Jue-yi (Awakening to the Meaning).
Their duties were specifically dedicated to the affairs of Buddhist doctrine and they belonged to the Ministry of Rites (*Li-bu*).

Their headquarters in Nanjing was established at Tien-chieh Temple; after the Yongle era, it was established at Ta-hsing-lung Temple in Beijing. Today, Ta-hsing-lung Temple having been destroyed, [the office] has been relocated to...
Dalong Shan Temple: All officials of this office shall be selected from among those who are thoroughly proficient in the scriptures and whose moral conduct is upright and pure;
they shall not receive stipends. For official correspondence, monks shall serve as the administrators, and tenant farmers shall be employed for labor services.
There are three grades of monks: Chan, Jiang, and Jiao. Monks residing outside [the capital] are under the jurisdiction of the local prefectures.

The *Kōshi* (Office of the Director) is under the jurisdiction of the *Sōjōsho* (Office of the Head of the Clergy) at the provincial level and the *Sōkai-sho* (Office of the Clergy Council) at the county level;

all are governed by this primary office (*Honsho*). Regarding the officials of this primary office: they attend court only on the first and fifteenth days of each month, taking their places in the western ranks.

On occasions such as celebratory rites or the promulgation of imperial edicts, they always take their positions in advance in the eastern ranks. In all sacrificial rites performed within the capital, the officials of this primary office [participate].

Not to be included among those outside [the jurisdiction]. All internal and external monastic officials are solely responsible for the supervision and restraint of all monks throughout the realm, ensuring they strictly observe the precepts and monastic regulations.
Those who violate these shall be punished by their respective offices. However, if an offense involves matters pertaining to the military or the common people, [it shall be handled accordingly].

Regarding the disciplinary measures taken by the authorities, according to the *Mingtong ji*: In the fifteenth year, an imperial edict was issued to select eminent monks to serve as attendants to the various princes.
The monk Dao Yan went to the Yanfu (the future Yongle Emperor’s residence) and took up residence at Qingshou Chan Temple.

In the twentieth year of the Hongwu era, it was decreed that those among the populace aged twenty and above were not permitted to become monks. According to the *Ming Huidian* (Veritable Records of the Ming Dynasty),
in the twenty-fifth year of the Hongwu era,
the regulations for the attire of monastic officials and monks were established, and furthermore, the *Zhouzhi Ce* (Register of Universal Knowledge) was ordered to be compiled and distributed.
On Monastic Temples Throughout the Empire: According to the *Ming Huidian* (Veritable Records of the Ming Dynasty), regarding the attire of monastic officials and monks:
in the twenty-fifth year of the Hongwu era, it was decreed that *yogācāra* monks were permitted to wear boots. Regarding the issuance of ordination certificates (*dujié*) to monks:

in the twenty-fifth year of the Hongwu era, it was ordered that the relevant office compile a *Zhouzhi Ce* (Register of Known Persons) to catalog the monasteries and monks within and outside the capital.
For each person, record their age, surname, given name, and conduct, as well as the year they became a monk and the number of the ordination certificate (duce) issued to them.
Display these records throughout all monasteries in the empire for reference. Whenever a traveler or itinerant monk arrives, verify his identity against this register.

If there is any discrepancy, he shall be escorted to the local authorities to be sent to the capital, where he will be punished with severe penalties. Those who harbor or shelter such individuals shall also be held liable.

It was done accordingly. Thereafter, for many years, no [registers] were produced. Yet, there were still those who practiced fraud and deception. In the fifth year of the Zhengtong era, an order was issued to produce registers according to the former practice.
In the twenty-sixth year of the Hongwu era, an order was issued that monks who could master the classical scriptures should be granted certificates (*jiedie*). (According to the *Ming Huiyao*)

[The] Regulations: In the twenty-sixth year of the Hongwu era, an edict was issued ordering that every three years, each administrative office must examine those who can master the classical scriptures.

Those who pass shall be submitted to the Ministry, which will prepare a memorial for the issuance of *duòdì* (ordination certificates). Regarding all temples established in various locations, each must have a monk serving as abbot.
The Sangha officials (*sēnggāng*) and others shall recommend from among the monks of each temple those who possess virtuous conduct and mastery of the classical scriptures.
The Office shall apply for and issue a warrant from this office. For major monasteries possessing funds and grain, an application shall be forwarded to the Ministry of Rites to issue a warrant.
In the sixth month of the fourth year of the Huizong Jianwen era, the Prince of Yan ascended the throne; in the tenth month, he appointed the monk Daoyan as a [state] monk.
Recorded by the Left Supervisor of Goodness (Zuoshanshi).

According to the *Mingtongji* (General Record of the Ming), in the second year of the Yongle era of Emperor Chengzu, the monk Daoyan was promoted to the rank of Imperial Prince of Lesser Security (Taizai Shaobao). According to the *Mingtongji*.
In the fourth month of the second year of the Yongle era, the monk Daoyan was promoted to the rank of Taibao Shaobao (Junior Guardian of the Crown Prince).
He then resumed his secular surname, Yao, and was granted the name Guangxiao. From that time on, the Emperor addressed him as "Master Yao" (Yao Shaoshi) rather than by his given name.

Furthermore, he never again grew his hair or married a wife; he resided mostly in monasteries and, although two palace women were constantly granted to him, he did not approach them. The Emperor then—
He summoned him back.
In the fourth year of the Yongle era, the Western monk Shangshi Halima was welcomed to the capital. According to the *Mingtongji*:
"In the fourth year of Yongle, the Western monk Shangshi Halima was welcomed to the capital. Previously, when the Emperor was still in the Prince’s residence..."

The Imperial Residence [reported]: "It is heard that in U-Tsang there is a Master Shang Ha-lima, an extraordinary monk. Upon his accession to the throne, he dispatched the eunuch Pu Xian with letters and gifts to go and welcome him.

After five years, passing through both cold and heat, he finally arrived. When the imperial carriage went to see him, he did not perform the rites of prostration or kneeling, but merely joined his palms.

According to the *Ming Waishi*, in the "Biographies of Arts and Techniques," it is recorded that the monk Zhiguang... [the Emperor] bestowed upon him the title of "Wu... (The text here appears to be truncated).

As a person of settled virtue, during the Hongwu era he was commissioned on two missions to the kingdoms of Uṣaṅga (U-si-tsang), Baṅgala (Bengal), Ni-pa-la (Nepal), Di-yong-ta (Tibet), and other lands.
During the Yongle era, he again served as an envoy to Uṣaṅga to welcome the Imperial Preceptor Ha-li-ma (Hsüan-tsang).

Consequently, he became proficient in the various scriptures of the foreign nations and performed extensive translations. Having served six successive reigns, his imperial favors and gifts surpassed those of all other monks.
In the fifth year of the Yongle era, one thousand eight hundred monks who had requested ordination certificates were dispatched to garrison duty in Liaodong and Gansu.

The Emperor commanded the Western monk Shangshi Halima to establish a Dharma altar; he was subsequently granted an honorary title and appointed as the Overseer of Buddhist Teachings throughout the realm.
According to the *Ming Tongji*, in the first month of the fifth year of Yongle, [this occurred] across the various prefectures of Zhili and Zhejiang.
One thousand eight hundred sons of military and civilian families had shaved their heads to become monks and traveled to the capital to request ordination certificates (*duodie*).

When the Ministry of Rites reported this to the Emperor, he said in anger: "By the regulations of my late father, subjects were only permitted to leave the household life once they reached the age of forty.

Now that they have violated the prohibitions to such an extent, they clearly show no regard for the imperial court. He ordered that all of them be transferred to the Ministry of War, enrolled in the military registers, and dispatched [to the frontiers].

He was stationed in Liaodong and Gansu. In the second month, he commanded the Western monk, the Imperial Preceptor Ha Lama, to establish a Dharma altar at Linggu Monastery to offer memorial services for the late Emperor and Empress.
The Preceptor led the monastic community (*saṃgha*) of the realm in holding a fourteen-day Great Fast ritual for universal salvation.
There appeared auspicious clouds, celestial flowers, sweet rain, and nectar-like dew, as well as śarīra relics and auspicious light. Green...
Birds, white cranes, and other fowl gathered in great numbers day after day. One night, golden flowers bloomed upon the cypresses and pines, covering the entire capital.

Golden immortals and arhats manifested in the clouds above; white elephants and blue lions appeared with wondrous, majestic forms. Celestial lamps led the way as banners and canopies circled incessantly in every variety.
Furthermore, the sounds of Brahma-chants and celestial music resounded from the heavens. The ministers then presented [their offerings].
The memorial was presented as a congratulatory message. The Academician Hu Guang and others offered songs and hymns celebrating the auspicious responses of sacred filial piety.
From that time forward, the Emperor devoted himself deeply to the Buddhist scriptures and composed Buddhist melodies, which he had performed by the palace women through song and dance.

In the third month, the Western monk Ha Lama was enfeoffed as "The One Endowed with Myriad Practices, Most Supreme and Perfectly Awakened, Wondrous Wisdom Universally Responding to and Protecting the State."
To the Tathāgata Yanjiao, the Great Dharma King of the Western Heaven, the Great Benevolent Sovereign Buddha, who presides over the Buddhist teachings throughout the realm:
[I] bestow one hundred taels of gold, one thousand taels of silver, colored silks and precious currency, a brocade robe adorned with pearls, and vessels of gold and silver.

He was granted a ceremonial retinue equal to that of a Prince of the First Order. His disciples, including Bala and others, were all conferred the title of Imperial Preceptor of a Great State (Daguoshi).
They were each bestowed with seals, edicts, gold, silk, and other items, and entertained at the Huagai Hall.

In the sixth year of the Yongle era, it was prohibited for the children of military and civilian families, as well as servants and slaves, to shave their own heads and become monks. According to the *Ming Huidian* (Veritable Records of the Ming Dynasty):

In the sixth year of Yongle, an order was issued that those among the children of military and civilian families, as well as servants and slaves, who shaved their own heads to become monks, were to be sent to the capital along with their fathers and elder brothers.
They were to be dispatched to Mount Wutai to perform manual labor; upon completion of their service, they were to remain in Beijing as commoners to cultivate the land.
Furthermore, those monks who had illicitly harbored [the fugitives] at the Mulong Masi (Pasture Horse Temple) were also transported to Beijing to become commoners and cultivate fields.
In the eighth year of the Yongle era, he appointed a monk from the Tibetan regions as Guoshi (State Preceptor) and dispatched envoys to the western lands to summon Shangshi Kunze Sipha.

According to the *Ming Dazheng Ji* (Veritable Records of the Great Administration of the Ming), on the gengshen day of the ninth month in the eighth year of Yongle, he ordered the monk from the Tibetan regions...
Mian Si-ji and others served as the Imperial Preceptors (Guoshi) of Jingci and Miaoji; each was granted an imperial decree to allow them to practice freely.
An official from the Inner Palace was dispatched with a letter and silver silk to the Western Regions to summon the Master Shang Shun-ze-si-pa.
In the tenth month, he commanded the monk Banden Tsangbuk and others to confer the title of National Preceptor upon Jingjue Hongji and others,
and the title of Chan Master upon Ba Bian and others, granting each of them official edicts and seals.
In the twelfth month of the tenth year of the Yongle era, Kun dga' bzang po (Kunze Sipha), the Imperial Preceptor of U-Tsang, came to court.
He had previously sent an envoy to present śarīra relics and a Buddha image. (As recorded in the *Ming Dazhengji*, etc.)

In the fifteenth year of the Yongle era, the private establishment of hermitages and monasteries by monks and nuns was prohibited; according to the *Ming Huidian* (Veritable Records of the Ming), it states as follows.
In the sixteenth year of the Yongle era, the regulations for ordaining monks were established, along with the fixed quota of clerics;

according to the *Ming Huidian*, in the sixteenth year of the Yongle era, it was decreed that the procedure for ordaining monks shall occur once every ten years, with the Ministry of Rites submitting a petition for approval in advance.

For novices residing within the capital, their names shall be submitted from their respective monasteries; for those residing outside, they shall be submitted through the ecclesiastical authorities (*senggang*).

The compilation of registers and the issuance of certificates are both managed by this office, which shall forward the applications to the Ministry of Rites for implementation. The Ministry shall conduct examinations on filial piety;

those who can thoroughly master the scriptures shall be granted ordination certificates (*dudie*). Regarding the quota of monks: no more than forty per prefecture, thirty per commandery, and twenty per county.
Ten people.
In the seventeenth year of the Yongle era, Buddhist scriptures and Buddhist melodies were promulgated.

According to the *Ming Tongji* (General Record of the Ming), in the autumn of the seventeenth year of Yongle, the Emperor composed Buddhist melodies, which were published alongside the Buddhist scriptures for circulation. On the twelfth day of the ninth month, the Buddhist [scriptures] were solemnly promulgated.
The scripture arrived at Dàbào'ēn Temple. That night, within the temple pagoda, the light of śarīra appeared like precious jewels.

On the thirteenth day, five-colored rays of light manifested; auspicious clouds cradled the sun, and the wondrous forms of the thousand Buddhas, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and the Arhats gathered in full splendor.
Subsequently, Buddhist scriptures and hymns were issued for distribution upon reaching Huāi'ān, where again a five-colored circular halo appeared.
Colorful clouds filled the sky. Within the clouds appeared Bodhisattvas and Arhats, celestial flowers, and jeweled stupas, as well as dragons, phoenixes, lions, and elephants.
Furthermore, crimson birds and white cranes circled and fluttered about.
Subsequently, he commanded Minister Lü Zhen and Censor-in-Chief Wang Zhang to carry the *Songs of the Names of the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, and Honored Ones* to Shaanxi.
The edict was issued in Henan. Heaven and earth responded in harmony, and auspicious "ministerial clouds" repeatedly appeared, manifesting the omens of the radiant halo and the precious stupa.
The civil and military officials presented a memorial to offer their congratulations. The Emperor was greatly pleased; consequently, the eunuchs increasingly revered the Buddha and honored the monks.
They established Buddhist monasteries throughout the inner and outer cities of the two capitals to pray for blessings.
In the nineteenth year of the Yongle era, the Western monk, the Great Treasure Dharma King (Dabao Fawang), came to court.

According to the *Ming Tongji*: "In the nineteenth year of Yongle, the Western monk, the Great Treasure Dharma King, came to court. Someone requested that the Emperor personally go out to welcome him. Xia Yuanji said:

'These barbarians have come from afar out of admiration for our righteousness; we ought to demonstrate to them the principles of human relations. If the Sovereign of Ten Thousand Chariots were to stoop once, there would surely be [those below who]..."*
"He would have run away and died without looking back. The Emperor said, "Do you wish to emulate Han Yu? Then do not come out to pay your respects.

On another day, when the Dharma King entered the audience, the Emperor commanded Yuan Ji to prostrate before him. Yuan Ji replied, "Even a minor envoy from a foreign state ranks above the feudal lords;
how much more so one from among the barbarians? He merely performed a long bow and withdrew.
In the first year of the Hongxi era of Emperor Renzong, Shi Zhiguang was granted the title of Grand State Preceptor (Da Guoshi) and bestowed with a golden seal.
According to the "Biographies of Arts and Techniques" in the *Ming Waishi*, Emperor Renzong was quite credulous toward heterodox teachings.
A Buddhist monk named Zhiguang was likewise granted the title: Yuanrong Miaohui Jingjue Hongji Fuguo Guangfan Yanjiao Guanding Guangshan Da Guoshi.

He was appointed National Preceptor (Guoshi) and bestowed with a golden seal. When Emperor Yingzong succeeded to the throne, he further conferred upon him the title "Son of Buddha from the Western Heaven" and bestowed a jade seal.
Such was the extent of his veneration and trust.
In the fourth year of the Xuande era of Emperor Xuanzong, Wu Zhong memorialized regarding the repair of the pagoda at Yuan’guo Temple; it was not permitted. According to the *Ming Tongji*:
"In the second month of the fourth year of Xuande, Wu Zhong, Minister of Works, submitted a report stating:

'Yesterday, I went to the Western Yuan’guo Temple and reported that this temple is an ancient site and a place of practice for making prayers for the longevity of the Emperor on behalf of the state. The old pagoda is dilapidated; I request labor [to restore it].'"
The people did it for him, and the superior said: "Do you wish to seek blessings by relying on this? I regard the security of the people as my own blessing.
Let it cease; do not exhaust my people."

In the eighth year of the Xuande era, an edict was issued ordering that all local officials and at river and road passes throughout the empire must arrest and send back to their original places of registration anyone encountered with shaved heads, to be punished according to the law. (As stated in the *Ming Huidian*, etc.)
In the first year of the Zhengtong era of Emperor Yingzong, the *Zhouzhi Ce* (Register of Monastic Personnel) was recompiled for monks. According to the *Mingtongji*:

In the tenth month of the first year of the Zhengtong era, the Emperor ordered the Senglu Si (Bureau of Monastic Records) to once again compile the *Zhouzhi Ce* for monks in accordance with the old regulations established during the Hongwu era.
During the Hongwu period, whenever monks were granted ordination certificates (*duodie*), the Bureau was required to compile their *Zhouzhi Ce*. From that time on...
The names of the monks from the temples in the capital and those in the provinces shall be compiled in sequence.

Their age, surname, given name, and monastic lineage, as well as the year they first became monks and the number of the ordination certificate (duce) they were granted, shall all be recorded following each monk’s name.
An edict was issued to all monasteries throughout the empire: "Whenever itinerant monks arrive, they must be verified against this register.

Those who do not match the records shall be seized and sent to the authorities to be taken to the capital for trial and punishment by heavy penalty. Those who harbor them shall be punished in the same manner.

Subsequently, as many years passed, those who forged and falsified [the registers] became numerous. Consequently, an order was given to re-examine and reissue them according to the old format. (Note: According to the *Huidian*, this was ordered in the fifth year of the Zhengtong era.)
(These differ from the records previously compiled).
In the tenth year of the Zhengtong era, the Tripitaka was bestowed upon Ganlu Temple. According to the *Xu Wenxian Tongkao*:

"In the second month of the spring of the tenth year of the Zhengtong era, the Tripitaka was bestowed upon Ganlu Temple. The imperial edict stated: 'I, the Emperor, embodying the Way of Heaven and Earth...'"

With a heart to protect the people, I reverently fulfill the will of my late Emperor Great-Great-Grandfather, Great-Grandfather, Grandfather, and Father by carving and printing the Great Canon of Scriptures to be distributed throughout the empire for wide circulation.
This Great Canon is now installed at Gānlù Chan Monastery in Zhènjiāng Prefecture, Zhílì, to serve as a perpetual offering.
May the local monastic officials and monks read, recite, and extol it, and offer prayers on behalf of the State.
This is to rectify [the situation]. For the sake of praying for the welfare of the common people, you must diligently and respectfully venerate and protect [this object].

You are not permitted to tolerate the presence of idle or miscellaneous persons who might privately borrow it for viewing or play, treating it with negligence or profanation, thereby causing damage or loss. Should anyone dare to violate this, they shall certainly be severely investigated. Thus, this edict is issued.
In the thirteenth year of the Zhengtong era, the Daxinglong Temple was renovated and Buddhist rites were performed.

According to the *Ming-shan-zang Dian-mu-ji*, in the second month of the thirteenth year of Zhengtong, the Daxinglong Temple was repaired; Buddhist services were held within the Forbidden City, and the Emperor visited in person.
Originally named Qingshou, the temple had been founded during the reign of Emperor Zhangzong of the Jin dynasty. Wang Zhen remarked that it was dilapidated and in need of repair.

The Great Construction Bureau mobilized both military and civilian forces for its reconstruction at an expense of tens of thousands of materials. Once completed, its magnificence was preeminent within the capital.
In the fifth year of the Jingtai era of Emperor Daizong, the imperial carriage selected a day to visit Longfu Temple;

however, following a memorial submitted by Yang Hao and others, the visit was canceled that very day. According to the *Ming Daoji*, in the fourth month of the fifth year of Jingtai, Longfu [Temple] was newly constructed.
The temple was completed. The Emperor selected a day to visit it in person; the officials had already prepared the carriage early and cleared the roads.

Yang Hao, a student at the Imperial Academy from Jining, submitted a memorial stating: "At the very beginning of Your Majesty’s reign, you first visited the Imperial Academy, and scholars throughout the realm heard of this and beheld it with joy.
Now, however, you have abandoned the arts of Confucius to prioritize Buddhist teachings. How can there be a sagely and enlightened sovereign who serves barbarians?"
"Could the ghosts of the Di barbarians provide a model for posterity? Zhang Lun, Director of the Bureau of Rites and Ceremonials, also submitted a memorial stating:

"Buddhism is the law of the barbarians, not the Way of the Sages. For the Emperor of ten thousand chariots to preside over a place that is not the domain of the Sages—if the court historians record this and it is transmitted for ten thousand generations, it will truly tarnish the sagely virtue. Upon reading the memorial, the Emperor dismissed [the project] on that very day.
According to the *Ming-shan-zang Dian-mu-ji* (Records of the Canons and Edicts of Famous Mountains): In the third month of the fourth year of the Jingtai era, Dalingfusi was completed.

This temple was the foremost in the capital, with expenses amounting to several hundred thousand [units of currency]. (Note: According to the *Tongji*, this was the fourth month of the fifth year; these two accounts differ.)
In the first year of the Tiānfùn era of Emperor Yīngzōng, imperial edicts were issued to bestow temple names upon monasteries throughout the central and provincial regions.
