According to the *Míngshān Zàng Diǎnmó Jì*, on the tenth month of the first year of Tiānfùn, edicts were issued for the following temple names:
Zhēnqìng, Jiāfú, Yuánlín, Guānyīn, Jìngjué, Pǔshòu, Nánquán, Yúnjiān, Qìngníng, Yǒngqìng, Miàohēng, Chánglè, Xiǎnníng, and Huìmíng.
Zhao-ling, Zhao-ning, Bi-feng, Hu-guo, Jing-hui, Fu-yan, Ling-yun, Bao-yin, Bao-guo, Da-sheng, Qing-yuan, Pu-li, Ying-tai, Ci-hui, Xing-shan,
Jing-ye, Guang-fu, Chong-hua, Fa-kong, Guang-hui, Yan-shou, Long-quan, Pu-ji, Jing-ren, Ye-qing, and Long-xing—
altogether forty temples. In the eleventh month, they were granted [imperial patronage].

The temple names from both within and outside [the capital] are: Qingguang (Pure Light), Yongtai (Eternal Peace), Longquan (Dragon Spring), Lingyan (Spiritual Rock), Guiyi (Return to Righteousness), Long’an (Prosperous Peace), Dizang (Earth Store), Zhongxi (Reign of Prosperity), Fachtang (Dharma Banner), Yanguo (Extended Offerings), Huaguang (Flower Light), Putuo (Potalaka), Dayun (Great Cloud), Huihui (Ocean Assembly), Zhi’an (Wise Peace), Fusheng (Blessed Victory), Puying (Universal Response), Qingta (Blue Stupa), Yangpo (Sunny Slope), Guji (Grain Accumulation), Shifo (Stone Buddha), Xizhao (Setting Sun), Pu’an (Universal Peace), Tongfa (Penetrating Dharma), Puren (Universal Benevolence), Jiafu (Auspicious Fortune), and Faning (Dharma Tranquility). Open!
Huà, Dàníng, Fǎbǎo, Wǎngjí, Yǒngfēng, Yuánguǎng, Guānyīn, Xiǎnfǎ, Yǒngfú, Bǎo'ān, Chóngqìng,
Guǎngfú, and Yuánzhēn— altogether forty temples.
In the second year of the Tiānshùn era, an imperial edict was issued stating that henceforth, the monastic community shall undergo inspection once every ten years.
According to the *Míng Dàzhèngjì*, on the first month of the second year of Tiānshùn, an edict was promulgated: "Henceforth, the monastic community shall undergo inspection once every ten years.

During the Jiǎngtài era, the eunuch Xīng'ān held great faith in Buddhism and conducted inspections every three years for tens of thousands of monks; consequently, the ranks of the clergy became greatly inflated.
In the second year of the Tiānshùn era, the monastics from throughout the empire again gathered in the capital as scheduled, numbering in the tens of thousands.
The Emperor summoned Lǐ Xián and said, "How can the monastic community be so vast and unrestrained? Lǐ Xián replied, "Your Majesty’s insight is most correct;

it is indeed necessary to prohibit this. Thereupon, he issued a public notice to inform the populace that henceforth, the tonsure ceremony shall only be permitted once every ten years, and no one shall undergo it arbitrarily.
Those aged twenty and above were all ordered to return to lay life. Those who violated this decree were to be dispatched to frontier garrisons to serve in the army.
Those who had ordained others were all subject to the fixed quota and investigated for dismissal. Thereupon, the monastic community dispersed.
In the eighth year of the Tiānshùn era, it was decreed that monks aged twenty or above who lacked a *dùcí* (ordination certificate) were to be compelled to return to lay life.

According to the *Míng huìdiǎn*, in the eighth year of the Tiānshùn era, it was ordered that in all regions, monks aged twenty or above who did not possess a *dùcí* were to be returned to lay status immediately.
Furthermore, those who concealed their actual age, along with their preceptors, were to be punished.

In the third month of the second year of the Chenghua era of Emperor Xianzong, an edict was issued by the Ministry of Rites to grant *duòdì* (ordination certificates) for the sale of monkhood to provide relief for famine-stricken commoners.
According to the *Ming Dazheng Ji* (Great Account of State Affairs of the Ming), it says as follows...

In the fourth year of the Chenghua era, a Western monk was enfeoffed as the Dharma King, Son of the Buddha, and State Preceptor. According to the *Ming-shan-zang Dianmu Ji* (Records of the Monastic Histories and Imperial Edicts),

on the fourth day of the fourth month in the fourth year of the Chenghua era, the Western monk Zhaba Jiancan was enfeoffed as the "Wanxing Zhuangyan Gongde Zuisheng Zhixue Yuanming Nengren Ganying Xianguoguang Jiaohongmiao Dawu" (One of Wondrous Great Enlightenment Who Propagates the Teaching,
Manifests National Splendor, Responds with Compassion, and Possesses Perfectly Clear Wisdom of Supreme Virtue Adorned by Myriad Practices).

The Dharma King, the Most Virtuous Vajra of the Western Heaven, the Buddha of Universal Salvation and Great Wisdom, issued a decree appointing Zhabs-drung as the Great State Preceptor (Guoshi), a Son of the Buddha from the Western Heaven, for the purpose of purifying and rectifying the path to perfect enlightenment, through wondrous compassion, universal salvation, the protection of the state, the propagation of the teachings, and the conferral of empowerment (abhiṣeka) for great goodness.
Sönam Gyan-tsän was appointed as the State Preceptor for Quiescent Cultivation and Great Goodness. On the day of Guihai in the ninth month, a comet appeared. Six.
The Court Supervisors Wei Yuan and others submitted a memorial stating: "The monastic community has become excessively prone to seeking patronage.
Whenever they encounter auspicious occasions for generating merit, they invariably squander limitless wealth to establish useless vegetarian feasts and incantation rituals.

Furthermore, figures such as Zhashipa of the Western Regions have been granted the title of 'Dharma King' and bestowed with lavish rewards; they travel in palanquins made of sedge and are escorted by the Golden Guards. If one calculates these expenditures..."
Their maintenance exceeds that of the princes of the blood, and the court’s bestowals of rewards are without restraint. Their amusements and curiosities are excessive;
they either print and distribute sutras and liturgical texts, or transcribe Buddhist scriptures, or commission painted images, or fashion objects of precious gems.
Furthermore, mining operations in places such as Yunnan continue without end. Under such conditions, it is impossible for the people to be wealthy or the state to be at peace.

I humbly submit that Your Majesty should abolish titles such as "Dharma King" and issue an edict to cease the construction of temples and monasteries, forbidding the performance of *jiao* and *zhai* rituals.

You should curtail useless rewards and abandon trivial pastimes. Furthermore, the Censors of the thirteen circuits, including Kang Yongshao, have also submitted memorials stating that Buddhism has been of no benefit since ancient times;
yet now, you bestow favor upon Tibetan monks by granting them titles such as "Son of the Buddha" and "National Preceptor."
The title of their king and his ceremonial retinue exceed those of princes and lords; his clothing and utensils rival those of the imperial court.

Clad in brocade and feasting on jade-like delicacies, his followers number several hundred. They exhaust the fat and essence of the commoners' neighborhoods to serve a host of empty, illusory, and delusional men.

Furthermore, many among them are people from the Middle Kingdom who have adopted foreign teachings merely to seek favor and high status. We humbly hope that you will provide the means for these foreign monks to be sent back to their own country. If...

The Chinese inhabitants were bound [in servitude]. Their previously granted edicts were rescinded, and they were forced to provide taxes and labor. [The Emperor] accepted this proposal, believing that in this way the livelihood of the people would be improved.
He then commanded Jaziba, a Buddhist monk from India, to return the lands sought for the state back to the common people.

The Ministry of Rites requested that Tibetan monks be dispatched [to the frontier], but the Emperor said, "I fear this might alienate the hearts of those in the distant regions; we need only prohibit acts of usurpation. (Left Yu, Censor-in-Chief)

I submit that recently, the Censorate presented a memorial requesting that the titles of Tibetan monks be abolished to resolve the doubts of the empire and eliminate the delusions of future generations.
Your Majesty approved this; yet when the Ministry of Rites was about to carry out the dispatch, the matter was once again suspended.

I humbly beseech you to follow the sublime maxims of the Masters Zhou and Kong, and to practice the eternal Way of Yao and Shun. If the Buddha possesses knowledge, he will surely recognize these words of yours. Is it not so?

Report. In the sixth year of the Chenghua era, the Emperor desired to build a Buddhist pavilion on the Western Hills. [The memorial was submitted] by the Six Sections of the Imperial Secretariat (Liukē Gěishìzhōng) after they had remonstrated against it.

According to the *Ming Dàzhèng Jì* (Veritable Records of the Great Administration of the Ming), in the fifth month of the sixth year of the Chenghua era, the Emperor desired to build a Buddhist [pavilion] on the Western Hills.

The Gate (Gé) reported that the Six Bureaus of the Secretariat for Imperial Edicts (Lìshìgōng) had submitted a memorial stating: "Drought and blight have afflicted the four quarters; there has been no harvest in summer or autumn.

The common people groan in distress, awaiting their next meal. In Jingzhou and Xiangyang, displaced persons have become violent and defiant; in Shaanxi, barbarian raiders have committed incursions and plundering, causing Your Majesty’s profound concern.

Great ministers have been dispatched to conduct inspections, and government troops have been mobilized and deployed. Yet now, you initiate nameless labor for urgent matters, resulting in nothing but..."

To waste the state’s resources is injurious to the fundamental principles of governance. If you claim that constructing this pavilion will indeed bring merit and benefit, how does it compare to using these funds to provide relief for the starving populace and to reward the laboring soldiers?
Would not the resulting merit and benefit be far greater? The Emperor said: "The year is one of famine and the people are starving;
as for the Buddhist pavilion on the Western Hills, let it be abandoned at once."

Imperial Edict of the Tenth Year of the Chenghua Era: To Construct a Stupa for the Burial of the Dashiying Fawang (Great Resonance Dharma King). Four thousand imperial troops were allocated for service.

According to the *Ming-shan-zang Dianmu Ji* (Records of the Canon and Statutes of the Famous Mountains): In the third month of the tenth year of the Chenghua era, Zhashiba, the Dashiying Fawang of Chongwang, died.

An imperial decree was issued that he be buried in a stupa according to the precedent of the Daci Fawang (Great Compassion Dharma King), and four thousand imperial troops were allocated for the service.
Four thousand men were assigned to serve him. Wang Tan, a Censor of the Ministry of Rites, submitted a memorial stating:
"Zhashiba is a person of the barbarians who has falsely assumed the name of a follower of Śākyamuni. Your Majesty treats him with extraordinary courtesy and confers upon him a prominent title;

this is done specifically to pacify his kindred and ensure they do not trouble the borders. It would suffice to provide him with funeral rites according to precedent, yet the items for the sacrifice exceed [the prescribed limits]."

"The King’s expenditure on constructing this stūpa nearly equals that required for a royal mausoleum. Now, famine has plagued the capital region for years, and the roads are filled with the corpses of those who have starved to death.
Would it not be far better to use these funds to rescue the people currently suffering in such calamity and on the brink of death, rather than lavishly supporting a single eccentric foreign monk?
The Emperor replied, "The remarks of the Secretariat Drafter are excessive. The construction of the stūpa for the Dharma-King Da-ying is comparable to [the state's own] great..."
The Compassionate Dharma King had already reduced [the number of monks] by two-thirds and would not permit it.
In the twelfth year of the Chenghua era, Grand Secretaries Shang Lu and others petitioned to prohibit the granting of gold and silver seals of office to Tibetan monks and the construction of stupas.
According to the *Ming-shan-zang Dian-mu-ji*, in the seventh month of the twelfth year of the Chenghua era, the Grand Secretaries...
Shi Shanglu and others submitted a memorial on six matters concerning current administration. The first point stated:
"When the people of Hami and other regions come to the capital, they bring jade and stones with them. These are frequently enticed by petty officials to be presented as tribute.

The intermediaries are then instructed to sell them to government offices at high prices to secure substantial profits. Furthermore, retired Tibetan monks often rise from the rank of Du-gang Chan-shi to that of Guoshi."
The Sons of the Buddha and the Dharma Kings have been granted gold, silver, seals, and official insignia. When they die, their disciples inherit these and further seek to construct stupas;
both of these practices deplete the wealth and resources of the imperial court. It is fitting that prohibitions be enacted to govern them.
In the sixth month of the fourteenth year of the Chenghua era, the Chan masters Nanke Lingzhan and others of the Great Ci’en Monastery requested that silver seals be granted to them;
this was permitted. According to the *Ming-shan-zang Dianmu Ji* (Records of the Ancestral Models of Famous Mountains), it says as follows...
In the fifteenth year of the Chenghua era, more than twenty individuals obtained official rank through imperial favor.

According to the *Ming-shan-zang Dian-mu-ji* (Records of the Monastic Archives), in the ninth month of the fifteenth year of Chenghua, by imperial decree, Chan Master Jiegan Lingzhan was promoted to State Preceptor (*guoshi*) and granted ceremonial robes and headgear.
In the tenth month, by imperial decree, the monk Jixiao was promoted to Left Jueyi of the Sengluosi (Bureau of Buddhist Affairs). [Intercalary Month]
In the tenth month, Lunu Banden was promoted to State Preceptor (Guoshi) of the Great Ci’en Monastery;
Jueyi Chogji Jiancen was appointed as State Preceptor; Dalong Shanhuo Guosi was appointed as State Preceptor for Consecration (Guanding Guoshi);
Banzhu’er Zangbu was appointed as State Preceptor of the Buddha’s Son (Fuzi Guoshi); and Zhuode Lingzhan was appointed as State Preceptor for Consecration. As for those...
Four individuals obtained official rank through imperial favor. In the eleventh month, seventeen individuals obtained official rank through imperial favor.

In the ninth month of the eighteenth year of the Chenghua era, Daci'en Si Guanding Da Guoshi Zhashi Jiancuo Runu Banban Dan was promoted to the rank of Xitian Fuzi (Son of the Buddha from the Western Heaven) and was granted an edict, ceremonial robes, and other items.
In the second month of the nineteenth year of the Chenghua era, he commanded Li Jin, the Marquis of Xiangcheng, to lead ten thousand laborers and soldiers to repair the Daci’en Monastery.
(The above is recorded in the *Ming Shanshang Zang Dianmu Ji*, etc.)
In the twentieth year of the Chenghua era, the Great State-Protecting Yongchang Temple was constructed. In that same year, thirty-seven individuals received official appointments by imperial decree.
According to the *Mingtongji*: "In the twentieth year of the Chenghua era, the Great State-Protecting Yongchang Temple was built;
[the Emperor] summoned Lin Jun, Vice Director of the Ministry of Punishment, and Zhang Fu, Assistant in the Rear Army Commandant’s Office."
They were both imprisoned and banished to distant provinces. Previously, there was a monk named Jixiao who had begun by deceiving the Prince of Chu with lewd arts.
When his schemes failed, he fled to hide in the capital, where he was introduced into the inner palace through the influence of Liang Fang and others; thus his arts found favor.
He was honored as "Dharmarāja" (Fa-wang) and granted more than ten fine pearls and an incalculable amount of gold and jewels. He then petitioned the Emperor to open the Inner Treasury.
Hundreds of thousands of taels of silver were spent outside the Xihua Gate to demolish private residences and construct Buddhist temples.
Fearing punishment, the high officials remained silent. Thereupon, Lin Jun submitted a memorial stating: "Since this year, calamities and anomalies have arisen one after another.

Earthquakes have shaken both capitals and the imperial mausoleums have trembled; the sun and moon have been eclipsed in succession, and wild bears have entered the city. These are clear warnings and admonitions—"
This is truly lamentable. For years, Shaanxi, Shanxi, and Henan have suffered from famine; the people have been displaced and perished of hunger by the roadside.

With no means for relief, it is enough to move one to tears. Yet, the monk Jixiao has deceived Your Majesty’s sagacious virtue, drawing hundreds of thousands of taels of silver from the Inner Treasury to construct the Great Zhen'guo Yongchang Temple—using resources that serve a vital purpose to fund something of no benefit.

The expenses for this project have been immense; labor and service have never ceased, and public resentment grows daily. I submit that if Jixiao is not executed, the calamities of a future day cannot even be described.
Yet, he who enabled him was Liang Fang. Fang is treacherous and malevolent by nature, employing only the wicked and depraved.

He expelled the loyal and virtuous. Within a few years, under the pretext of receiving tribute and purchasing goods, he plundered the imperial treasuries accumulated over more than a hundred years of his ancestors until they were nearly exhausted.
His private wealth was piled high like mountains; even the engraving of it would not suffice to record its magnitude. Everywhere there was turmoil and unrest.
Wang Zhizhi could not prevail over them. Now, from the court officials within the palace to the commoners in the villages, all feel heartache at the deaths of the starving people;
none do not wish to eat the flesh of Liang Fang and Ji Xiao.
Yet, they ultimately dare not advance such words because what they cherish is their office and what they fear is death. How can I, your servant, bear to fear death and remain silent? Thus...
"Is this not a stain upon Your Majesty’s benevolence and sagacity? Upon reading the memorial, the Emperor was greatly incensed and cast Li Jun into the custody of the锦衣卫 (Jin-yi-wei).
Zhang Fu submitted a memorial pleading for their release, and both were subsequently arrested and brought before the court. Each was flogged several dozen times;

Li Jun was demoted to the post of Administrative Assistant (判官) in Yao Prefecture, Yunnan, while Zhang Fu was reduced to the rank of Magistrate (知州) of Zong Prefecture. According to the *Ming-shan-zang Dian-mu-ji*, this occurred in the twentieth year of the Chenghua era.

In the eleventh month, thirty-seven individuals who had received official rank through imperial decree were demoted to the status of *Dafeng* (Great Ascendant) *Fawang* (State Preceptor) and *Chanshi* (Zen Master).
In the first month of the twenty-first year of the Chenghua era, Jixiao was stripped of his title as State Preceptor and reduced to commoner status; his edict of appointment was confiscated.

Imperial Edict: According to the *Ming-shan zang-dian-mu-ji* (Records of the Mountain Names and the Canon of Statutes), etc., in the ninth month of the twenty-third year of the Chenghua era, the monk Jixiao was returned to his original domicile as a commoner.

The Tibetan monks, National Preceptors (*guoshi*), and Dharma Kings (*falawang*) such as Lingzhan Zhu and others were all demoted and stripped of their offices, and the successive imperial edicts previously conferred upon them were confiscated.

The seals of office and ceremonial insignia were returned, and she was ordered to reside at her original home, Kuangxiang Temple, in Sichuan. According to the *Ming Tongji* (General Record of the Ming),
in the eighth month of the third year of the Hongzhi era of Emperor Xiaozong, the Ministry of Rites’ Minister of State, Geng Yu, issued an edict to demolish the nunnery at Huangcun.
The Vice Ministers Ni Yue and Zhou Jing were both upright men. They exerted great effort in supporting the proposal to dismiss him.

According to the *Ming Dazheng Ji* (Veritable Records of the Great Administration of the Ming), in the sixth year of the Hongzhi era, an imperial edict was issued to summon the Tibetan monk Lingzan Zhu; upon this, Ni Yue, Chai Sheng, and others submitted a memorial.

The extreme discussion was thus brought to an end. According to the *Ming-shan-zang Dian-mu-ji* (Records of the Canons and Edicts of Famous Mountains), in the tenth month of the sixth year of the Hongzhi era, the Tibetan monk Lingzhan Zhu was summoned from afar to reside at Da Cien Temple.
Ni Yue, the Minister of the Court of Ceremonies, and others submitted a memorial stating: "Lingzhan Zhu had been impeached and sent back;
to now receive a summons once more will cause turmoil for the postal stations and open the door to favoritism, making it difficult to prevent such occurrences in the future."
The Imperial Mother sent a decree for [the monk] to come in person. At that time, Xia Ang, a Censor of the Ministry of Rites, submitted a memorial of impeachment, stating:
"Previously, Leng Zhanzhu obtained an official promotion and reward by offering a human skull, a rosary, and a dharma-bowl.

Upon Your Majesty’s accession to the throne, he was stripped of his office and sent back, bringing joy to those far and near. That Yue obstructed this matter—how could it have been merely a single decree? We pray that Your Majesty..."

This was intended to strictly establish a defense against the confusion between heterodoxy and orthodoxy and between order and negligence. However, the Emperor still did not grant his approval. Chai Sheng, a Grand Secretary of the Ministry of Works, and others submitted a memorial arguing the matter vehemently, whereupon the project was finally abandoned.
In the eighth year of the Hongzhi era, Wang Yunfeng and others submitted a memorial to prohibit the issuance of ordination certificates (*duòdié*). According to the *Ming Dazheng Ji*:
in the second month of the eighth year of the Hongzhi era, Wang Yunfeng, Director of the Rites Bureau’s Sacrificial Section, submitted a memorial prohibiting the issuance of ordination certificates.
There was no response. Initially, the Minister of Revenue Ni Yue submitted a memorial regarding the maladministration caused by natural calamities, proposing four measures:

to punish wickedness and depravity; to prohibit the issuance of ordination certificates (*dudie*); to suspend and reduce ritual feasts and incantations (*zhaiqiao*); and to deliberate on the management of the imperial clan. His words were exceedingly poignant and direct.

Later, when the ordination of monks did not cease, he alone submitted a memorial of over a thousand words. He presented it three times, yet there was still no response. When the imperial decree finally arrived, the number of monks ordained was not large.
Everyone marveled at his power to turn the heavens.
In the twelfth year of the Hongzhi era, as the Qingning Palace was completed, an imperial edict was issued for the National Preceptor to establish an altar for celebratory praise.

According to the *Ming-shan-zang Dianmu Ji* (Records of the Sacred Mountains and Imperial Edicts), in the tenth month of the twelfth year of the Hongzhi era, following the completion of the Qingning Palace, the Great [Preceptor] was commanded...
The State Preceptor Nambul Gyen-tsang and others of the Insa Temple established an altar for three days of celebratory rites. The Grand Councilors Liu Jian and others remarked:
"Buddhism and Daoism are heterodox teachings. The palace precincts are a forbidden area; that these barbarian and heretical followers should occupy it for successive days and mornings is improper."
The clamor and confusion of the inner palace disturb the ancestral temples, abolish the laws of our ancestors, and add further burden to the sacred virtue of the Sage.

Moreover, since Your Majesty’s supreme filial piety and pure sincerity have been protected by Heaven itself, why must you rely on heterodox arts within the palace precincts before you can serve your revered parents and pray for their eternal fortune and longevity?
This servant has long been a mere figurehead, consuming his salary while lacking any plan when faced with affairs of state.

These imperial edicts were issued suddenly without prior consultation. We humbly pray that Your Majesty will swiftly issue a clear decree to dismantle the altar and expel the monks. We, your subjects, are overcome with a sense of guilt and await your command.

At that time, the officials of the Censorate and the Court of Judicial Review all spoke to this effect. The Emperor said, "Your words are correct. However, such things occurred even during the Yongle era.
Since the officials of the Six Ministries, the Censorate, and the Court of Judicial Review had all spoken with great urgency, the Emperor said, "There is a precedent; let us wait for a while."
Later, in the fourteenth year of the Hongzhi era, Eunuch Li Xing requested the construction of a temple, which was granted the name Longxi.
The monk Dingqi was promoted to the position of Right Lecturer of the Sengluosi. According to the *Ming-shan-zang Dianmu Ji*, on the fifth month of the fourteenth year of the Hongzhi era:

Eunuch Li Xing requested the construction of a temple in Donggao Village, Daxing County, to offer prayers for the Emperor’s longevity. He further petitioned for the bestowal of a name plaque and imperial protection.

By imperial decree, Ding Qi, the Left Jueyi of the Senglu Si (Office of Buddhist Records), was appointed as the abbot. Upon receiving the edict, Ding Qi was promoted to Right Jiangjing (Preacher). The temple was named Longxi.
In the fifth month of the fifteenth year of the Hongzhi era, the Imperial Preceptor Lingzhantan from Fan was summoned to the Da Cien Temple;
Zhang Sheng, Minister of the Ministry of Rites, remonstrated against this, but it was not granted.

According to the *Ming Shan-zang Dian-mu Ji*, in the sixteenth year of the Hongzhi era, an edict was issued to construct a longevity pagoda, which was subsequently abandoned. According to the *Ming Tong-ji*, the Hongzhi...

In the sixteenth year, an edict was issued to construct a Longevity Stūpa outside the Chaoyang Gate; however, it was subsequently abandoned. At that time, Grand Secretaries Liu Jian and others submitted a memorial stating:
"Among the sovereigns of previous dynasties, none believed in Buddhism more than Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, yet he ultimately starved to death in Taicheng.
He sought blessings, yet instead brought about calamity. By observing past events, one may take them as a clear mirror. Our imperial ancestors..."
It is traditionally held that the Way of Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius alone suffices for governing the world. Buddhism is a heterodox teaching that wastes wealth and deludes the masses;
what relevance does it have to governance? To wish to construct Buddhist stupas is not the means by which to instruct the world or leave a legacy for posterity.
The memorial was submitted. An imperial decree arrived, ordering its rejection.

In the second year of the Zhengde era of Emperor Wuzong, a new temple was constructed within the Inner Garden, and the Chan masters of the Ci'en, Nengren, and Huguo temples were promoted to the rank of National Teacher (*Guoshi*).
According to the *Ming-shan-zang Dian-mu-ji*, this occurred in the third month of the second year of Zhengde.
A new temple was constructed within the inner gardens, where the Emperor practiced the Buddhist teachings.
Consequently, the Chan Master of Daci'en Monastery, Lingzhan Zhu, was appointed as the State Preceptor for Consecration (Guanding Da Guoshi).
The Chan Master of Darenen Monastery, Mati Boritashi Majaya Bukjian, and the Chan Master of Dalong Shan Huguo Monastery, Puxiao Zangbu, were appointed as [State Preceptors].
The Master. All were granted edicts.
In the eighth month of the fourth year of the Zhengde era, Dalai Lama Lobzang Gyatso was promoted to State Preceptor (Guoshi) of Dulong Shan Huguo Si and appointed as Dharma King (Fawang).
Lama Lhatsün Panchen Danzin Chökyi Gyaltsen was appointed as Lhatsün. Lama Dorje Gyaltsen was appointed as Lhatsün. Dorje Tenpa was appointed as Lhatsün. And Jigme Gyaltsen was appointed as Lhatsün.

In the fifth year of the Zhengde era, the various monks were promoted to the ranks of Dharmarāja, Buddhaputra, and Jueyi Dugang.

The Emperor himself appointed [him] as the Great Celebration Dharmarāja and issued tens of thousands of monastic certificates (*du-chie*) to propagate the foreign teachings. According to the *Ming-shan-zang*.
Record of the Imperial Decrees and Edicts. In the fourth month of the fifth year of the Zhengde era, the National Preceptor of Daren Monastery, Naxiao Jian, was promoted;
the Chan Master Zhaba Cangbo was appointed as the Metropolitan Superintendent (Du-gang) of the Dharma Kings; Nabulingzhan was appointed as a Son of the Buddha (Fuzi);
Gongge Duanzhujian Bozhashi was appointed as a Chan Master; and Lamochuo Jiluo was appointed to the Dalong Shan Huguo Monastery.
Zhu was appointed as a Son of the Buddha. Guoshi Ruru Lingzhan of Daci’en Temple was appointed as a Son of the Buddha from the Western Heaven.
Formerly dismissed Guoshi Halazha was appointed as a Son of the Buddha. Lama Yeshewo was appointed as a Chan Master.
In the sixth month, Chan Master Xingji Bandan of Dalongshan Temple was promoted to Guoshi. Luo Zhu Band and others were appointed as Left Jueyi.
Lama Ge-’dzub was appointed as the Left Jueyi; San-zuo She-la as the Right Jueyi; Lun-zhu Jian-can as the Dugang;
and the disciples of the Great Ci’en Monastery, Ru-nu Ling-zhan, She-la-za, and Ju, were all made Dharma Kings.
Lama Shel-xing-ji was made a Disciple (Fuzi); Ye-fu Duanzhu was made a Chan Master. The Great...

He was also granted an official edict engraved with the seal-mark "Heaven One" (Tianyi). In the tenth month, Luo Zhubanzhuodan Duanzhu was promoted to State Preceptor (Guoshi).
He was appointed as the Grand State Preceptor and Chan Master for the Consecration Rite. Zhang Lugzhu was appointed as State Preceptor.
Thirty thousand *fandeng* (monastic certificates) were granted to Tibetan monks, and five thousand each to Chinese monks and Daoists, in order to propagate the Tibetan teachings.

In the sixth year of the Zhengde era, a monk from the frontier regions submitted a memorial requesting one hundred *qǐng* of land to establish a subordinate monastery for the Dàqìng Fǎwáng (Great Celebration Dharma King).
According to the *Míng tōngjì* (Comprehensive Record of the Ming), during the Zhengde era, the Emperor was personally devoted to Buddhism and had assumed the title "Dàqìng Fǎwáng" for himself;

no one in the outer court dared to remonstrate. It happened that a monk from the frontier regions submitted a memorial requesting one hundred *qǐng* of land to establish a subordinate monastery for the Dàqìng Fǎwáng. Consequently, [Chén] Chuánguī...
The official remonstrated against the monk, saying: "What is this 'Dharma King'? To place him in parallel with the Imperial Honorific Title is a great violation of the Way and deserves execution.
Although there was an imperial decree not to pursue the matter, the monk’s reckless pursuit was thereby brought to an end.
In the eleventh month of the seventh year of the Zhengde era, the Dharma King of Da Cien Monastery requested permission to repair the monks’ quarters; this was granted.
The Ministry of Works remonstrated against it, but his advice was not heeded. This is recorded in the *Ming-shan-zang Dian-mu-ji* (Records of the Canons and Edicts of Famous Mountains), and so forth.

In the eighth year of the Zhengde era, for the purpose of repairing a temple and constructing a pagoda for a monk from the frontier regions, the title of "Daqing Fawang" (Great Joy Dharma King) was bestowed upon him, along with a *duodie* (ordination certificate) for a novice (*xingdong*).

He was granted permission to receive full ordination at his own convenience. According to the *Ming Dazheng Ji* (Veritable Records of the Great Administration of the Ming), on the seventh month of the eighth year of the Zhengde era, Western monks sought to seize the fields and lands of the common people of Ganzhou and dispatched an official to supervise the construction of a Buddhist monastery. Liu Chun, the Minister of the Court of Ceremonies (*Libu Shangshu*), opposed this.
"It must not be done; stop it. At that time, there was a famine in Guanzhong. In the spring, [the officials] struggled over the matter, deeming it improper.

Their general argument was that halting [the project] would not merely harm the people, but that upon the arrival of border alarms, it could not be sustained and would inevitably lead to chaos and disaster. Although the memorial had been submitted for nearly two months, the imperial decree finally arrived and the project was suspended.
According to the *Ming-shan-zang Dian-mu-ji*, in the fourth month of the eighth year of the Zhengde era, a great military mobilization was undertaken.
The Gentleman (Shi) served as the supervisor for the番僧 (Fan-seng) in the restoration of Daci’en Temple. He sold noble titles to redeem his sins, using the proceeds to cover the expenses.
In the tenth month, the Grand State Preceptor (Da Guoshi) Yeshe Wo of Daci’en Temple died; an edict was issued to construct a stupa for his burial.

The Director of the Ministry of Works and the Secretaries of the Ministry of Works submitted a memorial stating that this was not according to established precedent. The Emperor said, "Let it be made into a regulation. In the eleventh month, [an edict] was granted to the Da...
Qingfawang Lingzhan Bandan petitioned for a certificate of ordination (*dudie*) for his attendant novice, requesting permission to ordain others at his own discretion.

however, this proposal could not be implemented. (As recorded in the *Mingtongji*, etc.)

he was granted a golden seal and a *kāṣāya*. According to the *Ming-shan-zang Dianmu Ji*, on the second month of the tenth year of the Zhengde era, the Dade Fawang Chokyi Aba of Bao’an Temple [bestowed these honors] upon his disciple Lingtsen Chokje’er Chok...
The memorial for the investiture was lost. [The Emperor] requested that he be appointed as the Senior and Junior Envoys; he returned to reside in U-Tsang (Uṣ-ka-tsaṅ).

The Minister of Rites, Liu Chun, argued that this was improper and ordered a review of the matter. At that time, Shangxi was translating scriptures and wearing the robes of a Tibetan monk, including the *chokyi aser* (auspicious scarf) and other accoutrements, as he moved in and out of the Leopard Room (*Baofang*) and mingled among the high officials.
When Lingzhan Chuo Jier and others returned, their carriages and baggage followed one after another, causing great expense for the postal relays.
In the fifth month, the Right Dharma Master (*Youjueyi*) Banden Lhundrup of the Great State-Protecting and Peace-Securing Temple (*Daguo Anbangsi*) acted on behalf of his ancestral teacher.

The Great Sage Dharma King Wang Jiban Dan requested to perform a sacrificial burial ceremony. The Ministry of Rites submitted a memorial stating that there was no precedent for such a rite, yet the Emperor granted it as an exceptional favor.

In the eleventh month, a favorite courtier reported that there was a Western monk from the regions beyond the Pamirs who possessed knowledge of three lifetimes; the people of the West call him a "Living Buddha.
The Emperor dispatched the Eunuch Liu Chong to welcome him, leading over a hundred men, including commanders, thousand-households, and armored soldiers.
A thousand men were provided, with pearl necklaces used for banners and streamers, and gold used for the seven types of offerings.

The Dharma King was granted a golden seal and a *kāṣāya* robe, and his followers were bestowed with gifts amounting to tens of millions. In the thirteenth year of the Zhengde era, the Imperial Censor Liu Chong was dispatched to welcome the Living Buddha. Food and tea were bestowed upon the Tibetan monks of the Western Regions.

According to the *Ming Dazheng Ji* (Veritable Records of the Great Administration of the Ming), on the third month of the thirteenth year of Zhengde, the Emperor dispatched the Imperial Censor Liu Chong as an envoy to Uṣaḍza to welcome the Living Buddha. He traveled...

He was regarded as a Living Buddha (*ho-shih*). The Emperor dispatched an envoy to welcome him. At every station along the way, the envoy demanded tributes by every possible means, and his power grew exceedingly great.
Lan issued a proclamation to the relevant authorities, forbidding them from complying with his desires. Upon reaching Huai, he took his leave.

As for the uninterrupted tribute missions from the Tibetan monks, these are merely a means of keeping the distant barbarians submissive; it is not out of reverence or deluded faith.

In the seventh month, the monk Jueyi and others, including Lengzhaba, were dispatched to invest the chieftain of the country of U-tsang as the Prince Who Propagates the Teaching (Chanzhao Wang). Lengzhaba and his companions requested the provision of fast ships for their journey.

For thirty years, salt had been used as capital for purchasing provisions on the frontier. The Ministry of Revenue submitted a memorial objecting to this practice, but an imperial edict specifically granted permission for it.
In the fourteenth year of the Jiajing era of Emperor Shizong, Xinglong Temple was demolished and merged with Cien Temple; all associated ritual feasts were abolished.
According to the *Ming Huidian*, in the fourteenth year of the Jiajing era, Daxinglong Temple was destroyed, and an order was issued that it shall never again be permitted [to exist].
Furthermore, the Great Ci'en Monastery was abolished, and all its ritual observances were reformed. The monks were notified that they should return to reside in their respective original temples.
Those who chose to return to their former monasteries were granted landholdings commensurate with their previous status, and the fields were exempted from corvée labor and taxes for six years.
In the fifteenth year of the Jiajing era, the Buddhist halls within the imperial palace were abolished, and the Buddha images, relics, teeth, and other such objects were destroyed.

According to the *Ming Dazheng Ji* (Veritable Records of the Great Administration of the Ming), in the fifth month of the fifteenth year of Jiajing, the Emperor desired to remove the Buddhist temples from within the palace in order to establish the Ciqing and Cining Palaces on that site. He ordered the court officials to convene a discussion; they all agreed that—
"Very well. The Emperor immediately ordered them to be removed. He soon summoned Li Shi and Xia Yan to inspect the Dàshàn Hall.

There they saw over a thousand golden cast Buddha images, all of which he ordered to be melted down and destroyed. Among the tables, stands, and suspended gilded caskets were still many relics, such as fragments of bone and teeth.
Xia Yan withdrew and submitted a memorial, earnestly requesting that they be burned and buried. The Emperor followed his advice. Thereupon—

The heterodox and impure elements within the inner palace were almost entirely expelled. According to the *Chunming mengyu lu*, in the memorial by Minister of Rites Xia Yan regarding the burial of Buddhist relics, it states:

"Recently, we have the honor of witnessing Your Majesty consult with your ministers, desiring to remove the Buddhist halls from within the palace and to establish two palaces [for the Empress and Empress Dowager] to serve as the model for a unified era. At that time, the court deliberations looked up to and praised Your Majesty’s profound sincerity.

He perfected the filial piety of total restraint and established a transformation that repels the heterodox and exalts the orthodox; his magnificent virtue and great achievements illuminate the past and stir the future.
On the eleventh day of this month, we humbly received the Imperial Decree commanding Grand Secretary Li Shi and your servant Yan to enter for an audience.

Regarding what is called the Hall of Great Goodness (*Dàshàn Diàn*): Your servants have observed that within this hall there are cast images of gold and silver, numbering no fewer than a thousand or ten hundred in total, many of which depict the forms of heterodox spirits and lewd obscenities.

We humbly entreat Your Majesty’s sagacious wisdom to perceive their absurdity and lack of canonical basis, and to act with resolute vigor to remove them all at once; this would be a most magnificent undertaking. However, as your servants observe the various tables and desks...
Above these, as well as within the spaces between the hanging beams and arches, and those stored within golden caskets, there were many objects that could not be identified;
when questioned of their guardians, they simply said these were "Buddha-bones" and these were "Buddha-teeth."
It was withered, decayed, shattered, and split; its strange fragments were jagged and massive, weighing no less than a thousand *qīn*.

Your servant considers that the entry of the Buddha-dharma into China began during the time of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty; yet it did not go beyond individuals reciting its scriptures and practicing its teachings.
It was not until the time of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang that the Buddha’s relics were welcomed to the capital, where his minister Han Yu spoke most vehemently of their inauspiciousness.
"It is not appropriate for him to enter the palace precincts. Emperor Xianzong could not accept this advice and, moreover, severely censured Han Yu, ultimately banishing him far away.
It was my intention that thereafter no one would dare to feign such heterodoxy; yet all these Tibetan monks continue to use it to deceive and delude the people of China.
As for what are called the Buddha’s skull and bones, they are associated with the Way;

thus they have flowed into the inner precincts of the Son of Heaven’s palace, and this has been so through successive generations without being considered strange. What currently exists within the palace halls was likely not left behind by a defeated state.
Since successive reigns, it has certainly been treated as a model of that dharma, yet no one has ever investigated it deeply to prolong [the inquiry].
Up to this day, I respectfully reflect that Your Majesty possesses the innate endowments of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, and practices the Way of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu.
From the outset, you have deliberated upon the destruction of Buddhist halls and the removal of defiled images, ensuring that these heterodox practices may not further profane the imperial precincts.
This is truly a vision transcending all ages, surpassing the ordinary by tens of thousands of times.
This is so. Now that the halls and their images have been removed, all the aforementioned items such as Buddha-heads and Buddha-teeth are defiled and should not be allowed to remain.

I request that Your Majesty issue an edict to the relevant authorities to bury these objects in the wilds, sweeping them away entirely to eliminate the source of ignorance and doubt; this would truly be for the greater good.

The actions of the Sage are extraordinary; they provide immense benefit to the teachings and his merit is boundless. Your servant is exceedingly fortunate, and future generations will likewise be fortunate.
Upon the submission of this memorial, the Emperor replied: "The Buddha relics stored in the Great Hall and various other items that do not conform to the Classics shall be buried in the wild fields.
I fear that in the future, those who seek out curiosities may still exhume them. It would be better to cremate them."
To eliminate this perpetual affliction, an edict was issued to the Ministry of Rites to have both [the pagodas] burned outside the city walls.

In the sixteenth year of the Jiajing era, an imperial decree permitted monastics to return to lay life and prohibited the repair of monasteries as well as the private tonsure of individuals into the clergy.

According to the *Ming Huidian*, in the sixteenth year of the Jiajing era, it was formally approved by the relevant local authorities that—*Qin* (imperial decree)—[the aforementioned measures be implemented].
In accordance with the Imperial Decree: those among the monastic community who wish to convert to lay life shall be permitted to seek their own comfort and convenience.
In all temples, regardless of how long they have stood, no repairs or renovations are permitted for the aging halls and palaces; they shall be allowed to fall into ruin.
It is forbidden to enshrine young children from common households as monks. Should anyone privately shave their heads in violation of this, the parents and the neighbors shall be held culpable.
In the twenty-second year of the Jiajing era, an edict was issued to demolish the Daci'en Monastery; according to the *Ming Huidian* (Imperial Compendium of Rites and Institutions), it states...

In the tenth month of the forty-second year of the Jiajing era, the dispatch of Tibetan monks (*fan seng*) and the conferral of titles upon them were abolished, and this was established as a formal decree;
according to the *Ming Shanming Zang Dianmu Ji* (Records of the Sacred Mountains and Imperial Edicts of the Ming Dynasty), it states...

In the twelfth month of the forty-third year of the Jiajing era, an edict was issued stating that those among the Tibetan monks who come to pay tribute shall be limited in number upon entering the frontier, following the precedents established during the Chenghua and Hongzhi reigns.
This is recorded in the *Ming-shan-zang Dian-mu-ji* (The Records of the Sacred Mountains and Imperial Edicts), which states as follows.

In the forty-fifth year of the Jiajing era, an edict was issued prohibiting ordination platforms for monks and nuns. According to the *Ming Huidian*, regarding all prohibitions on ordination platforms:

in the forty-fifth year of the Jiajing era, it was ordered that the provincial Surveillance Commissioners (Fuzhi) and Inspecting Commissioners (Anzhi) outside the capital must supervise and direct the local officials.
Each [jurisdiction] shall investigate the number of monasteries and the number of monks within its domain, recording them clearly in registers and conducting periodic inspections.

Those who fail to appear shall be held accountable by the abbot, who must set a deadline for their registration. All itinerant monks residing temporarily shall be sent back to their original places of origin.
The various guards and commanderies (*zhānwèi*) in the capital, as well as the Censors of the Five Prefectures (*wéng yǔshì*), shall [oversee] the areas both inside and outside the capital city.

In all monasteries for both monks and nuns, large and small, strict patrols and investigations shall be maintained. Should anyone be accused of violating the precepts through lewdness or unlawful conduct, they shall be apprehended upon inquiry and severely punished.

According to the *Ming Tong Ji*, in the ninth month of the forty-fifth year of the Jiajing era, an imperial edict was issued to the judicial officials of the Capital Prefecture (Shun天府) to strictly prohibit the preaching of the Dharma at ordination altars for monks and nuns;
furthermore, the factories, the guard corps, and the city-inspecting censors were ordered to conduct a comprehensive investigation.

An inspection was conducted of the monasteries both inside and outside the capital city. Those who were found to be residing there while still receiving ordination under the previous [illicit] system were arrested and imprisoned.
Wandering monks from all quarters were ordered by the local authorities to be sent back to their original places of registration. At that time, the White Lotus sect was flourishing;
the Censor Bao Chengyin, believing that heretics and bandits followed the same path, feared they might join the heterodox group and incite a popular uprising.
This became a great source of trouble, and consequently, it was forbidden. In the seventh year of the Shenzong Wanli era, the monk Sonam Gyantsok from Ü-Tsang requested to open a tribute mission.
According to the *Ming Tongji*: "In the seventh year of the Wanli era, the monk Sonam Gyantsok from Ü-Tsang requested to open a tribute mission.
Sonam Gyantsok was none other than the King of Propagation, Dalai Lama; thus he was popularly known as the 'Living Buddha' (Huofo)."

The Buddha, who transmits the sutras and preaches the Dharma while forbidding lust and killing, was honored and venerated by the barbarians as the "World-Honored One of the Wheel-Turning Dharma-Merit Realm" and the "Great State Preceptor.

In the fifth year of the Wanli era, the chieftain of the Tümed, Chichin Huang Taiji, conspired with Altan Khan to welcome Gendün Drup (Gian-ts'o) to the western sea to drink the water of longevity; Altan Khan led several hundred thousand tribesmen in this endeavor.
As for the people, simply because they followed the teachings of [the Emperor] Jian and Cuo and refrained from licentious excesses, their transformation through instruction can be known.
The Seventh Year of the Tiantong Era of the Imperial Qing Dynasty.

The Grand Code of the Great Qing. Regarding the prohibitions for lamas: In the seventh year of the *Tiancong* era, it was decreed that lama *bandits* (officials) must reside outside the city walls in clean and secluded locations.
Should there be those who invite lamas to recite sutras for the purpose of curing illness, the head of the household shall be punished.
Furthermore, it was decreed that lama *bandits* who harbor women or fail to report their presence to the authorities [shall be punished].
Section. Those who build temples for me as a lama shall be punished.

In the fifth year of Chongde, the Great Qing Compendium of Ordinances (Daching Huidian) records that in the fifth year of Chongde, it was approved by memorial that newly enrolled monks must pay silver, which is to be sent to the Ministry of Revenue for inspection.
Collected. Distributed according to the Indian certificates provided, to be issued by the Office of the Monastic Administration (*Senggangsi*).

The *Da Qing Huidian* (Great Qing Compendium of State Ceremonial) of the fourth year of the Shunzhi era: In the fourth year of the Shunzhi era, it was decreed that *lamas* were not permitted to travel privately; those who traveled...
Those who arrived in the capital were ordered to be sent back to their original places of residence.

In the *Da Qing Huidian* (Imperial Code of the Great Qing) of the eleventh year of Shunzhi, it was decreed that the construction of new temples was prohibited; however, the repair of dilapidated [temples]...
They destroyed temples and took advantage of the situation.
In the eighteenth year of the Shunzhi era,
according to the *Da Qing Huidian* (Great Qing Compendium of State Ceremonials), it was formally approved that lamas residing at the White Stupa within the capital city [were to be regulated].
The nine named [lamas], the eight lamas residing at the Great Dada Temple in the west, and the Emechi Lama shall remain in their current residences as before.
All other lamas and panditas shall be ordered to reside outside the capital city.
If there are any lamas currently residing within the precincts of the capital, they shall be sent to the Ministry of Punishment (Xingbu) for processing according to the regulations.
Examples of violations. Punishment.

The Great Qing Compendium of State Ceremonies (Da Qing Huidian), Year 6 of the Kangxi Emperor’s reign. In the sixth year of the Kangxi era, it was deliberated and approved that all lamas and bandits shall be placed under the jurisdiction of the local Grand Lama.
Ma. Conduct detailed inspections every day. The Ministry of Rites shall conduct detailed inspections each month.

Should there be those who request to recite scriptures for the purpose of curing illness, they must obtain authorization from the Dalai Lama before departing; furthermore, they must be required to return to the Dalai Lama.

The Grand Qing Compendium of Rituals (Da Qing Huidian), Year 23 of the Kangxi Emperor. Year 23 of the Kangxi era: It was re-authorized that henceforth, wherever lamas travel, they shall not remain for more than three days and must immediately depart.
Those who violate this shall have the head of the household, the temple, and the abbot held accountable.

Officials who fail to exercise due supervision shall all be punished. As for Lamas, except in cases where they commit a crime punishable by death, other offenses shall not result in their being taken into state custody;
instead, they shall be punished according to the law and transported back to their place of origin.
Furthermore, it was decreed that Bandi shall not wear garments of golden-yellow or yellow, nor shall Wu-pa-shi or Wu-pa-san-ca do so.
It is permitted to wear garments of golden-yellow or yellowish-red.
Those granted such colors as mentioned above may use them accordingly; those who violate this shall be punished.
