*Record of the Buddhist Kingdoms*,
the Kingdom of Shanshan.
The king of that country reveres the Dharma; there are some four thousand monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna.

Both the laypeople and the śramaṇas of the various countries practice the Indian dharma, though there are differences in their degree of refinement. From here to the west, the various countries are for the most part like this.
Although the spoken languages differ from country to country, those who have left the household life all study the scripts and languages of India.
In the country of Kucha (Kao-ch’ang), there are more than four thousand monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna; their discipline is uniform and orderly. As for the śramaṇas of the land of Qin:
Upon arriving there, he was not included among the ranks of the monastic community at all.
In the kingdom of Khotan, the people all faithfully uphold the Dharma and delight one another with the joy of the Dharma. The number of monks there reaches tens of thousands, for the most part.
The Mahāyāna students all receive communal meals. In that country, the people have erected small stupas before the doors of every household;
even the smallest are about twenty feet high. They have constructed monastic quarters for the Saṃgha of the four directions to provide for visiting monks.
The monastery in that country is named Gomatī, which follows the Mahāyāna teachings. Among the fourteen great monasteries in the kingdom, it is... [not included in the provided fragment].
Regarding those who count as few: from the first day of the fourth month, they sweep the roads within the city and adorn the streets and alleys.
Above the city gates, large canopies are spread and everything is solemnly decorated. The King, his consort, and their attendants all reside therein.
The Saṃgha of Gomatī are followers of the Mahāyāna and are held in high esteem by the King; they are the first to lead the procession of the sacred image. Three *li* outside the city...

Four *li* away, they constructed a four-wheeled image-carriage over three *zhang* in height, appearing as if it were moving. It was adorned with the seven treasures and draped with silken banners and canopies.
The image stood within the carriage, attended by two bodhisattvas, while various celestial beings served as attendants;

all were carved and polished from gold and silver and suspended in mid-air. When the image was a hundred paces from the gate, the King removed his celestial crown, changed into new garments, and went barefoot.
Carrying flowers and incense, they followed as attendants out of the city to welcome the image. They prostrated themselves with their heads at its feet, scattering flowers and burning incense.
As the image entered the city, ladies and handmaidens atop the gate towers shook and scattered various flowers, which fell in profusion.
Such were the magnificent offerings, each chariot being distinct from the others; one monastery would conduct the procession of the image for one day, beginning on the first day of the fourth month.
The procession of the images began on the fourteenth day and was finally completed. Once the procession was over, the King and his consort returned to the palace.

Seven or eight *li* to the west of the city is a monastery named the New King Monastery (*Rājanava-vihāra*). It has been under construction for eighty years, having been completed only after three successive kings;
it stands approximately twenty-five *zhang* high, adorned with intricate carvings and engravings, its surface covered in gold and silver, and embellished with various precious gems.
The stupa was constructed, followed by the building of a Buddha hall that was exquisitely adorned. Its beams, pillars, doors, panels, windows, and casements were all covered with gold leaf.
Separate monastic quarters were also built, equally magnificent and well-ordered, beyond the power of words to fully describe.
The kings of the six kingdoms to the east of the ridge offered many of their most precious treasures as acts of devotion.
The king of the country of Zihe is diligent in his practice. There are over a thousand monks there, most of whom study the Mahāyāna.
[This is] the country of Kiecha.
The king of that country held a Pañcavārṣika festival. "Pañcavārṣika" means, in the language of Han, a "Great Assembly every five years.
When the assembly was held, he invited śramaṇas from the four quarters, who gathered like clouds; he then adorned the seating places for the saṃgha, hanging silk streamers, banners, and canopies.
Having fashioned lotus flowers of gold and silver and placed them upon a seat covered with silk, he spread out a pure sitting mat.
The king and his ministers made offerings according to the Dharma for one month, two months, or three months, mostly during the spring season.

Once the king had completed the assembly, he further exhorted his ministers to establish offerings and make worship for one day, two days, three days, or five days. When the offerings were fully concluded, the king—
He took the horse he was riding, complete with its saddle and bridle, and had it ridden by a high-ranking official of the kingdom;
together with various white woolen cloths and diverse precious treasures—articles required by śramaṇas—he made a vow and offered them as a gift along with the assembled ministers.

Having completed the offering, he redeemed them from the Saṃgha. Because the mountains and lands there are cold and do not produce other grains, only wheat ripens. The assembly of monks accepted [the gift].

When the year has ended, frost invariably falls on that morning; therefore, the king always praises the assembly of monks, commanding them to ripen the wheat before he himself observes the *varṣā* (rain-retreat) ceremony.
In this country there is a spittoon belonging to the Buddha, made of stone, its color resembling that of the Buddha’s almsbowl. There is also one tooth of the Buddha;
the people of the country have erected a stūpa for the Buddha’s tooth. There are more than a thousand monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna.
In the country of Tālikya,
there are many monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna. [The same applies to] the country of Udyāna.
The Buddha-dharma flourished greatly in that country. They called the dwelling places of the Saṃgha *saṃghārāma*.
There were five hundred such *saṃghārāmas* in total, all of which followed the teachings of the Hīnayāna. Whenever visiting bhikṣus arrived, they were provided with offerings for three days;
once the three days had passed, the visitors were then required to seek out their own accommodations.
In the kingdom of Pūṣkaravatī, the Buddha formerly traveled with his disciples; the Buddha’s bowl is still located here.

The King of the Yuezhi raised a great army and came to attack this country, desiring to take the Buddha’s bowl. Once he had subdued this country, the King of the Yuezhi became deeply devoted to faith.

Regarding the Buddha-Dharma, [the king] wished to take the bowl and depart; therefore, he offered worship. Having completed his offerings to the Triple Gem, he adorned a great elephant and placed the bowl upon it.

The elephant then prostrated itself on the ground and was unable to move forward. He further prepared a four-wheeled carriage to carry the bowl, with eight elephants pulling it together, yet it still could not advance.
The King, realizing that the karmic conditions for the bowl had not yet matured, felt deep self-reproach and sighed in admiration. Thereupon, at...
A stūpa was erected here, as well as a saṃghārāma, which remained as a site for various offerings. There were more than seven hundred monks residing there.
When midday approached, the assembly of monks would bring out their alms bowls to receive various offerings from the laypeople (*avadātavasana*), after which they took their midday meal.
At evening, during the time of burning incense, the same occurred again. [The bowls] could hold about two *dōng* (pecks) of capacity; they were of various colors, though mostly black. 4.
Its boundaries were distinct and its thickness was about two inches; it was translucent and lustrous. When a poor person threw a few flowers into it, it was immediately full.
Yet when a great wealthy man wished to make offerings with many flowers—even a hundred thousand million *hu*—it could never be filled.
In the city of Kheṭaka within the kingdom of Nāgadīpa, there is a shrine for the Buddha’s cranial bone, entirely adorned with gold leaf and the seven precious jewels.

Out of reverence for the cranial bone and fearing it might be seized or plundered by others, the king selected eight men of noble lineage from among the people of the realm, each of whom was entrusted with it.
It was sealed with a single seal for protection. At dawn, eight people arrived together; each inspected the seal before opening the door.
Having opened the door, they washed their hands with scented water. They brought forth the Buddha’s cranial bone and placed it upon a high throne outside the vihāra.
A circular anvil made of the seven precious gems was used as a base, covered above by a bell of lapis lazuli, both adorned with pearls and jewels. The bone was yellowish-white in color.
It is four inches square and bulges upward at its center. Every day after sunrise, the attendants of the vihāra ascend a high tower to beat a great drum, blow conch shells, and strike bronze cymbals.
Upon hearing this, the king proceeds to the vihāra to make offerings of flowers and incense.

Having made his offerings, he circumambulates it by placing it upon his head in succession before departing. Entering through the eastern gate and exiting through the western gate, the king performs this rite every morning.
Having made offerings and performed prostrations, he would then attend to the affairs of state. Householders and elders likewise first made offerings before attending to their domestic affairs.
They did so every day without ever becoming weary or indolent. Once the offerings were fully completed, he returned the cranial bone to the vihāra.
Within it stands a stūpa of liberation made of the seven precious gems, which is sometimes open and sometimes closed; it is about five feet high and used to contain [relics].
Every morning, before the gate of the vihāra, there are always vendors of flowers and incense, from whom anyone wishing to make offerings may purchase various items.
The kings of various countries also constantly dispatch envoys to make offerings at this site, which measures forty paces on each side. Even when heaven shakes and the earth trembles...
It is cracked; this place is immovable.
In the kingdom of Rāyī, there are approximately three thousand monks, who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
In the kingdom of Banna,
there are also approximately three thousand monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna.
[In] the kingdom of Piṭa...
The Buddha-dharma flourished in that country, encompassing the study of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Upon seeing the Chinese monks arrive, they felt great compassion and spoke thus:
"How is it that people from a remote land can understand the path of renunciation and seek the Buddha-dharma from afar?
They provided everything necessary for their needs and treated them according to the Dharma. There were many monasteries in the southeast, with tens of thousands of monks.
In the kingdom of Mathurā, on both banks of the river Pūrṇa, there were twenty monasteries with approximately three thousand monks; the Buddha-dharma was flourishing there.
Generally, the kings of all the various kingdoms of India to the west of the Sandy Desert were all devoted believers in the Buddha-dharma and provided offerings.
When providing for the Saṃgha, he would then remove his celestial crown and, together with his kinsmen and ministers, personally serve the food with his own hands.
Having finished serving the food, he would spread a mat upon the ground and sit before the Elder (Upādhyāya), not daring to sit on a seat in the presence of the Saṃgha.
This tradition of how kings made offerings when the Buddha was in the world has been passed down to this day. From this point southward, it is called the Middle Kingdom (Madhyadeśa).
In China, the cold and heat are harmoniously balanced; there is no frost or snow. The people are prosperous and happy. There are no household registers or official laws;

those who cultivate the King’s lands merely pay a share of the produce. They may leave whenever they wish and stay whenever they wish. The King’s governance does not employ punishments or legal snares;
those with offenses are simply fined according to the gravity of their deeds. Even for those who plot evil or rebellious acts, the punishment does not exceed amputation.
[He uses] only his right hand. The king’s attendants on both sides all receive stipends.
All the people of the kingdom refrain from killing living beings, do not drink alcohol, and do not eat onions or garlic—except for the *caṇḍālas*.
The *caṇḍālas* are called "evil men" and live separately from others. When they enter a city or marketplace, they strike wood to distinguish themselves; thus, people recognize them and avoid them.
They do not jostle one another. Within the kingdom, they do not raise pigs or chickens, nor do they sell living beings.
In the markets, there are no butchers or wine-sellers. For trade, they use cowrie shells; only the *caṇḍālas* and hunters sell meat.
Since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, kings, elders, and lay devotees have built monasteries for the Saṃgha and provided offerings. Supplying...

They were granted fields, houses, gardens, orchards, households, oxen, and calves, along with iron-bound title deeds and records. These have been handed down from king to king without interruption, continuing to this day without ceasing.
For the monks who reside there, their dwellings, bedding, food, drink, and clothing are entirely free from lack.
It was thus everywhere. The resident monks constantly performed meritorious deeds, recited scriptures, and practiced seated meditation.

When visiting monks arrived, the resident monks would go out to meet them, carry their robes and bowls for them, provide water for washing their feet, oil for anointing their feet, and non-time (pre-meal) refreshments.

After they had rested for a short while, the residents would inquire about the sequence of their seniority (the number of years since ordination) and assign them rooms, bedding, and various other necessities accordingly.
At the monastic residence, they constructed a stūpa for Śāriputra, as well as stūpas for Maudgalyāyana and Ānanda, and stūpas for the Abhidharma and Vinaya scriptures.
One month after the summer retreat (varṣā), families seeking merit were exhorted to provide offerings. The monks prepared non-seasonal medicinal drinks (vikāla-pāna).
A great assembly of the Saṃgha gathered to preach the Dharma. Having finished preaching the Dharma, they made offerings of various incenses and flowers to the stūpa of Śāriputra.
Lamps were kept burning throughout the night. He had that person act as Śāriputra when he was formerly a brahmin, approaching the Buddha to seek ordination;
Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Mahākāśyapa did likewise. Among the bhikṣuṇīs, many made offerings at the stūpa of Ānanda.
Because Ānanda requested that the World-Honored One permit women to leave the household life, many śrāmaṇeras offer support to Rāhula;
those who are masters of Abhidharma offer support to the Abhidharma; and those who are masters of Vinaya offer support to the Vinaya.
Each year they make offerings once, each having their own designated day. Those of the Mahāyāna, however, offer support to the Prajñāpāramitā and to Mañjuśrī.

[The assembly] was benefited. After the monks, including Avalokiteśvara and others, had completed the *varṣā* (the rains retreat), the elders, householders, brahmins, and others each brought various garments and requisites required by śramaṇas to offer as alms to the monastic community. The monks likewise each gave offerings themselves.
Since the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha, the rules of conduct and ritual protocols practiced by the noble assembly have been handed down in succession without interruption.
One thousand two hundred paces from the south gate of the city of the kingdom of Kosala, to the west of the road, the elder Sudatta constructed the Jetavana Vihāra.
When the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, King Prasenajit, longing to see the Buddha, immediately [summoned] the ox-headed [guardian].

An image of the Buddha was fashioned from sandalwood and placed in the Buddha’s seat within the Jetavana Monastery. The wooden structure had seven stories, and kings and commoners from various nations vied with one another to offer worship.
They hung silk banners and canopies, scattered flowers, burned incense, and lit lamps that continued to shine day after day without ceasing.

A mouse gnawed at the lamp wick, setting fire to the flowers, banners, and canopies, which eventually reached the monastery itself until all seven stories were completely consumed by the flames. In the various kingdoms...
The king and his people were all filled with great sorrow and distress, believing that the sandalwood image had already been consumed by fire.

Four or five days later, they opened the door of the small eastern vihāra and suddenly beheld the original image; everyone was filled with great joy and together renovated the vihāra, enabling it to be constructed with two stories.
He then moved the image back to its original location.
In the kingdom of Magadha,
when King Aśoka was once a young child, he encountered Śākyamuni Buddha walking for alms while playing along the road.
The child was filled with joy and immediately offered a handful of earth to the Buddha. The Buddha took it and used it to repair the ground where he practiced walking meditation (*caṅkrama*).
By virtue of this karmic fruit, he became an Iron-Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) who ruled over Jambudvīpa.

Riding upon his iron wheel, he traveled throughout Jambudvīpa and saw people being punished in the hells between the two Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*). He then asked his ministers, "What is this? and they replied: "This is..."
The King of Ghosts, Yama, governs those who have committed offenses. The king thought to himself, "If even a king of ghosts can create a hell to govern offenders, I am a lord of men;

why should I not create a hell to govern offenders? He immediately questioned his ministers, "Who among you is able to create a hell for me to govern offenders? The ministers replied, "Only one of extreme evil can do so."

[The King] heard this. The King immediately dispatched his ministers to search everywhere for a wicked man. Along the banks of the leaking water, they saw one who was tall and sturdy, black-complexioned, with yellow hair and blue eyes;
he used a foot-hook and a fish-mouthed blowpipe to snare birds and beasts. Whenever a bird or beast approached, he would shoot and kill it;
none could escape. Having captured this man, they brought him before the King. The King secretly commanded him: "Build a high wall on all four sides."
Within it are planted various flowers and fruits, along with fine grain fields and ponds; it is so magnificently adorned that it inspires longing in those who behold it.
Its gates are made secure, and anyone who enters is immediately seized and punished in various ways, never permitted to leave.
"Even if I myself enter, punish me as well and do not release me! Now I appoint you as the Lord of Hell. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who entered while going on his alms round in sequence.
When the wardens of hell saw him at the gate, they sought to punish him. The bhikṣu was terrified and pleaded with them, "Please allow me a moment to eat my midday meal.
Before long, someone entered; the wardens placed him inside a mortar and pounded him, until red froth emerged.
Having seen this, the bhikṣu contemplated that this body is impermanent, suffering, empty, like a bubble, and like foam; he immediately attained arhatship.
Thereupon, the hell-wardens seized him and cast him into a cauldron of boiling water, yet the bhikṣu’s countenance was joyful and serene; the fire was extinguished and the water grew cold.
A lotus flower sprang up from within, and a bhikṣu sat upon it. The wardens immediately went to inform the king, saying, "There is a marvel in the prison;
we pray that Your Majesty will go to see it. The king said, "I have a prior commitment; I do not dare go now. The wardens replied, "This is no small matter;
Your Majesty should go quickly and alter your previous engagement. The king then entered with them. The bhikṣu preached the Dharma for him, and the king attained faith and understanding.
The hells were immediately destroyed. [The king] repented of the many evils he had previously committed;

because of this, he came to revere the Triple Gem and constantly went beneath the peepal tree (*pippala*) to repent his transgressions and reproach himself, observing the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*).
When the queen asked the king where he was always going, the ministers replied, "He is constantly beneath the peepal tree. While the king was away, the queen sent men to cut down that tree.
[The tree] fell over. When the king came and saw it, he fainted and collapsed to the ground. The ministers sprinkled water on his face, and after a long while, he regained consciousness.
The king immediately piled bricks around its four sides and poured a hundred jars of cow’s milk onto the roots of the tree. He prostrated himself on the ground and made this vow:
"If this tree does not grow, I shall never rise. Having finished his vow, the tree immediately began to sprout from its roots. Because...
To this day, it is now ten *wen* shorter.
The King of Siṃhala sent an envoy to China to take seeds of the *pāṭala* tree and plant them beside the Buddha hall; their height is approximately...
It was twenty *zhang* high. The tree leaned toward the southeast; fearing it might fall, the king propped it with pillars each eight or nine *guan* in circumference.
Where the tree met the supports, new growth sprouted from its trunk, eventually boring through the pillars and descending into the earth to form roots nearly four *guan* in girth.
Although the pillars split down the middle, the tree remained encased within them, and people did not remove them. A vihāra was erected beneath the tree, in which there is a seated [image].
The images were revered by both monastics and laypeople without weariness. Within the city, a Tooth Relic Shrine (Dantadhātu-vihāra) was also erected, constructed entirely of the seven precious gems.

The King cultivated the pure conduct of the Brahma-faring with purity, and the devotion and faith of the people within the city were likewise profound. Since the establishment of this kingdom’s governance, there has been no famine or civil unrest.
The treasuries of the monastic community abound with rare jewels and priceless *maṇi* gems. When the King entered [the shrine]...
While touring the monastic treasury, he saw a *maṇi* jewel and immediately conceived a greedy desire to seize it. Only after three days did he realize his error;
he then went before the community of monks, prostrated himself, and repented for his former sinful intent. He addressed the monks, saying:

"I pray that the Sangha will establish a regulation so that from this day forward, the King shall not be permitted to enter the treasury to look about. Only after a bhikṣu has completed forty years of seniority (*varṣa*) shall he be allowed to enter. His...
Within the city dwell many lay devotees, elders, and wealthy merchants. The houses are magnificent and beautiful, and the streets and lanes are level and well-ordered.

At the crossroads of every thoroughfare, preaching halls have been constructed. On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, high seats are set out for offerings, and the fourfold assembly of both monastics and laity gathers there to listen to the Dharma. The people of that country say there are approximately fifty or sixty thousand monks in total. All...
There is a communal meal provided by the King within the city for five or six thousand people. Those who require food take their own bowls and go there to receive it;
each bowl is filled to its capacity before they return. The Buddha’s tooth relic is regularly brought out during the third month.
Before ten days had passed, the king adorned a great elephant and had a skilled orator dressed in royal garments mount it.
As the drum was beaten, he proclaimed: "For three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, the Bodhisattva practiced austerities, not sparing his own body or life;

he gave away his kingdom, his wife, and his children, as well as gouging out his eyes to give them to others; he cut off his flesh to ransom a dove, severed his head as an act of charity, and threw himself before a starving tigress."
Without begrudging even his marrow and brain, he practiced such various asceticisms for the sake of sentient beings.

Having attained Buddhahood and remained in the world for forty-nine years, he preached the Dharma to teach and transform them, bringing peace to those who were not at peace and delivering those who had not been delivered.

When his karmic affinity with sentient beings was exhausted, he entered parinirvāṇa. One thousand four hundred and ninety-seven years have passed since his parinirvāṇa; the sentient beings of the world [continue to...]
"Alas! Ten days hence, the Buddha’s tooth relic shall emerge and arrive at the Vimalagiri Monastery.
All monastics and laypeople within the kingdom who wish to plant the seeds of merit should each level the roads and adorn the streets and alleys, preparing various flowers, incense, and offerings.
Having thus proclaimed, the King then had five hundred forms of the Bodhisattva fashioned along both sides of the road, manifesting in various transformations."
Manifesting himself, he sometimes took the form of Sudāna, sometimes that of Śyāmaka, sometimes that of a king of elephants, or of a deer or a horse;

such were his manifestations, all painted and adorned so that they appeared like living beings. Only then did the Buddha’s tooth emerge and proceed along the middle path, receiving offerings as it went.
Upon reaching the Buddha hall of the Abhayagiri Monastery, monastics and laypeople gathered like clouds, burning incense and lighting lamps.
Lamps were lit for various religious rites day and night without ceasing. After ninety days had passed, they returned to the monastery within the city.
On fast days, the gates of the city’s monastery were opened, and worship was performed according to the Dharma. Forty *li* to the east of the Abhayagiri Monastery is a mountain;
on this mountain is a monastery named Badrī, which can accommodate approximately two thousand monks. Among these monks...
There was a great virtuous śramaṇa named Dharmagupta, whom the people of that country all revered.

He dwelt in a stone cave for about forty years, constantly practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and was able to move snakes and mice so that they lived together in the same room without harming one another.
Seven *li* south of the city, there was a monastery named Mahāvihāra. There...
Three thousand monks resided there. Among them was a śramaṇa of great virtue whose conduct and observance of the precepts were pure; the people of the country all suspected him to be an arhat.
At the time of his death, the king came to visit him and, having assembled the monks according to the Dharma, asked: "Has this bhikṣu attained the Way?"

He then answered truthfully, saying, "He was an Arhat. After he had passed away, the King followed the sūtras and vinaya to bury him according to the rites for an Arhat, four or five *li* to the east of the vihāra.
He piled up fine, large firewood, measuring more than three *zhang* in length and breadth, and the same height.
Near the top, he placed sandalwood, aloeswood, and various other fragrant woods. Steps were constructed on all four sides, and upon them were placed pure, high-quality white [cloths].
It is covered all around with layers of woolen cloth. On top is constructed a large hearse-couch, resembling the *chuanche* (hearse-carriage) used here, though it lacks the dragon and fish motifs.
At the time of the cremation, the king, the people of the land, and the fourfold assembly all gathered together, making offerings of flowers and incense.

From the funeral bier to the burial site, the king himself made offerings of flowers and incense. Having completed the offerings, the bier was placed upon a pile of wood; it was then drenched everywhere with ghee and oil before being set ablaze.
As the fire burned, everyone’s hearts were filled with reverence, and each person removed their upper garments, as well as their ceremonial regalia, parasols, and canopies.
He cast it from afar into the fire to assist the cremation. Once the cremation was complete, he immediately collected the bones to erect a stūpa.
The King, possessing deep faith in the Buddha-dharma, wished to construct a new vihāra for the Saṃgha.

Having first convened a great assembly and provided a meal as an offering to the monks, he then selected a pair of excellent, superior oxen, adorned their horns with gold, silver, and precious gems, and had a fine golden plow fashioned.
The King himself plowed the four borders, and thereafter he allotted fields and residences to the households of the people, recording this on iron bonds.
From that time forward, it was handed down through successive generations, with none daring to abolish or alter it.
*Continued Records of the Wondrous and Extensive*:

Regarding the origins of the Śākya [Buddhist] tradition, in the twenty-first year of the Qin dynasty, twelve golden *dik* (statues) were cast. The origins of the Śākya tradition originally stem from Huo Qubing’s campaign against the Xiongnu.
The butcher-king obtained the golden man used for the sacrifice to Heaven. Emperor Wu regarded it as divine and enshrined it in the Ganshui Palace.

In the first year of the Huangchu era of the Wei dynasty, the bronze figures of the Di were moved from Chang’an; because they were too heavy to transport, some claimed that the golden Di wept, and thus they remained at the south of Beiyang City.
Someone saw Ji Zixun with an elderly man rubbing the bronze figure of the Di, saying: "I am clearly seeing this being cast."
It has been nearly five hundred years since that day. Dong Zhuo destroyed nine of them to make coin; Fu Jian destroyed two of them to make coin.
As for the remaining one, the common people pushed it into the river north of Shan. Some say that the topknot of the statue’s head would occasionally emerge;
when the Jin army arrived, the topknot no longer emerged.
In the *Yekè cóngtán*,
regarding the entry of Buddhism into China,
both Fu Yi and Han Yu state that it first entered China during the time of Emperor Ming of the Later Han dynasty. This is...
To discuss what is evident: one does not know that the Buddha-dharma entered China long ago. Observing the "Account of the Western Barbarians" (*Xirong zhuan*) in the *Wei lüe*, it says:

"In the first year of the Yuanshou era of Emperor Ai of the Han, the Court Scholar Jing Lu received the oral transmission of the *Futu jing* (Buddha-sūtra) from I-chun, an envoy of the King of Greater Yuezhi.
Furthermore, observing the "Preface to the Arrayed Immortals" (*Lie xian xu*) by Liu Xiang, it says: "Those who attained immortality numbered in the hundreds..."

Forty-six persons. As for the seventy-four persons, since they are already mentioned in Buddhist scriptures, we know that Buddhist scriptures already existed during the reigns of Emperors Cheng, Ai, and Ping of the Han dynasty.
Observing the *Han Wu Shiji* (The Story of Emperor Wu of Han), it records that King Kunya killed King Xiutu and surrendered with his host.
They obtained the spirit of a golden man and placed it atop the Ganquan Palace. These golden men were each over ten feet tall;
their worship did not involve oxen or sheep, but consisted solely of burning incense and prostrating. The Emperor ordered that they follow the customs of their own country.

Furthermore, in the third year of the Yuanshou era, when the Kunming Pond was excavated, black ash was found at its bottom. The Emperor questioned Dongfang Shuo, who said, "You may ask the Daoist practitioners from the Western Regions."
One knows this to be the "ashes of the kalpa. Furthermore, one knows that the Buddha-dharma had already entered China during the time of Emperor Wu.
People today know only that the Buddha-dharma entered China starting from Emperor Ming; they do not realize it began with Emperor Wu. Xue Zhengji recorded:
"Confucius took Laozi as his teacher, and Laozi took Zhuqian as his teacher. If this is examined, then the Buddha’s entry into China [is even earlier]. Furthermore—
It ends with Emperor Wu;
the "Waves of Ink" are idle talk regarding the entry of the Buddha-dharma into China.
The entry of the Buddha-dharma into China did not begin with Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty.

This can be verified by the fact that *Liezi* states there was a sage in the West, whom Laozi took as his teacher from Zhugan (India). Indeed, during the time of King Mu of Zhou, Mañjuśrī and Maudgalyāyana came to convert him;
these were the "transformed persons" (*huaren*) mentioned in *Liezi*. These transformed persons showed King Mu that the High Four Terraces were the teaching of Kāśyapa Buddha.
Regarding the Dharma-realm: he established three assemblies at a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*). During the time of Duke Mu of Qin, a stone Buddha was found in Fufeng;
the Duke did not recognize it and cast it away in the horse stables. When the Duke fell ill, he ordered Youyu to go and examine it. Youyu said, "This is truly a divine Buddha.
The Duke took the image, bathed it, and placed it in a pure location. The image subsequently emitted light, whereupon the Duke slaughtered livestock to sacrifice to it. It was divine.
He lifted it up and discarded it in a distant place. Youyu spoke again, saying, "I have heard that for the Buddha’s pure body, all offerings consist merely of burning incense.
Your Majesty now wishes to create a Buddha image. Thereupon, Youyu went to the village south of Gaosita and found an old man surnamed Wang and named An, who was one hundred and eighty years old.
The man said of himself, "I once saw people making one at the site of the Three Assemblies. The minister [then proceeded].
He was old and lacked strength. To the north of the village lived four brothers who had previously worked as craftsmen within a monastery.
They now requested that he join them in creating a bronze statue with all its marks and signs perfectly complete. Gong Yue greatly rewarded them.
On an earthen platform, these men constructed a multi-storied pavilion three hundred feet high; at the time, people called it the "Gao-si Platform" (The Four Highs). These men...
His surname was Gao; because he was the fourth among four brothers who established themselves together, he was named Gao Si.
Thus, during the time of Duke Mu of Qin, the Buddha-dharma had already entered China.
(Taishō Tripitaka, Section on Buddhist Teachings, Comprehensive Examination Volume Seven, End)
